20126-the-cave-of-gold-a-tale-of-califor:
Everett McNeil wrote The Cave of Gold, a tale of California in '49. The gold rush year gives the tale its heat and risk. Bud hears fearful screams from a hill and turns pale at the sound. Yet he vows to find the cause and climbs at once.

With rifle ready, he fixes his eyes on the spot above. Boys' gold rush tales mix mines, caves, and sudden peril freely. McNeil sets greed, courage, and wild country in a fast plot. Readers get a vivid taste of how '49 looked to young readers years later.
23192-gold-seekers-of-49:
Gold Seekers of '49 is an adventure story about the California gold rush, told through a boy named Charley. Its chapter list promises a full journey west: a mysterious stranger, a call to the golden west, an unwelcome companion, and an attack by an enemy early on the road.

The route runs by Panama, up a river, and through the Golden Gate into San Francisco. Later chapters take Charley on to the diggings, where he hears a key talk, follows an enemy's trail, and makes a great discovery. Readers get the rush as a young traveller's string of risks, races, and finds.
anthem-pg1249: Ayn Rand's 1938 novella: in a collectivist future, Equality 7-2521 rediscovers the word "I." Stark, passionate, and prophetic, it is her hymn to the individual. The seed of Atlas Shrugged, and a powerful fable. Rand's fable burns with the intensity of her later novels.
arxiv-2510-00149:
Kumud Singh Porte, R. B. Sandeep, and Kamal Santra wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on flipping colors in two-colored graphs. Each vertex carries one of two colors, and a move at a vertex flips its neighbors' colors and rewires their links. The question is how few moves can reverse every color while keeping the graph itself fixed. A 1987 result by Sabidussi set the classic bounds for this puzzle.

The authors improve both of Sabidussi's bounds by wide margins. Full color reversal now needs at most about four moves per vertex, down from about six. Turning one coloring into any other also gets a sharper cap in their proof. For stars and complete graphs, they bring the cost down to three moves per vertex. Tighter bounds like these clarify how powerful purely local changes can be in reshaping a network.
arxiv-2510-00349:
Felix Reichel wrote this 2025 economics paper modeling a triathlon as a two-stage contest. After the swim, each athlete chooses whether to continue or withdraw from the race. That choice is endogenous, shaped by how the swim went for them. The bike and run legs then form a Tullock contest, where effort buys win probability.

Swim drafting enters the model as a discount on the cost of later effort. Athletes who drafted more face cheaper effort in the second stage. Reichel derives closed-form equilibrium strategies for the two-player case. For many asymmetric players, he shows the equilibrium exists, is unique, and responds sensibly to parameters. The continuation choice produces athlete-specific cutoff rules based on drafting intensity. The analysis links drafting benefits, exposure, and field size to effort in the final contest.
arxiv-2510-00749:
Navarrete Ramos and eleven co-authors test whether carbon enrichment hardens timing detectors against neutron damage, in this 2025 arXiv paper for Nuclear Instruments and Methods A. Low Gain Avalanche Detectors give timing for collider experiments, but radiation deactivates their boron gain layer. The team manufactured sensors at IMB-CNM with a broad, shallow, carbon-enriched multiplication layer and compared them with non-carbonated devices. Both sets went to the TRIGA reactor in Ljubljana for neutron irradiation.

Exposure reached a fluence of 2.5 times ten to the fifteenth neutrons per square centimetre. Carbonated samples showed less deactivation, and the acceptor removal constant dropped by more than a factor of two. Timing resolution and collected charge degraded with fluence, yet the carbonated parts tolerated radiation better. A noise study traced spurious thermal pulses to a gap between the gain layer edge and the p-stop implant, without hurting device operation.
arxiv-2510-01049:
Werby, Rotondi, Scaparro, and Arras at the University of Stuttgart present KeySG in this 2025 arXiv paper on robot world models. Robots in homes and offices need scene representations that are both geometrically precise and rich in meaning. Three-dimensional scene graphs provide that mix, but they usually hard-code one fixed set of relationships between objects. Their text form also overflows a language model's context window in large buildings.

KeySG organizes a scene hierarchically, from floors and rooms down to objects and functional elements. Selected keyframe images supply multimodal detail at each node, gathered by a vision-language model. A hierarchical retrieval pipeline then feeds only the relevant slice of the graph to the language model for each query. Across four benchmarks, including 3D segmentation and complex query retrieval, KeySG beat prior approaches on most metrics.
arxiv-2510-01149:
Teiletche and six co-authors question how visual document retrievers are usually built, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Teams typically fine-tune large generative vision-language models with contrastive losses and use them as embedding models. The authors argue that repurposing inherits design choices, such as causal attention masks, that quietly bottleneck retrieval quality. Through controlled experiments they measure what actually matters, including attention masking, image resolution, alignment data, and late-interaction objectives.

Their recipe produces ModernVBERT, a compact vision-language encoder with only two hundred fifty million parameters. Fine-tuned for document retrieval, it outperforms models up to ten times larger on their benchmarks, including the ViDoRe suite. A late-interaction variant, ColModernVBERT, leads its size category on the efficiency frontier. The team releases the models and training code so practitioners can cut cost and latency in real deployments.
arxiv-2510-01349:
Lawrence and co-authors test the hidden assumption behind symmetry tricks in machine learning: that transformed data points are just as likely as originals. Augmentation and equivariant designs help only when the test distribution truly respects the symmetry. Their diagnostic measures a dataset's anisotropy with a two-sample neural classifier.

The classifier tries to tell real data from randomly transformed copies, and its success quantifies symmetry breaking. Synthetic validation came first, then standard point-cloud benchmarks showed surprisingly strong alignment. Theory proves broken symmetry can cap invariant methods even when labels are truly invariant. Empirically, augmentation hurt on only two benchmarks, making the answer dataset-dependent. ModelNet40 and MNIST are the two benchmarks where augmentation backfired. Invariant ridge regression carries the infinite-feature theory case. Rotations and permutations are the transformations under scrutiny. Measure first, then decide whether to augment at all.
arxiv-2510-01649:
Furqon and co-authors define continual learning across shifting domains when the original source data may never be touched again. Privacy rules increasingly forbid carrying source samples into deployment, yet models must keep learning new domains without forgetting. Their system, REFEREE, pairs a source-pretrained model with a large vision-language model.

Frequency-aware prompts emphasize an image's stable low-frequency structure and suppress fragile detail. The prompting makes pseudo-labels on new domains less noisy. Uncertainty-aware weighting then downweights the labels that remain doubtful, using their spread. The combination learns continually with no rehearsal data at all. CLIP's zero-shot skill powers the vision-language branch of the design. Dual branches compensate for each other's generalization weaknesses. Pseudo-labels are unavoidable when target domains arrive unlabeled. Mean and covariance of predictions carry the uncertainty signal. Forgetting is fought without storing a single old source example.
arxiv-2510-01749:
Delchevalerie and five co-authors bring generative models to photonics in this 2025 paper. Photonic crystals are patterned materials that control how light moves through them. A band diagram maps which light frequencies can pass through a given crystal. Computing each diagram means solving Maxwell's equations thousands of times, which makes design searches slow and costly.

The authors generate band diagrams directly with a latent diffusion model. A transformer encoder reads the crystal structure and builds context-rich embeddings to guide the generation. Treating a three-dimensional crystal as a stack of two-dimensional slices keeps the method cheap and extensible. The work is the first diffusion-based approach to this task. It offers a fast surrogate for full simulations, which could speed inverse design of photonic and quantum devices.
arxiv-2510-02149:
Ryabchenko and Mou study learning when actions decide whether the agent gets to see the state in this 2025 reinforcement learning paper. In many real systems, observations arrive only when triggered, stochastically, by the agent's own actions. Standard Markov decision processes assume the state is always visible. Their action-triggered framework assigns each action a probability of producing an observation.

Tailored Bellman equations describe optimal behavior under this sporadic visibility. A key idea is the action-sequence paradigm: agents commit to a whole sequence of actions until the next observation lands. Under linear structure, value functions stay linear in an induced action-sequence feature map. The authors build off-policy estimators with statistical guarantees on those features. Their algorithm, ST-LSVI-UCB, adapts a classic optimistic method and achieves a stated regret bound. Sensing on demand, from medical monitoring to robotics, fits the model.
arxiv-2510-02349:
Fard, Schalau, and Wunder test self-taught learning methods for spotting network intrusions. Their 2025 security paper focuses on non-contrastive methods. Classic detectors learn from labeled attacks. They then miss attack types never seen before. Self-supervised learning instead studies normal traffic patterns first. Vision research inspired this shift toward unlabeled training. The team varies three ingredients across experiments. They swap augmentation tricks, encoder designs, and learning methods. A frozen encoder plus simple clustering then separates normal from attack traffic.

Results differed sharply by dataset and recipe. Random shuffle augmentation performed poorly across all methods. Gaussian noise gave the best average result for one model on a standard dataset. A mixup pairing topped another dataset on detection scores. No single recipe won everywhere. Augmentation choice shapes what the model learns. Practitioners must tune it for their own network.
arxiv-2510-02449:
Bandi and co-authors validate the galaxy target lists for a major cosmology survey. Their 2025 astronomy paper serves the 4MOST Cosmology Redshift Survey. That survey will gather nearly five point four million redshifts. Its maps cover about fifty seven hundred square degrees. Two target families anchor the program. Bright galaxies and luminous red galaxies fill the catalogues. The team drew targets from DESI Legacy Survey imaging. They checked photometry, masking, and redshift distributions carefully. Angular clustering tests measured how targets bunch on the sky.

Careful masks veto bright stars and imaging artefacts. Those masks suppressed fake small scale clustering power. They left large scale structure signals clean. Cross-checks with DESI spectroscopy recovered the redshift distributions. The catalogues behave uniformly across the survey footprint. Baryon acoustic oscillation and growth studies can now proceed. Clean targets are the foundation of precision cosmology.
arxiv-2510-02549:
Dong and co-authors grade retrieval augmented generation systems with knowledge graph scores. Their 2025 paper extends the known RAGAS evaluation framework. Judging RAG output is hard because answers sound fluent even when wrong. Standard metrics miss reasoning depth and source use. The new framework scores answers through a knowledge graph lens. Multi-hop semantic matching checks chained facts across sources. Community based semantic overlap measures topic coverage in clusters. A language model acts as the evaluator under these metrics. Human annotated samples validate the automated scores.

The graph based subscores tracked human judgment well. Agreement with RAGAS scores ran moderate to high. The two subscores complemented each other across cases. They also reacted sharply to relevance differences in inputs. Builders of retrieval systems need such finer gauges. Entity level matching is only the current scope. Triplet level scoring is the planned refinement.
arxiv-2510-02749:
Bujtás and three co-authors study a placement problem on graphs. They ask for the smallest set of points that can watch the whole network. Each chosen point must cover all points within a set distance. The chosen points must also stay far enough apart from each other. The paper studies this number for strong products. A strong product builds a big graph from two smaller ones.

The team proves a clean upper bound for the product. The number for the product never beats the product of the two numbers. For products of paths, they compute the exact value. The bound is thus shown to be sharp. For some torus-shaped products, though, the true value falls below the bound. The gap can grow without limit in one family. The authors end with a conjecture about cases where no valid set exists at all.
arxiv-2510-03349:
Chen presents a 2025 arXiv paper that tests large language models on tornado forecasting, a high stakes real world task. The framework, AgentCaster, gives models live style access to forecast maps and air soundings from a detailed weather archive. Models could query thousands of maps across a forty day test span with major outbreaks. Over five hundred tornado reports fell inside that span. Each day, models drew risk polygons for the next twelve to thirty six hours.

New scoring tools measured both forecast skill and made up risk. Human experts beat the best models by a wide margin. Models tended to hallucinate danger, overstate risk strength, and misplace risk areas on the map. Their sense of space and change over time stayed weak in fast moving storms. The benchmark sets a hard, clean test for agent reasoning in fields where errors carry real costs.
arxiv-2510-03449:
Jamshidian presents a 2025 arXiv paper borrowing from data sets to fit regressions for small samples, while guarding against borrowing. Transfer learning can backfire when a source biases the target, a failure called negative transfer. The proposed framework, BLAST, weighs sources inside a Bayesian model. Global local shrinkage priors enforce sparsity, and Bayesian source selection discounts sources that would mislead. Model averaging then folds selection and fitting into one posterior, sampled with a Gibbs algorithm.

Simulations show stronger posterior inference for the target coefficients than target only methods give. Predictive performance stayed competitive with transfer methods, and uncertainty estimates were better calibrated. A case study estimated tumor mutational burden from gene expression in cancer atlas data. Uncertainty matters in genomics, where a wrong coefficient can misdirect a study. Selecting sources inside the model, rather than beforehand, makes the borrowing auditable. The framework suits a field where regressions beg to be pooled.
arxiv-2510-03549:
Nishigomi and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on cobalt based coordination nanosheets, atom thin materials built from metal atoms linked by sulfur rich organic rings. The team studies two crystal forms of the sheet, one dense and one sparse, with first principles calculations. Stretching a sheet, called strain, offers a knob to retune its electronic behavior. The dense form behaves as a metal, while the sparse form acts as a semiconductor with a small band gap.

Both forms show band patterns reminiscent of a Kagome lattice, a geometry prized in quantum materials. Adding spin orbit coupling opens gaps at key points and feeds a topological character. A model analysis confirms an anomalous Hall effect driven by Berry curvature in the dense form. Pulling the sheet along one axis shifts magnetic moments and boosts that Hall response under hole doping. Strain engineering could tailor these sheets for electronics, optics, and catalysis.
arxiv-2510-04649:
Mateo Torres Ruiz, Robin Piedeleu, Alexandra Silva, and Fabio Zanasi wrote this 2025 paper on a picture language for mixed probability models. Many models blend a discrete choice with values that follow a bell curve for each choice. Gaussian mixtures are the best known case, used in clustering and signal work. Reasoning about when two such models agree has stayed informal. The authors build a calculus of string diagrams for these hybrid models.

Boxes and wires in a diagram stand for model pieces, and diagrams compose like the models do. They give the diagrams a meaning as probability distributions. They supply equations that can rewrite one diagram into another. The equation set is sound and complete: two models match exactly when the equations can prove it. Nested mixtures can flatten or reshape without changing meaning, and the calculus certifies it. The result gives tools for software that must verify models.
arxiv-2510-04749:
Samy Ateia and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on using language models to mine concepts from research papers. Publication volume keeps climbing, and readers cannot track fields by hand anymore. The team builds a system that pulls concepts out of scientific documents. Their approach leans on in context learning: show the model a few examples and it adapts. A new field can be served with few examples, or none.

The work sits inside a German national project for research data in computer science. It aims to support the FAIR goals of findable, reusable scholarship. Tests focused on business process management papers. The authors compared commercial and open models on the extraction task. They built a demo and gathered feedback from users. A workshop with the research community supplied stories that steer the design. Planned services include structured literature reviews and concept based search. Extracted concepts would flow into knowledge graphs.
arxiv-2510-04849:
Elisei Rykov and eight coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on catching the exact words a language model makes up. Hallucination checks usually flag an answer as wrong, and only in English. Users need finer tools: which span of text is invented, in their own language. The team built PsiloQA, a data set of hallucinated spans across fourteen languages. An automated pipeline built it from Wikipedia questions and model answers.

One model wrote question and answer pairs, and several models answered without context, inviting invention. A strong model then marked the invented spans by comparing with gold answers and sources. The authors tested many detectors on the result. Methods ranged from uncertainty scores to tagger models and fine tuned encoders. Encoders won across languages in their evaluation. The data also transferred well to other benchmarks, showing real teaching value. Building the set by machine cost far less than human annotation would.
arxiv-2510-04949:
E. E. Nokhrina and co-authors at the Lebedev Physical Institute present an analytical model of relativistic jets in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such jets are narrow streams of plasma fired from the centers of active galaxies. Their model describes the jet's magnetic fields, motion, and plasma density along its length and across its width.

The team checked their formulas against full numerical simulations of the same physics. The fits matched closely, which means the model can replace heavy computing in many studies. It also predicts how a jet should look on the sky. The inner part appears bright at the edges, while the flow farther out glows along its spine. Researchers can now compute light and polarization maps for a jet far more cheaply.
arxiv-2510-05049:
Ahmed Elhussein and five co-authors improve how AI reads medical records in this 2025 arXiv paper. Health records are full of structured codes for diagnoses, drugs, and procedures. Models need compact numeric versions of those codes to learn from them. Older methods lean either on formal medical knowledge or on raw data patterns, never both.

Their framework, KEEP, starts with embeddings built from a medical knowledge graph. It then adapts those embeddings on real patient records while protecting the formal relationships. The result needs no extra task-specific training before use. On UK Biobank and MIMIC-IV records, KEEP beat both traditional and language-model methods. It won on semantic relationship tests and on clinical outcome prediction, with modest computing needs.
arxiv-2510-05249:
Bhavya Matam and seven co-authors build VR training that adapts to the learner's brain in this 2025 arXiv paper. Manufacturers face a widening skills gap, and virtual reality offers scalable practice. Most VR trainers follow fixed step-by-step scripts, though. They ignore cognitive load, a key factor in learning and retention.

Their system, CLAd-VR, trains a precision drilling task with animations, text, and video. A wearable EEG headset streams the trainee's brain activity to an LSTM classifier. The classifier labels load as low, optimal, or high in real time. The system then adjusts difficulty and picks guidance, from voice prompts to ghost-hand demonstrations. The design aims to keep each learner in the productive zone.
arxiv-2510-05549:
Blackwell and Haah bring order to a young kind of quantum memory. Floquet codes store quantum data through a repeating cycle of measurements. Errors can strike across space and time, and some hidden errors quietly corrupt the stored data. Their 2025 paper asks which hidden errors are actually harmless.

The authors prove that every harmless hidden error splits into two simple kinds. One kind repeats the measurement itself, and the other sandwiches a measurement between twin errors. They call such errors benign, after the stabilizers of older static codes. The code distance then equals the smallest harmful hidden error, by weight. No assumptions about time boundaries are needed for the main dichotomy to hold. The result also covers wider families of dynamical codes with bounded inference time. That clarity helps designers judge how much noise a Floquet memory can survive.
arxiv-2510-06249:
Nakai and six co-authors improve low-resource machine translation by aligning internal model layers in a 2025 language technology study. The work joins the MMLoSo challenge targeting India's many low-resource languages. The team asks whether forcing cross-lingual similarity in specific layers improves translation into high-resource languages.

Their method TRepLiNa combines Centered Kernel Alignment with the REPINA regularizer. Alignment pulls different languages' representations together, while REPINA keeps updates near the pretrained model. They experimented on Aya-23 with QLoRA in zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuning settings. Pairs covered Mundari, Santali, and Bhili with Hindi or English pivots. Aligning mid-level layers proved a low-cost, practical improvement. Gains were clearest in data-scarce settings, where these languages need help most. The recipe needs no new parallel corpora, suiting the world's many under-resourced languages.
arxiv-2510-06349:
Samadi and Schuppert argue decentralized swarm learning may beat foundation models on essential adaptive tasks in a 2025 machine learning paper. Foundation models excel broadly, yet gains remain modest in domains like intensive care. Such settings demand self-adapting models of strongly interacting systems with little data and partial mechanistic knowledge.

The authors name the curse of dimensionality as the fundamental barrier to self-adaptation. Monolithic foundation models face conceptual limits against that barrier. Their alternative is a decentralized architecture of small agent networks. Each agent covers only a specialized subset of system functions, mirroring its substructure. Mathematical learning results, plus evidence from applications, support the proposal. Diverse swarms of self-adapting agents should deliver superior decisions in dynamic environments. The admitted cost is reduced reproducibility in detail. AI, they insist, should prove superiority here before claiming broader decision-making roles.
arxiv-2510-06749:
Eitan Klinger leads a large team formalizing how to grade grammar correction software. Their 2025 paper addresses a flaw in current scoring. A sentence can be corrected correctly in many different ways. Metrics that reward closeness to one reference answer punish other valid fixes. Edit-based scores also lean heavily on English.

Their framework treats scoring as an aggregation problem over many accepted corrections. It measures fluency through shared word sequences rather than exact edit matching. A known metric, GLEU, is rebuilt inside the framework in four versions. The versions pick the best reference, average plainly, average with weights, or merge counts. The authors check each version for boundedness, steady improvement, and sensitivity to new references. Tests on Czech, Estonian, Ukrainian, and Chinese data show the versions capture different strengths. Some reward fluency, while others reward coverage. The framework gives a principled base for multilingual, generative correction tools.
arxiv-2510-06849:
Pierre Charbit, Michel Habib, and Amalia Sorondo extend a classic graph theorem to networks that change over time. Their 2025 paper concerns comparability graphs and their orientations. An orientation assigns a direction to every edge. It is transitive when a two-step path always comes with a direct shortcut edge.

A 1962 theorem by Ghouila-Houri covers the static case. Any graph with a loosely transitive orientation, where the shortcut's direction is free, also has a transitive one. Temporal graphs add time labels to edges, which complicates every direction choice. A 2025 model by Mertzios and co-authors defined transitivity for such networks. Charbit and colleagues prove the matching characterization for that temporal setting. Their structural theorem encodes all the constraints as a 2-SAT formula. That encoding yields an algorithm to find orientations, improving on the earlier approach. Information flow in real networks is rarely timeless, so the extension has bite.
arxiv-2510-07049:
Xingran Xu, Chunyu Jia, and Xin-Xin Yang track hybrid light-matter particles gliding on an optical conveyor belt. Their 2025 paper studies exciton-polaritons, quasiparticles formed when light couples strongly to excitations in a material. Moving them in controlled ways matters for future photonic devices. A moving periodic light pattern creates the conveyor belt effect.

The team derived the band structure that the patterned potential imposes. They used Bloch theory for the static lattice and checked dynamics in Fourier space. Watching the intensity over time confirmed the dispersion curves. For potentials that change with time, a Lagrange method shows the motion. Polaritons follow mostly straight trajectories at steady speed. Small wiggles ride on top of that linear drift. Dispersion and transport behavior are closely linked, their analysis shows. Condensate paths were computed two ways, with matching results. Precise steering of polaritons could one day route signals in quantum photonic circuits.
arxiv-2510-07249:
Chen and co-authors release TalkCuts, a large data set for generating videos of people speaking across changing camera shots. Their 2025 paper notes that older sets use one static viewpoint. Real films cut between close, half-body, and full-body views. The set holds about one hundred sixty-four thousand clips and over five hundred hours of speech video. More than ten thousand identities appear in it.

Each clip carries rich labels: text descriptions, body keypoints, and full 3D motion records. To show the set's value, the team built Orator, a baseline generator. A language model acts as director, planning camera moves, gestures, and voice changes. Models trained on TalkCuts produced multi-shot speech videos with stronger visual flow. They beat earlier baselines in both pose-guided and audio-driven tests. It should help researchers build talking-head videos that feel like edited films.
arxiv-2510-07549:
Chen, Xu, Zhang, and Xiu build targeted digital twins: small learned models that predict only the outputs an engineer actually cares about. Their 2025 paper uses flow map learning, which teaches a model to step a system's key quantities forward in time. The full digital twin of a physical system may be a heavy fluid simulation. A targeted twin skips the interior entirely. Short bursts of full simulation, run repeatedly offline, generate training trajectories of just the target quantities.

The demonstration is a classic fluid benchmark: two-dimensional flow past a cylinder. The target quantities are the hydrodynamic forces on the cylinder. The resulting twins are compact dynamical systems that evolve those forces accurately over long horizons without ever seeing the flow field.
arxiv-2510-07949:
Sakaue and Carlon wrote this 2025 statistical physics paper on active polymers, long molecules kicked by persistent forces. Chromatin, the DNA-protein fiber inside cells, is their motivating example. Its motion shows odd crossovers and bursts of superdiffusion from molecular motors. Tracking one tagged point gives tangled statistics for the chain. The authors propose an analytical framework based on a compounding formula.

The formula connects the chain's dynamics to the behavior of a single monomer through tension propagation. That link yields scaling laws with physical pictures attached. Both transient and steady regimes show distinctive exponents from the memory of the noise. The active Rouse polymer serves as the example. The authors expect the machinery to fit semiflexible polymers, crumpled globules, growing interfaces, and single-file particle arrays. Simple formulas that survive contact with experiments are rare in active matter, and this one aims to travel widely.
arxiv-2510-08149:
Laskar and Bouvier Tremblay wrote this 2025 paper presenting AI Knowledge Assist, a system that builds a chatbot knowledge base automatically from past customer conversations. Contact centers want retrieval-powered agents, but many lack any company-specific knowledge base, and building one by hand is slow. The system extracts question-answer pairs from historical transcripts. A lightweight open model, fine-tuned on internal data, outperformed larger closed-source models on the task.

Evaluation across twenty companies showed the system reaching above ninety percent accuracy in extracting information-seeking pairs. That performance closes the cold-start gap, letting centers deploy retrieval chatbots immediately from their own archives. Every support organization already owns the raw material, its conversation history, and leaves it unused. Turning transcripts into searchable knowledge converts a compliance archive into a working asset.
arxiv-2510-08449:
Noor Islam Mohammad presents a modular toolbox for spatial image processing in a 2025 arXiv paper. The framework chains classic operations: quantization, enhancement, sharpening, transformation, and feature extraction. A stepwise intensity map first compresses grayscale images into eight discrete levels. This posterization simplifies the picture while keeping its main structure intact.

Color enhancement equalizes histograms in RGB space and in YCrCb space. The YCrCb route improved contrast while preserving color fidelity better, the study reports. Brightness is tuned through the value channel of HSV space, and a small convolution kernel sharpens fine detail. A two-way pipeline combining unsharp masking, gamma correction, and noise reached accuracies near seventy-six percent forward and seventy-five percent back. Feature tools include Canny edges, Hough lines, and Harris corners. Cue isolation in billiard images matched ground truth with 81.87 percent similarity.
arxiv-2510-08549:
Zilin Kang, Chonghua Liao, Tingqiang Xu, and Huazhe Xu boost models by constraining output entropy through activation design, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Entropy, the spread of a model's output distribution, shapes exploration and confidence. Their method, ERA, applies specially designed activations to model outputs. These activations keep sampling entropy above chosen thresholds during training and generation.

The gains span three very different domains with less than seven percent extra compute. For language models, ERA raised the AIME 2025 math score of Qwen2.5-Math-7B by 37.4 percent, a large jump. For continuous control, it improved strong baselines like SAC by over thirty percent on HumanoidBench tasks. For image classification, ImageNet top-1 accuracy of ResNet-50 rose by 0.69 percent. The authors present output activation as a simple, general tool for entropy control in algorithm design.
arxiv-2510-09249:
Bukhsh, Daneva, and van Sinderen survey who falls for phishing emails in Pakistan, finding the usual stereotypes about likely victims misleading, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Phishing, fraudulent messages that steal credentials or money, thrives on human rather than technical weakness. The team collected questionnaire responses from one hundred sixty-four people, probing demographics, technology habits, past victimization, and reactions to email features. The goal was to identify which groups need protection most.

Contrary to common assumptions, men, people over twenty-five, employed respondents, and frequent online shoppers showed relatively high susceptibility. The message itself mattered too: authority and urgency cues raised susceptibility, while risk cues sometimes sharpened vigilance. Emails appearing to come from services such as Gmail or LinkedIn fooled users more readily than ones mimicking government sources. The authors call for awareness campaigns aimed at the groups and email types their data flags.
arxiv-2510-09549:
Andrew Stasiuk, Garrett Heller, Lance Berkey, Bo Xing, and Paola Cappellaro observe unusual diffusion in a disordered spin network in a 2025 arXiv paper. In typical systems with few conserved quantities, excitations spread diffusively, at a steady random-walk pace. Strong disorder can instead slow transport and block thermalisation, the settling toward equilibrium, which makes disordered systems a sharp probe of how thermodynamics emerges.

The team studies a strongly disordered three-dimensional nuclear spin ensemble, using local measurements made possible by a disordered-state technique. They observe what looks like a phase transition into a sub-diffusive regime, where spreading runs slower than diffusion. They model it as a random walk on a fractal network that emerges as dipolar-coupled spins percolate through the ensemble. The framework offers a way to characterise how thermalisation emerges in closed quantum systems even under strong disorder.
arxiv-2510-09849:
Zhu investigates text prompt injection in this 2025 arXiv project on the safety of large vision language models. These models take in both images and text and answer questions about what they see. A prompt injection hides crafted text that tricks the model into wrong or unsafe behavior.

Zhu developed an algorithm that carries out this kind of attack. Tests then showed that the attack works well and runs with little wasted effort. The results point to a simple weak spot: text placed where the model reads it can steer the model away from its task. The work frames the attack as easy to mount, which raises the stakes for guarding such models.
arxiv-2510-10049:
Li, Zheng Ning, Yuan Tian, and Toby Jia-jun Li present Alloy in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI agents. Language models let end users hand complex tasks to autonomous agents in plain words. But users often cannot specify the procedure they want, above all for tasks with no single right answer that hinge on personal taste, like posting content or planning a trip.

Alloy generates reusable agent workflows from user demonstration instead of written instructions. The user shows the task once, and the system captures the steps as a workflow that can run again. This shifts the burden from describing preferences to demonstrating them. The authors target repeatable personal tasks where taste, not fact, defines a good result.
arxiv-2510-10449:
Ricardo Alonzo Fernández Salguero reviews a decade of austerity policy in this 2025 arXiv paper. Austerity means deep cuts to public spending meant to shrink government debt. Such cuts spread across much of the rich world after the 2008 financial crisis. Salguero gathers a wide body of past studies, sorts them by theme, and asks what the cuts did to economies, daily life, and politics.

Most studies he reviews find that austerity shrinks economies, above all during a crisis, and can deepen a downturn instead of curing debt. The cuts are linked to wider inequality, worse public health, and weaker safety nets, with women hit harder than men. They are also tied to falling trust in institutions, rising populism, and unstable elections. Salguero concludes that the costs are high and the gains doubtful, and he argues for fairer policies shaped to each country's situation.
arxiv-2510-10849:
Donald Loveland, Yao-An Yang, and Danai Koutra ask when a graph neural network should phone a language model for help, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Learning on graphs whose nodes carry text has pushed researchers to fuse the two model types. Most fusion applies the language model uniformly to every node and gains little overall. The authors argue that averages hide the truth: each model type excels on different structural patterns, such as nodes whose neighbors share their label.

Their framework, GLANCE, adds a lightweight router. Given cheap per node signals, the router decides whether querying the language model is worth it for that node. It trains on an objective comparing the utility of asking versus trusting the graph model alone. Across benchmarks, GLANCE achieved the best balance across node subgroups. It gained up to 13 percent on heterophilous nodes, where neighbors differ, while also reaching top overall performance.
arxiv-2510-12049:
Lu Fang, Zhe Yuan, Kaifu Zhang, and colleagues measure what generative AI actually did for a retailer's bottom line. Anecdotes abound; causal evidence at scale is rare. Their 2025 arXiv paper reports randomized field experiments at a top cross-border online retail platform, spanning millions of users and products over six months in 2023 and 2024.

Generative enhancements were woven into seven consumer-facing workflows, from content generation to customer interaction. Sales effects ranged from zero to over sixteen percent, depending on how much the AI added beyond existing practice. Because inputs and prices were held constant between experimental arms, the sales gains translate directly into total-factor productivity gains. In the four applications with positive effects, the implied value was roughly five dollars per consumer per year. That is modest per person, enormous at platform scale. The study gives executives a rare randomized benchmark for what these tools earn.
arxiv-2510-12249:
Cyffers and co-authors study how regularization should be chosen when the data reacts to the model itself, in a 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. In performative learning, deploying a model changes the distribution it will face, for example when users adapt their features to game the system. A good model must therefore anticipate the shift it causes, without knowing exactly what that shift will be.

The authors analyze high dimensional ridge regression, a standard method that penalizes large coefficients to control overfitting. They show that performative effects worsen test risk in the classical population setting. Yet in the overparameterized regime, where features outnumber samples, those same effects can actually help. The optimal regularization strength scales with the total strength of the performative effect, so it can be set in advance if that strength is estimated. Experiments on synthetic and real world datasets illustrate how the optimal parameter moves as predicted.
arxiv-2510-12449:
Demirci and co-authors use dark matter detectors' electron recoil data to constrain the electromagnetic properties of neutrinos, in a 2025 arXiv particle physics paper. When a neutrino scatters elastically off an atomic electron, any magnetic moment, tiny electric charge, or charge radius it carries would change the recoil rate. These properties follow naturally from neutrinos having mass, but they are far too small for direct measurement.

The authors fold each property, one at a time, into the Standard Model prediction using the measured solar neutrino flux. They then analyze the latest datasets from the PandaX-4T experiment along with new XENONnT results, both built to detect dark matter but equally sensitive to these recoils. They present bounds that ignore flavor and bounds that marginalize over the three neutrino flavors separately. The new limits are comparable to or better than previous studies, tightening what neutrinos' electromagnetic behavior can still be.
arxiv-2510-12749:
Yang, Dai, and Zhang unify three perception tasks for city scenes into one framework that segments video, tracks the camera, and renders new views, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Systems that understand urban scenes for embodied agents suffer when the tasks run separately: weak segmentation, interference from moving objects, sparse data, and limited viewpoints.

Their SPORTS framework tightly integrates the three tasks so each helps the others. The segmentation stage aligns features across frames using pose, depth, and optical flow through an adaptive attention mechanism. A matching step stabilizes object identities. Segmentation results then help the odometry stage judge which objects move, improving camera pose accuracy and depth completeness. Rendering converts the sparse point clouds into neural fields that synthesize high fidelity color views and matching panoptic views. On three public datasets their fusion outperformed most leading methods across odometry, tracking, segmentation, and novel view synthesis.
arxiv-2511-00349:
Weiyou Kong, Weijia Kong, Lukas Chrostowski, and Xin Xin chase a fabrication failure in photonic devices built on barium titanate films. A routine oxygen plasma clean, meant to prepare the surface, caused photoresist to lift off during gentle rinsing and ultrasound. Optical microscopy and two spectroscopy methods let them separate bulk changes from surface changes in the film.

The bulk stayed the same, but the surface did not: plasma created a nanometer-thin layer rich in barium carbonate that weakened the resist bond. Each plasma step recreated the weak layer, while simple solvent cleaning removed it. The practical guidance is direct: avoid routine oxygen plasma on this material, use gentler cleans such as UV-ozone, or tune the plasma with care.
arxiv-2511-00749:
Tanvi Dinkar, Aiqi Jiang, Gavin Abercrombie, and Ioannis Konstas audit how image generators encode beauty and erase its opposite. Social media already promotes Western beauty norms with documented harms, and AI-generated content now floods the same feeds. The team prompts three language models and two image models through two generation pipelines, structured by a beauty taxonomy they built, producing nearly six thousand images.

Women and non-binary social media users then rated twelve hundred of the images in a within-subjects study, with high agreement. More than eighty-six percent of generated people had lighter skin tones, and about three quarters read as young. Explicit content appeared in over a fifth of images despite safe-for-work training. Non-binary figures were rated younger and more sexualized, and prompts with so-called negative traits drew higher unsafe ratings across genders.
arxiv-2511-00849:
Zhexiao Huang and colleagues propose P-OCS, a method for flagging out of distribution inputs, data unlike anything a model was trained on. Spotting such inputs matters when deep learning systems run in open environments, where strange cases appear without warning.

The method works in the space left over after the main feature directions of normal data are removed. A single small nudge applied only inside that leftover space sharpens the faint differences between normal and foreign samples, without disturbing the geometry of the normal ones. The authors prove a one step update suffices in the small nudge regime and give convergence guarantees. Across designs and data sets, they report top detection scores at almost no extra computing cost and with no retraining.
arxiv-2511-01049:
Andrei Lebed predicts an unusual magnetic effect in quasi one dimensional conductors, materials where electrons move far more easily along one direction than across it. Under magnetic breakdown, electrons tunnel between two open orbits. He finds that the electron scattering time can then oscillate in a way that Fermi liquid theory, the standard picture of metals, cannot explain.

The oscillations come from electron electron interactions in the metallic phase under that breakdown condition. Lebed works the effect out in formulas and in numbers for the known electron spectrum of the organic conductor (TMTSF)2ClO4. He also argues that similar resistivity oscillations should appear in another quasi one dimensional organic conductor, giving labs a concrete place to look for non Fermi liquid behavior.
arxiv-2511-01449:
Riddhi Jain and colleagues judge fruit freshness from photographs, a non-invasive way to cut waste of perishable produce. Fine grained freshness labels from experts are costly, so training data are scarce. Proprietary vision language models do well at the task, but food retailers cannot send their data to closed services, and open models lag behind.

Their algorithm, model agnostic ordinal meta learning, trains smaller vision language models by meta learning across tasks while exploiting the ordered nature of freshness grades. It is designed for both zero shot and few shot use under data sparsity. The reported accuracy, averaged across fruits, is about ninety two point seven percent, which the authors describe as industry standard, with state of the art results for this classification task.
arxiv-2511-20249:
Bonte, Devillez, Dusollier, Hertz, Mélot, and Schindl ship a web tool for extreme molecule graphs. Their 2025 paper presents ChemicHull for chemical graph theory. Topological indices summarize molecular structure as numbers. Degree-based ones add edge weights from endpoint degrees. Chemists use them to predict physical properties.

The tool studies graphs where vertices have degree at most three. Such graphs model conjugated molecular systems. Each graph maps to a point in three-dimensional space. Extremal index values become linear optimization over a polyhedron. Only a small family of graphs can ever be extreme. Some graphs provably never win for any index. ChemicHull finds and displays the extremal graphs interactively. Known results for trees and unicyclic graphs were recovered easily. A published Randić index result fell to a counterexample. The tool exposed that error directly. Anyone can now test extremal hunches online. Mathematical chemistry gains a shared proving ground.
arxiv-2511-20349:
Kherchouche, Galpin, Dumas, and colleagues speed up video encoding by guessing block splits. Their 2025 paper attacks VVC intra partitioning complexity. The Versatile Video Codec gains about fifty percent efficiency over HEVC. Its encoder pays with a far heavier search. Trying every block split is the main cost.

Two learning methods estimate split costs cheaply. A regression network predicts normalized rate-distortion costs per block. Neighboring blocks' costs feed in as features. The design works for any block size uniformly. A second method frames splitting as a decision process. A deep Q-network agent learns from split trajectories. It sees two depths of decisions before choosing. Fixed thresholds turn estimates into split decisions. Both methods skip most of the exhaustive search. Quality losses stay controlled by the thresholds. Future work aims at rate control reuse. Encoder designers get size-independent acceleration tools. Real-time VVC encoding moves closer.
arxiv-2511-20449:
Rigutto, Ratz, and Mendez rebuild smooth flow fields from scattered measurements. Their 2025 paper improves radial basis function regression for fluid data. Such meshless methods reconstruct velocity fields from particle tracking. Round, identical kernels struggle near sharp gradients, though. They produce spurious wiggles where flows turn anisotropic. The new method adapts kernels to the flow itself.

Local polynomial fits estimate gradients at the data points. Those gradients guide smarter resampling of the measurements. Dense sampling lands near steep gradients; smooth regions thin out. Each basis function stretches along the local flow direction. Observed gradients enter the fit as soft extra constraints. Tests included simulated turbulent channel flow data. A measured turbulent jet provided the experimental case. The method beat isotropic versions on accuracy and smoothness. It used ten times fewer basis functions overall. Computation time dropped by about half on average.
arxiv-2511-20649:
Hidir Yesiltepe and colleagues at Virginia Tech describe in 2025 a way to let video-generating models run without a built-in time limit. Today's autoregressive video models hit a wall because their position code, called 3D RoPE, fails past 1024 latent frames. Long videos also react slowly when the prompt changes, and they cannot jump between scenes like edited film.

Their fix, named Infinity-RoPE, works at run time and needs no retraining, so an already trained model can use it directly. One part recodes each new block of frames against a moving reference point, removing the 1024-frame ceiling so generation can continue indefinitely. A second part keeps only two frames in memory, the first and the newest, so fresh prompts take effect at once. A third part deliberately breaks the position code to create clean scene cuts inside one stream, and the system beat earlier models on overall VBench scores.
arxiv-2511-20849:
Dong Dong and Weijie Su redesign in 2025 the tokenizer, the component that chops text into the tokens a language model actually reads. Standard Byte Pair Encoding builds its vocabulary by frequency alone. Length-MAX instead optimises average token length, choosing a vocabulary that covers text with as few, long tokens as possible, cast as a graph partitioning problem with a greedy solver.

On FineWeb and other domains it produced 14 to 18 percent fewer tokens than BPE for vocabularies of 10,000 to 50,000, and 13.0 percent fewer at 64,000. GPT-2 models trained from scratch at three sizes reached a fixed validation loss in up to 18.5 percent fewer steps, with inference latency down as much as 13.7 percent and throughput up 16 percent at the smallest size. Downstream quality rose too: LAMBADA perplexity fell 11.7 percent and HellaSwag accuracy gained 4.3 points. Coverage hit 99.62 percent of vocabulary with only 0.12 percent out-of-vocabulary rate, and inference memory dropped 18 percent.
arxiv-2511-21349:
Dario Corona, Stefano Nardulli, Ramon Oliver-Bonafoux, and Giandomenico Orlandi count the many ways a superfluid-like system can swirl on a curved surface, in 2025. Their equation is the time-independent Gross-Pitaevskii equation, a Schrödinger-type model of superfluidity and nonlinear optics, posed on a closed Riemannian manifold. Solutions arise as critical points of the Ginzburg-Landau energy that carry a prescribed momentum set by a background velocity field.

Corona and his coauthors prove lower bounds on how many distinct solutions must exist. The count is governed by the topology, the hole-and-handle structure, of the set where the velocity reaches its maximum. Their regime assumes small momentum and tiny vortex cores. The proof blends critical point theory with Gamma-convergence for Ginzburg-Landau energies, plus new results on codimension-two isoperimetric problems in the small-flux regime that may interest geometers independently.
arxiv-2511-21449:
Steffen Tillmann, Felipe González, and Stefanie Elgeti ask what shape a 3D printer nozzle should be, and answer with simulations in 2025. In fused deposition modeling, molten plastic is squeezed through the nozzle, and pressure loss inside it caps printing speed. Most printers still ship standard nozzle shapes. The authors built an optimization framework that tunes the nozzle two ways: by a single cone angle, or by a flexible spline curve describing the whole profile.

Tillmann and his coauthors compared two melt models. Under a shear-thinning viscous model, the best half-opening angle depends strongly on feed rate: fast feeding favors angles near 30 degrees, while slow feeding prefers wider cones. A viscoelastic model showed a much weaker dependence. Surprisingly, the fancy spline profiles bought only marginal pressure savings over the single-angle designs, a useful reality check for nozzle engineering.
arxiv-2511-21549:
Jason Yik and ten coauthors give brain-inspired chips their first proper performance manual, in 2025. Neuromorphic accelerators compute with event-driven, brain-like architectures that exploit sparse activity, promising efficient machine learning at the edge. Yet engineers optimizing workloads for them relied on crude network-wide sparsity counts whose link to real speed was never checked. The team set out to find what actually limits these chips.

Yik and his coauthors combine analytic modeling with measurements on three real accelerators: BrainChip's AKD1000, SynSense's Speck, and Intel's Loihi 2. They identify three bottleneck states, memory-bound, compute-bound, and traffic-bound, and which workload settings trigger each. Their floorline model, modeled on the classic roofline chart, shows at a glance where a workload sits and how to improve it. Applying the method yielded up to 3.86 times faster runtimes and 3.38 times lower energy at equal accuracy compared with hand-tuned configurations.
arxiv-2511-21649:
Mohamed El Jbari, Fernando García, Hugerles Silva, and Felipe de Figueiredo work out exactly how to detect bits sent as modulated noise, in 2025. Thermal noise communication powers ultra-low-energy wireless links for Internet of Things devices by varying the noise level itself instead of transmitting a carrier. Real channels fade, though, and earlier analyses leaned on Gaussian approximations that ignore fading and inflate errors.

Working under Rician fading, the team derives the optimal detection threshold from chi-squared statistics, plus a bit error probability formula evaluated by Gauss–Laguerre quadrature. The model eliminates approximation error and stays accurate even at small sample counts. Simulations by Monte Carlo confirm the analysis and show significant error-rate improvements over Gaussian-based detectors. The study also quantifies how sample size, resistance ratio, and the Rician K-factor each move performance, giving receiver designers a rigorous foundation.
arxiv-2511-21749:
Svitlana Volkova and six coauthors build BRIES, a compound AI system that detects influence attacks and tests whether defenses against them work, in 2025. As language models generate convincing content at scale, reactive takedowns lag behind. BRIES instead borrows inoculation theory from psychology: exposing audiences to weakened attacks works like a vaccine.

Four dedicated agents divide the labor. A Twister generates adversarial content using targeted tactics. A Detector identifies attack types with tunable settings. A Defender crafts resistance-building content, and an Assessor uses causal inference to measure whether it worked. Experiments used the SemEval 2023 Task 3 technique taxonomy on a synthetic dataset. Skill varied sharply by model. GPT-4 excelled on complex techniques like Appeal to Fear and Whataboutism. Open models such as Llama3 and Mistral struggled with subtle tricks, including Equivocation and Red Herring, suggesting architectures differ in the speech patterns they encode.
arxiv-2511-21849:
Saberi asks a practical question about networks: with eleven published measures of centralization, the extent to which a network is dominated by a few hub nodes, which ones can actually be trusted? Saberi normalizes all eleven onto a common scale, then tests them against six basic postulates any sound measure should obey.

The second test runs them on textbook graphs, stars, rings, and complete networks, plus disturbed versions with known answers. The measures disagreed sharply despite sharing the same goal. Three came out as most reliable: normalized betweenness centralization, which captures dominance over paths, normalized closeness centralization, which captures ease of reach, and normalized degree centralization, which captures raw hub connectivity. Applied together to real networks from different fields, the three gave complementary views that no single measure provided, so Saberi recommends reporting them jointly rather than picking one favourite.
arxiv-2511-22049:
Richland, Kiiskinen, Wang, and colleagues, including Hastie and Tibshirani, adapt uniLasso, a two-stage sparse regression method, to computing polygenic risk scores at biobank scale. The method first fits each genetic variant alone, then uses those univariate coefficients and their sizes to guide a second. Penalized fit, which stabilizes feature selection when predictors are heavily correlated, as neighboring variants in the genome typically are.

Applied to the UK Biobank, with over a million variants measured on hundreds of thousands of people. The adapted method matches the standard Lasso's predictive accuracy while selecting substantially fewer variants, giving sparser and more interpretable risk scores. Standard multivariate methods tend to smear one causal signal across its whole correlated neighborhood. It also outperforms the widely used PRS-CS competitor, and folding in external summary statistics improves prediction further while keeping the model sparse, a practical combination for large genomic studies.
arxiv-2511-22249:
Lai, Wang, Rambhatla, and colleagues diagnose why bigger latent spaces make worse pictures. Latent diffusion generates images inside an autoencoder's compressed space, and raising that space's dimensionality keeps improving reconstruction while generation quality deteriorates. Through controlled perturbations in both pixel and latent domains, the team traces the mismatch to frequency: decoders lean heavily on high-frequency latent components to restore fine detail. Encoders under-represent those bands, so diffusion training barely sees them and underfits them.

Their fix, FreqWarm, is a warm-up curriculum that front-loads exposure to high-frequency latent signals during diffusion or flow-matching training, with no autoencoder changes or retraining. Across high-dimensional autoencoders it cuts generation FID, by 14.11 points on Wan2.2-VAE, 6.13 on LTX-VAE, and 4.42 on DC-AE, with gains growing at higher dimensionality. The authors argue autoencoders and diffusion models should be co-designed around frequency budgets.
arxiv-2511-22549:
Feng and colleagues design one image codec serving both human viewers and machine vision systems. Compression is tuned for one audience: pictures that look good to people, or pictures algorithms read well. The authors argue the two goals share a foundation, because preserving a scene's semantic content matters for both, and quality even helps machines extract features. Their Diff-ICMH framework builds compression on a pre-trained diffusion model, whose generative prior supplies realistic detail.

Two additions keep meaning intact at low bit rates. A Semantic Consistency loss penalises reconstructions whose semantics drift from the original. A Tag Guidance Module feeds the diffusion model tags, nudging generation toward the right content for very few extra bits. Across diverse machine tasks, a single bitstream from this one codec supported analysis with no task-specific retraining, while humans still saw high-quality images, a route to versatile compression.
arxiv-2511-22849:
Al Asif and colleagues profile the Mamba architecture to find where its time goes. Selective state space models promise Transformer-level quality with linear scaling. Nobody had mapped Mamba's runtime behaviour in detail: which components dominate, and how costs grow from 64 to over 16 thousand tokens. They profiled computation, memory access, and I/O across that range for Mamba-1 and Mamba-2.

The state space module is the bottleneck, accounting for more than half of total computation and memory. Acting on that, the authors prune low-activity states inside the module, removing redundancy while leaving expressive power intact. Within a moderate pruning regime the result was a 1.14 times speedup and 11.50 percent lower memory usage across sequence lengths, with accuracy maintained. The study doubles as a design guide: optimise the update rule first; dynamic cache allocation and hardware-optimised sparse-state computation are next steps.
arxiv-2511-22949:
Zhao and colleagues propose a new way to get rid of axion domain walls. These sheet-like defects formed in the early universe. They would otherwise grow to dominate its energy and wreck standard cosmology. Axions are hypothetical particles invented to solve a puzzle in the strong force and are also a dark matter candidate, so their leftover walls are a real problem to clear away.

Instead of adding a bias term that breaks the underlying symmetry, as earlier fixes do, they couple the axion to a twisted primordial magnetic field. They run three-dimensional lattice simulations of the wall network. The coupling drives the walls to collapse. The decay speed depends strongly on the field's correlation length, with both very short and very long lengths slowing the collapse. The process also yields a gravitational wave signal that future pulsar timing experiments could detect.
arxiv-2511-23149:
Del Vecchio and colleagues project how precisely the FCC-ee electron-positron collider could measure the Higgs boson's decays into quarks and gluons. These hadronic modes probe how the Higgs gives fermions their mass. Their combined fit is the first to cover all hadronic decays at once, using both Higgs-strahlung and vector-boson-fusion production and treating interference effects in the neutrino final state.

Assuming four detectors of the IDEA design collecting data at 240 and 365 giga-electronvolts, the study reaches percent-to-per-mil precision for the modes, with expected uncertainties of 0.21 percent for bottom-quark decays and 1.75 percent for charm decays in Higgs-strahlung at the lower energy, both stated alongside the gluon and strange results. It also establishes first sensitivity to the rare decay into strange quarks, opening a path to evidence for the strange-quark Yukawa coupling that the LHC cannot reach.
arxiv-2512-00449:
Turbulence is usually studied in three dimensions, but its character changes with the number of dimensions available. Richard Ho and co-authors measure that effect with direct numerical simulation in 2025. They solve the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with forcing at different spatial dimensions.

The team measures turbulent and chaotic properties, including Lyapunov exponents, which quantify how fast nearby flows diverge. Those exponents fell with dimension in their runs, turning negative in six dimensions at modest Reynolds numbers. Such results test basic theories of chaos and turbulence in a clean, controlled setting. Direct numerical simulation resolves every scale, which is why dimension studies use it. Lyapunov exponents turn the vague word chaos into a measurable number. For folks who study storms in air or sea, the gain is a clean lab. The spin of chaos can be weighed as the room it plays in gains new sides.
arxiv-2512-00649:
Mutual information measures how much two parts of a quantum system know about each other. Beau Leighton-Trudel introduces a geometric scaling relation for correlations in one-dimensional quantum spin chains in 2025. The construction defines an informational distance from the mutual information between regions.

A geometric conversion factor quantifies the local scale behavior of that distance. Turning information into geometry echoes ideas from holography, where distances emerge from entanglement. A clean scaling relation in spin chains could give physicists a new ruler for criticality and correlation, tested in systems simple enough to compute exactly. One-dimensional chains are the systems where such informational geometry can be computed exactly. Mutual information is zero for independent regions, so the distance responds to correlation alone.
arxiv-2512-00749:
G Bande and G Franzoni present a physical model of the Reeb foliation in a 2025 math paper. A foliation slices a space into surfaces stacked like pages in a book. The Reeb foliation is a famous example on a solid torus, often shown only in drawings and proofs.

The paper first explains basic ideas from the modern theory of foliations, in order to describe the Reeb example clearly. Then the authors build what they call the first full physical model of it. They use geometric methods tied to 3D printing. Holding a model in hand can make an abstract shape far easier to grasp.
arxiv-2512-00849:
Yunbo Long, Jiaquan Zhang, Xi Chen, and Alexandra Brintrup tackle private clustering across sites in a 2025 paper. Federated clustering groups data held by many owners without pooling it. Local differential privacy adds noise at each site to protect individual records before anything is shared.

The challenge is keeping clusters accurate under strong noise and uneven data, without many rounds of communication. Older one-shot methods lean on unstable pairwise distances or rankings and degrade badly. The team's topological method uses gravitational potential fields to guide cluster centers. A steadier method could let hospitals or banks cluster jointly without exposing raw data.
arxiv-2512-01049:
Heman Shakeri and four coauthors give a fast algorithm for finding light cycles in graphs in a 2025 paper. Cycles are basic features of networks, shaping robustness, information flow, community structure, and dynamics. Tools that probe cyclic structure are in demand across graph mining, network optimization, bioinformatics, and social network analysis.

Their algorithm finds minimum weight cycles, the cheapest loops under edge costs, in cyclic graph topologies used in mining. Faster cycle finding helps analysts spot feedback loops and redundant paths in huge networks. The paper aims for efficiency without losing exactness about which cycle is lightest.
arxiv-2512-01849:
Klaas De Kinder and Christophe Caloz build a framework for dispersive space-time varying media. Space-time media can steer waves in unmatched ways. Most studies assume ideal, nondispersive matter. Real platforms disperse, with response shifting by frequency. That gap limits design claims.

Their framework finds which frequency transitions are physically allowed. Waves scattered at moving boundaries are the test case. Allowed-transition rules guide real device design. Dispersive honesty brings space-time optics closer to lab-ready filters and switches. Moving boundaries model Doppler and lens effects together, so allowed transitions guide both communication links and exotic lens designs.
arxiv-2512-01949:
Multimodal language models turn images and video into long streams of visual tokens, and processing all of them is slow and memory-hungry. Zhongyu Yang's 2025 paper, called Script, prunes those tokens, discarding the redundant ones, while keeping the ones that matter for the user's actual question.

Earlier pruning methods often ignored the query, cutting tokens by generic importance, or leaned on attention scores with known limits. Script instead builds a graph over the tokens and conditions its choices on the query's meaning. Smarter pruning promises faster, lighter multimodal models that still answer with the visual detail the question needs.
arxiv-2512-02049:
Waves bouncing off several objects at once, multiple scattering, are costly to simulate across a whole volume. Rémi Marsal and Stéphanie Chaillat work in 2025 with the boundary element method, which needs values only on the objects' surfaces, and build a physics-inspired network around it, called PIBNet.

In the boundary approach, one first solves an integral equation for the wave's trace on each boundary. The full solution everywhere else then follows cheaply from a boundary integral formula. A network designed around that structure inherits the method's efficiency. Faster scattering simulations serve acoustics, electromagnetics, and any field where waves meet cluttered geometry.
arxiv-2512-02449:
Brendon McBain, Yi Hong, and Emanuele Viterbo study how users switch between satellites in low Earth orbit networks. Their 2025 study tackles handover, the moment a link passes from one fast moving satellite to the next. Older theory often assumed short serving times, or grew too hard to compute for real plans.

The authors build a general math framework that works for any handover rule a network might use. It measures long term average capacity, meaning the data rate users can expect over time. People who design or run large satellite fleets get a cleaner way to compare switching rules first. It also gives teams a fair way to test new rules side by side.
arxiv-2512-02949:
G. Q. Garcia and three co-authors study fermions living on a spacetime where time and space scale differently. Lifshitz spacetimes break the usual balance between space and time scaling. The authors examine two dimensional Weyl fermions in such a background, in two space and one time dimensions.

Using the Dirac phase method, they show how geometric phases arise from coupling to the Lifshitz geometry. They also check for well behaved fermionic zero modes. Zero modes and phases of this kind matter for topological matter, where geometry leaves fingerprints on quantum states. Odd space time is more than a game. Such back drops test if our rules for spin and phase hold when the stage is bent out of shape.
arxiv-2512-03549:
Long coding tasks need agents that check their own work. Yuki Orimo and co-authors introduce PARC in this 2025 work. PARC is a coding agent built for autonomous, robust execution of long-horizon computational tasks.

Its design is hierarchical, with planning, execution, and self-assessment layers. A separate mechanism evaluates actions and outcomes from an independent context and feeds back. Self-reflection could cut the silent errors that plague long agent runs. That matters as firms delegate longer software tasks to AI. Independent feedback contexts reduce self-deception, a known risk when agents grade themselves.
arxiv-2512-03749:
Image generators trained on web-scale data absorb the stereotypes present in that data and reproduce them in their pictures. Korada Sri Vardhana, Shrikrishna Lolla, and Soma Biswas introduce SelfDebias in a 2025 computer vision preprint. Their method reduces biased outputs from text-to-image diffusion models without any human-labelled training data.

SelfDebias works at test time and fits any diffusion model that uses a UNet to predict noise. It finds clusters of meaning inside an image encoder's representation space, then steers generation so the output distribution spreads more evenly across those clusters. No external classifiers or concept-by-concept annotation are needed. Experiments across prompts and model designs show the method generalises to both conditional and unconditional models. It softens demographic stereotypes while keeping images sharp, and it also helps with subtler, abstract biases that are harder to name.
arxiv-2512-03849:
Spacecraft can ride halo orbits around a planet-moon pair, but the highly tilted versions of those orbits behave in complicated ways. Chankyu Joung, Dayung Koh, and Otto van Koert chart that behaviour in a 2025 dynamical systems preprint. Their setting is the circular restricted three-body problem, where a small craft moves under two larger bodies, sometimes passing dangerously close to the lighter one.

Using a Hamiltonian formulation with Moser regularisation, the team built tools that trace periodic orbits and their stability even near collision. They describe vertical collision orbits and the families budding from them through pitchfork, period-doubling, and period-tripling bifurcations, including halo and butterfly families. Those families are then continued into real systems such as Saturn-Enceladus, Earth-Moon, and an equal-mass pair. The resulting maps give mission designers groundwork for polar orbits, including future flights through the plumes of Enceladus.
arxiv-2512-03949:
Jets at the Large Hadron Collider start either from quarks or from gluons, and telling the two apart sharpens nearly every analysis. The ATLAS Collaboration reports a transformer-based tagger for that job in a 2025 experimental preprint. The algorithm reads properties of a jet's constituents, gathered by the detector's tracker and calorimeter, and classifies the jet's origin.

Performance is measured on dijet data from proton-proton collisions across the collider's second and third runs. Two routes estimate what pure samples look like in data. One is a simulation-heavy matrix method. The other, jet topics, leans less on modelling the underlying physics. Efficiencies in data differ from simulation by factors the paper tabulates. The jet topics method carries notably smaller systematic uncertainties in places. The collaboration presents the tagger as a robust instrument for precision measurements and searches for new physics.
arxiv-2512-04049:
TT Arietis is a nova-like binary whose brightness flickers on many timescales, including puzzling quasi-periodic oscillations. I. Vega-Manubens and colleagues reanalyse those oscillations in a 2025 preprint, using far more complete data than earlier studies. The MOST space telescope watched the star continuously for hundreds of hours during its bright state in October 2012.

Their method searches short stretches of data for frequencies, then groups neighbouring detections into frequency groups: episodes of steady or slowly drifting oscillation. They catalogue about one hundred sixty groups with periods between roughly fourteen and fifty-three minutes, lasting a few hours each and often wandering in frequency. Sometimes two groups run at once. Tests on randomised data show chance explains only a fraction of the groups. Their appearance shows no link to the superhump phase, leaving the oscillations' origin open.
arxiv-2512-04249:
An underactuated robot that must repeat a motion forever, a walking cycle or a flapping wing, needs its periodic trajectory stabilised against disturbances. Maksim Surov and Leonid Freidovich present a control design for that job in a 2025 robotics preprint. Their systems have one degree of underactuation, and the standard optimal control design for such cycles is computationally heavy.

The method combines partial feedback linearisation with subspace stabilisation. Studying motion across the reference orbit yields a linear time-varying system possessing a stable subspace. Sliding-mode control then drives trajectories toward that subspace. The design avoids solving costly regulator problems, the expensive step, and improves robustness to matched shocks. Experiments on the Butterfly robot validate the methodology.
arxiv-2512-04449:
Suyeon Lee, Kangkyu Park, Kwangsik Shin, and Ada Gavrilovska present AXLE, a system that moves work into smart memory chips and streams results back without stalling the host. New CXL links let computers add far-off memory that can also compute in place. That near-memory work can cut the cost of hauling data back and forth. Yet older offload schemes ignore trade-offs between distinct CXL routes. Their 2025 arXiv paper maps those trade-offs first.

AXLE pairs two CXL protocols so results flow back while new work flows in, a scheme the team calls Asynchronous Back-Streaming. Light host-side control keeps the pipeline full across both sides. In tests, end-to-end run time fell by as much as half on fitting workloads. Gains hinge on data size and compute weight, which the study charts. The design points toward data centers that treat memory as an active partner.
arxiv-2512-04649:
Yarden Sheffer, Ruihua Fan, and Ady Stern devise new ways to detect the chirality of exotic quantum phases straight from their ground-state wavefunctions. Two-dimensional chiral topological phases are famous for the gapless modes that run along their edges. How that edge anomaly hides inside the bulk wavefunction was only partly understood. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds entanglement measures that expose it without touching an edge.

The trick is to take several copies of the wavefunction in neighboring regions and permute how they join. The seams left behind are called permutation defects. The measures built on those seams stay robust under small changes. Standard topological field theory misses the chiral piece, yet the authors' field-theory frame recovers it exactly. Reading chirality from the bulk could help identify new topological materials, where edge access is hard and bulk data is what experiments give.
arxiv-2512-04849:
The PandaX Collaboration, with Zhe Yuan, Zihao Bo, and many co-authors, reports the most precise measurement yet of double beta decay in xenon-136, from deep underground in China. In this rare decay, a nucleus sheds two electrons at once. Its smooth energy spectrum tests the Standard Model and may hide signs of new physics. Their 2025 arXiv paper analyzes the full spectrum recorded by the PandaX-4T detector over a large exposure.

The team measured the two-neutrino half-life with an uncertainty half that of their prior result, the tightest value to date. They also extracted a ratio that compares the subleading and leading parts of the nuclear matrix element, and it agrees with theory. A search for Majoron-emitting decays, a channel beyond the Standard Model, accompanies the main result. Precision spectra like these discipline the nuclear theory that any future discovery claim must use.
arxiv-2512-05749:
Dexuan Zhou, Huajie Chen, Cheuk Hin Ho, Xin Liu, and Christoph Ortner speed up a trusted method for finding the ground state of quantum systems. Variational Monte Carlo guesses a wave function and tunes it to lower the energy. The best tuning method, stochastic reconfiguration, corrects the gradient with a large covariance matrix. Inverting it again and again is unaffordable for large networks.

Their 2025 fix is to warm start the linear algebra. A singular value decomposition from the previous step gives a head start, and a low rank picture of the matrix is refined as iterations proceed.
