The costly inversion shrinks to updating a compact approximation. Tests on typical atomic and molecular systems show the method works well inside real variational Monte Carlo runs. The advance matters because the method is prized for steadiness where plain gradient methods stall. Making it cheap lets deep wave functions use it in practice.
arxiv-2512-06049:
Laura Rinaldi, Alvise Sommariva, and Marco Vianello release ORTHOCUB, a software package for computing integrals and derivative values over polynomial spaces in several variables. Cubatures sit underneath much of computational physics. It computes its rules from orthogonal polynomial moments, with near minimal cubature inside a bounding box. The design avoids the usual numerical trap: no matrix inversion or factorization is ever needed, so conditioning problems do not arise.

It all reduces to moments and matrix vector products. Matlab and Python codes are free, as building blocks for larger solvers. The value is the combination: a clean construction, no standard failure modes, liftable code. Cubature in many variables is a quiet bottleneck across applied mathematics; a stable, ready made tool for it is infrastructure, and infrastructure compounds.
arxiv-2512-06249:
Matthew Prest and four co authors study how disorder changes the way light matter hybrids push on each other inside a tiny cavity. The hybrids, called polaritons, form when light trapped in a cavity mixes with excited states in a thin semiconductor layer. Random flaws in that layer are usually seen as a nuisance, something engineers try to smooth away.

The team works out the energy patterns of both the bare excitations and the hybrids, this time with disorder built into the math. Their sums show that the flaws do not weaken the hybrids. Instead, disorder makes the push between two polaritons stronger than it would be in a clean layer. That result matters for devices that rely on these particles bumping into each other, such as low power switches and simulators built from light. It hints that a bit of mess can be a feature, not only a flaw.
arxiv-2512-06649:
Camellia Zakaria and five co authors estimate a harmful soot pollutant from traffic cameras that cities already run. Black carbon pours from traffic, gathers near big roads, and falls hardest on nearby marginalized neighborhoods. Measuring it takes pricey specialist gear, so most streets have no readings at all, and policy flies blind on local sources. Traffic video, by contrast, is everywhere.

Their system reads vehicle behavior and conditions from the video and blends those features with weather data. The model then estimates black carbon at street level, matching held out readings with solid accuracy. The point is leverage: no new sensor network, just new value from infrastructure cities already pay for. Estimates at this grain can guide pollution cuts, street planning, and health work where the burden actually falls, block by block rather than city by city.
arxiv-2512-06749:
Ming Ma and eight co authors debug teams of AI agents by intervening, not just by reading logs. When a multi agent system fails, the trace of who said what is long and branching. The usual fix is to have a language model read the log and blame one agent at one step. That blame is an untested guess, and it may be ill posed: the authors find several distinct fixes can each rescue the same failed task.

Their framework, DoVer, pairs each failure hypothesis with a targeted intervention, such as editing a message or altering a plan, and runs the system again to see whether the fix works. Success is then graded by outcome: did the task get solved, or measurably closer? Inside a known agent framework, on two benchmark suites, DoVer turned a solid share of failures into successes and settled many of its hypotheses by direct test.
arxiv-2512-07049:
T Nagao and co-authors report that a massive star spent its last decades throwing off giant clumps of itself before exploding as the supernova called 2024qiw. Theory says some stars shed mass heavily near death, but the mechanism is unknown. Light curves, spectra, and polarization measures for this event all point the same way: the blast wave is plowing into clumpy material the star had already expelled, at a furious rate.

The bumpy brightness, the broad hydrogen signature, and the shifting polarization fit several major eruptions rather than a steady wind. Such eruptions resemble those of luminous blue variables, rare unstable giants. That raises a dilemma: either those giants can explode directly, against standard expectations, or some other late stage of stellar life erupts the same way. Oddly, despite the heavy shedding, the explosion registered as an ordinary Type II supernova rather than the interacting kind.
arxiv-2512-07449:
Mukta Debnath, Krishnendu Guha, Debasri Saha, Amlan Chakrabarti, and Susmita Sur-Kolay wrote this 2025 computing paper. It concerns deep neural networks split across small edge chips and cloud machines. Splitting saves time and energy, but faults in the hardware can quietly spoil the results.

Their tool, AFarePart, chooses how to split a network with faults in mind from the start. It weighs accuracy loss under faults alongside energy use and delay. During the search it injects fake faults at runtime to test each candidate split. A feedback loop then favors splits that survive faults best. The team tried it on three well-known image networks running on accelerators. Fault tolerance rose clearly, with only a small cost in speed. Safety-critical edge systems, they argue, should plan for faults at partition time.
arxiv-2512-07549:
Miles Gould wrote this 2025 mathematics note on operator algebras, the algebra of quantum observables. It lifts a classic result, the Kadison transitivity theorem, into an infinite setting. The stage is a class of very large algebras that includes the Calkin algebra.

The infinite version grows out of a saturation property of pure states. Massive algebras inherit that countable saturation from their states through excision. Gould shows the saturation matches several order-based traits of a linked filter. One of those traits earns the state the name quantum P-point. Such states cannot be proved to exist from the usual axioms alone. Under mild extra assumptions from set theory, they exist in abundance. The note ends with a cautionary example on the other side. One representation of the Calkin algebra fails the infinite transitivity property. The result maps both the reach and the limits of the theorem.
arxiv-2512-08149:
Milan Rosko, a researcher in logic and the foundations of computing, posted a short paper on arXiv in December 2025. His subject is uniform separation, a hoped for principle in constructive arithmetic, the system known as HA. He argues that a strong structural barrier blocks any such principle from working as intended.

The barrier, he shows, does not depend on what the separated classes mean. It appears whenever two distinct evaluator predicates run in parallel and inference stays uniformly representable in an extension of HA. Under those conditions, any uniform separation principle turns into a special case of a fixed point construction, the kind that breeds paradox. Rosko argues this limit is stricter than classic barriers in complexity theory, because it constrains the logical form of uniform separation itself. Those older results only restricted particular proof techniques.
arxiv-2512-08249:
Sagnick Mukherjee, Jonathan J Fortney, Theron W Carmichael, and colleagues, planetary scientists, posted a modeling study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is transiting brown dwarfs, whose sizes can be measured directly when they cross their host stars. Because those sizes are direct, these objects test theories of brown dwarf and giant planet interiors.

The team built atmospheric and evolution models for this population. Intense host star light, they show, can inflate a brown dwarf radius at all masses, especially past a high flux threshold. Irradiation also changes burning rates, lowering the minimum masses for deuterium and hydrogen burning. That shift moves the boundaries between planets, brown dwarfs, and stars more than metal content or clouds do. Fitting the known sizes of dozens of transiting brown dwarfs, the irradiated models matched better than star ignoring ones. A stubborn set of objects still disagreed, pointing to gaps for future work.
arxiv-2512-08549:
J J Gomez Cadenas and a team of nine colleagues, particle physicists, posted a detector proposal on arXiv in December 2025. They work on xenon time projection chambers hunting for neutrinoless double beta decay, a rare process that would rewrite particle physics. These detectors can image particle tracks, telling a lone electron from the paired electrons of a true decay, but drifting electrons blur as they travel, softening the picture.

Their concept, ITACA, images the mirror track of ions as well. A trace of ammonia converts xenon ions into ammonium ions, which drift slowly toward the cathode without disturbing the electron signal. A sensor there captures them, and laser probing reveals an ion image with sub millimeter sharpness. The electron image still gives the event energy and center. Combining both views improves background rejection by about tenfold. Sharper topology could push these detectors toward much longer decay lifetimes.
arxiv-2512-08649:
Soumitra Ghara, Surjit Kumar, and Shailesh Trivedi introduce a new notion for tuples of bounded operators that commute with each other. The notion weakens a known homogeneity property tied to the unitary group, giving a broader class to study. The authors ask when such a weakly homogeneous tuple is in fact similar to a fully homogeneous one.

They give a sufficient condition for that similarity to hold in general. They then focus on multishifts, a concrete and important class, and fully characterize the weakly homogeneous cases. For multishifts, weak homogeneity holds exactly when the tuple is similar to a homogeneous one. The results are sharpened further for spherically balanced multishifts, giving a clear picture for that subclass of operators.
arxiv-2512-08849: Srijan Ghosh studies rational curves on low degree surfaces inside orthogonal Grassmannians, spaces that collect isotropic subspaces of a fixed dimension under a symmetric bilinear form. The author studies moduli spaces for rational curves in a general surface of low degree. Under a stated numeric condition linking the ambient size, the subspace size, and the degree, the surface is proved to be rationally simply connected. That property is a strong form of rational connectedness for the variety.
arxiv-2512-09049:
Gandham Sai Santhosh and coauthors introduce EMMap, a systematic method for mapping where electromagnetic fault injection affects a microcontroller and for classifying the resulting faults. Fault injection with electromagnetic pulses can flip bits and perturb instructions, making it a powerful security testing tool. Past literature lacks a unified method to map spatial sensitivity and classify fault behavior in a repeatable way.

Building on earlier insights, the method is designed to be platform agnostic, so the same workflow can be applied across embedded architectures. Pilot tests on three representative targets, including an ESP32 class chip and two research boards, are presented as illustrations rather than final reviews. Those early observations motivate a generalized, reproducible workflow for future studies. Researchers can adopt the method to analyze susceptibility of diverse devices in a consistent manner. The work aims to move fault injection testing from ad hoc probing toward a shared, comparable practice.
arxiv-2512-09149:
Anton Vasiliuk and coauthors introduce MindShift, a benchmark for how large language models react to mind based prompts. Language models can absorb and reflect traits and attitudes set by users, but measuring that ability needs robust test based tools. The study adapts the most studied test in mind literature, a major personality inventory, to examine model behavior.

Personality based prompts create detailed roles that vary in trait strength, letting the team measure how closely models follow each role. Results show a consistent improvement in role reading across models, credited to better training data and alignment methods. Responses to the test based assessment also differ greatly across model types and families. That variation suggests models differ in how well they can emulate human like personality traits. MindShift prompts and review code will be released publicly. The benchmark gives researchers a shared way to test role skill,.
arxiv-2512-09349:
Lin Li and four co-authors present COVLM-RL, a self-driving framework that pairs vision-language models with reinforcement learning. End-to-end driving systems struggle to generalize, train efficiently, and explain their decisions. Vision-language models reason well when supervised on big datasets but can be brittle in new scenes, while reinforcement learning adapts yet learns slowly and opaquely.

COVLM-RL uses the vision-language model as a critical-object reasoner. A chain-of-thought prompting strategy makes it pick out key traffic elements and produce semantic decisions, turning multi-view camera input into guidance for the learning loop. That guidance speeds training and makes the policy easier to interpret. A consistency loss keeps the model's semantic plans aligned with the controller's actual outputs. In the CARLA simulator, the system raised success rates substantially in trained and unseen environments alike.
arxiv-2512-09649:
Angiraben D. Mahida leads a team reporting the deepest radio search yet for accretion onto the intermediate-mass black hole in Omega Centauri, the Milky Way's most massive globular cluster. Fast-moving stars in the cluster's core gave the strongest evidence that such a black hole, between stellar and supermassive in size, sits there. How efficiently it feeds would show up as radio and X-ray emission.

With one hundred seventy hours of Australia Telescope Compact Array observations, the team produced the most sensitive radio image of the cluster to date, reaching noise near one microjansky. They detected no radio emission at any of the proposed center positions. That silence imposes limits: through the fundamental plane relation linking black hole activity across scales, the accretion efficiency around this black hole must be low. The result constrains how intermediate-mass black holes grow, or fail to grow, inside star clusters.
arxiv-2512-09749:
Katsuhiko Matsuzaki studies the Teichmüller space of smooth reshaping maps of a circle. The maps he allows have a mild regularity condition, called Zygmund continuity of their derivatives. The space collects all such maps up to a natural notion of sameness. Matsuzaki brings two tools to bear on it: simultaneous uniformization, a method from surface geometry, and composition operators acting on Besov spaces, a scale of function spaces.

From these tools he draws two main results. First, he gives a new proof of a known match between distortions inside the unit disk, fading at a steady rate, and boundary maps on the circle. The maps land in exactly the regularity class he studies. Second, he shows the whole space is real analytically equivalent to a standard Banach space of Zygmund continuous functions on the circle. The result gives the space a clean coordinate description for further work.
arxiv-2512-09849:
Naman Jain, Jin Zhang, Marcus Culemann, and Philipp M. Preiss demonstrate control over fermionic atoms held in optical tweezers. Their array holds lithium atoms in an eight by eight grid of light traps. The team prepares chosen product states with two internal components, atom by atom, in a fully programmable way. The atoms sit in their motional ground states with fidelity above ninety-eight percent. Large differences in magnetic moment between the components help them resolve spin at each site.

The setup also reads out spin, site, and atom number in a single short exposure, and experiments cycle in a few seconds. Low entropy state preparation has been a key hurdle for simulating fermions, the particle family that includes electrons. By combining deterministic assembly, high ground state fidelity, and fast detailed readout, the work establishes a scalable platform for fermionic quantum simulation. The results appeared in Physical Review Letters.
arxiv-2512-09949:
Yuma Sato and Shuichi Matsukiyo model a plasma probe called collective Thomson scattering inside a beam plasma system. The technique shines waves into a plasma and reads the scattered spectrum to infer conditions inside. Their tool is a particle in cell code on a flat grid. They formulate the shape of the scattered spectrum in wave number space for general setups, where the beam and wave paths can point any way.

In this flat setup, they find, the spectrum becomes lopsided. Looking along a fixed direction, the electron and ion signatures in the spectrum grow and distort when instabilities strike: the Buneman instability for electrons and the ion acoustic instability for ions. A second run, with a weak hot beam that stays linearly stable, still showed a lopsided spectrum. The findings should help interpret radar observations of ionospheric plasmas and laboratory measurements.
arxiv-2512-10049:
Jocelyn Nembe builds a unified theory of adaptive estimation that exploits symmetry. The setting is nonparametric functional estimation: recovering an unknown function from noisy data without assuming a formula. When the target function has structure along the orbits of a group action, a symmetry group moving points around the input space, estimation should be easier. Nembe builds a hierarchy of kernels transported along those orbits, calling the resulting setup Twin Spaces. A penalized model selection scheme, obeying a Kraft type inequality, picks among the transported kernels automatically.

Three contributions follow. Non asymptotic oracle inequalities with explicit constants bound the estimator's risk against the best choice in hindsight. New regularity classes capture smoothness along group orbits, and the estimator adapts to them without being told which class holds. Finally, the setup recovers the classic optimal rates in ordinary Euclidean problems, while improving on them when orbital structure is present.
arxiv-2512-10249:
Ellen C. C. Lin and colleagues compare the rhythm of repeating fast radio bursts with the pulses of a magnetar, hunting for a shared engine. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes of unknown origin; some repeat, irregularly. Magnetars, fiercely magnetized neutron stars and a leading suspect for the burst sources, emit similar but far fainter pulses. The team analyzed burst sequences from three repeating sources and from the galactic magnetar SGR J1935+2154. For arrival times, energies, and peak frequencies, they measured two diagnostics: an index of randomness and the largest Lyapunov exponent, a gauge of chaos.

Waiting times in every repeater show high randomness and low chaos, matching the magnetar pulses closely. Energies tell a messier story: bursts and magnetar pulses occupy the same region of the diagnostic plane but scatter far more widely than timings or frequencies. Beaming or varying emission efficiency may explain the scatter.
arxiv-2512-10349:
Quan Yuan, Zhenting Du, Daqian Cao, and Weibang Bai build a robot finger that bends all its joints in lockstep from a single motor. Tendon driven underactuated fingers promise dexterous hands with few actuators and simple mechanics. Their hard tradeoff is getting high load capacity and adaptive compliance together in a compact shape. The authors' answer is synchronous tendon routing: one tendon path mechanically couples every joint at fixed angular velocity ratios, so one actuator drives the whole finger. Their models cover the kinematics and statics, including tendon elasticity, which lets them predict the finger's stiffness before building it.

A prototype matched the models closely under static loading. Five such fingers were then integrated into a complete robotic hand, which manipulated objects across diverse scenarios.
arxiv-2512-10649:
Sisi Huang and Xiaohua Yao prove boundedness results for the wave operators of a fourth-order Schrödinger operator, the biharmonic operator plus a potential, on the integer lattice. Wave operators compare the perturbed dynamics with the free one. And their boundedness on sequence spaces is the backbone of scattering theory: it transfers decay and Strichartz-type estimates from the free equation to the real one.

The authors assume the potential decays. How fast it must decay depends on the type of zero resonance at the thresholds. Under those assumptions, the wave operators are bounded for every exponent strictly between one and infinity. If both thresholds are regular points, the result is sharp: boundedness fails at both endpoint spaces. The proof leans on asymptotic expansions of the resolvent near the two thresholds and on singular integral theory. Decay estimates follow for the beam equation, in a sixty-page analysis.
arxiv-2512-10749:
Merve Ipek Bal and Diogo Pacheco measure how bots bent political conversation in Brazil. Working with more than three hundred and fifteen million tweets from August 2018 to June 2022, spanning one presidential election and the run-up to the next, they compare the behaviour, sentiment. And topics of bot posts against human ones.

Bots leaned heavily on retweets and replies, and their reply activity spiked after the 2018 election, a pattern the authors read as conversational infiltration and amplification. Their emotional tone stayed narrow, while human sentiment swung with events. Topic modelling found bots repeating a tight, Bolsonaro-centred message set, while humans ranged across candidates, civic concerns, and personal reflections. The authors conclude that bots acted as amplifiers of narrow agendas, with a real potential to distort the online debate citizens saw.
arxiv-2512-10849:
Geoffrey Bomarito and Patrick Leser let a computer rediscover physical laws, and ask it to admit how unsure it is. Symbolic regression searches for a formula, written in symbols, that explains data, and it can surface real governing laws. Noise is its weakness: a formula that fits noisy data perfectly usually fits the noise too, and a single best answer hides that risk.

Their Bayesian version samples from the posterior spread over expressions instead of naming one winner. A sequential Monte Carlo engine does the sampling, combining random selection, adaptive tempering that slowly sharpens the target, and scaled marginal likelihood to score candidates. The result favours short expressions that generalise, with an honest spread of options. Against standard genetic programming baselines, the method handled noisy benchmark problems better, overfitting less and recovering accurate, readable equations more often.
arxiv-2512-11249:
Chandra Raskoti and Weizi Li present a model run setup that lets traffic flow and detailed vehicle physics run jointly on lifelike hilly terrain. Testing self driving systems needs both large scale traffic and faithful 3D perception, yet current tools rarely include real elevation. Flat virtual cities mislead developers working on places with steep, irregular streets.

Their automated process links the SUMO traffic simulator with the CARLA driving simulator. Open street map road networks and national survey elevation data are fused into steady 3D environments with smooth, checked height profiles. Model runs in two and three dimensions stay synchronised across the platforms. Demonstrations across several districts of San Francisco showed the setup scaling while reproducing steep terrain faithfully. The authors offer it as a useful base for high fidelity autonomous vehicle testing.
arxiv-2512-11549:
Marie Breum, Vanessa Didelez, Erin Gabriel, and Michael Sachs derive honest ranges for mediation effects when the usual identifying assumptions cannot be trusted. Mediation analysis asks how much of a treatment's effect flows through an intermediate pathway, such as a biomarker. Point estimates rely on assumptions, including ones about unmeasured confounding, that can fail even in randomised trials.

When an effect is not point identified, bounds give the range of values still consistent with the data. The authors study bounds under two leading frameworks, natural effects and separable effects. With unmeasured confounders of the intermediate variables, the sharp symbolic bounds for separable direct and indirect effects coincide with known bounds for natural effects in the matching setting. They also compare bounds when only the cross world independence assumption fails. A real trial of infant peanut consumption and allergy development, working through measured immune biomarkers, demonstrates the methods.
arxiv-2512-11749:
Minglei Shi and a large team scale up a new way to make images from text without a separate compressor. Most image generators first squeeze pictures into a compact code with a variational autoencoder. The SVG approach instead works in the feature space of a vision foundation model, a space rich with meaning.

Their system, SVG-T2I, runs a standard diffusion pipeline in that feature space. It scored 0.75 on GenEval and 85.78 on DPG-Bench, matching strong rivals. The result shows foundation model features can carry image making on their own. The team released code, models, and full training and testing tools for others to build on.
arxiv-2512-12249:
Partha Ghose reframes the quantum measurement problem as a problem of logic in a 2025 paper. The usual puzzle pits smooth Schrödinger evolution against a sudden collapse rule. Ghose argues the deeper clash is that quantum theory is contextual, set by the measurement setup, while classical thought assumes one global true or false value.

He recasts locality and completeness as a global section of a presheaf, a tool that tracks local data. When no global section exists, no context free description is possible, and cohomology measures the block. Classical physics is the sheaf case, where local data glue cleanly. Measurement then becomes sheafification, not a physical break in the rules.
arxiv-2512-12349:
Yidong Zhou and four co-authors settle cases in graph coloring in a 2025 math paper. A graph is vertex-critical when removing any part lowers the colors it needs. They study triangle free graphs that also avoid certain long path patterns as induced subgraphs, meaning patterns that appear with no extra edges.

They show exactly three 4-vertex-critical graphs avoid both P7 and triangles while holding a 7-cycle. That settles the first of two cases in a 2018 conjecture by Goedgebeur and Schaudt. They also prove all graphs avoiding P5 plus an isolated vertex and triangles are 3-colorable. Finally, they build an endless family of critical graphs avoiding four disjoint edges and triangles.
arxiv-2512-12449:
Joao Morais, Akshay Malhotra, Shahab Hamidi-Rad, and Ahmed Alkhateeb compare data sources for machine learning in wireless systems in a 2025 paper. Most studies train on standard stochastic channel models, which are easy to generate at scale. But their built-in assumptions may stray from how signals really travel, so test scores may mislead.

The team also uses ray-traced data, which simulates signal paths through a scene and acts as a stand-in for the real world. Two tasks anchor the study: channel state compression and channel prediction over time. Stochastic-only scores sometimes overshot and sometimes undershot ray-traced results. Their recipe: use stochastic data for scalable pretraining, but ground tests in ray-traced scenes when space-time coupling matters.
arxiv-2512-12549:
Shaif Chowdhury, Mushfika Rahman, and Greg Hamerly present a supervised contrastive method for video representation learning in a 2025 paper. Video models usually need costly transformers. Their trick arranges many frames from one video into a single image grid, so a standard pretrained image network like ResNet50 can process the whole clip at once, gaining temporal context cheaply.

A contrastive objective pulls together projections of videos with the same label and pushes apart the rest. Varied frame samplings of one video serve as natural positive views, cutting overfitting without synthetic augmentation. On Penn Action the method hit 76 percent accuracy against 43 for ViViT, and on HMDB51 it reached 48 against 37, with fewer resources.
arxiv-2512-12749:
Sahil Bhola and Karthik Duraisamy propose a new way to model physics systems with hidden uncertainty in a 2025 paper. Surrogate models are fast stand-ins for costly simulations. When data from the best simulations are scarce, plain neural operators give one answer and no sense of doubt, while generative models need many costly runs.

Their method learns only the residual, the gap between a cheap low detail solution and a costly high detail one. A flow matching model, conditioned on the input and the cheap solution, spreads that learning across input cases and can work at new grid resolutions. On advection, Burgers, and Darcy flow tests with random inputs, accuracy rose under the same costly data budget, and doubt was captured better when data were scarce.
arxiv-2512-13049:
Le Bin Ho uses quantum simulation to probe why a symmetry called CP is almost perfectly kept by the strong force. Theory allows a term that would break it badly, yet experiments show the effect is tiny. This puzzle is known as the strong CP problem.

Ho maps a simplified version of the theory, a one-dimensional analogue, onto qubits. Ground states prepared with a feedback based quantum method showed energy minima where the breaking term is zero or a full turn. Adding a dynamical axion field let the system relax to zero breaking on its own. That mirrors the Peccei-Quinn mechanism proposed to solve the puzzle.
arxiv-2512-13249:
Tomasz Kania and Natalia Maslany compute Raja's covering index for Lp spaces, a measure of how the unit ball of a space can be covered by smaller pieces. They handle classic scalar spaces, vector-valued versions, and non-commutative counterparts used in quantum probability.

For infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, they find the index exactly: it falls as one over the square root of the number of pieces, settling a question of Raja. For general Lp spaces they build an explicit splitting of the unit ball to prove a matching upper bound. Bochner spaces obey the same rate regardless of the inner space, giving a partial negative answer to another of Raja's problems.
arxiv-2512-13349:
David Barreiro-Villaverde, Antonio Cantiani, and Miguel Mendez model pressure buildup in cryogenic tanks, where heat leaking in slowly raises pressure with no venting. Predicting that rise means resolving heat flow, natural convection, and phase change together. Tuning knobs that merely fit past data are a common weakness.

Their segregated framework treats liquid with an incompressible solver and vapor with a compressible one, joining them at a sharp interface with jump conditions from first principles. Wall heat conduction is solved rather than imposed. Validated on small nitrogen and large hydrogen experiments, the model found two regimes: an early heating driven phase, then a boil-off driven phase governed by saturation.
arxiv-2512-13549:
Federico Alberto Astolfi, Sven Jandura, and Guido Pupillo study fastest state changes for qubits held in neutral atoms. Their work uses the Rydberg blockade, where one excited atom blocks nearby atoms from the same state. They seek laser controls that move two or many qubits from one state to another in the least time.

Using the Pontryagin Maximum Principle, they sort best paths into normal and abnormal types. For two qubits, some abnormal paths are absent or not best. For normal paths, laser detuning maps to a classical particle moving in a quartic potential well. Blending this math with numeric search gives fast, high-fidelity control plans.
arxiv-2512-13649:
Ali Partofard studies integral models of exceptional Shimura varieties, a class of geometric spaces tied to the Langlands program. He works in the meta-unitary case, using Scholze's fiber product conjecture as a lens. The aim is a clean geometric account of spaces that are not of abelian type.

Partofard restates Bultel's construction with moduli stacks of Shtukas and Igusa stacks, and proves the fiber product formula for this class. That extends work by Zhang, Daniels, Van Hoften, Kim, and Zhang. He then derives local-global compatibility results. Adapting a strategy of Zhu and Yang, he applies the unipotent categorical local Langlands correspondence to prove a vanishing theorem for generic cohomology.
arxiv-2512-13849:
Adam Cushman gives new exponents for the sum-product problem and for convex sumsets in additive combinatorics. The sum-product question asks how much a finite set of real numbers must grow under either addition or multiplication. A set cannot stay small under both operations, and pinning down the growth rate is a central open problem.

For a finite real set A, Cushman bounds the larger of the sumset and product set. It grows at least like the size of A to the power 4/3 plus 10/4407, up to a small loss. For convex sets, he gives a sumset exponent of 46/29 and a difference set exponent of 8/5 plus 1/3440. The note is short and purely focused on these improved bounds.
arxiv-2512-13949:
Zachariah Malik, Quinn Langfitt, and Zain Saleem generalize how readout noise in quantum devices is modeled. Standard models assume measurement noise is purely classical: observed counts come from ideal populations passed through a column-stochastic assignment matrix. That premise makes the effective measurement blind to quantum coherences.

The authors relax it and derive a general formula for observed chances under any noise before a basis measurement. The probability vector splits into a classical part from populations plus a coherence-response matrix times the coherences. The classical model returns only when all POVM entries are diagonal. Using the new matrix in readout recovery improved fidelity over classical inversion in their tests, and enabled chosen Pauli twirling with far less circuit overhead.
arxiv-2512-14049:
Rajesh Kumar Bhagat develops a theory of hydraulic jumps in thin films driven by surface tension, not gravity. Hydraulic jumps are traditionally explained by gravity-driven shallow-water theory, with surface tension cast as a minor Laplace pressure effect. Recent experiments suggest surface tension can instead be the primary mechanism.

Starting from full interfacial stress conditions, Bhagat shows the deviatoric part of the normal stress enters at leading order and changes the balance fundamentally. A dominant-balance analysis in the zero-gravity limit gives parameter-free governing equations with a similarity solution for the velocity profile. Depth-averaged momentum conservation reveals a singularity at unit Weber number, read as the criterion for hydraulic control. A non-trivial pressure gradient at the jump regularizes that singularity.
arxiv-2512-14349:
Federico Califano, Camilla Rota, Riccardo Zanella, and Antonio Franchi present a geometric port Hamiltonian formulation for redundant robot arms in a 2025 paper. Redundant manipulators have more joints than a task needs, which gives freedom but complicates modeling and control.

Their model starts from canonical Hamiltonian dynamics and changes coordinates to a task space view. The momentum variable splits into a task space part and a null space part, which captures motion that does not affect the task. They highlight traits of the model and its links to Lagrangian forms in the literature. As a test, they use it in a passivity based control design that stabilizes a 7 degree of freedom Emika Panda robot and shapes its impedance in simulation.
arxiv-2512-14449:
Sean Thrasher, Ioannis Kolotouros, Julien Michel, and Petros Wallden compare adiabatic inspired quantum methods for molecular ground states in a 2025 paper. Quantum chemistry problems like electronic structure can defeat classical solvers, and ground state preparation is a central target.

The Variational Quantum Eigensolver often struggles with non convex landscapes and barren plateaus, while full Adiabatic Quantum Computing needs circuits too deep for current devices. The authors first unify the adiabatic inspired family in one framework, then benchmark three methods. They add a new variant, G AQC PQC, with adiabatic inspired initialization and a low memory BFGS optimizer that cuts quantum cost. On beryllium hydride, the new method beats conventional VQE, though a zero gradient problem still limits some regimes.
arxiv-2512-14649:
Yoann Launay, Gerasimos Rigopoulos, and Paul Shellard put stochastic inflation into numerical relativity in a 2025 paper. Stochastic inflation adds random noise to the growth of the early universe. A full treatment must include all metric and matter degrees of freedom at once, not just a single field.

The authors re derive a set of 3 plus 1 equations for this process in a gauge invariant way. They then build the equations into the BSSN form of numerical relativity, a standard code frame. Tests cover both a slow roll and an ultra slow roll case. The evolution is correctly reproduced for all variables, and the energy and momentum constraints stay well satisfied. Their runs give real space views of the fully nonlinear dynamics, with gradients and uneven expansion kept.
arxiv-2512-14949:
Tomasz Kania and a coauthor revisit a famous 1981 counterexample by Bourgain about how sequences converge. Bourgain showed that a mode of convergence on the l1 space, pointwise plus domination, is not sequentially complete. The authors recast the question in vector lattices, ordered spaces where elements can be compared and joined.

In that setting, the Bourgain style convergence for sequences matches plain order convergence. They then define a stronger Cauchy notion that must survive taking subsequences. Any space that is sequentially complete in this stronger sense must be sigma order complete, so free Banach lattices on spaces of dimension above 1 fail. On the bright side, the classic spaces c0 and l infinity pass. For bounded Lipschitz function lattices, the test passes exactly when the underlying space is uniformly discrete.
arxiv-2512-15449:
Margot Teunisse and Martin van Hecke study interacting hysterons in two limiting cases in a 2025 paper. Hysterons are small elements that switch between two states at different thresholds on the way up and down. Linked together, they model memory effects in complex materials and can guide the design of smart metamaterials.

The authors look at spans, the gap between the two switch points, that are either very large or nearly zero. Large spans limit the paths the system can take, since many avalanches vanish. Tiny spans make hysterons act like interacting binary spins. They also show that pairs of strongly linked spins can mimic hysterons, mapping n hysterons to 2n spins.
arxiv-2512-15749:
Abiel Kim studies a special case of quadratic extrapolation under the neural tangent kernel in a 2025 paper, dated December 11. ReLU multilayer perceptrons are known to extrapolate linearly far from their training data. Extrapolation near the origin is a different, less explored case, because the kernel feature map is not translation invariant there.

Rotation invariance still holds, so the near origin and far away cases form two canonical extremes of ReLU kernel extrapolation. Kim shows the near origin case produces quadratic, not linear, extrapolation for an out of distribution evaluation point. The result clarifies how the geometry of the feature map shapes what a network predicts outside its data.
arxiv-2512-15849:
Orion Ning, Kailash Raman, and Benjamin Safdi search for diffuse axion X-ray signatures from cosmic neutron stars in a 2025 paper. Axion like particles could be made in neutron star cores. Ultralight ones would convert to photons in the stars' magnetic fields, and heavy ones would decay into photons on the way to Earth.

Summing over the whole cosmic neutron star population, the team predicts the axion induced X-ray signal with cooling and magnetic field models. They compare it with the cosmic X-ray background measured by NuSTAR, HEAO, Swift, and INTEGRAL. No evidence for axions appears. The null result sets strong limits for both light and heavy cases and rules out an axion account of one known excess.
arxiv-2512-15949:
Tejas Anvekar and co authors present the Perceptual Observatory, a framework for characterizing perception in multimodal language models, in a 2025 paper. Many model families scale the language part while reusing nearly identical vision encoders. Leaderboard accuracy cannot tell whether gains reflect true visual grounding or borrowed text knowledge.

The observatory tests models on simple vision tasks such as face matching and reading text inside images. It also tests local to global skills: image matching, a grid pointing game, and attribute localization. Ground truth face and word data are perturbed with pixel changes and diffusion based illusions. The framework probes robustness and attribution fidelity rather than end task scores alone.
arxiv-2512-16549:
D Schaerer and nine co-authors test a clue to ancient star clusters in a paper uploaded to arXiv in 2025, a letters journal version. Some distant galaxies glow unusually strong in nitrogen, and their chemistry resembles stars inside globular clusters. That resemblance, plus their compactness and dense gas, hints these nitrogen emitters mark globular clusters being born.

Using a recent census of how common such emitters are and how their numbers evolve with redshift, the team predicted the globular cluster population's history from the cosmic star formation record. The predicted ages peak at about 11.5 to 12 billion years with a tail toward younger ages, matching observed patterns in the Milky Way and elliptical galaxies. The total mass formed, 2 to 7 times 10 to the 5 solar masses per cubic megaparsec, lands within a factor of about two of today's globular cluster mass. The hypothesis gains support.
arxiv-2512-16649:
Bingxiang He and a large team from Tsinghua and partner labs ask whether training large language models with reward learning needs to be complex. Recent recipes stack stages, shifting knobs, and staged lessons, and the team tests a far simpler path they call JustRL.

JustRL trains in one stage with fixed settings. On two 1.5 billion parameter reasoning models it scored 54.9 percent and 64.3 percent on average across nine math tests, while using half the compute of fancier recipes. The same settings worked for both models, and training rose smoothly over more than 4,000 steps. Tests that added standard tricks, such as length penalties, made results worse.
arxiv-2512-16749:
Ulrich Bunke studies coarse homology theories, tools that read the large-scale shape of spaces while ignoring fine detail. The focus is on transgressions, maps from such a theory into one that factors through the Higson corona, a boundary at infinity.

Bunke checks whether a square of maps commutes, linking analytic and topological transgressions with algebraic and homotopy Chern characters. A Chern character here turns K-theory-like classes into ordinary homology classes. Pinning down that square matters because it ties index-style analytic data to topological data at large scale. The long paper sorts several theories and the natural maps between them into one coherent picture.
arxiv-2512-17549:
Albert Huber and Paul Schreivogl show that a quantum system's motion can be read as the wobble of a classical spinning top. The Bloch vector picture turns a quantum state into an arrow, and its path obeys equations any mechanic would know. One form matches a swarm of point masses; another matches the Euler-Poinsot equations of a free top.

That match lets the authors import two centuries of top theory wholesale. They prove the motion is integrable, meaning an exact closed-form solution exists, and they build it. Stability tests come along for free. For linked multi-part systems, special solutions swing between fully entangled and fully separate states, an oscillating entanglement they connect to the top's famous middle-axis flip.
arxiv-2512-18149:
Kento Okuyama and coauthors build a forecasting tool for models of psychological change, such as a student's drift toward dropping a math course. Such processes jump between hidden states, and regime switching state space models capture the jumps with intensive longitudinal data.

Their filter is the first frequentist one for this model class, built on Chow and Zhang's extended Kim filter. It lets the hidden Markov switching depend on latent traits measured both within and between people. Forecasts can then update in real time while data are still being collected. In a study of math dropout, the filter forecasts emotions and behavior tied to quitting. Simulations check how well it recovers parameters and predicts the hidden regimes.
arxiv-2512-18249:
Anuradha Mahasinghe leads a six author team finding a leaner way to apply math functions to matrices on quantum hardware. Tasks from physics simulation to solving linear systems need a matrix raised to some polynomial form. Top methods first pack the matrix into a larger block code, a step that eats spare qubits and hard angle math.

Their route, built on a broad signal processing frame, skips the packing step entirely. Set patterns of circuits add up to the wanted polynomial, and the chance of success stays steady no matter how high the degree climbs. Closed form rules for even polynomials smooth the build. The savings matter most when the matrix arises from tidy sums of basic gates.
arxiv-2512-18449:
Masoud Bahari and three co-authors study how electrons with large total angular momentum behave in crystals that lack a center of symmetry. Standard theory treats spin-1/2 electrons and the Rashba effect. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in Physical Review B, builds a fuller theory for heavy-element crystals with C3v symmetry that keep time-reversal symmetry.

Using multiplets with j equal to 1/2, 3/2, and 5/2, they construct every symmetry-allowed spin-orbit coupling term up to fifth order in momentum. For j above 1/2, the coupling reshapes Fermi surfaces and makes the spin texture band-dependent, going far beyond a single Rashba helix. They classify the textures by vorticity, finding phases with values 1, 2, and 5, and show the crossovers boost the Edelstein effect, where current induces spin polarization.
arxiv-2512-18649:
Oleg S. Balashov and Andrei V. Faminskii study inverse problems for a wave equation in this 2025 analysis paper. The equation is the generalized Korteweg-de Vries equation on a bounded interval, a model for shallow water waves with a general nonlinear term. In an inverse problem, extra integral measurements of the solution over time are given, and unknown controls must be recovered from them. The controls can be the right-hand side of the equation, the boundary data, or both.

The authors prove well-posedness for three such problems, with no restriction on how fast the nonlinearity may grow. Their solutions are regular in time, though the results need the input data, or the time interval, to be small. The work extends control theory for dispersive equations on finite domains.
arxiv-2512-18949:
Michael Neilan and Hongzhi Wan build a finite element method for fourth-order problems living on curved surfaces, like bending a thin shell that exists only as a surface in space. The surface biharmonic equation is the model case. Their TraceFEM approach, posted to arXiv in December 2025, uses ordinary quadratic elements on a three-dimensional background mesh and reads the solution off a polyhedral approximation of the surface.

Stability comes from penalties: surface edge terms plus bulk penalties on jumps in the gradient and Hessian. The authors prove optimal first-order convergence in a discrete H2 norm and quadratic convergence in the L2 norm, the best rates the spaces allow. For computational scientists modeling membranes, interfaces, and surface flows, a proven method on background meshes avoids the pain of meshing the surface itself.
arxiv-2512-19149:
Genevieve Quiñones and Peter Olmsted derive equations for a dense suspension of rods under shear flow. Think of short fibers packed tightly and dragged sideways, rubbing as they turn. Their tool is Onsager's variational method, in the form set out by Doi for liquid crystals.

Two friction kinds get separate treatment: dry solid friction, and lubricated friction that grows with sliding speed. A mean-field step yields a dissipation function for each, and from a single Rayleighian they obtain both a Smoluchowski equation for rod directions and the stress tensor. The results appear as corrections to Doi's classic model, plus a new contact-count formula.
arxiv-2512-19349:
JiaWei Zhu and ZiHeng Liu close the loop between inventing hidden confounders and checking them. Confounders are unseen factors that can fake a cause-and-effect link in observational data. Language models can propose plausible ones from domain knowledge, yet plausible is not the same as useful.

Their framework, VIGOR+, pairs a language model with a CEVAE, a variational model that scores how much a proposed confounder helps. Scores, consistency checks, and diagnostic notes return to the language model as plain-language feedback for the next round. The loop runs until the candidates settle. The authors formalize the feedback, prove convergence under mild assumptions, and give the full algorithm.
arxiv-2512-19549:
Jibril Ben Achour, Adolfo Cisterna, and Hugo Roussille present a new exact rotating black hole in a modified gravity theory. Kerr's solution anchors every test of general relativity with spinning holes, yet exact alternatives are scarce. Their hole lives in a Horndeski scalar-tensor theory, a broad family that adds a scalar field to gravity.

The construction applies a disformal transformation, a metric reshaping tied to the scalar, to a stealth Kerr seed. Unlike earlier attempts, the reshaping keeps circularity, the tidy symmetry that makes Kerr so workable. The authors name the result the Circular Disformal Kerr solution and argue its familiar structure suits observational tests.
arxiv-2512-19849:
Ziming Mao leads a thirteen-author team making mixture-of-experts AI run on mixed hardware. Expert parallelism spreads a model's experts across graphics chips. The champion system, DeepEP, is fast. But it is welded to set pairs of chips and network cards. The cause is in its design. The chips start the data transfers themselves, which demands tight links to the card drivers.

Their system, UCCL-EP, routes control through the CPU instead. Small routing commands cross a fast chip-to-CPU channel. Threads on the CPU then issue the real transfers for the chips. Order rules that some cards lack are faked with spare data fields. The system runs on NVIDIA and AMD chips with two brands of cards. It matched DeepEP on its home turf. On Amazon's fabric it beat the best rival. It also lifted serving and DeepSeek-V3 training speeds by large margins.
arxiv-2512-19949:
Zixuan Huang, Xiang Li, Zhaoyang Lv, and James Rehg probe how much three-dimensional understanding hides inside video models. A video is just a flat projection of a three-dimensional world, frame after frame, so a model trained on enough video might internalize depth, shape, and layout without ever being taught them. The team built the first model-agnostic framework for measuring that awareness, reading several three-dimensional properties out of model features with shallow probes.

Benchmarking major video foundation models across multiple axes produced a headline surprise: state-of-the-art video generation models understand objects and scenes three-dimensionally with striking strength, despite no three-dimensional training data. On some measures they surpassed large expert models built specifically for three-dimensional tasks. The authors offer the benchmark as guidance for building scalable 3D models from video.
arxiv-2512-20049:
Bo Fu, Chang-An Li, and Björn Trauzettel propose growing Majorana modes out of a magnetic cousin. Their platform is a three-dimensional altermagnetic topological insulator. It is coated with a plain s-wave superconductor. Altermagnetism stamps highly uneven gaps on the paired state. At the outer faces, Bogoliubov Fermi surfaces form. They differ from facet to facet. That is raw material for topology.

A wire cut thin from this system can switch its topology under confinement. Majorana zero modes then sit at its two ends. Vortices give a second stage. The magnetic order lets the system swap between two kinds of such modes. One kind lives on the vortex line. The other lives at the outer faces. The authors argue that crystal shape plus confinement gives new knobs for this field.
arxiv-2512-20349:
M Kotur and co-authors cool the spins of atomic nuclei inside a gallium arsenide quantum well to extreme cold, using light. The sample is an undoped GaAs layer held between layers of aluminium gallium arsenide. Two optical methods, Kerr rotation and the orientation of emitted light, track how strongly the nuclei line up.

In a near-Faraday setup they measured a very large Overhauser field, above three tesla, in a well about twenty nanometres wide at a bath heat of 1.6 kelvin in magnitude. Slow sweeps of the field then drove the spin heat down to millionths of a kelvin, as spin temperature theory predicts even with quadrupole splitting. At still colder baths, down to a few hundred thousandths of a kelvin, the nuclei began to line up on their own, a self-driven effect that grows as the lattice gets colder.
arxiv-2512-20449:
A Deur, M M Dalton, and S Širca show how a sum rule can interrogate the inside of a nucleus. The Gerasimov-Drell-Hearn rule ties the spin-dependent photoproduction cross-section of a particle to its anomalous magnetic moment and mass. For a nucleon buried in a nucleus, the rule involves an average over all the nucleons inside.

That average is quadratic, which turns out to be a lever. Different mechanisms for how the medium modifies a nucleon predict different quadratic averages, so measurements can discriminate between them. The authors also note that global properties of the embedded nucleon, such as axial charge, mass, and magnetic moment, are themselves observable through sum rules. The work guides experiments probing how nuclei reshape their constituents.
arxiv-2512-20549:
Jaime E Muñoz Rivera and Maria Grazia Naso examine the long-time fate of solutions to the Signorini problem, a model of elastic contact with an obstacle. Their version adds pointwise damping, dissipation applied at selected points. The question is whether all solutions settle into a compact pattern that attracts everything else.

Both the semilinear Signorini problem and the elastic obstacle problem with normal compliance turn out to decay exponentially to zero and to admit compact global attractors. The proofs detour through a hybrid system coupling a partial differential equation to ordinary differential equations. That approximation makes well-posedness and long-time behaviour tractable. Attractor results like these certify that damped contact systems forget their initial conditions in a structured way.
arxiv-2512-21249:
Xinyao Zhang maps spaces that parametrize deformations of two-dimensional Galois representations of Eisenstein type, the reducible corner of the Langlands landscape. Two questions drive the work: how large are the components, and do modular points fill them densely? Over the rationals, under explicit generic hypotheses, every component is claimed to have dimension four and characteristic zero, with modular points Zariski dense.

A R equals T theorem is reported over abelian totally real fields, identifying deformation rings with Hecke algebras. Then come claimed cases of famous conjectures. One is the irregular Fontaine-Mazur conjecture, in a residually reducible setting for primes at least five. Another is Mazur's dimension conjecture over the rationals. A third is Emerton's equidimensionality conjecture for the Hecke algebra at every odd prime. All rest on a new finiteness theorem for pseudo-deformation rings. If the proofs hold, several long-standing hopes become theorems.
arxiv-2512-21449:
Takayuki Hibi, Francesco Navarra, Ayesha Asloob Qureshi, and Sara Saeedi Madani study ideals generated by adjacent two-by-two minors of a grid. Such ideals arise from collections of cells, and their algebra mirrors the collection's geometry. The paper asks which of these ideals have especially nice structure.

The authors describe all the minimal prime ideals in this family completely, using admissible sets and associated lattice ideals. They prove five desirable properties, being unmixed, Cohen-Macaulay, level, Gorenstein, and complete intersection, are equivalent here: an ideal has all of them or none. They characterize combinatorially which convex collections of cells enjoy these properties. Finally, they study when such an ideal is radical, meaning it hides no repeated factors, deriving necessary conditions from the smallest non-radical configurations. The results link algebra, combinatorics, and cell geometry.
arxiv-2512-21749:
Konstantin Yakovlev and Nikita Puchkin determine how well feedforward neural networks with GELU activations can approximate basic functions, together with all their derivatives at once. GELU is the smooth activation used in most modern transformers. Approximation theory usually bounds the error in function values alone; bounding derivatives matters when networks are used inside differential equations.

The authors derive error bounds that hold at once for a function and its derivatives up to any fixed order. The functions covered include polynomials in several variables, the exponential, and the reciprocal. They also report the needed network size, the size of the weights, and the behavior far from the origin. The engine of the proofs is a constructive multiplication scheme valid on growing domains. From it they build division and the exponential, with the approximators' higher derivatives bounded throughout. Such guarantees underpin certified uses in computing.
arxiv-2512-21949:
Valenitn D. Ivanov, in a conference talk write-up, proposes that the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope should issue variability alerts from spectra, not just images. Imaging surveys already alert on changing brightness. A multiplexed spectrograph could go further, flagging changes in spectral profiles and strengths, which reveal different physics.

The science cases range from emission-line stars such as Be stars, Wolf-Rayet stars, and luminous blue variables, to galaxies and quasars, including changing-look objects that switch between spectral types. Ivanov lays out what the facility's data flow system must do to make this possible. Processing must be fast enough for timely follow-up. Alerts require comparison against an updated reference spectral database, drawn from the telescope's own archive, other surveys, or user submissions. He considers automated archive searches and user-supplied references. Modeling the spectra and comparing physical parameters, rather than raw data, could rank alerts.
arxiv-2512-22149:
Guilin Zhang, Wulan Guo, and Ziqi Tan present a system that hands out graphics processor time to teams of cooperating AI agents running on serverless platforms. Such multi-agent systems mix light coordinator agents with heavy specialist ones, and demand swings fast. Static schedules waste expensive hardware, while naive rotation leaves agents waiting.

Their allocator adjusts shares in real time from workload traits, agent priorities, and minimum resource guarantees, using an algorithm whose cost grows only linearly with the number of agents. In simulations of a four-agent workflow, the approach cut latency by about 85 percent compared with round-robin scheduling. It also held throughput close to static allocation while improving cost and hardware use.
arxiv-2512-22249:
Zheng Xing and Weibing Zhao improve unsupervised human motion segmentation by letting a language model label what the body is doing. Cutting motion sequences into meaningful segments is often done with subspace clustering, but classic methods ignore temporal semantics. Their idea is to ask a large language model, working from images, whether consecutive frames show the same motion, and feed that judgment back into the clustering.

The resulting method adds a temporal regularizer that pulls each frame's subspace embedding toward its neighbors' embeddings, and a matching constraint during segmentation itself. A feedback loop keeps refining the embedding from the segmentation output. On four benchmark motion datasets, the approach outperformed current state-of-the-art methods for unsupervised segmentation.
arxiv-2512-22349:
Alaa Alahmadi and Mohamed Hasan color-code heart signals so neural networks learn the way clinicians see. Deep networks reading electrocardiograms usually need large training sets and cannot explain their calls, which limits clinical trust. The authors reuse a pseudo-colouring technique that encodes features like QT-interval duration into structured colors, a trick earlier shown to help human readers of ECGs.

Their test case is acquired long QT syndrome, a drug-induced condition with messy signal shapes, variable heart rates, and few positive examples despite its link to dangerous arrhythmias. With prototypical networks and a ResNet-18, models learned from as few as one or five examples. Attention maps showed the coloring steered models toward clinically meaningful features, and pooling several heartbeats helped, echoing how humans average across beats.
arxiv-2512-22749:
Rui Ai, David Simchi-Levi, and Feng Zhu examine how a third-party platform should set its service fees when sellers and buyers react strategically to prices. The platform wants maximum revenue and can see market features that move demand, yet it only observes completed transactions. Learning demand from such data is confounded, because the prices the platform itself chose helped generate the observations.

The authors give an algorithm whose regret, the revenue lost versus knowing demand in advance, is provably optimal up to small factors. Their analysis shows supply-side noise changes how learnable demand is, producing a phase transition in regret. Non-random platform actions turn out to work as instrumental variables, and a new construction yields the first efficiency guarantee for demand learning with deep neural networks. Tests on Talabat and Lyft data illustrate the revenue at stake.
arxiv-2512-23049:
TJ Bai and Jason Eisner speed up workflows that chain many large language model calls together, as in multi-agent systems. Such workflows waste most of their time re-encoding messages that earlier calls already processed. Their framework, Prompt Choreography, keeps one dynamic global cache of key-value encodings, and each new call may attend to any reordered subset of previously encoded messages, with parallel calls supported.

Reusing cached encodings in a new context can change results, since the model originally encoded each message in its own setting. The authors show across varied settings that fine-tuning the model to work with the cache largely restores the original behavior. The payoff is substantial. Time to first token per message fell by factors between about two and six. Some workflows dominated by redundant computation ran more than twice as fast end to end.
arxiv-2512-23949:
Maxim Burke continues work on a classical theorem of Hoischen. The theorem concerns approximation by entire functions. Any smooth function on the real line can be matched by one. The match covers the function and its derivatives. It can even be made exact at scattered chosen points.

Entire functions rise and fall in stretches. A natural extra demand follows. The approximant should rise and fall on the same intervals as the original. That property is called comonotonicity. The same demand can be placed on the derivatives. Burke pins down when this can be arranged. The range covered runs up to three derivatives. The proof also settles the general case conditionally. It assumes a conjecture about endpoint values of derivatives. That conjecture is already verified in the range treated here.
arxiv-2512-24149:
Changhao Song and four colleagues argue that world models, the systems AI uses to predict what happens next, are missing half the story. Physical laws govern how states change, but human actions are steered by feelings. A model that learns only physics can mimic the physical world, not the human one, so the team builds emotion in as a state variable.

They first construct a dataset of more than ten thousand emotion-aware transitions, each recording the situation and feeling before an action, the action, and the feeling and situation after. Their model then predicts in two linked steps: first the future emotion, then the future state given that emotion. Across tests the approach improved world-state prediction, emotion understanding, and general reasoning, with large gains on the new dataset. The authors see emotion-aware prediction as a route to more realistic simulation of human settings.
arxiv-2512-24249:
Fuqiang Gu and five colleagues tune drone controllers with Bayesian optimization. Quadrotors are hard to control well. They are underactuated, nonlinear, and tightly coupled. Classical PID controllers often track trajectories poorly as a result. The team's method keeps the PID structure. It tunes the parameters far more cleverly.

Their algorithm wraps the controller in a heteroscedastic Bayesian optimizer. The optimizer models noise that varies with the input. That makes it adapt better to dynamic, complex settings. A two-stage strategy speeds the search for good parameters. Simulation and real-world flights both tested the method. Position accuracy beat state-of-the-art rivals by wide margins. Angular accuracy improved even more strongly. The gains held across both test settings. Robust trajectory tracking is the practical payoff.
arxiv-2512-24549:
Maor Ben-Shahar, Lucile Cangemi, and Henrik Johansson develop a worldline action for a spinning Kerr black hole that works to all orders in spin. Their starting point is a proposed tree-level Compton amplitude, a measure of how the black hole scatters waves, drawn from higher-spin field theory.

Inside, the authors give the action in closed form and sort its many curvature-squared terms by helicity. They argue some of those terms have no deep meaning and only cancel unwanted pieces from simpler terms. Readers get a careful account of why loop corrections, counter terms, and matching to general relativity still matter.
arxiv-2512-24749:
Illya Plotnikov, Alexis Rouillard, Athanasios Kouloumvakos, and others examine the strong solar eruption of 31 December 2023 near the Sun's eastern limb. The event brought a very strong X-ray flare, a global extreme UV wave, and a coronal mass ejection moving near three thousand kilometers per second. Radio bursts, energetic particles, and long gamma-ray emission followed.

By combining a reconstructed coronal shock with background solar wind runs, they produce synthetic radio spectra from shock emission. Comparing those spectra with records links the shock to particles and radio signals. Space weather readers get a full case linking one eruption's many signatures.
arxiv-2601-07149:
Zhaoyan Li and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with rewarding creativity. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. While Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate fluent text, producing high-quality creative stories remains challenging.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) offers a promising solution but faces two critical obstacles: designing reliable reward signals for subjective storytelling quality and mitigating training instability. The work introduces the Reinforcement Learning for Creative Storytelling (RLCS) framework to systematically address both challenges. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07549:
M. Raczyński and colleagues measure how quantum coherence travels through a semiconductor, in a 2026 optics preprint. Coherence transfer matters across chemistry, biology, and physics. In quantum technology, linking solid-state qubits without contact is a major goal. The team studies excitons, bound pairs of an electron and a hole inside a quantum well.

Using non-local four-wave mixing micro-spectroscopy, they track exciton coherence propagation. Their abstract states that excitons can carry mesoscopic optical coherence transfer in semiconductors. Mesoscopic means a scale between single atoms and bulk material. Showing coherence can move this way points to new links between quantum devices. The paper speaks to scholars building quantum networks and light-based quantum hardware.
arxiv-2601-07649:
Hui-Ming Zhang and colleagues model how the Sun's activity alters cosmic rays reaching Earth, for both matter and antimatter. They build a unified charge-dependent solar modulation model. It solves the three-dimensional Parker transport equation, the standard description of cosmic ray movement through the heliosphere. A realistic wavy heliospheric current sheet lets the model treat drift effects consistently.

The team fits the model to time-resolved proton and antiproton fluxes from the AMS-02 instrument. The data cover the quiet solar period from May 2011 to June 2022. A local interstellar spectrum from GALPROP, constrained by Voyager data, supplies the starting point. Matching both charges with one model tests whether drift physics is captured correctly. Cosmic ray physicists use such models to read antimatter data as a probe of new physics.
arxiv-2601-07749:
Agnieszka Kaliszewska and Monika Syga classify two-dimensional curves using distances borrowed from optimal transport. Their 2026 preprint applies variants of the Wasserstein metric to curve classification. The variants let the comparison focus on chosen fragments of each curve. Discrete probability measures encode how much each fragment matters. That focus is the paper's main device.

Many curve tasks care about one section more than the rest, such as a signature stroke or a heartbeat segment. A global distance can drown that section in irrelevant differences. Weighting fragments lets the classifier attend where experts attend. The authors analyze several variants of the distance for this purpose. The work speaks to scholars in shape analysis, medical signals, and pattern recognition. It offers a principled way to compare curves in part, not just as wholes.
arxiv-2601-07849:
Giuseppe Castagnoli argues that quantum speedup has a goal led character, in a 2026 preprint on the base of physics. That word means led toward a goal. He claims quantum algorithms move toward their goal, the solution of the problem. An attractor sits in that very goal, which the algorithm will produce in the future. On this view, quantum mechanics gives the physical base for such goal led change.

The claim is philosophical as much as technical. It recasts the known speedup of quantum algorithms as future led acts. Such readings are much debated, since they touch on time and cause in quantum theory. The paper will interest readers in quantum foundations and philosophy of physics. It gives a lens for why quantum computation beats classical computation. The argument proceeds from the structure of quantum algorithms themselves. The claim is bold, and it will draw pushback.
arxiv-2601-07949:
Spencer Tamagni gives a careful study of fermion path integrals in a noncommutative instanton background. The fermions are chiral and sit on holomorphic curves in a complex space. Such instantons warp the usual instanton solutions of gauge theory. His 2026 preprint treats the path integrals with full rigor from math. The goal is to read them as instanton versions of known scattering quantities.

In detail, the integrals give analogs of matrix coefficients of monopole scattering matrices. Scattering matrices code how monopoles bend each other's paths in gauge theory. Such an analog would extend that picture to a new class of backgrounds. Such bridges help geometers and physicists translate results between fields. The paper serves scholars in geometry and theoretical physics. It is a technical work, building a dictionary rather than reporting an experiment. No lab test sits at its heart; the gain is a clean map between two hard fields.
arxiv-2601-08149: Chaoqun Fei and four co-authors learn graph structures from data through resistance curvature flow. Their 2026 arXiv paper sits in geometric representation learning, which fits graph structures to high-dimensional data. The field rests on the manifold hypothesis, that data lie near a low-dimensional curved surface. Static graphs built from Euclidean distance often miss the manifold's true curvature. The authors use a dynamic flow based on resistance curvature to reshape the graph. Better graphs could improve learning on data where shape, not raw distance, carries the signal.
arxiv-2601-08849:
Manas Khatore and four co-authors test how foes can game an AI grader. The grader reads a free text reply and checks it next to a right reply. Such checks scale well and match human marks in fair play. But a sly user can pad a reply with long words, repeat key terms, or guess in a bold style to lift the score.

The team tries such tricks and tracks how marks move when the true worth of a reply stays the same. Tricks that work show a flaw in the grader, not skill in the user. A reader who uses AI checks gets a list of weak points. It helps them build checks that prize true right replies, not slick text.
arxiv-2601-08949:
Laurence Boxer writes a fix note on a fix note, and finds the fix note flawed. The first work was by S.-E. Han, on cover spaces in digital shape work. Digital shape work deals with shapes made of grid points, not smooth lines. Han aimed to mend past slips in that field with his note.

Boxer says the mend has slips of its own. Some math steps are wrong, and some cites are used in a poor way. He lists the flaws one by one so the record is clear. A reader in digital shape work gets a guard post. Claims in the Han note should not be used till they are checked with care.
arxiv-2601-09049:
Kaiyu He and four co-authors ask if slow, deep learn in a small net is worth its cost. Some nets learn a task fast by rote. A few keep train for long past that point, then snap to a true rule. That snap is called grokking. Past work says grokked nets build a shared circuit for two step thought, a known weak spot for chat models.

The team tests if a grokked net beats a plain net on new tasks. They pull the circuit out and check if it moves to fresh work. A reader who trains nets gets a cost call. Long grok train is dear, so its gain must be real and must move.
arxiv-2601-09949:
Griffin Kearney tackles a clash in how machines read time based data. Many nets work on tokens, which are short fixed chunks. But real world signs are smooth flows, seen through noise. Chunks cut from raw values can break when noise is high.

Kearney gives a new way to cut tokens from the flow. The cuts come from a fit step, not from fixed rules. Each token tracks a span of the smooth path. The goal is a token set that holds up in noise. It should also suit tasks where a wrong call costs more than a pass, so the model may best hold back.
arxiv-2601-10449:
Clémentine Grethen and co authors learn how the moon bounces light, from its shape. How a surface bounces light is named its BRDF. The moon's dust has a rich bounce that shifts by place. Past moon maps use a plain bounce for all spots. Their terms are hard to set and miss local shifts.

The team learn the bounce from shape facts. Shape comes from maps of the moon's heights. The learned bounce can then shade each spot as it is. That gives truer shots for craft that land by sight. It also aids maps that read the moon from its hues.
arxiv-2601-10649:
Darshan Singh and co-authors present CURVE, a benchmark for video reasoning across cultures and languages. Video models have made fast progress on long clips. Yet most tests lean on western content and English text. That skew can hide weak spots when models face other cultures or tongues.

CURVE stands for Cultural Understanding and Reasoning in Video Evaluation. It tests models on long videos drawn from many cultures, with questions in many languages. Scores on it show whether a model truly grasps scenes beyond its home turf. The benchmark gives builders a fairer way to measure progress in global video understanding.
arxiv-2601-10849:
Cuong Le, Symeon Chatzinotas, and Thang X. Vu study drone teams that gather data from remote sensors. Several unmanned aerial vehicles must plan paths and share bandwidth to be energy-efficient. A catch sets this work apart: the drones cannot act in sync. In real deployments, action synchronization across all UAVs is impossible.

The authors build an asynchronous multiagent learning framework for the joint task. Paths and bandwidth are tuned together, since a drone far from its peers needs both time and channel space. Asynchrony matches how real fleets behave, with each craft on its own clock. The results target data collection for farms, disasters, and remote sites where power is precious.
arxiv-2601-11049:
Stephen Pilli and Vivek Nallur test whether language models can predict biased human decisions in conversation. People fall for classic cognitive biases, and the load on their minds can change the effect. The authors ran a pre-registered study with 1,648 participants. Each person completed six classic decision tasks through a chatbot, with dialogues of varying complexity.

The question is twofold: do model predictions capture the biases, and do they capture how the biases shift under cognitive load? Complexity of talk acts as that load here. A model that tracks both could help design chatbots that warn users at risky moments. The work links behavioral science with the evaluation of conversational AI.
arxiv-2601-11149:
Lei Xie, Hengtao He, and Jun Tong quantify sensing power in integrated sensing and communication signals. ISAC systems use one waveform to talk and to sense. Their signals mix deterministic pilots with random data payloads. Past work mostly treated purely random or purely deterministic waveforms. Real signals are a blend, and the blend changes what sensing can extract.

The authors measure the sensing mutual information of such mixed signals. Mutual information caps how much a receiver can learn about the scene. Pilots are known in advance and help sensing; payloads are random but still bounce off targets. The results guide 6G designers who must split one signal between two jobs.
arxiv-2601-11449:
Jeff Maki, Lidia Stocker, and Oded Zilberberg seek Kondo physics in atom chains. Their 2026 preprint uses ytterbium atoms with spin impurities. The Kondo effect is a classic of strongly correlated physics. A magnetic impurity locks into a many-body singlet with its host.
