Cold ytterbium gases are a proposed ideal stage for it. Unlike states of the atom can play impurity and host. But a wrinkle stands in the way of that plan. The impurity interacts through both magnetic and potential scattering. The team maps a pathway past that dual coupling. Chains of atoms with repulsive impurities are the test bed. Their route could let labs build the Kondo effect on demand.
arxiv-2601-11749:
Anil Khachi, Shikha Awasthi, Tarachand Verma, and Ranjana Joshi build wave forms for a pair of alpha parts. Alpha parts are the cores of helium atoms. When two such parts scatter, their wave form tells how they act on each other.

The team use the phase function method, a math route to such waves. They state that this is the first use of the method to build these waves in a direct way. Their inputs come from fits to past phase shift data. The result gives a clear tool for work on alpha-alpha scattering.
arxiv-2601-11849:
Jarrod C. Lewis, Steven D. Conradson, Jacek Wasik, and their co-authors probe how extra oxygen changes uranium oxide films. They grow thin, single crystal films by DC magnetron sputtering. Heat steps after growth tune the oxygen level in a set range.

They then check the local sites round uranium atoms in the film. Small shifts in those sites can change how the film acts. Such films model nuclear fuel at a clean, small scale. The work links oxygen dose to local form with care.  That local view helps explain how the film may act in use.
arxiv-2601-11949:
Asim K. Dey builds a risk tool for home insurance in a time of more wild weather. Storms, floods, and long rain spells now hit more homes. Claims tied to such events are rising, so firms need sound views of future risk.

His frame joins deep learning with copula models. Copulas track how risks move as one, such as flood and wind in one storm. Deep nets can spot complex traits in claim and weather data. The pair could price risk with more care as the climate shifts.  A clear gauge of doubt helps staff trust the risk calls.
arxiv-2601-12049: Chenchen Zhao, Muxi Chen, and Qiang Xu explain visual model calls with logic, with no need to open the model. Clear grounds matter most in high-stakes use. Past tools need white-box access, or lack strict counts of how much each trait drove the call. Their frame, called FocaLogic in the work, turns model acts into logic forms. It can work on any model from the outside. It also counts the weight of each part in firm terms.
arxiv-2601-13249:
June Huh gives survey notes on a rich class of sums called volume polynomials. Such sums are marked by a bend rule, log concavity, that gives them strong traits. Huh tours the open tasks of how such sums can be built from real shape data.

He also sets out the core bounds that such sums obey. He then shows how they play in the study of algebraic matroids, a bridge of combinatorics and algebra. The notes rest on talks given at a 2025 summer school in algebraic geometry at Colorado State. For maths readers, the piece is a guide by a lead voice to a class that links shape, sums, and counts.
arxiv-2601-13349:
Leonardo Teixeira Viotti and co-authors map where care for wild land best blocks disease jumps to folks. Ills born in wildlife cost lives and vast sums each year. A jump, called spillover, takes place where folks, farm stock, and wild hosts meet. Both land traits and life webs shape that risk.

The team ranks land by how much a guard there cuts jump risk. Such a rank lets scarce funds go where they block most risk. It joins maps of hosts, stock, and folks with the land traits that drive meets. For health and land teams, the map is a joint plan, not two plans that clash.
arxiv-2601-13649:
Xiaolin Zhou and co-authors test whether AI judges favor some languages over others in 2026. In LLM-as-a-judge setups, a model grades text quality for a given task. Past work shows such judges can be biased by traits of the text. Those biases may not match what human readers prefer.

The team asks if fluency, smooth and easy prose, can crowd out fairness. A judge might rate slick text high and plain text low for the wrong reasons. Their study probes language bias in pair-wise judging, where two texts face off. Clear proof of bias would push for fairer ways to grade with models.
arxiv-2601-13749:
Benaya Trabelsi, Jonathan Shaki, and Sarit Kraus test if large language models favor AI itself in 2026. These models now aid choices in many fields, from hiring to health. A bias toward AI could skew those choices in a hidden way. The team checks for a systematic pro-AI bias in model outputs.

They ran three complementary experiments to probe the tilt. Across them, they found consistent evidence of pro-AI bias. A model that boosts its own kind could mislead users who trust its neutral tone. Naming the bias is a step toward checks that keep it in line.
arxiv-2601-14449:
Patrycja Potępa reports for the ATLAS Collaboration in this 2026 paper. The topic is top-quark pair production in heavy-ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Top quarks are the heaviest known elementary particles. Making pairs of them in heavy-ion collisions gives a unique probe. It can test nuclear parton distribution functions, the maps of quarks and gluons inside nuclei.

Such collisions also let physicists study the time evolution of strongly interacting matter, including the quark-gluon plasma. The work presents the observation and measurement of top-quark pairs in two systems. They are proton-lead and lead-lead collisions, both recorded by the ATLAS experiment.
arxiv-2601-14549:
Nilesh Prasad Pandey and four co-authors design edge AI hardware in this 2026 paper. Deploying small language models on edge platforms is critical for real-time, privacy-sensitive generative AI. Edge devices face tight memory, latency, and energy budgets. Quantization reduces model size and cost, but it suffers from device noise in emerging non-volatile memories.

Conventional memory hierarchies further limit efficiency. The team's system, QMC, co-designs outlier-aware quantization with emergent memories. Outlier-aware means the number format protects the few extreme values that matter most. Readers get a joint design of model format and memory hardware for small models that must run well on the device itself.
arxiv-2601-14749:
Menglong Zhao and five co-authors report a discovery about tokamak divertors in this 2026 paper. The divertor is the exhaust region of a tokamak, where hot plasma is guided to target plates. Detachment, a cooled state at the target, protects those plates. The team reports the trigger for detachment bifurcation, found through steady-state and time-dependent UEDGE simulations.

The team saw an electron temperature cliff at the outer target in DIII-D H-mode plasmas. The ion drift there runs into the active divertor. They trace the cliff to a bifurcation-induced temperature drop above the X-point. In plain terms, the sudden cooling starts higher up than the plate itself. Readers get the mechanism behind a key protection state for fusion reactors.
arxiv-2601-14949:
Leqi Zheng, Jiajun Zhang, and a large team ask a plain question: what should a scholar cite? Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the flood of new work on the web. Each year brings more papers, and finding the right prior work gets harder.

Citation prediction aims to suggest apt references on its own. The team builds a benchmark for this task based on retrieval-augmented generation. The benchmark tests how well a system can pick the sources a paper needs. It is meant to help scholars steer through the growing literature.
arxiv-2601-15049:
Isaac Baglin, Xiatian Zhu, and Simon Hadfield test how private data can leak from shared model updates. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with federated learning, where many devices train one model together. In a deep leakage attack, a foe rebuilds a client's raw data from its updates.

Past attack methods can be unstable or blurry. They also fare poorly under realistic settings. The authors pair the attack with a generative flow matching denoiser. The denoiser cleans the rebuilt data, which tests just how strong and how sharp such leaks can get.
arxiv-2601-15549:
Ryo Fujii, Hideo Saito, and Ryo Hachiuma teach video models with very few labels in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their method is called VIOLA. Multimodal large language models need to adapt to new video domains for real use. Labeled data in those domains is scarce. In-context learning offers a training-free path to adapt. Standard versions still need large pools of annotated examples.

Large label pools are out of reach in many settings. Industrial and surgical video, for instance, needs expert annotators. VIOLA aims at video in-context learning with minimal annotations, per the title. The goal is to pick and use a small set of examples well. If that works, specialist teams can adapt big models without big labeling budgets.
arxiv-2601-15649:
Weihu Ma and Yu-Gang Ma quantize spacetime structure through scaling in a 2026 arXiv paper. At the Planck scale, the smooth picture of spacetime breaks down. Quantum fluctuations suggest a microstructure beneath it. The authors build a framework that encodes those fluctuations. Their move is to promote local scale factors to fundamental variables. The metric tensor, the usual core variable, steps back.

General covariance is preserved in their setup. That symmetry is a bedrock of relativity and cannot be dropped lightly. Making scale the basic variable reframes how quantum spacetime might work. If scale fluctuates first, geometry follows from it. The paper is theoretical and aimed at quantum gravity readers. It offers a language for structure at scales no experiment can yet reach.
arxiv-2601-15749:
Hiroshi Okada and Yoshihiro Shigekami build a neutrino mass model in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neutrinos have tiny masses that the Standard Model does not explain. Their model generates those masses at two loops, in a rainbow pattern. The mechanism uses a non-invertible symmetry. It comes from gauging a Z6 symmetry down to Z2. Such symmetries are a recent frontier in particle theory.

The model adds several new particles. It introduces three families of vector-like fermions with isospin doublet form. It adds heavy right-handed neutrinos. It also adds bosons in doublet and singlet forms. Each piece plays a role in the mass pattern. For theorists, the paper tests whether exotic symmetry can do concrete work in a classic problem.
arxiv-2601-15849:
Tsung-Hsiang Chou, Chen-Jui Yu, Shui-Hsiang Hsu, and Yao-Chung Fan improve table search in a 2026 arXiv paper. General embedding models do well at text retrieval. Tables are harder for them. Structured content leads to semantic compression and query-table mismatch. Recent methods generate synthetic queries with language models to help. They often pick partial tables by heuristic, though. They also rarely use the synthetic queries as training supervision.

Their framework is CGPT, built on cluster-guided partial tables. The partial views are chosen by clustering, not guesswork. LLM-generated supervision then improves the embedding model itself. Table retrieval matters wherever data live in spreadsheets and reports. Better matching between questions and tables saves analysts real time.
arxiv-2601-15949:
Yiran Wang and a large team map Mars with language in a 2026 arXiv paper. Planetary scientists think in high-level concepts and words. Orbital image archives, though, are organized at the pixel level. That mismatch limits open-ended exploration of planetary surfaces. Archives are vast, and pixel search cannot answer concept questions. Their framework is MarScope. It enables natural-language-driven, label-free mapping of Martian landforms at planetary scale.

A vision-language framework bridges words and pixels. Users can ask for landform types in plain terms. No hand labels are needed for each new concept. That opens the archive to faster, broader study. Mars science has more images than humans can inspect. Tools that search by meaning multiply what scientists can learn from them.
arxiv-2601-16049:
Niels Sorgenfrei and a large team track how a key layer in a photon sensor wears out. Their 2026 preprint deals with Low Gain Avalanche Diodes, built for use in high energy tests. Blast of rays harms the gain layer and cuts sensor life. No one yet knows the harm at the flaw level. Past tests used stuff with far less charge than real sensors.

The team sets out to close that gap with new tests. They probe the gain layer as rays break it down step by step. Clear flaw level proof would guide how to build tougher sensors. It would also help teams guess sensor life in hard ray fields. The work serves groups who build tools for big test halls.
arxiv-2601-16349:
Gopinadh and coauthors test for place bias in large language models. Their 2026 preprint deals with fair acts of such models. Place bias means a model treats folk or facts by place in a slanted way. Slants can stem from the text hoards the model learned from. The team probes model replies for place tied slants.

Probes span prompts that vary place cues in set ways. Slants found in replies mark where guards are needed. Fair tools must serve users of all places with same care. The study gives a check list for place bias in new models. It comes from a team based in Andhra Pradesh, India.
arxiv-2601-16549:
Meet Raval, Tejul Pandit and Dhvani Upadhyay weigh ML and base models for med sorts. Their 2026 preprint deals with sorts that join pics and text. New vision and language tools open fresh paths for such sorts. Past tests oft span few sets or one data type. A fair test must span both text and pic sets at once.

The team runs one strict test on four open med sets. Sets span both types and both two class and more class sorts. Joint scores show where each tool type leads or lags. That map guides teams to the right tool per task. The work is a shared bench for med sorts.
arxiv-2601-16649:
Amin Rakhsha and a team at Qualcomm AI Research study AI agents that act over long spans. Large language models do well on short, single tasks. They still fail on jobs that run through many turns. Such jobs need plans, memory of state, and long text in mind. The team's 2026 preprint probes why these jobs stay hard.

The study asks which skill counts most for success. It weighs the worth of plans, state tracking, and long context use. The aim is to learn where gains will help most. That guide can shape how labs train the next agents. It also helps buyers judge what agents can truly do.
arxiv-2601-16749:
Pedro Picchetti builds a clean frame for cause work in two hard trial types. Some trials give each unit a mix of more than one cure. Others track the same units through time in steps. In both, some units skip their set cure. Their 2026 preprint sets out cause marks for such trials as fixed pools.

Fixed-pool marks treat the test crowd as the whole world. No vast unseen crowd sits in the back. The marks gauge how cure chains stack up. Which chain works best is the core ask. Clean marks help drug and policy trials read right. They curb claims that reach past the test crowd.
arxiv-2601-17049:
Christina Garcia and a team of six co-authors sum a contest on spot-the-odd-act tools. The contest ran at ISAS 2025 with pose data as its base. Pose data tracks body joints with no face shots. Care homes for folks with growth traits need such tools. Odd acts there can flag harm or pain fast. Their 2026 preprint sums how teams fared on the task.

Teams had to split plain acts from odd ones. Plain acts span meals, play, and rest moves. No-touch pose reads guard the privacy of those in care. Contest sums show what works and what fails. Homes gain a guide to tools that truly help.
arxiv-2601-17549:
Narek Maloyan and Dmitry Namiot give the first formal security analysis of the Model Context Protocol. MCP is now a common standard. It links language models to outside tools. No one had checked its design for flaws in a rigorous way. The authors find three protocol-level vulnerabilities. They call them fundamental, tied to the design itself.

Design flaws are worse than code bugs. Every tool built on the spec may share them. Prompt injection is a key concern in the study. Tool-linked models act on files and apps, so stakes are high. The analysis gives vendors a fix list. It also warns users to guard MCP links today.
arxiv-2601-17649:
Xiaoli Han and Yang Wen prove that weakly stable Yang-Mills fields cannot exist near the round sphere metric. Yang-Mills fields model gauge forces in physics and geometry. Weak stability is a mild calm trait for such fields. The authors look at the Euclidean sphere in five or more dimensions. Near its usual metric, in the C2 topology, no nontrivial weakly stable connections exist for any nearby metric.

A nonexistence result is a strong guide. It tells geometers not to hunt where nothing lives. It also sharpens what makes the sphere special. Stability questions drive much of gauge theory. This proof trims the search space in a clean way. Nearby metrics inherit the ban, which adds force.
arxiv-2601-17749:
Kyriakos Stylianopoulos and co-authors build over-the-air extreme learning machines with metasurfaces. Goal-oriented communication sends data for a task, not for its own sake. Inference can run right in the physical layer of MIMO systems. That in-air computing faces hard practical challenges. Their design uses nonlinear cascaded metasurfaces with extra-large reception.

Metasurfaces shape radio waves as they pass. Cascades can act like layers of a neural network. If inference rides the wave itself, delay and energy can drop. The work joins antenna design with machine learning. It points to radios that compute while they listen. Such fusion could serve dense 6G networks.
arxiv-2601-17949: Wenjie Fang studies a new statistic on Dyck paths called 0pt. His 2026 preprint places the statistic among the q,t-Catalan statistics, a family tied to counting path shapes. The 0pt statistic was proposed by Pappe, Paul, and Schilling in 2022. It was shown to share its joint distribution with the well-known area statistic. Fang extends the study to Łukasiewicz paths, a broader class of lattice paths.
arxiv-2601-18149:
Tomokazu Kiyota and a large team catalog faint dusty galaxies with the JWST telescope. Their 2026 preprint reports a spectroscopic census in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field. The targets are sources first seen at one millimeter by the ALMA telescope under deep survey programs. The team took rest-frame optical spectra of a flux-limited sample with JWST's NIRSpec instrument. Such spectra reveal star birth, gas state, and black hole activity in galaxies too faint for older tools.

A census ties the dusty, far-off population into the wider story of galaxy growth. Many of these galaxies hide behind dust that blocks normal light. Pairing ALMA's finds with JWST's spectra opens them up. The sample sets a base for studies of early, hidden star formation.
arxiv-2601-18349:
Piotr Bacik and Anton Varonka take on two linked asks in the maths of change and reach. The first ask is old: start with a point, apply a fixed rule again and again, and ask if the path ever hits a set mark. When the mark is one point, past work showed the ask can be solved, and fast. Later work stretched that proof to wider marks.

The pair look at a harder form in which the space is cut by a rule at the same time. They also take on a twin ask about paths that must hit more than one mark in step. These asks sit at the base of checks on code and on plans that must be safe. A firm yes or no here helps prove that a design can or cannot reach a bad state.
arxiv-2601-18449:
Mrinmoy Basak and three colleagues set up a fresh frame to study a classic toy world of quantum fields. The toy world has one space dim and one kind of field that pulls on it-self. Staff have long used it to test tricks that fail on the full world of bits and force. The team build the frame from small wave bits that live in push space, not in plain space.

Each wave bit is tagged by how fine it is and by where it sits. That double tag gives a built-in way to trim both the fine end and the broad end of the field. A trim that maths can trust is key for work that skips small-step tricks. The frame could let teams study strong pulls with less guess work. It may also serve as a test bed for new quantum kit.
arxiv-2601-18549:
Elvise Berchio and three colleagues study how heat-like spread runs on webs that go on for ever. The webs are sets of points with links, like road nets or power grids stretched with no end. On such a web, a value at each point can spread to its linked points and can grow or fade by a rule that leans on the value it-self. The team take on two kinds of rule.

One kind of rule is tame in a set way, and the next is tame in a rate way. For both, they prove that a start state leads to one sound path, and they chart how smooth that path is. The start can be quite rough and still give a good path. Such proofs back the use of web maths for heat, crowds, and spread on huge nets.
arxiv-2601-18749:
Haruhiko Yoshioka and six colleagues study what makes a code change count, for both human hands and smart agents. Code hosts now fill with change asks made by agents. Those asks are fast and cheap to make, but they are merged at a lower rate than asks by human hands. The team ask why, in a large study of past asks from a shared data set.

Their set holds tens of thousands of asks, by both kinds of maker. They weigh traits such as size, tests, and the words that go with each ask. Traits that track with a merge for one kind may not track for the next. A clear map could help agent teams write asks that land. It could also help hosts set fair bars for all makers.
arxiv-2601-18949:
Cole Granger and three co-authors build a test set where human bugs and model bugs mix. Large language models now help write code, but they add sly logic slips that differ from the slips people make. To study how the two kinds of error play off each other, the team made a hybrid set.

The new set, Tricky squared, grows an older corpus of human written defects. Two large models then inject fresh errors into code in three languages. The mix lets researchers see when model bugs hide near human ones, and when each kind is caught or missed by checks.
arxiv-2601-19249:
Xingkun Yin and Hongyang Du check the memories of language model agents against a changing world. Memory boosted models store notes to guide later acts. Most systems assume those notes can be validated, either by outside scores tied to one task or by the model's own reflection.

In live settings with drifting facts, both assumptions often break. Their verifier, GLOVE, realigns stored memory with the environment as it now stands. Stale memory is a quiet failure mode for agents: they act with confidence on facts that used to be true.
arxiv-2601-19449:
Celia Rubio-Madrigal and Rebekka Burkholz show that fixed features can match graph neural networks at their own game. Graph networks are prized for learning how to pool each node's neighborhood. The team challenges that belief with fixed aggregation features: set summaries of a neighborhood that need no training at all.

Their approach turns graph tasks into table tasks, where classic classifiers take over. The gains are strong interpretability and free choice of classifier. If much of a graph network's power sits in the features, simpler and clearer tools may serve many graph jobs just as well.
arxiv-2601-19549:
Fengling Li, Andrei Vesnin, and Xuan Yang work in knotoid theory, a young branch of knot theory. Knotoids are like knots drawn with open ends, a generalisation proposed by Turaev in 2012. Researchers have since built many ways to measure and classify them. This paper focuses on how hard a knotoid is to undo.

The measure is the unknotting number: the fewest unknotting moves needed to simplify the knotoid fully. The authors study this count for a class called plus-welded knotoids. Knowing the count tells us how tangled an object truly is, beyond how tangled it looks. Such numbers are basic data for any classification effort. The work adds to the slow build of knotoid theory's core tables.
arxiv-2601-19849:
Haya Alyoussef and five colleagues build a vision transformer that lives in curved space. Much real data is hierarchical: images, text, and graphs all contain tree-like structure. Flat Euclidean geometry represents such structure poorly. Hyperbolic geometry, which expands exponentially, fits trees naturally.

Their model, HexFormer, is a hyperbolic vision transformer for image classification. Its key novelty is aggregation using the exponential map inside the attention mechanism. Attention decides which parts of an image inform each other. Doing that step in hyperbolic space should respect hierarchical relations among features. The work tests whether curved geometry earns its keep on vision benchmarks. The tests are plain image tasks. They sort cats, cars, and the like into groups. The scores show how well it works.
arxiv-2601-19949:
A speech corpus paper tackles a long-standing comparison problem in reverberant speech research. Echoey rooms distort recordings and challenge recognition systems. Comparing methods across studies is hard because most corpora lack per-file acoustic annotations. Documentation for reproducing results is often thin as well.

The new corpus, RIR-Mega-Speech, pairs speech with rich acoustic metadata. It was built by convolving LibriSpeech recordings with thousands of simulated room impulse responses from a companion collection. The result is over a hundred hours of reverberant speech with known room properties. Every file's acoustics are documented, and the evaluation is reproducible. Such a corpus lets researchers isolate what really helps in echoey conditions. Each file comes with notes on the room that made it. That is rare in this field. It makes fair tests much more easy to run.
arxiv-2601-20049: A methods paper presents a new data assimilation scheme built for ice and snow science. Particle-based assimilation tracks many candidate states and weights them by fit to data, but the method can collapse onto a few states. The new scheme is an adaptive particle batch smoother that draws on recent advances in importance sampling to resist that collapse. Though built for cryospheric problems, it applies directly to land surface and hydrological assimilation, and to geoscience inference more broadly.
arxiv-2601-20349:
A. A. Saharian and three colleagues study topological defects in higher-dimensional cosmological backgrounds. These backgrounds are described by a set of angle deficit parameters. As special cases, the defects include higher-dimensional versions of cosmic strings and global monopoles, flaws in spacetime that may have formed in the early universe.

The authors present the complete set of mode functions for a massive scalar field in these settings. The field has a general coupling to curvature. Mode functions are the building blocks for computing quantum effects near the defects, such as vacuum energy. With them, researchers test how quantum fields behave in curved space.
arxiv-2601-20449:
Fatima Ezzeddine, Obaida Ammar, Silvia Giordano, and Omran Ayoub study fairness in counterfactual explanations of machine learning decisions. Such explanations tell a user which changes to their inputs would flip a model's decision, offering a path to recourse. They hold a pivotal place among explanation tools because they point to action.

The authors aim to ensure fairness at both the individual and group levels. Recourse that is cheap for one group and costly for another quietly bakes bias into the system. Their work matters for lending, hiring, and other fields where a denied applicant deserves a fair route back.
arxiv-2601-20549:
Wies Claeys and ten colleagues compare radionuclide calibrators and SPECT/CT protocols for quantitative imaging of lutetium-177 across multiple centers. Therapies based on this isotope now succeed against neuroendocrine tumors and prostate cancer. Accurate measurement of the dose is a first need for correct treatment delivery and dosimetry.

Yet a lack of standardization introduces variability between systems, which can compromise multi-center clinical trials. The authors compare how centers measure and image the same isotope. Harmonized protocols would let hospitals pool results and give patients doses that mean the same thing everywhere. Each site was checked in the same way, so the gaps that show up are real gaps, not quirks of one lab.
arxiv-2601-20749:
Tawfiq Ammari and three co-authors study how students learn to work with AI in daily life. Their 2026 paper asks how AI literacy grows through practice, not formal lessons. The team analyzed more than ten thousand ChatGPT messages. The messages came from thirty-six undergraduates over one academic year. That long view shows real habits, not lab behavior.

The authors find five genres of use in the chats. Students used the tool as an academic workhorse and as an emotional companion. They also used it as a partner for thinking, for repair and negotiation, and for calibrating trust. Each genre is a distinct way students learn to work with AI. The study gives teachers a grounded picture of skills students build on their own.
arxiv-2601-20849:
Yapeng Zhang and a large team measure fierce winds on a scorching giant planet. Their 2026 paper studies KELT-9 b, an ultra-hot Jupiter. Fine spectroscopy can probe the air of such a planet. It reads Doppler shifts in the planet's signal. Those shifts change as the planet moves through its orbit. The team used the Keck Planet Finder.

The study is a pilot run on phase curve spectra. A phase curve tracks the planet across its full orbit. The emerging dayside is where night turns to day. Winds there can reach extreme speeds. Measuring them tests models of air flow on worlds with huge day-night gaps. The work shows what the new tool can do.
arxiv-2601-21149:
Maria Despoina Siampou and four co-authors teach a model both what a place is and how it is used. Their 2026 paper learns embeddings for points of interest from human movement. Such models need general-purpose pictures of real places. Points of interest, where activity piles up, matter most. Old approaches lean on static text about place identity. Or they tie the picture to paths, which capture movement habits. Neither captures a place's function well.

Movement data can reveal function at once. A site busy at dawn differs from one busy at night. Visit rhythms show if a place serves work, food, or rest. The authors embed that usage in the model. Their model knows a cafe from an office by rhythm, not just by name. Such embeddings can power maps, tips, and city planning.
arxiv-2601-21249:
Enzo Nicolás Spotorno and Antônio Augusto Medeiros Fröhlich argue that big unified models are a risky fit for safety-critical physical systems. Foundation models now handle time series and physical change well in smooth, slow settings. Real systems, though, shift over their life cycle and must meet strict reliability demands.

The authors make a position case for a modular design instead. Separate parts hold their own state, and that state can be checked and certified. A single large model must stay flexible yet stable, and the paper calls that tension the core problem. Modularity, they argue, is how both needs can be met at once.
arxiv-2601-21749:
Laurent R. Bergé, Kyle Butts, and Grant McDermott present fixest, an R package for fast econometric estimation. The package covers a wide toolkit for applied researchers. Its strength is fixed-effects estimation, a workhorse for panel data across economics and policy work.

A new fixed-point acceleration algorithm, written in a fast compiled language, drives the speed. It converges quickly across many data settings and handles complex models, even ones with varying slopes. Fast estimation changes what researchers can try in a day. Models that once ran overnight become interactive, which invites more careful checking of results.
arxiv-2601-21949:
Christian Schröder and co-authors watch a molecule vibrate in step right after its bond breaks. When methyl iodide absorbs ultraviolet light, it splits and releases a methyl radical. That radical comes out excited in its umbrella mode, a flapping motion where the hydrogens swing through the carbon's plane.

The team reports observing these vibrations staying coherent, moving together in phase, after the break. They probe the motion with femtosecond spectroscopy, which snapshots events lasting millionths of a billionth of a second. Their 2026 preprint shows that a violent break does not always scramble molecular motion. That matters for photochemistry, where coherent motion can steer which products a reaction forms.
arxiv-2601-22149:
Hang Ding and co-authors train web agents inside a model of the web instead of the web itself. Autonomous agents powered by language models and reinforcement learning promise general-purpose assistance online. Training them on the live internet is inefficient, costly, and risky, since real sites change, charge, and sometimes bite back.

Their 2026 preprint, DynaWeb, applies model-based reinforcement learning to web agents. The agent learns a world model of web dynamics and practices inside it, reserving real browsing for what matters. Model-based practice has transformed game and robot learning. Bringing it to the web could produce agents that are both more capable and far cheaper to train.
arxiv-2601-22249:
Ruiyi Zhang and four co-authors tackle a weak spot in code written by large language models. Their 2026 preprint notes that these models still fail often on hard coding tasks. They build on an idea that worked well for math: score each step, then pick the best full try.

Their method, FunPRM, treats each function as one step to be scored. A fix step then cleans up flaws in those scores. The goal is to lift the odds that the picked code is right. The work speaks to teams that rely on model-written code.
arxiv-2601-22349:
Andreas Habring and Martin Zach prove how fast a class of samplers settles to its target. Samplers draw fair samples from a spread; many use drifts that shift over time, set by cooling plans. Their 2026 preprint gives a joint, non-asymptotic account of these Langevin diffusions and their step-wise forms.

They measure the gap with forward KL divergence, a standard odds-based yardstick. Firm rates tell users how long to run a sampler for a set trust level. They also show which cooling plans help or hurt. The work backs tools used across stats and physics.
arxiv-2601-22449:
Tristan Shah and Stas Tiomkin reframe what drives an agent to act when no outside goal is set. Intrinsic motivation lets agents explore and learn on their own. Their 2026 preprint notes that most theory rests on information flow between picked variables, a choice left to the designer.

They propose a view based on information production, not transmission. The shift aims to free the drive from hand-picked variables. A cleaner base could yield agents that explore in richer, less biased ways. That matters for robots and game agents alike. The work is theory, with design in view.
arxiv-2601-22549:
Mu-Yang Wang and four co-authors study chaos in a particle trapped near the edge of a charged, magnetized black hole. Their 2026 preprint uses the dyonic AdS-Reissner-Nordström hole, set in anti-de Sitter space. A light probe particle sits in a harmonic trap just off the horizon.

Three dials — the particle's energy, a chemical term, and the field — tune how wild the motion gets. The team map where order gives way to chaos. Such maps test deep links between black holes and chaos theory. They may also hint at quantum signatures of chaos.
arxiv-2601-22649:
Henning Krause and Balduin Stoye count subfamilies of interval multisets, and find both known and brand-new number sequences. For any finite ordered set, multisets of its intervals form an abelian category. Their 2026 preprint gives natural combinatorial accounts of many classes of subcategories.

Counting those classes yields familiar integer sequences — and, in some cases, sequences never seen before. The count problem leads to a universal category of poset representations. New sequences are a small thrill in pure math. The work ties counting to deep structure. It gives peers a rich new playground.
arxiv-2601-22749:
Riki Matsui, Shigeo Kimura, Kohta Murase, and B. Theodore Zhang predict the light that follows a gamma-ray burst across many bands. Gamma-ray bursts are the most extreme flashes known, yet their jets stay poorly understood. Their 2026 preprint focuses on X-ray flares and extended emission, which glow hundreds of seconds after the main burst.

They forecast what those phases should emit from radio to high energy. Matching forecasts to real sky data can reveal the jet's makeup. The work gives observers a checklist for the next bright burst. It ties theory to telescope time.
arxiv-2601-22849:
Christian Dietz and four co-authors plan how robots can put parts together with care. Assembly planning has long leaned on learning methods and random sampling, both hungry for simulation time. Their approach uses optimal control that accounts for contact between parts.

The method uses exact second-order derivative data, which sharply cuts the number of simulation steps needed. It also stays robust, so plans hold up when the real world differs a little. Sample-efficient planning could make factory robots faster to program for new products. Contact-implicit planning treats contact forces as part of the optimization itself, rather than as an afterthought added later.
arxiv-2601-23249:
Hongyu Cheng and Amitabh Basu examine the theory gaps in learning to guide branch-and-cut solvers. Branch-and-cut is the workhorse method for mixed-integer linear programming. Machine learning now guides its choices, like which variable to branch on or which cuts to add.

Many approaches train on local signals from lookahead rules, then judge success by local score accuracy. The authors argue that local accuracy may not predict whole-solver performance. Their critique pushes the field toward training goals tied to end-to-end solving speed. Local score accuracy is the metric under critique, because a policy can score well locally while slowing the whole solver.
arxiv-2603-01449:
Restoring a clean image from an MRI scan often uses models that mix facts from across the whole picture. Xiangjian Hou, Chao Qin, Chang Ni, and colleagues ask in 2026 when that wide mixing truly helps. MRI jobs differ a lot, so a design that helps one job may add little to the next.

The group built a fair test bed with a small local model and a wider variant beside top global models. For fast scans and for sharper images, the small local model held its own against global rivals. For noise removal with uneven noise, global models did best, since they can judge how trust in each spot varies. The lesson is to match the model to the scan task and its physics.
arxiv-2603-01549:
Robots that take orders in words and act on what they see often miss how the world moves when they act. Jisoo Kim, Jungbin Cho, Sanghyeok Chu, and colleagues add that missing sense in this 2026 work. Their method, Pri4R, trains vision-language-action models with extra four-dimensional facts not used at run time.

During training, a light extra head predicts how points in space will move in three dimensions. Robot features feed that head, so the shared code learns how scenes shift under actions. At run time the model reverts to its plain form, with no extra inputs or cost. Tests in simulation and on real robots show clear gains on hard handling tasks. Extra checks confirm that point-track training is what teaches the action-world link.
arxiv-2603-01649:
Alvaro Pernas and Ricardo Puebla shape single photons so quantum network nodes can swap information despite mismatched tones. Their 2026 work sits in superconducting waveguide networks, where nodes pass single light particles along guides. When nodes ring at different frequencies, direct exchange fails and the network cannot scale.

The pair derive the controls needed to shape a photon at any chosen offset from its natural tone. That shaping allows on-demand, precise exchange between nodes that do not resonate with each other. They map which control settings suit common photon shapes and which suit real lab setups. Simulations support high-fidelity transfer between distant, off-tone nodes. A simple extension of the same controls also creates remote entanglement, a linked state shared across the network.
arxiv-2603-01949:
Cristiana Diaconu, Miles Cranmer, Richard Turner, and colleagues turn fixed physics simulators into probabilistic ones without retraining. Their 2026 work starts from a gap: learned PDE simulators predict one outcome, yet many real systems are chaotic and uncertain. Training probabilistic models from scratch wastes the strong deterministic models already built.

Retrofitting fine-tunes a pre-trained model with a proper scoring rule for distributions, called CRPS. The same recipe applies across unlike backbones with minimal code changes. On single-system models, rollout scores and error measures improve by wide margins over matched deterministic tuning. A PDE foundation model retrofitted on a target data set shows the same pattern at larger scale. The result says probabilistic physics modeling can be an upgrade, not a rebuild.
arxiv-2603-02049:
Yisu Zhang, Chenjie Cao, Tengfei Wang, and colleagues link camera-guided video generation with 3D scene reconstruction. Their 2026 framework, WorldStereo, attacks a split: generated videos look great, yet rebuilding consistent 3D scenes from them fails. Camera control is loose and content shifts between viewpoints in raw generator output.

Two geometric memory modules bridge the gap inside the generation process itself. A global memory injects coarse structure through point clouds updated as generation proceeds, enabling precise camera control. A spatial-stereo memory constrains attention with 3D correspondence, so fine details stay consistent across views. The control branch design stays efficient by reusing a distilled video backbone without joint training. Benchmarks for camera-guided generation and reconstruction both favor the approach, from single and panoramic inputs alike.
arxiv-2603-02149:
Namhoon Kim, Narges Moeini, Justin Romberg, and Sara Fridovich-Keil present a cleaning method for noisy 3D scans in this 2026 paper. Many scans, from medical CT to electron imaging, suffer heavy noise. Their method, 3D Field of Junctions, fits each small block of a volume with joined wedge shapes. Wedges meet at sharp edges, so real structure is kept, not blurred.

No training data is needed, which avoids the risk of invented detail. Nearby blocks are pushed to agree, so the full volume stays coherent. Tests covered low-dose CT, electron tomography, and laser point clouds in bad weather. In each case the method beat a mix of classic and neural rivals. It can also plug into wider scan repair tasks.
arxiv-2603-03549:
Edoardo Gargiulo and Efe A Ok settle when order-preserving maps can be extended without stretching them further. Extending a Lipschitz map, one that never stretches distances by more than a fixed factor, from a subset to a whole space is a classic problem. Their 2026 paper adds two demands at once: the map must stay order-preserving, and its values live in a Hadamard poset, a curved ordered space.

In one dimension the extension always exists. In two or more dimensions, with only weak conditions on the target space, a universal extension exists exactly when the domain's order is trivial, meaning no real ordering at all. Hilbert posets satisfy the conditions, so the result covers them directly. One corollary stings: there is no order-respecting generalization of Kirszbraun's classic extension theorem.
arxiv-2603-03849:
Yao Ma computes what neutron stars are made of inside a chiral model of nuclear matter, and finds a tension worth chasing. His 2026 analysis uses an extended linear sigma model in mean-field approximation, where baryon and meson masses arise from spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking. Several couplings between mesons and nucleons steer the results, and one newcomer, the delta meson, reshapes the symmetry energy in a decisive way.

The delta produces a plateau in symmetry energy at intermediate densities. That plateau reconciles two stubborn measurements at once: the neutron skin thickness of lead-208 and the tidal deformability of a typical neutron star. An explicit symmetry-breaking term then links to the pion-nucleon sigma term. Matching astrophysical limits demands that term be negative, stiffer stars and larger maximum masses, against its positive vacuum value. The mismatch hints how model parameters must run with density.

arxiv-2605-08849: In swirling flows — think of water draining or air in a turbine — the swirl sometimes flips direction without warning. The 2026 paper is fluid-dynamics research on a phenomenon engineers would love to predict.
arxiv-2605-08949: Teaching a language model new tricks usually erases old ones — catastrophic forgetting. bronte-shirley-1849:
Charlotte Brontë published Shirley in 1849, her ambitious condition-of-England novel of the mills. The tale is set in Yorkshire against the Luddite risings of 1811 to 1812. It was the first major industrial novel by a woman in English letters of the time.

Mill owner Robert Moore brings new machines as starving weavers plot to smash them at night. Shirley Keeldar, a brisk heiress, and meek Caroline Helstone view his world from two sides. Caroline pines in a parsonage while Shirley runs her estate and teases her old tutor. A shooting, a mad dog's bite, and two weddings close the social panorama of Yorkshire. Brontë wrote it in grief, as her brother and sisters died around her.
buddhist-mahayana-texts-sbe-49:
E. B. Cowell, F. Max Muller, and J. Takakusu translated the Buddhist Mahayana Texts of 1894. The volume closed the Sacred Books of the East series as number forty-nine. Key Mahayana scriptures of the Greater Vehicle appear in English here.

The Larger and Smaller Sukhavati texts describe Amitayus and his Pure Land. The Vajracchedika, or Diamond Sutra, teaches emptiness in sharp dialogues. Other pieces include the Heart Sutra tradition's core ideas in early form. These scriptures shaped the Buddhism of China, Japan, and Tibet profoundly. Muller edited the whole Sacred Books series and contributed translations himself. The volume gives East Asian Buddhism in its own sublime words.
castro-de-iusta-haereticorum-punitione-1:
Alfonso de Castro, a Spanish Franciscan theologian, published De Iusta Haereticorum Punitione in 1549. The Latin title means on the just punishment of heretics. Castro advised Spanish rulers at a time when Spain's church courts pursued Protestant and other accused heretics.

Three books weigh what heresy is, which penalties the law allows, and how rulers and judges should act. Castro argued for firm punishment but also set limits and urged care in proof. He drew on scripture, church law, and past cases to build his rules. The work is a key source for how learned churchmen defended persecution in law, and why they thought mercy toward heresy was a public danger.

cia-0000009449:
Three American prisoners of war were sighted in An Xuyen province, an October 1972 CIA report states. An Xuyen, at South Vietnam's southern tip, was deep Viet Cong country in the Mekong Delta. Prisoners held that far south lived far from the known northern camps.

Southern sightings mattered because the Delta's camps were small, mobile, and rarely photographed. A confirmed trio added names and a place to the southern prisoner map. Officials cross-checked the report against men known missing in the south. The file shows the search reaching the map's bottom edge, where information was scarcest.
cia-0000009649:
Three American prisoners, identified with the US 25th Division, were sighted in a January 1972 report from a Cambodian place the title cuts short at Komp. The 25th Division fought in South Vietnam's III Corps region, near the Cambodian border. Prisoners taken there could be marched across that border.

Cross-border captivity hid men in sanctuaries American forces could rarely reach. A sighting naming their division gave officials a strong check against unit loss records. The report shows the war's geography spilling past Vietnam's edge. It also gives three ground soldiers a dated trace inside Cambodia's camps.
cia-0000009749:
Inside Cambodia stood a Viet Cong prisoner of war camp, described in a November 1969 CIA report. Viet Cong sanctuaries across the border held supplies, hospitals, and prisoners beyond South Vietnam's reach. American forces would strike those sanctuaries the following spring.

A camp in Cambodia proved captivity already crossed borders years before that strike. Prisoners held there vanished from both countries' open records. Reports like this one were often the only sign of their location. The file adds a Cambodian site to the prison map at an early date, when the border war was still officially secret.
cia-0000009849:
Unidentified American prisoners were observed in Sam Neua and in Hanoi in 1965, an item filed in April 1971 recalls. Sam Neua is the main town of Houa Phan province in Laos; Hanoi needs no placing. Two capitals of captivity appear in one backward-looking report.

Retrospective reports helped fill the early years, when record keeping lagged the fighting. A witness recalling 1965 in 1971 could still add faces and places to thin files. Memory fades and shifts, so analysts handled such recall with care. This file preserves it as filed, an attempt to recover the prison story's first chapter.
cia-0000012249:
Five years after the Berlin Wall split Germany, a CIA paper from January 1966 takes stock of East Germany's outlook. Walter Ulbricht's communist regime ruled the smaller German state under Soviet protection. The Wall had stopped the flood of refugees westward, and with it the regime's worst crisis.

The paper weighs the regime's stability and finds it resting on concrete and Soviet backing. It also looks at the economy and at East Berlin's drive to be treated as a real state. The study captures a workers' state that endured by force, judged coolly by the other side.
cia-0000014749: Anatoliy Antonovich Yatskov, also named Yakovlev, fills a CIA file dated July 1, 1973. The title calls him Julius Rosenberg's handler. cia-0000036849:

Inside, the story is told as Hanoi wanted foreign readers to hear it. Comparing such dispatches lets readers see how one event was shaped for export. The file adds a further layer to the record of McCain's first days in captivity. Read beside the other dispatches, it shows the same story being shaped for different audiences abroad.

The theory of scientific socialism should be developed in practice, argues an item in a CIA record dated August 1, 1988. Scientific socialism was the Soviet system's name for its ruling doctrine. By 1988 that doctrine was under strain across the socialist world.

Inside, the item defends and develops the theory in the approved terms. American analysts collected such pieces to gauge the health of Soviet thought. The file shows ideology being argued over near the system's end. Within a few years the doctrine defended here would lose its state. cia-0000132749:
January 4, 1961 was the first full day after the United States cut diplomatic ties with Cuba, and the CIA marked it with this briefing. The break, made on January 3, ended formal relations between the two governments. The paper records the island as that new reality began.

Several Cuba briefings share this date, and together they form the agency's post-break baseline: what Cuba looked like once embassies closed and confrontation stood alone. Months later came the Bay of Pigs, planned in the shadow of this rupture. The declassified text was freed years later through the CIA Reading Room.

cia-0000136149: With a date of 4 April 1954, a CIA cable in the open files deals with a request that ODACID weigh the Central American situation. cia-0000136249: The CIA cable from 5 May 1954 deals with Instruction 10 for broadcast, the series running past eight with no beats skipped, in a file now declassified. dequincey-english-mail-coach-1849:
Two of De Quincey's late essays share this small volume, first issued together in 1849. The English Mail-Coach looks back on the fast coaching age, its speed, pride, and sounding bugles. Joan of Arc, the second piece, defends the French peasant heroine with warmth and force.

The coach essay builds toward a nightmare scene: a runaway coach rushing down on a tiny carriage in the dark. The Joan essay mixes history with praise, arguing for her worth against cold accounts. Side by side, the pair show De Quincey's rare gift for turning memory and feeling into visionary prose.
