Luther Gulick, an adviser on Pauley's reparations staff, sent him this undated memorandum, filed with the July 29, 1945 papers. It gathers new evidence on Soviet removals from Berlin. Three fresh reports are listed. One covers factory removals in the Russian sector. One covers art removals from the American sector. One covers property of American citizens and neutrals.

The new material reports raw materials, scrap, and cable machinery being taken in the Russian sector, even household sewing machines. Berlin's public art collections had been stored for safety, many in the zoo flak tower. The reports say the distinctive and valuable pieces were picked out and removed.
frus-1964-68v26-d149: A 1964-1968 FRUS document from the Indonesia volume. The archipelago's turmoil. This entry preserves that record. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
gao-gaoreports-b-295449: Abt Associates filed a March 2005 double protest — two dockets — and GAO's ruling answers the pair. The research firm's twin claims faced one referee. Two filings, one verdict, fully rendered. The verdict was rendered. The pair was answered. The referee was one.
gao-gaoreports-b-297849: TVI Corporation took its April 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298349: PAI Corporation took its August 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298949: Caddell Construction Company took its January 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Builders get the same full hearing as everyone.
gao-gaoreports-b-305349: The Social Security Administration's Gallup use got a fiscal ruling in this 2006 GAO call, which tests the polling expenditure. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the survey dollars were legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-306349: A No Child Left Behind newspaper article got a fiscal ruling in this September 2005 GAO call, which tests the Education Department's paid piece. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the article was legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-307849: The pension insurer owed its number-crunchers in this March 2007 GAO ruling, which settles who reimburses the financial analysis services. The call reads the fiscal law against the bill. The ruling decides which purse pays for the watchdog's hired math.
gao-gaoreports-b-400049: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Barnesville Development Corporation. The June 30, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-249: Capital project funding could be simpler in 2005, and GAO's report says the benefits of acquisition funds could come through easier means. The review finds the shorter path. The brick-and-mortar dollars deserved the simple route. The means had to be simpler.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-349: Predatory lenders were still circling troops in 2005, and GAO's report says the Pentagon's anti-gouging tools were not fully used. The review calls out the underused shields. The young soldiers deserved the protection. The tools had to be used. The young soldiers deserved the protection.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1049: The Chesapeake Bay gateways needed better oversight in 2006, and GAO's report says the Park Service had to improve accountability for grantees. The findings demand the watch. The report warns that the bay's dollars deserved tracking. The grants had to be guarded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-149: Veterans' claims processing needed structural help in 2006, and GAO's report says changes in the field office structure could improve disability claims. The findings prescribe the reorganization. The report warns that the waiting veterans deserved faster answers. The structure had to help.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-349: The Expeditionary Fighting Vehicle hit design troubles in 2006, and GAO's report says the program faced difficulties in demonstration. The findings document the struggles. The report warns that the swimming tank needed to swim. The design had to be fixed. The swimming tank needed to swim.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-449: Tactical space capabilities needed a strategy in 2006, and GAO's report says the Pentagon needed a departmentwide approach for low-cost responsive space. The findings demand the plan. The report warns that the quick-launch eyes should not be improvised. The strategy had to be built.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-49: Military drones needed better teamwork in 2006, and GAO's report says the Pentagon had to promote interoperability and improve performance assessment. The findings demand the coordination. The report warns that the unmanned eyes should work together. The teamwork had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-649: Foster care funds needed guarding in 2006, and GAO's report says federal oversight was required to safeguard the money and ensure consistent support. The findings demand the watch. The report warns that the vulnerable kids' dollars deserved protection. The oversight had to be real.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-149: The railroad watchdogs were sharpening their aim in 2007, and GAO's report says the administration was targeting oversight better, though the impact assessment lagged. The findings balance credit and caution. The report demands proof that the smarter watch saved lives. The rails had to show results.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-49: New cures were stuck in 2007, and GAO's report says science, business, rule, and patent snags were slowing the making of new drugs. The findings map the holdups. The report warns that the future drug shelf needed new drugs fast. The cures had to flow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-549: Winning the peace needed a better plan in 2007 — GAO's report says the Pentagon's stability-ops approach and interagency teamwork wanted work. The findings target the day-after doctrine. The report's lesson from Iraq: the battle plan is only half the war.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-349: GAO published its findings on federal Real Property: Corps of Engineers Needs to Improve the Reliability of Its Real Property Disposal Data in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-49: GAO wrote this 2007 report on the Small Business Administration's Women's Business Centers — the offices that coach women starting firms. It finds the SBA could run the centers better and link its many aid programs more tightly. The core question: were tax dollars for advice and training truly reaching the women owners they were meant to lift up?
gdr-constitution-1949:
The German Democratic Republic adopted its first constitution in October 1949, founding East Germany out of the Soviet occupation zone. The text was approved days before the state itself was proclaimed, as Germany split into two rival republics. Its drafters modeled parts of it on the Weimar charter, in the hope of claiming all-German legitimacy.

On paper, the charter promises a democratic republic with free elections, basic rights, and a parliament of the people. In fact, the Socialist Unity Party, backed by Soviet power, ruled without real opposition from the start. The founding law of the workers' and peasants' state thus wore a democratic form over a Leninist reality. A new constitution in 1968 dropped the pretense and named the party's leading role outright. The 1949 text closed the founding act of socialism's forty-year German experiment.
geneva-convention-1-1949:
The first of the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 protects wounded and sick soldiers in armies on land. Nations redrafted the rules in Geneva after the Second World War, building on a line of agreements going back to 1864. The aim was to make sure that a soldier out of the fight through wounds or sickness is never treated as fair game.

The articles require armies to collect and care for the wounded of both sides, without favor. Medical staff, ambulances, and hospitals are protected, and the red cross emblem marks that protection. Attacking the wounded or those who care for them is forbidden. Nearly every nation on earth has accepted the 1949 conventions.
geneva-convention-2-1949:
The second Geneva Convention of 1949 carries the protection of the wounded to warfare at sea. It adapts the older Hague rules and the land convention to sailors, marines, and others fighting on the water. Two world wars had shown how exposed the wounded and shipwrecked were when ships went down far from help.

Under its articles, the wounded, sick, and shipwrecked at sea must be rescued and cared for by whichever side finds them. Hospital ships are protected from attack and capture, and their crews must be respected. The convention also covers coastal rescue craft and medical aircraft over the sea. Together with its three sister conventions, it forms the core of modern war law.
geneva-convention-3-1949:
Prisoners of war are the subject of the third Geneva Convention of 1949. Written after a war in which prisoners had been starved and murdered in great numbers, it sets firm limits on captors. The text builds on earlier prisoner rules from 1929 that had too often been ignored.

Captured fighters must be treated with respect, given enough food and shelter, and shielded from insults and public display. They may send and receive mail, and the Red Cross may visit their camps. Torture and medical experiments are banned outright. When the fighting ends, prisoners must be sent home without delay, a standard still cited in every modern conflict.
geneva-convention-4-1949:
Civilians in wartime gained their own full shield in the fourth Geneva Convention of 1949. Earlier war law had guarded soldiers and prisoners, while civilians in occupied lands were left with thin protection. The deportations and mass killings of the Second World War made the gap impossible to ignore.

The articles ban murder, torture, hostage-taking, and collective punishment against civilians under an army's control. Forced deportation from occupied land is forbidden, and children, the sick, and the wounded get special care. Occupying powers must keep food and medical supplies flowing to the people under their rule. The convention remains the main legal guard for civilians caught in modern wars.
german-basic-law-1949:
West Germany adopted its Basic Law in May 1949, written by a Parliamentary Council at Bonn. The drafters avoided the word constitution, since the country was divided and the law was meant to be temporary. Its lessons came straight from the Nazi years: never again a republic too weak to defend itself, never again a state above human dignity.

The text opens by declaring human dignity beyond all touch, the clause every other article serves. Power is split between the federation and the states, and the charter arms democracy against its foes, banning parties that seek to destroy it. A powerful constitutional court guards the whole design. The charter of the Federal Republic's economic and moral recovery still governs united Germany today, its temporary name now a badge of permanence.
haddock-somnolism-psycheism-1849:
Joseph Haddock lectured on mesmeric clairvoyance in Somnolism and Psycheism, first printed in 1849. His titles name the states he studies: somnolism, the mesmeric sleep, and psycheism, its mental wonders. Haddock treats clairvoyance as a subject for physiology and philosophy alike. An appendix adds mesmeric and psychical experiments of his circle.

Haddock worked in Bolton, far from London's learned societies. His book gives the movement a provincial English voice of real weight. His case reports rest on sittings with entranced subjects from his own circle. The lectures argue that the soul's powers show themselves in trance. Readers meet mesmerism as small town practice and print. The first edition holds his case entire.
hahnemann-organon-1849:
Samuel Hahnemann was a German doctor who broke with the harsh cures of his day. His Organon of Medicine lays out the scheme he called homeopathy. Charles Dudgeon's English dress of 1849 brought the work to British readers. The book is the root text of the whole school.

Like cures like, Hahnemann holds: a drug that makes a sign in health can cure that sign in the sick. He bids the doctor use the least dose that can still act. Rules for case work and drug tests fill the text. Homeopaths still treat the book as law.
hartley-observations-on-man-vol1-1749:
David Hartley, an English physician, published the first volume of Observations on Man in 1749. The title promises a study of man's frame, his duty, and his hopes. Hartley aimed at nothing less than a full science of the mind built from two simple tools: vibrations in the nerves and the association of ideas.

Volume 1 lays out the theory that all thought grows from linked sensations. Simple impressions join into complex ideas, feelings, and habits through repeated pairing. The scheme made the mind look like a machine of habit, which thrilled some readers and alarmed others. James Mill and later psychologists built on Hartley's foundation, and the book stands as the founding work of association psychology.
hartley-observations-on-man-vol2-1749:
The second volume of Hartley's Observations on Man appeared in 1749 with the first, completing his great system. Hartley was a physician who wanted one theory to cover body, mind, and faith. Volume 1 had set out his psychology of association; the second half puts that psychology to work.

Volume 2 applies the laws of association to religion and morals. Duty, hope, prayer, and the expectation of a life to come are all explained through the linking of ideas and feelings. Hartley, a devout man, meant the system to strengthen faith, not to dissolve it. The result is psychology in the service of religion, unusual for its age. Together the two volumes founded the associationist school that shaped British thought about the mind for a century.
heart-sutra-muller-sbe49:
A few hundred words hold the core of Mahayana Buddhism in the Heart Sutra. The Heart Sutra, in the English rendering of Friedrich Max Müller from 1894, gives that core text in full. Müller's version stood in the Sacred Books of the East, the great Victorian shelf of world faiths.

The sutra says form is emptiness and emptiness is form, and sweeps away each prop the mind would clutch. Monks and lay folk chant it daily from Tibet to Japan. Its end is a mantra that promises passage to the far shore of waking. No Buddhist text so short carries so much weight.
herodian-history-hart-1749:
Herodian lived through the wild years he writes about. His History, finished around 238 CE, tells the Roman Empire from the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 to the rise of Gordian III. J. Hart turned it into English in 1749, and he added an appendix that carries the story on to Constantine.

Eight books hold Commodus on the throne, the year of five emperors, the Severan house, and the chaos of the third century. Herodian writes as a minor official who saw courts at close range. His tale is vivid, moral, and often sharp. For these years he is one of the few full sources that survive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenstein-baru:
Baruch Solomon Löwenstein, a Russian mathematician born at Wolodarka in the second quarter of the nineteenth century, is the subject of a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. The article, by Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer, records a scholar who worked where Jewish learning met mathematics and astronomy.

Löwenstein wrote “Bikkure ha-Limmudiyyot,” a work explaining mathematical passages in the writings of Abraham ibn Ezra, Moses Maimonides, and Joseph Delmedigo. He also annotated and published a second edition of “Shebile di-Reḳia,” a book on the rules of the calendar with the elements of geometry, trigonometry, and astronomy, issued at Warsaw in 1863. The entry preserves the name and books of a little-known figure who explained older Jewish texts through mathematics, and it gives readers a compact record of that work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mandans-10349:
Mandaeans, an eastern religious sect of lower Babylonia, are described in a long Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The sect mixes Christian, Jewish, and heathen doctrines and customs. Its members live around Wasit and Basra, speaking Arabic and Persian. Their sacred books use an Aramaic dialect close to the Babylonian Talmud's.

The article untangles their names and books. Mandaean comes from Manda, the word of life, a central figure in their system. To outsiders they call themselves Sabians, and their learned men Nasoraeans. Europeans long misnamed them Christians of Saint John, for their reverence for John and their frequent baptisms. Their chief book, the Treasure, dates from between 650 and 900. Part serves the living and part the burial of priests. The system it teaches is a form of ancient Gnosticism. Jewish influence shows plainly inside it. The entry remains a rich early survey of a small, secretive faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marx-berthe-104:
Berthe Marx, a French pianist, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 from Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn. Born at Paris on July 28, 1859, she started piano at four with her father, a cellist in the Conservatoire and Grand Opera orchestras. At the Conservatoire she studied with Henri Herz and won first prize at fifteen.

Her career turned on a meeting in Brussels with the violinist Sarasate, who engaged her as soloist and accompanist. She toured with him through Europe and America, reaching Mexico and California, and played in about 600 concerts in all. The entry also credits her with several Spanish rhapsodies of her own and with piano arrangements of Sarasate's Spanish dances.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-zioni-z:
Menahem Zioni of Speyer was a cabalist of the middle of the fifteenth century. He takes his name from his work, the "Ziyyuni." That work is a cabalistic commentary on the Pentateuch. Joseph Jacobs and A. Biram treat it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The book builds on Rashi and Nahmanides. It builds on the older cabalistic literature of the geonic age too. It opens with acrostic poems. With Maimonides quoted at length, it argues for the doctrine of creation. Short poems bridge the weekly portions.

The book had a violent birth in print. Vincentio Conti issued it at Cremona in 1559, in rabbinic type. Marauding Spanish soldiers burned that edition the same year. It was reprinted there in 1560. Quoted often in the "Yalkut Re'ubeni," it became a standard cabalistic gloss. The entry ends with a separation. It parts its author from a twelfth-century hymn-writer of a similar name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-annie-nee:
Annie Nathan Meyer, born in New York City on February 19, 1867, was an American writer profiled by Cyrus Adler and M. H. Harris in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She published early in The Critic, Harper's Bazar, Lippincott's, and The Bookman. Her best-known short story was Vorbei, and some of her tales drew on Jewish life.

She married Dr. Alfred Meyer in 1887 and went on to write the novel Robert Annys, Poor Priest in 1901 and to edit Woman's Work, a standard book of 1898. Her public work mattered as much as her books: she chaired a literature committee at the Chicago World's Fair congress. Most of all, her energy helped found Barnard College, gathering its promoters and raising its first-year funds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minerbi-hirsche:
Hirschel de Minerbi, Count of Oscarre, was an Italian diplomat from a wealthy and illustrious Jewish family of Triest, born on April 25, 1838. Isidore Singer and Vittore Castiglione sketch him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took a law degree at Padua in 1864 and entered the Italian government service three years later.

His postings carried him to Paris, Bern, Constantinople, London, and Brussels, and back to London, where he stayed until he left the service. The entry's most telling detail comes at the end: before retiring to private life, Minerbi set aside 80,000 lire as the seed of an institute for the widows and orphans of diplomats. It is a short entry for a long career of quiet postings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monogamy-10949:
Monogamy in Judaism was custom outrunning law, Joseph Jacobs and Israel Abrahams argue in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Law tolerated polygamy without enacting it; the people, from the return from Babylon onward, made one wife the ideal and the practice. Scripture itself leans that way from its first page, the creation of one man and one woman.

Even the patriarchs' plural marriages are told, the writers note, with apology, as infringements needing excuse. The Wisdom books assume monogamy entire: Proverbs' perfect wife of chapter thirty-one has no rival in her house, and Ben Sira and Tobit confirm the picture. A social-history entry arguing that practice reformed the law long before any statute did.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-11049:
Moses, the lawgiver who led Israel out of Egypt, is the subject of one of the Jewish Encyclopedia's central articles. Six scholars share the byline, among them Wilhelm Bacher, Kaufmann Kohler, and Crawford Howell Toy. The article tells his life from the Bible: hidden by his mother Jochebed, set adrift on the Nile, and found by Pharaoh's daughter.

It follows his flight to Midian after he killed an Egyptian, and his call at the burning bush. Then come the ten plagues, the crossing of the sea, and the giving of the Law at Sinai. The article ends with the wilderness years, the fighting east of the Jordan, and Moses' farewell address and death on Mount Nebo. It is a full period retelling of the Exodus story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-simha:
Moses ben Simhah of Lutsk was a Karaite scholar of the first half of the eighteenth century. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach give him a very short Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He is remembered partly through his son, Simhah Isaac, author of the Orah Zaddikim.

His own work, the Torat Mosheh, is divided into four parts. It contains liturgical poems and prayers, together with a number of sermons. That is all the entry tells us about him. Such brief notices still matter: they keep the names of Karaite writers of Poland from being lost entirely.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-myers-maurice-w:
Maurice William Myers was an American librarian born in London in 1821 and dead at Cincinnati in 1899. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Jacobs wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He came to New York in 1833 and to Cincinnati in 1837. Trained for the law, he instead became librarian of the Cincinnati Law Library in 1861.

When the library burned in 1884, Myers drove its rebuilding. At his death it held thirty thousand volumes, almost all chosen by him. He knew those books so well that the lawyers of Cincinnati leaned on his knowledge daily. The entry is a tribute to a librarian who was himself a reference work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nethaneel-ben-i:
Nethaneel ben Isaiah was a Yemenite writer on the Pentateuch. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked in the fourteenth century. His book's title means Light out of Darkness, Lamp of Wisdom. Saphir first saw its manuscript in Yemen in 1863.

That copy lacked its start, so its title was misheard. Berlin and Oxford copies give his true name and title. He began the work on June 23, 1328. He wrote in a mix of Arabic and Hebrew. His method was midrashic more than plain exposition. Maimonides was his chief guide, copied at length. He added letter-number readings and sharp strokes at rival faiths. Drawings of the altar and candlestick fill his pages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nineveh-11549:
Nineveh was Assyria's most famous and last capital. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and J. Frederic McCurdy for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its native name was Ninua in Assyrian speech. It stood where the Choser meets the Tigris. The mounds of Koyunjik mark its ground today.

Gudea of Lagash named it about 2900 B.C. Sennacherib made it truly great after 705 B.C. He built two palaces and a splendid aqueduct. Assurbanipal added splendor that eclipsed old Babylon itself. Medes destroyed the city by fire in 607. Its river, dammed and loosed, helped breach its walls. Layard began digging its mounds in 1845. Assurbanipal's great library came out of Koyunjik's ruins.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-obornik-obernik:
Meïr Obornik was a writer on the Bible and a Biurist. The board and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Biurist was one who gave plain notes on the text. Obornik was born in 1764. He died at Vienna on November 6, 1805. He wrote much for the journal Meassef.

Obornik was among the most keen of the Biurists. He put the books of Joshua and Judges into German. He added short notes of his own to both. With Samuel Detmold he did the same for Samuel. He then brought out the whole Bible with such notes. That set, Minḥah Ḥadashah, came out at Vienna. Its parts came out from 1792 to 1806.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pagel-julius-le:
Julius Leopold Pagel was a German doctor and writer on cures. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Pollnow, in Pomerania, in 1851. He read at Stolp and at the University of Berlin. He took his medical degree in the year 1875.

In 1876 Julius set up as a doctor in Berlin. In 1891 he won the right to teach at that school. In 1898 he gained the high title of professor there. In 1902 he taught the past of cures as his field. He helped run a great book of lives of doctors. He ran a German paper for doctors of his land. His own books treat old works on the art of surgery. One treats the work of H. von Mondeville in that field.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-patto-samson-go: Samson Gomez Patto was a rabbi in Jerusalem in the eighteenth century. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He sat on the city's college of rabbis. In 1705 he gave his formal approval to Peri Hadash. That legal work was written by Hezekiah de Silva. It was published the next year, in 1706. Nothing more about Patto's life is recorded here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perugia-12049:
Perugia is a town in Umbria, in Italy. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It held a Jewish congregation by the fourteenth century. Several Jewish scholars lived and worked there.

One scholar served as judge there about 1400. Moses Rieti won fame as poet and physician in 1436. A cabalist and a liturgical poet followed later. Some Hebrew manuscripts were copied in the town. When Jews were expelled from the Papal States, many moved to Rome. The Da Perugia family in Rome keeps the name alive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pilgrimage-1214:
Pilgrimage meant a journey to a shrine for blessing. Gotthard Deutsch, Judah David Eisenstein, and M. Franco wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Every Israelite male owed three such journeys yearly. He went up to the Temple at Jerusalem.

The three feasts were Passover, Shabuot, and Sukkot. The Mishnah excused minors, the blind, and the lame. Women and children still came along in practice. Each pilgrim brought an offering of set worth. Jeroboam set calves at Dan and Beth-el instead. His guards watched the roads to stop the journeys.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pollak-leopold-:
Leopold Pollak was a painter of scenes and portraits, born at Lodenitz in Bohemia in 1806. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied under Bergler at the Academy of Prague. Later he worked in Munich and, after 1833, in Rome. He became a citizen of Italy and died at Rome in 1880.

Several of Pollak's paintings were made into prints by other artists. His Shepherdess with Lamb hangs in the Hamburg art hall. His Shepherd Boy is in a Berlin gallery. He painted Zuleika from a poem by Byron. He also painted Maternal Love. His portrait of Riedel is held by a Munich gallery.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-presbyter-judor:
Presbyter Judaeorum was the chief officer of the Jews of England. Joseph Jacobs wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The office held sway before the expulsion of 1290. The man who held it kept it for life, as a rule. Only six men held it in near a hundred years.

Scholars have argued over what the office truly was. Prynne held that it was a lay post in the Jews' exchequer. Its holder kept the rolls of control there, he said. Tovey pointed to Latin words used for the office. Words like priest and pontiff suggest a church-like role. The article weighs both views against the records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-purim-plays-124:
Purim plays are folk comedies made for the feast of Purim. Gotthard Deutsch and Henry Malter wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They were staged in Jewish homes or before a Jewish crowd. The month of Adar was their season. Stage plays were held frivolous by the strict, as a rule.

Purim formed the one great exception to that rule. The Talmud names shows and pranks that were common then. In geonic times the tale of Esther was turned into a play. Later ages made whole scripts from that tale. The article traces the plays from those roots to later stages. It names the lands where the custom ran strongest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ramath-lehi-125:
Ramath-lehi was a place on the border of Judah and Philistia. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its name means Jaw-Bone Height. It appears only in the story of Samson in Judges.

The article explains the name through Samson's fight there. Tradition says he killed a thousand Philistines with an ass's jawbone. He then threw the bone away on that hill. The writers suggest the hill's shape may explain the name instead. They also discuss a nearby spring and a proposed site. The entry shows how a place name can grow from a story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rehumai-ii-1264: Rehumai II was a Babylonian amora of the seventh generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied under Rabina I. For Rabina he explained a saying of Huna b. Tahlifa. The article says he led the academy at Pumbedita after Rafram II. He held that post from 443 to 456. He died during persecutions under King Yezdegerd II. Sherira often called him Nahumai instead, the writers note. Sources include Sherira, Grätz, and Halevy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-riemann-solomon:
Solomon Riemann was a traveler of the nineteenth century who died about 1873. Isidore Singer and Isidor Warsaw wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Vienna. He had once been a rich merchant.

The article says his wealth came from large investments in Siam. War with the English there ruined him completely. British authorities seized all his property in that conflict. He then traveled through Asia, Africa, and much of Europe. He finally settled in Vienna. Aid from Adolf Jellinek let him record his travels. He died suddenly before finishing that work. His style was tangled and nearly unreadable, they say. Wolf Schur rewrote the manuscript fully before publishing it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenfeld-morde:
Mordecai Jonah Rosenfeld was a Galician author of Hebrew books, born at Dynow on October 21, 1797. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied Talmud, Hebrew, and German at Brody as a boy.

Around 1830 Rosenfeld became ritual slaughterer at Sosnica, and he stayed there for life. He died at Sosnica on June 5, 1885, after decades of quiet writing. His books comment on Behinat Olam and on Or ha-Hayyim by J. Yabez. He also published a Job with his own commentary and notes on the Hebrew words. His essays appeared in papers such as Ha-Maggid and Ha-Ibri.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ryssel-carl-vic:
Carl Victor Ryssel was a German Protestant theologian born at Reinsberg, Saxony, on December 18, 1849. Crawford Howell Toy and Bernhard Pick wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He began teaching at Leipsic in 1878 in theology and Oriental studies.

In 1889 Ryssel was called to Zurich as professor of Old Testament and Oriental languages. His first book compared words for true and good across Semitic languages. A later critical commentary asked whether the book of Micah is genuine. He prepared new editions of Fürst's Hebrew dictionary for students. He also edited Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, and Exodus-Leviticus for a handbook series.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salvador-joseph:
Joseph Salvador was a French historian born at Montpellier on January 5, 1796. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. His family traced itself to the Maccabees and fled Spain's Inquisition for France.

Salvador took a medical degree at Montpellier in 1816, then quit medicine. Rich and independent, he refused public offices and gave himself to literature. He spent the rest of his life writing in Paris. Though his mother was Catholic and his siblings married Christians, he stayed staunch. The entry calls him the undisputed head of that mixed family.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-solo:
Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel ben Solomon Nasi of Carcassonne. He was a French scholar of the thirteenth century. Samuel wrote a commentary on the Moreh Nebukim, Maimonides' great work of philosophy. A copy of that commentary still exists in manuscript. It sits in the Library of the Neophytes at Rome.

The scholar Gross argued that Samuel Nasi was really Samuel Sekili. Menahem Me'iri counted Sekili among the finest scholars of his age. Me'iri said he knew both rabbinic writings and secular science well. Later law books, such as Orḥot Ḥayyim and Kol Bo, often cite his authority. The entry untangles two names that may belong to one man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schapiro-heinri:
Herman Rosenthal and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Heinrich Schapiro. He was a Russian physician. Schapiro was born at Grodno in 1853. He died at St. Petersburg on February 14, 1901. After the gymnasium at Grodno, he studied at the St. Petersburg medical academy. He studied there from 1871 to 1876.

During the Turko-Russian war, Schapiro served as a military surgeon. He then held long military medical posts at St. Petersburg and Odessa. In 1895 he became a privat-docent of medicine. In 1897 he rose to a professorship. Professor Eichwald trusted him to finish a textbook of general therapy. Schapiro completed that work after Eichwald's death. He also translated German medical handbooks into Russian. His own treatises appeared in Russian and German journals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwob-mayer-an:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Marcel Schwob. He was a French journalist and story writer. Schwob was born at Chaville on August 23, 1867. He died at Paris on February 27, 1905. His father edited the Phare de la Loire at Nantes. In Paris, Schwob wrote for the Echo de Paris and other journals.

Schwob took his degree in 1888 and taught at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes. His uncle Leon Cahun, of the Mazarin Library, guided his learning. His books include Cœur Double and Le Roi au Masque d'Or. Le Livre de Monelle and Mimes appeared in 1894. His Vies Imaginaires, or imaginary lives, came in 1896. He turned Shakespeare's Hamlet into French with Eugène Moran. Sarah Bernhardt starred in that version on stage. He also translated Stevenson, a friend of his.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sessa-karl-borr:
Karl Borromäus Alexander Sessa was a Breslau doctor who wrote against the Jews. Gotthard Deutsch wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Born in 1786, Sessa studied philosophy and medicine at several schools. He took his medical degree in 1807 and practiced in Breslau.

Alongside poems and medical essays, Sessa wrote a comedy mocking Jews. Its Jewish figures speak in jargon and chase only money. Staged in 1813, the play spread under a new title before police banned it. It was still reprinted long after his death that same year. The entry preserves the record of a popular play built on prejudice, and of efforts to stop it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shema-koli-hear:
Shema Koli, Hear my voice, opens the eve of Atonement service in Sephardic ritual. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the hymn. It comes just before Kol Nidre in that service. The hymn holds twenty-nine two-line verses in all.

Its verses build on an old Mishnah plea for mercy. May He who answered the Patriarchs answer us, it runs. Scholars call it the oldest complete timed hymn of its kind. They credit it to Hai ben Sherira, the gaon. Its tune is nearly as old as the words. Other famed hymns of the season borrow that same melody. The entry links text, tune, and the holiest night of the year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-oskar-137:
Oskar Simon was a German dermatologist born at Berlin on January 2, 1845. Isidore Singer and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1868. He then studied further at Vienna. In the Franco-Prussian war he served as an assistant surgeon.

In 1878 Simon became professor of dermatology at Breslau. He was also chief physician at the Allerheiligen Hospital there. His books dealt with where skin diseases appear on the body. He also wrote on molluscum contagiosum and on prurigo. He died at Breslau on March 2, 1882, still in his thirties.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-abr:
Solomon ben Abraham ibn Daud was a physician and translator. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Scholars link him to the family of Abraham ben David of Toledo. That family was famed for its translators from Arabic. Solomon rendered Averroes' medical work Kulliyyat into Hebrew.

His version bore the Hebrew title Miklol. Copies survive in Oxford and in Paris libraries today. Steinschneider thought he might be the Solomon Daud of another work. That work was a treatise on psychology and metaphysics. It survives in a manuscript in the Turin Library. The brief entry weighs that uncertain identification with care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stieglitz-ludwi:
Ludwig von Stieglitz was a Russian banker born in Arolsen, Germany, in 1778. Herman Rosenthal and H. Guttenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He emigrated to Russia as a young man. There he became court banker to the czar. He died at St. Petersburg on March 18, 1843.

After adopting Christianity, Stieglitz was made a hereditary Russian baron in 1826. He played a large part in Russian financial affairs. His efforts brought steam navigation between Lübeck and St. Petersburg. He bought an estate in Courland and joined its nobility register. His son Alexander later headed the family banking house. The firm wound up its business in 1863. The entry traces a migrant banker's rise to titled rank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-switzerland-141:
Switzerland is a republic of central Europe with medieval Jewish roots. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Jews lived at Basel as early as 1213. Records place them at Bern by 1259. Zurich, St. Gall, and Schaffhausen followed within decades.

Swiss Jews ranked as serfs of the Holy Roman Empire. The emperor protected them for a yearly tribute. Cities later bought the right to tax and guard them. Biel first granted Jews citizenship in 1305. Still, they lacked the full rights of citizens. Jews arrived from Alsace, Germany, and even France. One Schaffhausen Jew owned three houses in 1299. His son sold them to a bishop in 1340. The entry maps small communities under layered protection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tarnopol-14249:
Tarnopol is a town of eastern Galicia on the Sereth river. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Hetman Johann Tarnowski founded it in 1540. Polish Jews were admitted from the very start. They soon formed a majority of its people.

In the 1500s and 1600s some 300 Jewish families lived there. Chmielnicki's march destroyed Tarnopol among many towns. Its large Jewish population had run an extensive trade. Under John Casimir the town prospered again afterward. Its Jewish numbers passed all previous figures then. Hasidism dominated the community in that era. It opposed every import of Western culture. In 1770 confederates stormed and massacred many Jews there. Joseph Perl later founded a Jewish school in 1813.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-teweles-heinric:
Heinrich Teweles was an Austrian dramatist born at Prague in 1856. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He first reached the stage in 1881 with a play called Die Schauspielerin. He later served as dramaturgist of Prague's German Landestheater.

His output was steady across two decades. Comedies such as Eherecht and Der Ring des Polykrates came in the 1880s. The 1890s brought plays on Johann Strauss and Demetrius. He reworked Demetrius from Hebbel's version. Teweles also wrote a novel, Die Armen, in 1885. He edited the Prager Dichterbuch, a Prague poets' book, in 1893. The entry lists each work with its year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tordesillas-mos:
Moses ha-Kohen de Tordesillas was a Spanish defender of Judaism under persecution. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Christians tried to convert him by force. He held to his faith though robbed of all he owned. Poverty followed, but his community chose him rabbi at Avila.

Around 1372 he debated the convert John of Valladolid. Christians and Muslims watched the contest. Moses knew the Christian sources well and won easily. A second fight came against a disciple of Abner of Burgos. In 1374 he wrote up his debates as a dialogue. Ezer ha-Emunah treats 125 disputed Bible passages. Trinity, Mary's virginity, and Daniel's weeks all figure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vatican-library:
The Vatican Library is the pope's great library in Rome. Joseph Jacobs and Ignatio Guidi wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article focuses on the library's Hebrew manuscripts. An old catalogue from its Avignon years lists 116 Hebrew manuscripts. That was likely Europe's oldest such collection.

The library shrank over time and lost many treasures. Popes Martin V and Nicholas V rebuilt it in the fourteen hundreds. Sixtus IV completed the work in the Vatican Palace. By about 1550 the Hebrew holdings were large again. The library even kept a special copyist for Hebrew works. The entry traces that long, uneven history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weiss-max-14849:
Max Weiss was a Hungarian chess master. He was born on July 21, 1857, at Szered on the Waag. Isidore Singer and A. Porter wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He moved to Vienna and studied math and physics. He taught those subjects for a time. He had learned chess at age twelve.

Weiss entered many international chess tournaments. At Vienna in 1882 he beat Zukertort twice. He drew with Steinitz in that same event. At New York in 1889 he tied for first prize. He won first prize outright at Vienna in 1890. By 1905 he worked in Baron Rothschild's Vienna bank. The entry lists a decade of top finishes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wisconsin-14949:
Wisconsin is a state in the Upper Lake region. Joseph Jacobs and A. M. Hofmann wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It joined the Union in 1848. In 1792 a Jew named Jacob Franks reached Green Bay. In 1805 he built the region's first grist mill. Other Jews held interests there, but records are scant.

Milwaukee's B'ne Jeshurun is the state's oldest congregation. Settlers organized it in 1852. The entry then lists communities across the state. Appleton, Ashland, and Eau Claire each have congregations. La Crosse holds two congregations and a cemetery. Kenosha incorporated its congregation in 1904. Aid societies and schools fill out the picture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yah-shimeka-150:
Yah Shimeka is a hymn of five long parts in the New-Year rite. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Sephardic Jews sing it on the second day of the feast. It stands at the head of the Kaddish prayer then. A name set in its lines points to Judah ha-Levi.

The hymn's refrain is drawn from that Kaddish prayer. Its beat fits a dear form of Arab song craft. Its old east tune serves more than one hymn now. One is a work by Solomon ibn Gabirol for Atonement. One is a second hymn by Judah ha-Levi for day one. The tune serves the Kaddish and two close hymns too. So one strain marks the whole feast in that rite.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zadok-imani-or-:
Zadok Imani was an African hymn poet whose works live in one rite book. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Eight of his poems stand in the Tripoli prayer book. The entry lists all eight by their first words in turn.

One poem has thirteen parts in its verse form. Each of the rest has five parts in verse form. Four of them are sung on the Sabbaths of Elul. That month is a time of prayer for pardon each year. Just one bears his full name sign at its head. One more bears a part sign of his name there. The rest show the name Zadok and no more than that. The entry rests on the great hymn study of Zunz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zerika-15249:
Zerika was a scholar of Palestine in the fourth century of this era. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a pupil of Eleazar in his school years. He passed on the rules of that man to his peers.

He was a peer of Abba in the schools of that age. With Abba he judged a feud on the night watch count. That feud stood twixt Judah the First and Nathan of old. Abba told him of a fix in a rule told by Ammi. He knew Zeera and was close to Jeremiah in his work. In Babylon men told a tale of a quip of his. He set meek Palestine high above bold Babylon in that quip. No tale words of his live on in the books at all.
king-john-pg2249: The Bastard Faulconbridge steals this edition of King John: Richard's merry, ruthless son outshines the kings around him. From Angiers to the poisoned orchard, he carries England's honor. Shakespeare's most patriotic history, with its most vivid commoner-hero.
law-spirit-of-prayer-1749:
William Law wrote The Spirit of Prayer in 1749, late in his life. Law was the English priest whose Serious Call had moved a whole age. Here he turns to prayer as the core of all true faith. The book had force with mystics and with the Oxford men of a later age.

Law holds that prayer is not a set of words but the soul at work. The wish for God, he says, is prayer in its true form. He warns off cold rites and bids the heart burn with plain want. The short book is a deep draught of English soul lore.
letters-from-england-1846-1849:
Elizabeth Davis Bancroft wrote these Letters from England between 1846 and 1849. Smith, Elder published them in London in 1904, with portraits and views. She was the wife of historian George Bancroft.

Her husband served as American minister in London then. Her letters record court, society, and daily English life. A preface introduces her as the youngest child of her family. She writes as an insider at diplomatic gatherings. American readers get England's drawing rooms through a keen, friendly eye. Portraits and views of English scenes illustrate her record. Private parties and public ceremonies receive equal attention.
lot-no-249:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote this mummy tale in 1892, two years after he made Sherlock Holmes a star. It was cut from a set of his weird tales to stand as its own text. Doyle had a strong taste for tales of the East and of old Egypt.

An Oxford man buys a mummy case at a sale, lot number 249 by the sale list. Soon a tall, thin foe stalks his foes at night, and the case stands empty in his rooms. With Stoker's Jewel of a few years on, the tale founds the mummy horror kind.
michaelis-sendivogii-chymische-schriffte:
Michael Sendivogius's chemical writings appeared in this German edition at Vienna in 1749. Sendivogius, a Polish alchemist, had died about a century earlier. The title promises clear teaching on the origin, preparation, and completion of the blessed Stone of the Wise. The publisher's preface notes the writings had long been out of print and much sought after.

The volume gathers several works under Sendivogius's name. It includes his fifty-five letters and writings by Synesius on the Stone. It also prints Basilius Valentinus's Way of Truth. German readers in 1749 still bought such collections eagerly, a sign of alchemy's long afterlife.
nato-treaty-1949:
Twelve nations signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington in April 1949, founding the alliance known as NATO. The signers were the United States, Canada, and ten European states still rebuilding from the Second World War. Fear of Soviet power in Europe drove them to bind their defense together in peacetime.

The heart of the treaty is Article 5, which treats an armed attack on one member as an attack on all. Members promise to help the victim, including with armed force if needed. It was the first peacetime military alliance in American history, and it anchored the West through the Cold War. The alliance has grown many times since and still rests on this short text.
notes-and-queries-number-01-november-3-1:
Saturday, November 3, 1849, brought the first number of Notes and Queries, priced at threepence. The journal offered itself as a medium for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, ran: when found, make a note of. That rule became the paper's whole method.

The editors say their prospectus has stated the design fully enough. They would rather give a specimen than a description, they write. Wide ranging subjects and much correspondence are expected, so the specimen must grow gradually. A few words of introduction stand in place of a boast. Readers were invited to send notes and ask questions in print.
notes-and-queries-number-02-november-10-:
Number two of Notes and Queries came out on Saturday, November 10, 1849, at threepence. The editors head it A Few Words to Our Friends. They stress that their opening address avoided any boast of what they would perform. A specimen, not a description, was their promise.

By the second week they allow themselves honest satisfaction, short of boasting. Thanks go to friends who sent friendly advice and able writing. They have opened a literary exchange, they say, and leading men in many branches of inquiry have used it at once. That quick use, they argue, proves the need for such a paper. Notes upon the first number follow.
notes-and-queries-number-03-november-17-:
Saturday, November 17, 1849, brought number three of Notes and Queries, at threepence. Travelling in England leads its contents list. Sir F. Madden writes on Sanuto's Doges of Venice. The Reverend A. Gatty prints letters of Lord Nelson's brother, written just after the Battle of Trafalgar.

Misquotations get a note, and notes from fly leaves reach their third part. Other notes treat the abdication of James the Second and Queen Elizabeth's domestic establishment. The register of East Peckham church in Kent, pawnbrokers' golden balls, and lions in the Tower all appear. Belton Corney starts notes on authors and books. Great events and small curiosities sit side by side.
notes-and-queries-number-04-november-24-:
Number four, dated Saturday, November 24, 1849, opens with Our Progress and Prospects. John Bruce writes on Luther and Erasmus, and Hallam's Middle Ages gets a note. Writers of notes on fly leaves start a run called Adversaria. The origin of grog and ancient alms basins share a page.

Queries ask whether Shakespeare wrote clouds or shrouds, and chase a medal of the Pretender. Roger de Coverley, Gothic architecture, and Katherine Pegg all draw questions. Edward Hawkins asks about the curse of Scotland, the nine of diamonds in cards. Book sale notes close the number. The journal's mix of learning and trivia was already set by week four.
notes-and-queries-number-05-december-1-1:
December 1, 1849, is the date on number five, priced at threepence. An original letter about Lord Chatham and Queen Charlotte leads the notes, touching Cibber's Apology. J. R. Planché writes on ancient tapestry. Prison discipline and the execution of justice get a sober note nearby.

Edward Hawkins treats a medal of the Pretender, and J. Britton writes on John Aubrey. An unpublished song by Suckling and white gloves at maiden assizes follow. Joseph Hunter adds anecdotes of books. Queries chase Sanuto's Doges of Venice and the manuscripts of Sir Roger Twysden. Books wanted and notices to correspondents fill the back pages, as in each number.
notes-and-queries-number-06-december-8-1:
A few words of explanation open number six, dated Saturday, December 8, 1849. A letter from the Earl of Shaftesbury follows, about the ash of Monmouth. Drayton's poems and a passage in Goldsmith get notes. The Reverend Dr Todd writes on ancient libraries, and J. Payne Collier offers a defence of a bald head.

Royal household allowances and printers' couplets appear among the notes. Minor notes touch an ancient alms dish, ironworks in Sussex, and the Order of Minerva. Answers settle the curse of Scotland, Katherine Pegg, and humble pie. Minor queries ask after the genealogy of European sovereigns. Learning and jest share the page.
notes-and-queries-number-07-december-15-:
Number seven, for Saturday, December 15, 1849, leads with the marriage contract of Mary Queen of Scots. The Reverend L. B. Larking prints a bill of fare from 1626. T. Hudson Turner writes on the Moneta Sanctae Helenae, a coin matter. Translations of Gray's Elegy get a note as well.

Bolton Corney continues his notes on authors and books. Answers treat a lobster in the Pretender's medal and straw necklaces. Queries ask about Berkeley's theory of vision and suppressed passages in Cartwright's poems. Another asks whether Dr Johnson met Professor de Morgan. Minor queries hunt hexameter verses in the Scriptures. Church registers and old coins share space with poems.
notes-and-queries-number-08-december-22-:
Otloh the scribe leads the notes in number eight, dated Saturday, December 22, 1849. E. Rimbault adds notes on Cunningham's London. Wives of ecclesiastics, Tower Royal, and barnacles all get entries. Albert Way writes on an ancient inscribed dish, and Dorne the bookseller returns as a topic.

Minor notes touch the omission of Dei Gratia, florins, and John Hopkins the psalmist. Queries ask after Love, the king's fool, and the Advent bells. The Middle Temple draws a query from E. Foss. Other questions chase Henry Lord Darnley, coffee as black broth, and catsup. A peal of bells and the battle of Towton also appear.
notes-and-queries-number-09-december-29-:
Our Progress heads number nine, for Saturday, December 29, 1849, the last issue of the journal's first year. Sir E. Dering's household book leads the notes, in the Reverend Lambert Larking's hands. Berkeley's theory of vision and Bishop Barnaby follow. Mathematical archaeology and Gothic architecture get notes too.

Dr Burney's musical works and ancient alms basins appear among the notes. Minor notes record Cromwell's baptism register, a wassail song, and autograph mottoes of two dukes. Answers settle Scarborough warning and coffee as Lacedæmonian black broth. Queries chase Charlemagne's talisman and Turner's manuscript history of Westminster. The Strand maypole and Dr Dee's petition close the sampled queries.
openalex-w1931185549:
Aziz Bousfiha and a large expert committee wrote this classification. It appeared in the Journal of Clinical Immunology in 2015. Nearly three hundred single-gene immune errors are now known. They cause infection, cancer, allergy, and auto-immune disease. The field grows so fast that sorting is hard.

The IUIS committee publishes updated classifications for these disorders. This 2015 version sorts them by clinical phenotype. Five broad categories frame the many varied conditions. Clear sorting helps doctors name and treat rare diseases. It also helps researchers compare cases across countries. The paper is a reference standard for the field.
openalex-w1991460349:
Julián Maggini and co-authors studied healing cells from bone marrow. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in the year 2010. Mesenchymal stromal cells can become several tissue types. Their healing value also rests on calming immune responses. Macrophages are immune cells that can drive inflammation.

The team asked how marrow cells reshape macrophage behavior. Mouse marrow cells were tested with activated macrophages. The title reports a shift to a regulatory-like profile. Such calmed macrophages could help limit tissue damage. The finding supports cell therapy for inflammatory diseases. It clarifies one route by which these cells heal.
openalex-w2023611349:
Martin Prince, Cleusa Ferri, Daisy Acosta and colleagues set out the study design of the 10/66 Dementia Research Group. Their protocol paper appeared in BMC Public Health in 2007. Latin America, China and India were ageing fast. Dementia cases there were rising. Most people with dementia live in developing countries.

The paper describes surveys of older people in communities. The same methods were used at each site. Teams assessed memory, thinking and daily function. They also interviewed family informants. Shared methods let results be compared across countries. The work aimed to measure dementia fairly in poorer settings. Western tests alone can misjudge people with little schooling. The protocol became the base for many later 10/66 studies.
openalex-w2027642249:
Vania Pivello reviewed the use of fire in two Brazilian landscapes. Her paper appeared in Fire Ecology in 2011. One landscape is the cerrado, a fire-adapted savanna. The other is the Amazon rainforest, which fire harms easily. People have shaped fire patterns there for thousands of years.

Lightning fires are common in savannas but rare in wet rainforest. Human-set fires are now frequent in both regions. Pivello gathered scattered records of indigenous fire use. She traced how fire regimes changed over time. Farming and cattle ranching raised fire frequency after European settlement. Seasonal parts of the Amazon now burn more often too. The review weighs what changed fire habits mean for both biomes.
openalex-w2099708849:
Ya-Wei Luo, Scott Doney, Laurence Anderson and colleagues built a global database of nitrogen-fixing ocean microbes. Their paper appeared in Earth System Science Data in 2012. These microbes turn nitrogen gas into usable nitrogen. That input feeds life across the open ocean. Records of them were scattered across many studies.

The database gathers counts of the microbes worldwide. It also holds their biomass estimates. Nitrogen fixation rates are included too. Data came from cruises and labs across many institutions. A shared archive lets modellers test their ocean simulations. It also shows where observations are still missing. The resource supports global nitrogen budget work.
openalex-w2112602049:
Andres Ruiz-Linares, Kaustubh Adhikari, Victor Acuna-Alonzo and colleagues measured ancestry and appearance across Latin America. Their paper appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2014. The region's people descend from Africans, Europeans and Native Americans. Mixing took place amid strong social ranking. The team studied over seven thousand volunteers.

Each person got an estimate of their ancestry shares. Body and face traits were measured next to the gene data. People also reported the ancestry they felt they had. Self-image matched measured ancestry only in part. Clear geographic patterns in ancestry appeared. Social factors shaped both mixing and identity. The data link biology with lived social labels.
openalex-w2120013349:
Jérôme Chave, Diego Navarrete, S. Almeida, and colleagues published this study in Biogeosciences in 2010. They asked what controls litterfall, the leaves and other soft tissue that rain down in tropical forests of South America. Litterfall is a large share of how much new plant matter these forests produce each year.

The team combined published and unpublished data from eighty-one forest sites. Old-growth rain forest dropped more litter each year than younger secondary forest. Total rainfall did not explain the differences, but the poorest white sand soils had much lower litterfall. Seasonal patterns tracked how seasonal the rainfall was, and poorer soils favored leaves over seeds and flowers.
openalex-w2156520949:
Renata Pardini, Adriana Bueno, Toby Gardner, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2010. They revisit the fragmentation threshold idea, which holds that species losses accelerate once remaining native vegetation drops below a critical share. Despite its influence on conservation science, the hypothesis lacked a robust real-world test.

The authors present and test a new conceptual model of biodiversity change in broken-up landscapes. In their model, crossing the threshold is only the first step. It starts a positive feedback that erodes the system's resilience and can drive a full regime shift. Local patch size starts to govern which species persist once landscape connections fail, linking patch effects to landscape collapse.
openalex-w2302501749:
Mark Wilkinson, Michel Dumontier, and IJsbrand Jan Aalbersberg led the authors of these rules in Scientific Data in 2016. They set out the FAIR guide for science data: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. Science now makes data faster than anyone can reuse it. Poor care of that data wastes the effort spent.

The rules reach beyond data sets to the code, tools, and workflows that made them. Each research object should carry a full account and a lasting ID code. It should stay within reach through standard routes. Shared word lists should let machines merge it with other work. The guide speaks to scientists, journals, tool builders, and funders alike. Its aim: open, repeatable science that others can build on.
openalex-w2461419449:
Joeri Rogelj, Michel den Elzen, Niklas Höhne, and colleagues published this perspective in Nature in 2016. The Paris Agreement promises to hold warming well below two degrees, and to chase one and a half. Countries filed national pledges, called INDCs, describing their post-2020 climate action. The authors assess what those pledges actually add up to.

The assessed studies cover up to one hundred sixty pledges, spanning nearly all global emissions. Together they bend emissions below the current-policy path, but not nearly enough. The window for a high-probability, no-overshoot route to one and a half degrees already looks closed. Emissions must peak almost immediately and fall fast. Stronger pledges, the authors argue, are unavoidable.
openalex-w2765081049:
The LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration reported the first neutron star merger detection in Physical Review Letters in 2017. On August 17, 2017, their detectors heard two neutron stars spiraling into each other. The signal, GW170817, rang in all three detectors with exceptional strength. Its false alarm rate was under one per eighty thousand years.

The two stars' masses fell in the range expected for neutron stars. Earlier observing runs had found only black hole mergers, never this lighter class. Binary pulsars had predicted such systems exist and should eventually collide. The detection confirmed that neutron star pairs merge within the observable universe today. It also opened gravitational-wave astronomy to the events most likely to shine in light. Telescopes around the world swung toward this one, making it a landmark for multi-messenger astronomy.
openalex-w2792652949:
Raúl Cassia, Macarena Nocioni, and Natalia Correa-Aragunde, with Lorenzo Lamattina, reviewed greenhouse gases and plant stress in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2018. The greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life, but human emissions keep strengthening it. Carbon dioxide is the main long-lived driver. Nitric oxide, a small signaling gas, also interacts with plants under stress.

The review examines how these two gases act as friends and foes of plant oxidative balance. Rising CO2 can feed photosynthesis yet also shift how plants handle damaging reactive oxygen. Nitric oxide helps plants coordinate defenses against that damage. Methane and other gases widen the climate backdrop the authors sketch. Understanding these double roles matters as crops face hotter, harsher conditions. The paper helps plant scientists judge which gas-driven effects to harness and which to fight.
openalex-w2806458049:
Frank Edgar Muller-Karger, Patricia Miloslavich, and Nicholas J. Bax lead a large team on ocean observation in Frontiers in Marine Science in 2018. Our ability to monitor marine life remains primitive next to our ocean uses. Two global frameworks try to fix that: Essential Ocean Variables and Essential Biodiversity Variables. This review advances both, focusing on biological data needs.

Satellites, buoys, and drifters have transformed physical ocean monitoring since the 1980s. Biology has lagged, though the need now includes tracking recovery and resilience, not only decline. The authors examine how the two frameworks complement each other. They specify what should be measured, where, and to what standard. Shared rules let scattered monitoring programs add up to a global picture. The paper is a planning document for the ocean-observing community. Its goal: marine life data as routine and trusted as weather data.
openalex-w2951449549:
Michael Menden, Dennis Wang, Mike Mason, and colleagues published this community study in Nature Communications in 2019. It reports a shared test of computer methods that predict which pairs of cancer drugs will work well together. The test grew out of a large drug screening effort run with the AstraZeneca-Sanger DREAM consortium.

Matching single drugs to a tumor's genetics can produce strong responses, but most tumors later resist and the disease returns. Drug pairs may overcome that resistance, yet testing every pair in the lab is slow. The consortium therefore asked many teams to predict good combinations from screening data. The paper compares their methods and judges how far such prediction can guide the search for durable treatments.
openalex-w3011154449:
Katrina Grasby, Neda Jahanshad, Jodie Painter, and colleagues posted this preprint on bioRxiv in 2019, before peer review. It studies the genetic architecture of the human cerebral cortex, the folded outer layer of the brain where thought and perception take place. A very large author team signals a pooled effort across many brain research centers.

The cortex varies in surface area and thickness from person to person, and much of that variation runs in families. The authors combine brain scans with genome data from large groups of volunteers. Their goal is to find which common gene variants track with which features of cortical structure. Such maps help explain how genes build the brain and why its form differs between people.
openalex-w3017872349:
R. Abbott, T. D. Abbott, S. Abraham, and colleagues of the LIGO and Virgo groups published this paper in Physical Review D in 2020. It reports GW190412, a merger of two black holes with clearly unequal masses. The waves were caught on April 12, 2019, early in the detectors' third observing run.

A black hole of about thirty solar masses merged with a companion of only about eight. All earlier mergers had paired near-equals, so this system stood apart. Unequal pairs should radiate more strongly in higher wave patterns beyond the basic one, and the team found strong evidence of exactly that. The heavier black hole was also spinning at a fair rate. The event tests gravity in new territory.
openalex-w3041340349:
Christophe Béné wrote this review in Food Security in 2020, working alone. It explores what resilience means for local food systems and how that resilience links to food security. The trigger is the disruption that the COVID-19 pandemic brought to those systems in 2020.

The discussion centers on low- and middle-income countries, where food systems also face weather, economic, political, and social shocks. Reviewing early accounts of the pandemic, many from reports and media, Béné notes a striking point. Aside from families who lost members to the virus itself, the main harm by mid-2020 came from lockdowns and travel limits. The review uses that lesson to sharpen the concept of food system resilience.
openalex-w4323531449:
Marcus Eriksen, Win Cowger, Lisa Erdle, and colleagues estimate the plastic particles floating in the world's oceans, in PLOS ONE in 2023. Their title calls the result a growing plastic smog. The estimate now stands at more than one hundred seventy trillion particles afloat at sea. The team built the figure from ocean sampling data gathered across many expeditions and years.

Numbers like these matter because plastic fragments drift into food webs and remote waters alike. A rising count also tests whether policies and clean-ups are working. The authors argue that the trend demands urgent solutions, not slow incremental change. Their paper gives governments and campaigners a single global yardstick for ocean plastic.
openalex-w4409708349:
Sándor Beniczky, Eugen Trinka, Elaine Wirrell, and colleagues present the updated classification of epileptic seizures. Their position paper appeared in Epilepsia in 2025. Doctors worldwide name seizure types using the International League Against Epilepsy system. The league revised its 2017 framework using experience gained since then.

A working group of thirty-seven members from all regions drafted the update. They used a modified Delphi process, needing over two thirds agreement for any proposal. Public comments then brought seven more experts into the task force. The classification keeps four main classes: Focal, Generalized, Unknown, and Unclassified. Shared seizure names help clinicians communicate, compare research, and choose treatments consistently across countries.
openalex-w7204080149:
Fabiana Custódio e Silva led a Portuguese-language review, published in Brazil in 2026, on compliance and management in agribusiness. Compliance programs help firms follow rules and manage risk, but their place in farming businesses was unclear. Following standard review guidelines, the team searched three sources for studies from 2020 to 2025, screening over three thousand records down to seven empirical studies that qualified.

In structured settings such as cooperatives and agro-industrial companies, compliance is consolidating as a strategic governance tool. Family producers and informal operations, by contrast, show low adoption and face major problems. The authors conclude that compliance practices can strengthen management, cut legal and operational risks, and support environmental and social governance agendas in agriculture.
openalex-w7204221649:
Eduardo Sampaio Feques Carvalho Lima led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on physical activity in natural environments and its effects on health and quality of life. Regular exercise promotes health, but authors also ask whether where people exercise changes the practice, affecting mood, attention, perceived effort, and well-being. The review drew on four research records about outdoor and indoor exercise, connection with nature, results, and nature sports.

The analysis ran along three axes: physical health, mental health, and quality of life. Exercising in nature, the authors expect to show, can enrich the practice mainly in psychological and subjective terms, without justifying a blanket claim that outdoor exercise beats indoor exercise physiologically. Contact with nature, pleasure, adherence, socialization, and varied bodily experiences matter for physical education professionals.
openalex-w7204524849:
Eldiomar da Silva Carneiro Neto led a Portuguese-language study, in Brazil in 2026. Mapping how dissertations from a graduate program at the Federal University of Tocantins, in Palmas, used Piaget and Vygotsky between 2014 and 2025. The two thinkers anchor much writing on learning and growth. The team identified twelve dissertations engaging their thought.

Treatment of the two proved heterogeneous and mostly superficial, the authors find, often filtered through other thinkers and translators rather than read directly. The dissertations connect the theories to early childhood schooling, assessment, and teacher training, among other themes. Discussion of Piaget and Vygotsky remains shallow in this corpus, they conclude, and new, deeper engagement is needed.
openalex-w7212043449:
Gisele Karin de Moraes leads a team on the teaching of African culture in Brazil's basic schools. A 2003 law made Afro-Brazilian and African history and culture a must in all schools. The team read past studies, laws, and school texts on the theme. Their aim was to weigh what the law has changed, and what still blocks it in class.

Teaching this culture, they argue, builds respect for human variety. It backs racial fairness and fights racism at school. The blocks are real: thin teacher training, weak class texts, and slow take-up of anti-racist practice. Still, the authors see the school as a key place to build respect for difference. They close with a call for a school life that is more open, more fair, and proud of its roots.
openalex-w7212137049:
Alexandre Pepe Parabocz and Karoema Lourenco Dias Hedlund study how the Parana military police care for the health of their own ranks. Police work brings steady risk and a high load of strain. That load tests any plan to guard staff health and worth. The pair read the force's rules on health and well-being. They set them by the national public safety law of 2018 and the force's own plan for 2025 to 2027.

The rules on the books, they find, line up well with the national guide. They aim at whole care for the officer, in body and mind. The pair also see room for a goal tool used in firms, built on aims and key results. That tool could test how well the rules work in real life. Sound care, they argue, builds a force that can bend and not break.
openalex-w7212154649:
Orlene Veloso Dias leads a team that reviews hunger risk in LGBTQIA+ people. Food insecurity means a lack of sure, steady access to food of good kind and fair amount. It tracks with want, job loss, low school years, and deep gaps in how groups are treated. Queer people face bias, shut doors, and shaky work more than most. The team read studies from 2019 to 2024 in three databases.

The review sorts the social roots that push this group toward hunger. Bias at work and at home can cut the cash that buys food. So can the stress of life on the edge of a harsh world. The point of the map is sharp: food aid that skips these roots will miss its mark. To feed all with fairness, plans must name who is left out, and why.
openalex-w7212505349:
Antonio Narcellio Machado Portela leads a team on clear reading and the fight with false claims in school. Brazil's kids score low on world tests of reading and science, while false claims flood phones and feeds. The team read past work on science skill, sorting the field in three strands: terms, class work, and state rules.

Science skill, in their frame, is more than facts. It is the power to weigh a claim, test its source, and act on sound ground. Class work can build it: sharp reads of news, tasks that join fields, and a stance of test all. Their close is a call for joined work, year on year: trained staff, a new class plan, and funds held firm. A school that builds such skill builds free minds.
openalex-w7213394549:
Alva Valéria Moro Labs and co-authors trace the history of inclusive education in Brazil. Their 2026 article moves from exclusion and segregation through integration toward full inclusion. It also looks closely at daily practice in one state school, Vila do Lago.

Real inclusion, the authors argue, is more than formal equality or building changes. It needs fair chances to stay, belong, and take part in school life. Democratic school management and teacher practice are treated as key levers. The study concludes that schools must place diversity at the centre of teaching and confront structural ableism that still shapes many institutions.
openalex-w7213402449:
Vera Antônia Ferreira de Carvalho and co-authors study religion and popular culture in Salvador's carnival. Their 2026 article focuses on Afro-Brazilian religion, Afro blocos, and afoxés in the Bahia capital. It uses library and document research in a qualitative design.

Candomblé symbols, bodies, and ritual ideas are carried into the public festive space, the authors show. Religious blending is read as a historic strategy for survival and cultural protection. The carnival is also presented as a place to affirm Black identity and resist religious racism. Drawing on liberation theology, the study treats street festivity as a claim to dignity and rights, not mere entertainment.
openalex-w7213867149:
Bruno Luís dos Santos Gonçalves and colleagues ran an exercise workshop for teenagers in Duque de Caxias, Rio de Janeiro. Their 2026 project worked with pupils aged fourteen to sixteen at a municipal school. Questionnaires before and after the workshop measured habits, learning, and motivation.

Some pupils were already physically active, the data showed. Lack of time and lack of will still blocked wider adoption of exercise. World Health Organization guidance on activity by age frames the project. Teaching time management routines could help, the authors argue, alongside direct encouragement. Regular exercise is presented as a route to health and quality of life for this age group.
openalex-w7213904749:
Ana Caroliny de Souza Ribeiro leads a study of final-year public high school students and their hopes for university. Their 2026 descriptive study, in Duque de Caxias, Rio de Janeiro, used structured questionnaires and a conversation circle. Seventy-six students aged sixteen to nineteen took part.

Higher education is framed as a social determinant of health, tied to quality of life and social mobility. A striking information gap appeared: most students lacked knowledge about how to enter university. The project widened their grasp of entry routes, the authors report. Educational action of this kind can expand students' view of university access, they conclude, promoting health and cutting social inequality at the same time.
openalex-w7214452049:
