Fabrício Pereira Loiola and three colleagues reviewed, in 2026, the mental health symptoms reported by caregivers of children with autism spectrum disorder. Caring for an autistic child can be intense and constant, and the review asks what that demand does to the caregiver. The team searched studies published between 2015 and 2025 in Portuguese, English, and Spanish.

Stress, anxiety, depression, emotional exhaustion, and social isolation appeared often among caregivers. Heavy care demands, thin support networks, and difficulty reaching specialized services were linked to worse suffering and lower quality of life. The authors conclude that caring for autistic children is directly tied to caregivers' mental strain. They call for wider psychological and social support aimed at caregivers themselves, not only at the children they care for.
openalex-w7220743549:
Bruno Morais Silva led a 2026 applied study planning a leadership school for middle managers at a Brazilian university hospital. The hospital is the Professor Alberto Antunes hospital of the Federal University of Alagoas. Corporate education in the federal hospital network rests on asynchronous online compliance tracks. These collide with teams' scarce time and with a split culture between medical, care, and administrative areas. The documentary, propositive research builds its model on Peter Senge's five disciplines for learning organizations.

The result is an eighty-hour dialogical curriculum in four modules, with protected study hours, mentoring across teams, and monitoring criteria based on a standard model for judging training. Leadership development in public health, they conclude, depends on moving from prescriptive training to permanent spaces of collective reflection. In such spaces, respect for professional subcultures enables sustainable solutions to the health system's operational challenges.
openalex-w7221106149:
Maria Rosa da Luz Lopes da Conceição led a ten-author critical review, published in 2026, of how Brazilian scholars read the effects of neoliberalism and conservatism on public education this century. Rather than testing one policy, the team surveys the national literature and asks what story it tells as a whole.

The reviewed work converges on four effects: public education turned toward the market, heavier managerial control, standardized curricula, and teaching work made more precarious. Moral conservatism advances alongside, tightening ideological control over school content. Read together, the authors argue, the two forces form one project that weakens the school's social mission. Their synthesis is a map of the critique, drawn from the critique itself.
parkman-oregon-trail-1849:
Francis Parkman published The Oregon Trail in 1849, an account of his own journey west in 1846. Parkman, a young Bostonian in poor health, rode from St. Louis along the emigrant trail. He hunted buffalo, met wagon trains, and lived for weeks with a band of Oglala Sioux. Forts, prairies, and mountain passes mark the route.

Parkman writes what he saw with energy and sharp detail. His judgments reflect his age and class, and modern readers note his bias toward Native peoples. Even so, the book became the classic American frontier narrative. It gives the West as lived experience, not legend. Later western writing starts here.
pascal-provincial-letters-pearce-1849:
In 1656 and 1657 an unknown writer in Paris issued a series of letters that set France laughing and arguing. The writer was Blaise Pascal, and the Provincial Letters defended a friend accused of heresy. George Pearce translated them into English in 1849.

Letter by letter, Pascal pretends to learn from Jesuit teachers how their moral rules work. Their own words, calmly repeated, expose lax excuses for sin and easy pardons for the rich. The comedy is dry, the logic tight, and the damage lasting. The letters fixed Pascal's fame as a prose master. They also helped make satire a serious art in French writing.
phrenology-examined-and-shown-to-be-inco: In the hosted sample, only the Google Books notice pages and the first words of the title page of Phrenology Examined, with no argument text visible. The catalogue title completes the promise: shown to be inconsistent with the principles of physiology, mental and moral science. It names Nathan Lewis Rice, a Presbyterian minister and debater, as the author and dates the attack on phrenology to 1849.
plos-pbio-0020049:
Christopher V. Rao, John R. Kirby, and Adam P. Arkin compared how two bacteria steer toward food in PLOS Biology in 2004. E. coli and Bacillus subtilis both swim toward good chemicals and away from bad ones, a behavior called chemotaxis. They use related genes but wire them in different ways.

The study asks what stays the same when the same job is built twice. Core sensing steps match, yet the control loops differ in telling ways. That mix of sameness and variety is a gift for engineers of living systems. It shows which parts of a circuit are fixed by the task and which parts evolution felt free to change.
plos-pone-0000049:
Akiko Kashiwagi, Itaru Urabe, Kunihiko Kaneko, and co-authors offered a theory of how gene networks adapt, in a 2006 paper. A gene network is a web of genes switching each other on and off. When the environment changes, the network must settle into a new pattern of activity that keeps the cell alive.

Their proposal is fitness-induced attractor selection: the network wanders among stable states, called attractors, and the state that raises fitness is the one that sticks. Adaptation, on this view, is partly the network trying states and keeping what works. The theory gives evolution inside a single cell a mechanism, and it has influenced how theorists model flexible genomes.
plos-pone-0000149:
Marian Warsame, Omari Kimbute, Zena Machinda, and colleagues published this malaria study from rural Tanzania in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines how families and health workers recognize severe malaria, what they think causes it, and how they treat it. A focus is rectal artesunate, a drug given as a suppository before a sick child can reach a hospital.

Severe malaria kills fast, so what happens before referral often decides the outcome. The authors record local beliefs and treatment habits that a pre-referral drug program must work with. The findings guide how new treatments get introduced in villages, where custom and distance can matter as much as the drug itself.
plos-pone-0000249:
Susanne Prinz, Christine Aldridge, Stephen A. Ramsey, and colleagues published this systems biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. In yeast, the MAP-kinase pathway is a chain of signals that helps the cell respond to stress. The authors show that an RNA-binding protein controls signaling in that pathway, adding a layer of regulation beyond the kinases themselves.

RNA-binding proteins adjust which messages get used, and here one tunes a whole signal chain. The finding connects two control systems that were often studied apart. It matters for the basic wiring diagram of the cell, in an organism used to model processes in many others.
plos-pone-0000349:
Tini Garske, Paul Clarke, and Azra C. Ghani published this poultry flu study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It estimates the transmissibility of highly pathogenic avian influenza in commercial poultry in industrialised countries, how fast the virus spreads within and between industrial farms. The authors draw on outbreak data from such settings.

Transmissibility numbers decide culling and control policy when an outbreak hits a poultry-dense region. Industrial farms, with huge flocks in sheds, behave differently from backyard flocks. The paper supplies estimates fitted to that reality, for planners preparing for H5N1 and its relatives.
plos-pone-0000449:
Lusisizwe Kwezi and colleagues tested a plant hormone receptor for a hidden talent, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The receptor is AtBRI1 of Arabidopsis thaliana, which senses brassinosteroids, steroid hormones that steer plant growth. The team found that part of the receptor functions as a guanylyl cyclase in vitro, an enzyme that makes the signaling molecule cyclic GMP.

A receptor with its own enzyme activity can pass a signal in two ways at once. Showing the activity in the test tube is the first step; the bigger question is whether the plant uses it. The study adds a candidate pathway to how steroid signals move through plant cells.
plos-pone-0000549:
Matthew E. Hardee and colleagues blocked a blood-vessel growth signal and watched tumors stall, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Erythropoietin is known for making red blood cells, but it also helps trigger tumor angiogenesis, the growth of new vessels that feed a tumor. The team showed that erythropoietin blockade inhibits the induction of angiogenesis and tumor progression.

The finding cuts two ways. It flags a risk: anemia drugs that mimic erythropoietin might feed tumors. And it suggests an opportunity: blocking the signal could starve them. Work of this kind reshaped how oncologists thought about a routine supportive drug during the years that followed.
plos-pone-0000649:
Michaela Lucas, Axel Ulsenheimer, Katja Pfafferot and colleagues followed helper T cells through acute hepatitis C infection, in PLOS ONE in 2007. CD4+ T cells provide help that keeps antiviral immune responses going. In infections that resolve, that help is sustained. In infections turning chronic, helper responses appear absent or short-lived.

The team tracked virus-specific CD4+ T cells during the acute phase and after it. Watching the same response over time shows where chronic cases lose their support. The contrast matters for vaccine thinking, since a vaccine must raise help that lasts. It also helps explain why some hepatitis C infections clear and others settle in.
plos-pone-0000749:
Gregory P. Henderson, Lu Gan and Grant J. Jensen pictured the inside of one of the smallest eukaryotic cells in 3D, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Eukaryotic cells divide their functions among membrane-bound organelles. Modeling that ultrastructure accurately has been hard: light microscopy lacks resolution, and older electron methods introduce artifacts. Their subject, O. tauri, is a tiny marine alga.

Using electron cryotomography, they imaged an entire cell frozen in place, slicing the data into a three-dimensional model. A whole-cell map at molecular detail shows how organelles pack into minimal space. O. tauri's small size makes it a natural lower limit for eukaryotic design.
plos-pone-0000849:
Mamadou B. Coulibaly, Neil F. Lobo, Meagan C. Fitzpatrick and co-authors traced how a flipped stretch of DNA in the malaria mosquito may have been born. Anopheles gambiae, Africa's main malaria carrier, holds many such flips, called inversions. They help it thrive in many settings across tropical Africa. A first step to grasp how flips arise is to read the DNA at their break points in fine detail.

The team's title points to segmental duplication as the likely cause of one flip, named 2Rj. A copied stretch at a break point can make chromosomes misalign, and the piece between them can flip. How flips form sets how fast mosquitoes can lock helpful gene sets together.
plos-pone-0000949:
Mark Read, Gordon Grigg, Steve Irwin and colleagues tracked moved crocodiles by satellite, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Estuarine crocodiles are secretive, spread over remote country and easily disturbed. How far they can travel was poorly known, a gap that matters when problem animals are relocated.

The team fitted transmitters to translocated adults and followed their movements after release. The title tells the headline: the crocodiles made long coastal journeys and homed back. Moving a large predator may not solve a local conflict if it simply returns. Tracking data like this should shape how wildlife agencies handle crocodile removals.
plos-pone-0001049:
Olaf Sporns, Christopher Honey and Rolf Kotter mapped the hub regions of brain networks, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The cortex is wired by bundles of fibers linking region to region. Earlier analyses counted connections, motifs and path lengths in those networks.

The authors set out to identify and classify hubs, the heavily connected regions that hold a network together. Hubs carry the traffic between specialized areas. Damage to a hub should matter more than damage elsewhere, a prediction with clinical weight. Their classification gives brain mapping a shared vocabulary for the regions that sit at the center of the web.
plos-pone-0001149:
Most gene-expression studies of cancer focus on one tumor type at a time. Yan Lu and co-authors took a broader approach in a 2007 PLOS ONE article, searching for cancer genes shared across tumor types. They used integrated analysis of gene-expression data, the microarray measurements of which genes are active in a tumor.

Combining data sets across cancers offers more patients for validation than single studies usually have. The authors report common human cancer genes found by this integrated route. Genes that recur across many cancers are attractive targets, since a drug aimed at one of them might help in several diseases.
plos-pone-0001249:
The Anopheles gambiae species complex is a set of closely related mosquitoes, only some of which transmit malaria well. Rui Wang-Sattler and colleagues used fingerprint genotyping of 414 field-collected female mosquitoes to reconstruct the group's history, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Three decades of attempts had gone into that reconstruction, since it guides malaria control strategy.

The authors describe a mosaic genome architecture in the complex: different genome regions tell different evolutionary stories, because genes have crossed between forms. A mosaic history complicates the idea of fixed species boundaries. It also affects how resistance and other traits spread among these mosquitoes.
plos-pone-0001349:
How the descendants of a fertilized egg first commit to becoming nerve tissue is an old debate. Is neural induction merely the default path, or does it need instructive cues? Nibedita Lenka and Saravana Kumar Ramasamy used embryonic stem cells to address the issue, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their monoculture strategy avoided cell-cell interaction effects that complicate other systems.

The authors conclude that neural induction from ES cells portrays default commitment but instructive maturation. In other words, cells drift toward a neural fate on their own, but need signals to mature properly. Their answer splits the debate rather than settling it for one side.
plos-pone-0001449:
Timothy Lesnick and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study that extends a gene path test from Parkinson's disease to a second ill. The second ill, called ALS, kills the nerve cells that move muscles. The team had built models from variants in axon guidance genes. Those models had strongly flagged Parkinson's risk and course.

They asked whether the same path also flags ALS risk. A shared path would hint that both ills grow from like faults in nerve wiring care. Gene path tests look at sets of genes at once, not one by one. That wider lens can catch weak signals that single gene hunts miss.
plos-pone-0001549:
Fiona Lees, Mark Baillie, and George Gettinby published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on sea lice drugs in Scottish salmon farms. Sea lice are a pest that plagues farmed salmon and wild fish near farms. Farms lean on a few drugs to curb them, which risks the lice growing resistant. The team reviewed one key drug's record from 2002 to 2006.

They weighed how well the drug still worked across farms and years. A slow slide in effect would warn of resistance on the rise. Such reviews guide when to switch or rest a drug. They also serve wild fish health, since lice spill from farms to wild stocks.
plos-pone-0001649:
Mia Phillipson, Jaswinder Kaur, Pina Colarusso, and their co-authors filmed white blood cells leaving blood vessels in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Neutrophils, the most common white cells, exit the blood at sites of inflammation to fight infection. Swelling builds up at the same spots. Cells can leave between vessel wall cells or straight through them.

The team describes dome-like covers that vessel wall cells raise over neutrophils as they cross. These endothelial domes seem to seal the crossing point, limiting how much fluid leaks out and how much the vessel wall opens up. The full text gives the imaging and leak measurements. Sealing each crossing helps explain how tissues can call in defense cells without flooding themselves.
plos-pone-0001749:
Paola Finocchietto, Fernando Barreyro, Silvia Holod, and their co-authors studied insulin's control of muscle mitochondria in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Mitochondria are the cell's energy plants. In metabolic syndrome, with excess insulin in the blood, suppressed mitochondria may help muscle store fat and glycogen and speed the syndrome's progress. Nitric oxide had emerged as a reversible brake on mitochondria.

The team reports that insulin's control of muscle mitochondria entails activation of an Akt2 and mitochondrial nitric oxide synthase pathway. The full text gives the pathway tests and energy measures. Linking insulin to a mitochondrial brake helps explain how high insulin can paradoxically slow energy burning in muscle.
plos-pone-0001849:
Adele Murrell, Yoko Ito, Gaetano Verde, and their co-authors studied methylation changes at a growth-control locus in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Differentially methylated regions are associated with many imprinted genes, genes whose activity depends on which parent they came from. In mice, methylation at a region upstream of the H19 gene is acquired in the male germline. That region, the imprint control region IC1, influences methylation 100 kilobases away.

The team reports distinct methylation changes at the IGF2-H19 locus in congenital growth disorders and cancer. The full text gives the patient samples and methylation maps. This locus is the classic imprinting example; its faults cause both overgrowth and growth restriction syndromes.
plos-pone-0001949:
Colette Smit and co-authors modeled why HIV patients fare differently across Dutch clinics, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Once drug therapy starts, survival in the first three years varied by treatment center. One suspect was timing: how late people enter care after infection sets the stage for all that follows.

The team built a math simulation fed with data from the ATHENA cohort, a national record of HIV patients. As the title states, late entry to care limits what therapy can achieve. The model shows how much of the gap between clinics is set before the first dose is ever given.
plos-pone-0002049:
Irina Buhimschi and co-authors mined the fluid around unborn babies for signs of early birth, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Preterm birth has many routes, and new protein tools had lately shown some of them, such as inflammation and bleeding. Yet the cause of most preterm births remained elusive.

The team ran a multidimensional proteomic analysis of amniotic fluid. They charted many proteins at once in cases of idiopathic preterm birth, where no cause is known. Protein patterns may sort hidden causes into groups that can be treated. A clearer split of causes is a step toward stopping early birth.
plos-pone-0002149:
Arun Krishnan, Alessandro Giuliani, Joseph Zbilut, and co-authors looked at a protein as a network, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Their subject was ubiquitin, a small protein found in all complex cells, and the question was how it unfolds. Knowing how proteins are built inside may one day explain how they fold into shape.

Earlier studies by the group treated protein structure as a web of linked parts. Here they ran unfolding simulations and read them with network-based tools. The view shows which links hold the structure together longest. Work of this kind may help predict where a protein will give way under stress.
plos-pone-0002249:
Elife Bagci, Yoram Vodovotz, and Timothy Billiar modeled the double-edged effect of nitric oxide on cell death, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Nitric oxide is a small signaling molecule made throughout the body. It plainly matters in apoptosis, the orderly self-destruction of cells, yet it can both promote and block that death. The reason for the split was elusive.

The authors propose a mathematical model that simulates nitric oxide's competing effects. In the model, dose and timing decide whether the molecule pushes a cell toward death or shields it. A working model helps predict outcomes in inflammation and cancer, where nitric oxide is always in play.
plos-pone-0002349:
Allen Braun, Joe McArdle, Jennifer Jones, and co-authors recorded brain responses in people who cannot carry a tune, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Tune deafness is a central hearing disorder: sufferers cannot discriminate pitch, reproduce melodies, or notice wrong notes, despite normal hearing at the ear. Its cause was unknown.

The team used components of the auditory event-related potential, waves of brain activity after a sound, to see how melodic errors are processed. They found signs that such errors are handled outside conscious awareness. The result places the fault in the brain's early, automatic stages of pitch processing rather than in attention or memory.
plos-pone-0002449:
Poncela and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Julia Poncela, Jesús Gómez-Gardeñes, Luis M. Floría, among others. Its subject is complex Cooperative Networks from Evolutionary Preferential Attachment. How form and function interact during network formation bears on the origin of complex networks, yet it stays largely unstudied.

Past work added dynamics by rewiring a network that already exists, while this team studies network formation itself. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002549:
Krithika and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names S. Krithika, Suvendu Maji, T. S. Vasulu, among others. Its subject is a Microsatellite Guided Insight into the Genetic Status of Adi, an Isolated Hunting-Gathering Tribe of Northeast India. Tibeto-Burman populations of India provide an insight into the peopling of India and aid in understanding their genetic relationship with populations of East.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002649:
In 2008, Alberto Valbuena and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was the C/H3 domain of p300 is required to protect VRK1 and VRK2 from their downregulation induced by p53. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Alberto Valbuena, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The vaccinia-related kinase 1 (VRK1) protein, an activator of p53, can be proteolytically downregulated by an indirect mechanism, which requires p53-dependent transcription. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002749:
In 2008, Kristen L. Curran and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about circadian genes are expressed during early development in xenopus laevis. The catalog record names Kristen L. Curran first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Circadian oscillators are endogenous time-keeping mechanisms that drive twenty four hour rhythmic changes in gene expression, metabolism, hormone levels, and physical activity. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002849:
In 2008, Yueming Chang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was messenger RNA oxidation occurs early in disease pathogenesis and promotes motor neuron degeneration in ALS. Authorship is credited in the record to Yueming Chang and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Accumulating evidence indicates that RNA oxidation is involved in a wide variety of neurological diseases and may be associated with neuronal deterioration during the. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002949:
Géraldine Rauchs, Pierre Orban, Christina Schmidt and co-authors tested how sleep reshapes two kinds of memory in 2008. Sleep is known to reshape brain traces of memories gained while finding a way through a virtual place. But navigation mixes spatial memory with context memory, which are not the same.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team separated those parts and tracked their brain bases after sleep. Both spatial and contextual consolidation, the settling of memory, were modulated by sleep. The split helps sleep researchers say more precisely what a night of sleep does for place learning.
plos-pone-0003049: Meredith Nahm, Carl Pieper and Maureen Cunningham wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE methods article on quantifying data quality for clinical trials that use electronic data capture. Electronic capture replaces paper forms with direct digital entry during a trial. The catalog record provides title, authors, and year, but its abstract snippet repeats the title without added detail. The article addresses how trial teams can measure the quality of electronically captured data, a practical concern for anyone running or auditing modern clinical trials.
plos-pone-0003149:
Nico Melzer, Sven G. Meuth, Delany Torres-Salazar and colleagues test a common antibiotic class in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In multiple sclerosis and its animal model, glial transporters that clear glutamate work poorly while immune cells release excess glutamate. That excess causes excitotoxic damage in the central nervous system.

The title reports that a beta-lactam antibiotic dampened that excitotoxic inflammatory damage in the model. Readers find a drug-repurposing idea grounded in glutamate control rather than immune suppression alone. The study invites care, since a mouse model result is only a first step toward patient use.
plos-pone-0003249:
Thibaut Josse and co-authors study gene silencing at fly chromosome ends in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Work on the P element in the fruit fly led to a new effect: a gene placed near a telomere, the chromosome tip, can silence matching genes elsewhere. The placed gene sits in repeat DNA near the tip, called TAS.

The team test how this trans-silencing varies by tissue and by stage of growth, and how non-matching telomeres interact. Readers see chromosome tips act as control hubs for distant genes. That long-range action breaks the simple idea of one gene and one local switch.
plos-pone-0003349:
Marcello Siniscalchi, Angelo Quaranta and Lesley J. Rogers study brain sides in dogs in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Much test evidence shows functional cerebral asymmetries are widespread in animals. Activity of the right cerebral hemisphere has been linked with responses to novel stimuli. It has also been linked with showing strong emotions such as aggression, escape behaviour and fear.

The authors test hemispheric specialization in dogs for processing different acoustic stimuli. Readers learn which side of the dog brain handles various sounds, from conspecific calls to other noises. Dogs are a telling case because their social hearing is tuned to humans as well as to other dogs.
plos-pone-0003449:
Allan Jefferson Guimarães and co-authors studied a key fungal protein in this 2008 paper. The fungus Histoplasma capsulatum causes histoplasmosis, a lung disease. Doctors diagnose it by finding antibodies against its M antigen. What that antigen does for the fungus itself was unknown.

The team mapped the antigen in the fungus's yeast phase. They also probed its biological role in that growth form. Knowing the antigen's job could sharpen tests that rely on it. The work joins diagnosis and basic fungal biology in one study. Better knowledge of the antigen may also guide new drug ideas for a disease that is often missed early.
plos-pone-0003549:
Ben C. L. van Schaijk and co-authors weakened a malaria parasite in this 2008 study. Subunit vaccines have struggled to give lasting sterile protection against malaria. Interest has returned to vaccines using whole weakened parasites. Radiation-weakened parasites can induce strong protection.

Deleting the p52 gene stalled the parasite's liver stage development. Tests used cultured primary human liver cells. A parasite stuck in the liver cannot reach the blood stage. Such gene-deleted parasites are candidates for safer whole-parasite vaccines. The liver stage is silent, so a vaccine that stops it can block disease before any fever starts at all. Whole weakened parasites remain one of the few paths that have shown strong and lasting guard in early human tests.
plos-pone-0003649:
Rajasimhan Rajagovindan and Mingzhou Ding published this neuroscience theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Brain areas often fall into step, firing in sync with almost no time lag between them. Such tight timing is puzzling, since signals need time to travel between areas.

The authors break the synchrony into parts to explain the near-zero lag. Their account links this rhythm to tasks like binding what we sense into one scene and holding memories. The paper offers a framework for how far-apart brain areas can act as one network in time.
plos-pone-0003749:
Gabriel G. Perron, Sylvain Quessy, and Graham Bell published this bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Research on harmful bacteria has focused on the infections they cause. Far less attention went to carriage populations, bacteria that live in hosts without producing symptoms. The authors turned to those silent carriers.

They report drug-resistant pathogenic bacteria resting in asymptomatic hosts. Such hosts form a reservoir where resistance can persist unseen. The finding means resistance can spread quietly through healthy people, which complicates efforts to track and contain it. Carriage studies like this one were rare when it appeared.
plos-pone-0003849:
Yolanda López-Vidal, Sergio Ponce-de-León, Gonzalo Castillo-Rojas, and colleagues published this bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Helicobacter pylori is tied to chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, and gastric cancer. Two of its variable genes, vacA and cagA, are leading suspects in that cancer link.

The team assessed how the genotypes are distributed across regions of the stomach. They compared patients with gastric cancer against those without it. The high diversity they found complicates the hunt for which strain features actually drive tumors to form. Strain maps from one region can mislead when used for the next.
plos-pone-0003949:
Joseph H. Jeong, Zhenxiong Wang, Alexander S. Guimaraes, and co-authors modeled prostate cancer in mice in 2008. Prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death in men. A signal path called MAP kinase is active in advanced prostate tumors. Formal genetic proof of its role had been lacking.

Their PLOS ONE article switches on BRAF, a gene in that path, in mouse prostates. They report BRAF activation starts invasive cancer but does not keep it going. That split matters for drugs aimed at the path. A starter gene may be a poor target once tumors are established.
plos-pone-0004049:
Kathleen F. Brookfield, Michael C. Cheung, Relin Yang, and co-authors asked where gynecologic cancer care works best in 2009. Hospital quality can strongly affect cure chances in many cancers. Concentrating care in big centers is called regionalization. Whether it helps gynecologic cancer patients was the question.

Their PLOS ONE article weighed hospital volume and teaching status against outcomes. Five cancers were covered: endometrial, cervical, and others of the female tract. Outcomes at busy teaching centers could guide referral policies. Patients may gain from travel to high-volume hospitals. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004149:
Jaco Homsy and colleagues published this cohort study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Antiretroviral therapy, the drug treatment for HIV, may change the body, social, and behavioural factors that shape pregnancy in infected women. Long-term data on what women on this therapy intend and experience in Africa were scarce.

Following women in rural Uganda over time, the team recorded their reproductive intentions and the outcomes that followed. The study shows how treatment interacts with family plans in real life, not just in clinics. Its findings help health services support women who are living with HIV and weighing motherhood.
plos-pone-0004249:
Chi-Tang Tu, Tzu-Ching Yang, and Huai-Jen Tsai published this zebrafish heart study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Nkx2.7 is a gene related to tinman, the fly gene that starts heart development, and it is a counterpart of Nkx2.5. Both genes switch on in the zebrafish's heart-forming fields, in similar places and at similar times, though their separate jobs were unclear.

The team report that the two genes function redundantly and are both required for the heart to take shape in zebrafish embryos. When two genes back each other up, losing one hides the damage that losing both reveals.
plos-pone-0004349:
Yuan-Ping Pang and colleagues published this insecticide study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Aphids are among the most destructive insects in world agriculture, controlled mainly by organophosphate insecticides. Those agents disable the catalytic serine of acetylcholinesterase, an enzyme nerves need. But they also affect vertebrate versions of the enzyme, harming non-target species.

The authors work toward selective and irreversible inhibitors of aphid acetylcholinesterases. A compound that disables only the aphid enzyme would be a step toward human-safe insecticides. Aphids attack crops on every continent, and farmers spend heavily to keep them off. The study treats selectivity, not raw potency, as the design goal.
plos-pone-0004449:
A drug meant to block blood vessel growth had some surprising side effects on vessel walls, report Gian Carlo Alghisi, Lionel Ponsonnet, and Curzio Ruegg in PLOS ONE in 2009. The drug, cilengitide, blocks proteins called integrins that cells use to grip their surroundings. It was reported to suppress new vessel growth by causing vessel-lining cells to die.

Instead, the team found the drug switches on the integrin it targets, in a form called alphaVbeta3. It also pulls apart a joining protein, VE-cadherin, where cells meet, and makes vessel walls leakier. Those effects matter for any drug of this class. A blocker that partly acts like an activator may help some tumors, or help them in the wrong way, so the detail counts.
plos-pone-0004549:
Immune genes in the malaria mosquito carry the marks of a long arms race, report Tovi Lehmann, Jen Hume, Monica Licht, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The mosquito is Anopheles gambiae, the main carrier of malaria in Africa. Parasites that dodge the host's immune response are favored by selection, and so are host genes that cut the parasite load.

Those opposed pressures leave signatures on the immune genes involved. The team studied the molecular evolution of those genes, reading the signatures to work out what modes of selection acted on them. Deciphering that history can reveal the nature of the interaction itself. It may also point to mosquito defenses that could be strengthened to block malaria transmission.
plos-pone-0004649:
A duplicated stretch of DNA that comes and goes between mouse strains is tied to anxious behavior, report Richard Williams, Jackie Lim, Bettina Harr, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene in the stretch is Glo1, glyoxalase 1. It has been implicated in anxiety-like behavior in mice and in multiple psychiatric diseases in humans.

Using exon arrays across inbred mouse strains, the team identified a large tandem duplication as a copy number variant. The variant is common but unstable, gained and lost between generations. It is associated with differences in Glo1 expression and anxiety-like behavior, as the title reports. An unstable gene dose that tracks behavior is a caution and a tool for psychiatric genetics.
plos-pone-0004749:
Herschel Wallen and colleagues found that a chemo drug helps transferred T cells live longer in melanoma patients, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The therapy grows tumor specific killer T cells outside the body and returns them to the patient. How long those cells persist is linked to how well the treatment works against the tumor.

The team tested fludarabine, a drug that can shape immune response. It boosted response and stretched the survival of transferred cells in patients with spread melanoma. Longer lived cells may give the immune attack more time to shrink tumors. The approach needs care, since the drug also lowers immunity.
plos-pone-0004849:
Emilios Gemenetzidis and colleagues showed FOXM1 upregulation is an early event in human squamous cell carcinoma enhanced by nicotine, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cancer associated with smoking and drinking remains a serious health problem worldwide. Survival is very poor due to lack of effective early biomarkers. FOXM1 overexpression is linked to the majority of human cancers but its mechanism remained unclear in head and neck carcinogenesis.

Nicotine boosts FOXM1 during malignant transformation. Early rise makes FOXM1 a candidate early marker. Tobacco thus directly fuels a growth driver. Quitting may interrupt that pathway. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0004949:
DNA carries its code on a backbone built from sugars. Simpler backbones might also work. Glycerol nucleic acid, or GNA, swaps the sugar for glycerol. It still forms stable double strands by normal base pairing. Jesse Chen and co-authors tested enzyme-driven building of GNA. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used DNA templates for the primer-extension work.

GNA interests scientists who study life's origins. Its simplicity hints at chemistry from before life. Getting enzymes to extend GNA strands is a real step. It moves toward evolving functional GNA molecules in the lab. The work tests how far nature's copying machinery can stretch.
plos-pone-0005049:
The gut wall must keep germs out while letting nutrients in. That tightrope is called barrier function. Yutao Yan and colleagues studied a protein that helps control it. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The protein is SPAK, a kinase switched on by salty conditions. Its known jobs included cell differentiation and chloride transport.

SPAK's role in intestinal inflammation was largely unknown. The team found its gene is regulated by hyperosmolarity. SPAK proved involved in the gut's barrier function. The finding links a salt-sensing switch to intestinal disease. A leaky barrier is a hallmark of gut inflammation. SPAK may be one of its controllers.
plos-pone-0005149:
Blood vessels must stay sealed and alive. Cells lining them, endothelial cells, maintain that seal. Signals from neighboring pericytes help stabilize vessels. Tony Walshe and colleagues tested one signal's necessity in PLOS ONE in 2009. The signal is TGF-beta. Their earlier work showed it stabilizing vessels in dishes.

TGF-beta proved required for the adult microvasculature. Without it, the vascular barrier fails. Endothelial survival and vessel homeostasis fail too. Tiny vessels suffer first and worst. The finding names a master keeper of the vasculature. Leaky vessels appear in many diseases, from sepsis to diabetes. Knowing what holds the seal suggests how to repair it. The study moves a dish observation into living tissue.
plos-pone-0005249:
When cells divide, chromosomes are usually pulled apart by spindle fibers gripped at kinetochores. Egg cells build their spindles differently from ordinary dividing cells, though. Deng and colleagues reported a surprise in mouse eggs in PLOS ONE in 2009.

During the second meiotic division, chromosomes moved toward the poles even without kinetochore control. A backup route for moving chromosomes exists in these cells. The finding revises a textbook rule of cell division and may help explain errors that lead to abnormal egg cells. Egg cells must split their genes with great care, since one small slip can end a pregnancy or leave a child with the wrong gene count.
plos-pone-0005349:
Mycobacterium tuberculosis infects about a third of the world's people. Active disease involves fast-growing bacteria, while latent infection involves slow or non-growing ones. Beste and colleagues mapped the genes needed for each growth mode in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The genetic requirements for fast and slow growth differ, as separate gene sets keep each state alive. Drugs that kill fast growers may miss the latent reservoir entirely. Knowing the slow-growth gene list gives drug hunters targets against the hidden form of TB. Most TB drugs were found by their kill of fast-growing germs in a dish. So the slow set has long been a blind spot that this gene list at last brings into view.
plos-pone-0005449:
Daniel Williams and Peter Novick studied cell shipping in yeast in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Yeast cells grow and divide by moving materials to the right place at the right time. Proteins called SNAREs make membranes fuse, which is how those materials get delivered.

The team studied what happens when one SNARE gene, SEC9, is held back. Watching the effects showed how this one part links membrane fusion to the wider health of the cell. The work adds detail to the basic rules that all cells, not just yeast, use to move cargo inside themselves.
plos-pone-0005549:
Beth Tamburini and co-authors studied a blood vessel cancer in dogs for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Hemangiosarcoma is a fast-moving cancer of blood vessel cells in dogs. Earlier work found set chromosome changes in tumours from golden retrievers that were rarer in other breeds.

The team compared gene activity in tumours across breeds. The patterns of activity tied closely to breed, even for tumours that arise without a known inherited cause. Breed background shaping tumour behaviour matters for dog care and may hint at similar effects in people. Dog cancers arise naturally and share features with human cancers, so breed lessons may run both ways.
plos-pone-0005649:
Irene Granlund, Michael Hall, and Thomas Kieselbach studied proteins in a hidden plant compartment in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Photosynthesis runs in membranes inside leaf cells, and the space inside those membranes holds well over a hundred proteins. That lumen space is thin and hard to study.

The team measured how light changes protein levels there in a model plant. They also found that the genes for those proteins are regulated in a uniform way. Light reaching even this hidden space in a coordinated fashion helps leaves adjust to the day. The lumen was long a blank space in diagrams, and a full parts list changes how photosynthesis is taught.
plos-pone-0005749:
J. A. Scott Kelso and co-authors linked a person to a virtual partner in 2009 to study how new shared behaviors arise. The setup pairs a human's hand movements with a computer partner that reacts in real time. It borrows its logic from a device used to probe single nerve cells.

Subjects and the virtual partner had to coordinate, and fresh patterns of joint motion emerged. The team uses those patterns to test theories of coordination dynamics. A machine partner can be tuned precisely, which a human partner cannot. That control lets researchers probe the rules of social timing itself.
plos-pone-0005849:
Jackie Cheung and co-authors analyzed in 2009 a two-part signaling system that controls toxin output in a food-poisoning bacterium. Clostridium perfringens causes gas gangrene and food poisoning with a battery of toxins. The VirSR system, a sensor plus a responder, acts as the master switch.

The team worked out how the responder VirR passes the signal to its target genes. Knowing the relay's wiring shows where it might be jammed. Blocking toxin production, rather than killing the bacterium, is a gentler anti-virulence strategy. The functional details here guide that idea for a common and dangerous germ.
plos-pone-0005949:
Inherited changes in one gene form the most common known genetic cause of Parkinson's disease. The gene is LRRK2, and Xiaodong Ding and Matthew Goldberg studied how the cell controls its protein in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper asks what keeps LRRK2 levels steady, since the protein's exact day job is still unclear.

An enzyme called CHIP, which tags worn proteins for disposal, turns out to govern how stable LRRK2 is. A disposal route of this kind gives drug hunters a new handle on a key Parkinson's protein. If LRRK2 levels can be trimmed safely, that approach could one day sit beside drugs that only block the protein's action.
plos-pone-0006049:
Tbx1 is a gene best known for its link to DiGeorge syndrome, a birth condition affecting the heart and face. Gabriella Fulcoli, Tuong Huynh, Peter Scambler and colleagues found the gene doing unexpected work in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper shows Tbx1 binding Smad1, a signal carrier in the BMP pathway that patterns the growing body.

The surprise is the manner: Tbx1 damps the BMP-Smad1 signal without acting as a transcription factor, its usual trade. A gene with a second, quieter job helps explain why its loss causes such a wide pattern of defects. The result also adds a new kind of control to a pathway that guides bone, heart and much more.
plos-pone-0006149:
Hantaviruses were long thought to belong to rodents alone, until shrews broke the story. Hae Ji Kang, Shannon Bennett, Laarni Sumibcay and colleagues added a mole to the plot in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper reports a genetically divergent hantavirus harbored by the European common mole, and reads what it reveals about the family's evolution.

A virus far from the known branches, in a host outside the rodent order, pushes the family's roots deeper and wider. Each new host redraws the map of where hantaviruses hide, which matters since some cause severe human disease. The mole virus is a clue that the family's true host range is still being discovered.
plos-pone-0006249:
Spores of Clostridium perfringens survive cooking that kills most bacteria, then cause food poisoning. Jihong Li and colleagues studied a small spore protein called Ssp4 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Type A strains carrying a toxin gene make spores with exceptional resistance to heat and nitrites.

Earlier work tied much of that toughness to Ssp4. The team further characterised the protein's properties and when it is produced. Knowing what armours spores helps food makers design safer processing. It also explains why some strains survive where others perish. Food makers need such facts to set safe cooking and storage rules.
plos-pone-0006349:
Cattle deploy small RNA regulators when viruses attack, and cataloguing them shows the defence in action. Evgeny Glazov and colleagues surveyed bovine micro RNAs and similar small RNAs expressed upon viral infection, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Several classes of small regulatory RNAs had been discovered in recent years.

The study extends the repertoire of characterised small RNAs in mammals. Which regulators appear during infection reveals immune strategy at the molecular level. Livestock health has direct economic stakes in such knowledge. The catalogue also serves comparison with human antiviral responses.
plos-pone-0006449:
Frank ter Veld and co-authors improved newborn screening tests in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Screening now flags babies who may lack one of two fat-burning enzymes, MCAD or VLCAD. The screen uses a method called tandem mass spectrometry on blood markers. It has raised the number of babies found with fatty acid oxidation disorders, so confirming the result quickly matters.

The authors present a new tandem mass spectrometry method for rapid confirmation. A fast, sure second test separates true cases from false alarms. That protects babies who need care from being missed. It also spares healthy babies from needless worry and treatment. The method strengthens a screening program used on newborns.
plos-pone-0006549:
Sung-Cherl Jung and Dax Hoffman studied how nerve cells tune their own firing in PLOS ONE in 2009. When links between nerve cells grow strong for good, the cells also grow more apt to fire. This is called intrinsic plasticity. The team worked on cells in the hippocampus, a brain area key for memory. They focused on a kind of potassium channel in the cell body.

Their title says these channels are turned down in two phases, which lets the cell fire more with ease. Less braking by the channel is the core of the change. The work shows in fine detail how a cell's own tuning helps it learn. Such tuning works hand in hand with changes at the links between cells.
plos-pone-0006649:
Nicolas Marsollier, Nadim Kassis, Karima Mezghenna, and colleagues studied brain-liver cross-talk in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. Deregulation of hypothalamic fatty acid sensing leads to hepatic insulin resistance. That may partly contribute to further impairment of glucose homeostasis. The team investigated deregulation of hepatic insulin sensitivity induced by central lipid infusion in rats.

Their title reports the effect is mediated by nitric oxide signaling. Fat sensed in the brain changes how the liver handles insulin. The brain-liver axis is a promising target in diabetes. Their work traces one messenger in that conversation.
plos-pone-0006749:
Michael Czisch and co-authors studied how the sleeping brain reacts to odd sounds in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sleep needs reduced responsiveness to outside stimuli. Yet sleepers still process signals that could mean danger. The brain must filter without fully waking. The team used an acoustic oddball task during non-REM sleep.

Unusual sounds were mixed among repeated standard sounds. They recorded brain activity with EEG and fMRI together. Combining both methods shows timing and location of responses. The results reveal how the sleeping brain keeps watch. That watchfulness explains why a baby's cry wakes a parent while traffic does not.
plos-pone-0006849:
Hua Zhang and his team read the small RNAs of a child's blood cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. Small RNAs called microRNAs steer much of what cells do. In cancers, they can brake growth or feed it. The cancer here is acute lymphoblastic leukemia. It is the most seen cancer of childhood. A full list of its small RNAs could bring fresh leads.

Deep gene reads logged small RNAs through the whole genome. Brand-new microRNAs turned up in the reads. Each new one is a fresh lead on how this cancer grows. The list is a store for later lab work. In time, it may yield marks for diagnosis or aims for drugs.
plos-pone-0006949:
Laura Heath, Alan Fox, Jan McClure, and colleagues compared HIV in lung and blood in PLOS ONE in 2009. HIV-1 is often found in the lungs of infected people. The virus likely helps drive lung infections that strike these patients. The lung has its own environment, rich in alveolar macrophages and local immune responses.

The team asked whether lung viruses form a separate genetic compartment. Their evidence pointed to only limited separation from blood viruses. That finding shapes how doctors think about drug resistance and viral reservoirs. If lung and blood viruses mix freely, blood tests tell more about the lung than expected.
plos-pone-0007049:
Debojyoti Dhar, Musturi Venkataramana, Anand Ponnuswamy, and colleagues studied protein production control in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was interferon regulatory factor 2, or IRF2. Earlier work showed its RNA can start translation from inside, not just the usual start point. A protein called PTB was suspected to help with that internal start.

The team confirmed PTB's role in driving this route. Internal initiation lets cells keep making key proteins under stress. IRF2 helps balance gene expression in hard conditions. The mechanism is one way cells protect vital output when normal translation falters.
plos-pone-0007149:
Ricardo Dinis-Oliveira, Paula Guedes de Pinho, Liliana Santos, and colleagues reviewed fatal herbicide poisonings in PLOS ONE in 2009. Paraquat is a weed killer that kills people who swallow it, often in self-poisoning. Doctors try gut decontamination to block absorption. They also use anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing treatments to slow its toxic path.

The team analyzed postmortem evidence from human cases. Those analyses showed the therapies work poorly in practice. An honest verdict matters more than hope here. It pushes research toward new approaches instead of repeating treatments that autopsies show failing.
plos-pone-0007249:
Nicholas J. Hudson, Antonio Reverter, YongHong Wang, and colleagues mapped gene regulation in cow muscle in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Decoding causal transcriptional regulation remains hard, even with modern tools. The problem grows in less studied organisms, and when only gene expression data are available to researchers.

Muscle has only a small set of well characterized regulators. The authors integrate co-expression networks, groups of genes that rise and fall together. They infer the transcriptional landscape of bovine skeletal muscle from those patterns. Livestock scientists can use the map to study meat production and muscle biology.
plos-pone-0007349:
R. Prasobh and Narayanan Manoj cataloged signaling proteins in a marine animal in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Heterotrimeric G proteins and their regulators are key partners in GPCR signaling. GPCR receptors form a highly versatile system for sensing signals outside cells, from hormones to light and odors.

The versatility comes from coupling many receptors to varied G proteins. The authors compile the repertoire of both protein families in Ciona intestinalis, a sea squirt. This animal is a close invertebrate relative of vertebrates. Their catalog supports evolutionary comparisons of signaling systems.
plos-pone-0007449:
Stephen Gilmore and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on telling dangerous skin spots from harmless ones. Early diagnosis of melanoma is critical for survival. Doctors now rely on examining lesions by eye, but interest in automated help is growing. The team tested a mathematical measure called lacunarity, which describes how patchy or gappy a pattern looks.

Applied to images of moles and melanomas, the measure separated the two groups. Malignant lesions showed a different patchiness signature than benign naevi. An automated score of this kind could support clinicians screening large numbers of skin spots. It would not replace medical judgment, but it could flag lesions that deserve a closer look. The study offers a promising route toward computer-assisted skin checks.
plos-pone-0007549:
Sodiomon Sirima and colleagues published a clinical trial report in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a malaria vaccine candidate called MSP3. MSP3 is a protein on the surface of the malaria parasite's blood stage. An earlier trial in European adults showed the vaccine raised antibodies that kill parasites in the lab. The new trial moved to the group that needs protection most: children aged twelve to twenty-four months in Burkina Faso.

The trial checked safety and immune response in those young children. A vaccine meant for toddlers in malaria regions must clear this bar before wider testing. Favorable results move the candidate one step closer to the field. Malaria kills mainly small children, so a vaccine proven gentle and active in them is the real goal. The study is one careful rung on that ladder.
plos-pone-0007649:
Konstantinos Lefkimmiatis and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 introducing a tool for one of the cell's most universal messengers. Cyclic AMP, or cAMP, relays signals inside nearly every cell. To learn what a signal does, researchers need to raise it, lower it, and buffer it on demand. The team built a molecular buffer they named the cAMP sponge. It soaks up the messenger inside living cells.

By sponging up cAMP, researchers can damp the signal in a controlled way. That reveals which cell behaviors truly depend on the messenger's level. Tools that tune a signal are as valuable as tools that measure it. The cAMP sponge gives cell biologists a new hand on a universal pathway. Studies of hormones, heart cells, and neurons all use such control. The paper is a methods contribution with wide reach.
plos-pone-0007749:
Kwame Shanaube and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It measures the yearly risk of TB infection in Zambia and South Africa. Both countries carry heavy burdens of TB and HIV. The yearly risk figure is a key sign of how fast TB spreads in a community.

Surveys use the tuberculin skin test to estimate how many people are infected. Several methods can turn those test results into a risk figure. The authors compare what the methods imply in high-burden settings. Choosing the right method matters, since health programs plan around this number.
plos-pone-0007849:
John Waitumbi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It checks whether a malaria vaccine changes which parasite strains infect trial volunteers. The vaccine candidate, RTS,S, is built in yeast from part of a parasite surface protein. It is joined to a hepatitis B protein, and mixed with strong boosters called adjuvants.

The team compared parasite genotypes in adults given two vaccine formulas. They used the AS02A and AS01B adjuvant versions. If a vaccine blocks only strains matching its design, other strains may fill the gap. Tracking that shift early helps vaccine makers judge strain-specific protection.
plos-pone-0007949:
Eunsun Lee and colleagues studied a protein that can hold back cancer spread, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein, Nm23-H1, also does plain housekeeping work in cells and can switch genes on. Much about how the cell steers its many jobs stayed unclear.

The team found the steering comes from the cell's redox system, the set of reactions that add or remove oxygen-based tags. As that balance shifts, the protein's jobs shift with it. The link ties the protein's fight against tumor spread to the cell's inner chemistry, a tie drug makers may be able to use.
plos-pone-0008049:
Chengyun Li and colleagues put mixed planting to a large field test in PLOS ONE in 2009. Farmers have long grown several crops in one field, in rows or in turns, claiming bigger harvests and less disease. Hard proof at real farm scale was thin.

Field trials across wide areas showed the mixes did yield more than single crops grown alone. Diversity in the field paid in grain, not just in theory. At a time of tight land and food demand, the result backs a cheap, low-tech way to grow more on the same ground.
plos-pone-0008149:
Agnieszka Klosowska-Wardega and colleagues lowered the fluid pressure inside mouse tumors with a paired drug attack in PLOS ONE in 2009. Solid tumors build leaky vessels and trap fluid, so pressure inside runs high. High pressure keeps chemotherapy from soaking in, a plain physical bar to cure.

Blocking two vessel growth signals at once, PDGF and VEGF, dropped that pressure in mouse carcinomas. With the pressure down, drugs should reach more of the tumor. The pairing offers a way to open the door before the real medicine knocks. Timing the pairing well will be the next test.
plos-pone-0008249:
Gisela Pöll and colleagues studied ribosome building in yeast in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Ribosomes are the cell's protein-making machines. The large subunit contains three ribosomal RNAs and about forty-six proteins. Assembly is dynamic and involves more than one hundred fifty helper proteins. The team depleted yeast cells of large subunit proteins to see what happens.

They tracked how ribosomal RNA matures when those proteins are missing. Each missing protein stalls the process in revealing ways. Mapping those stalls shows the order of assembly steps. The work is basic research on how every cell builds its core machinery.
plos-pone-0008349:
David N. Ruskin, Masahito Kawamura, and Susan A. Masino fed rats a special diet in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The ketogenic diet is high in fat and low in carbohydrate. It forces cells to burn ketones rather than glucose. Clinically, the diet has proven effective for pediatric epilepsy and type II diabetes. Its wider effects were under study.

Rats on the diet showed reduced pain and inflammation. Both juvenile and adult animals benefited in their tests. A diet that eases pain without drugs would be valuable. The findings support more research on ketogenic therapy.
plos-pone-0008449:
Stuart Edelstein and co-authors write on signal systems in cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Cells sense signals when molecules bind to receptors on their surface. Often the binding is cooperative, so one binding helps the next. In the body, signal levels are often close to the level that half fills the receptors. At such levels, using up the signal matters.

The authors show that ligand depletion changes the range of signals a cell can sense. It also changes how sharp the response is. Their model helps explain real cell behavior. Lab tests that ignore depletion may give a false picture.
plos-pone-0008549:
Daniel Fernandez-Ayala and co-authors profile gene expression in a fly model in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. A point mutation in the fly gene technical knockout causes mitochondrial disease. That gene encodes a mitochondrial ribosomal protein called S12. Mutant flies show respiratory chain deficiency and developmental delay. They also show neurological abnormalities similar to human mitochondrial patients. The team measure gene expression across the whole genome in these flies.

Their profile shows which genes rise or fall when mitochondria fail. Coordinated changes reveal how cells compensate for lost energy. Some changes may themselves drive symptoms such as neurological problems. The fly model helps dissect human mitochondrial disease mechanisms.
plos-pone-0008649:
KyeongJin Kim and co-authors study a hepatitis B protein and insulin in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Hepatitis B virus X protein is a viral regulator made in infected liver cells. Diabetes and insulin resistance are more common in hepatitis B patients. The authors' abstract centers on hepatic insulin signaling, the liver's response to insulin. Two molecules feature in that signaling: IRS1, a relay protein, and SOCS3, a suppressor of signaling. The team test how the X protein affects both.

They find the X protein impairs hepatic insulin signaling. It does so through degradation of IRS1 and induction of SOCS3. Both hits weaken the insulin message in liver cells. That mechanism links chronic hepatitis B to diabetes risk.
plos-pone-0008749:
Eric Grossman, David Lee, Jing Tao, and colleagues asked whether steady blood sugar helps insulin cells regrow. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Insulin-making beta cells sit in the pancreas. A toxin called streptozotocin kills many of them, modeling diabetes. Some beta cells regrow afterward. Conditions favoring that regrowth could matter for patients.

Diabetic mice received insulin treatment to hold sugar near normal. Their beta cells regenerated better than in untreated mice. Good sugar control itself seems to create a friendlier setting for regrowth. The finding supports tight control as more than damage prevention.
plos-pone-0008849:
Siddharth Pathi, Christine Kowalczewski, Ramya Tadipatri, and colleagues built a mineralized 3-D model of tumors spreading to bone. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Advanced breast cancer often spreads into bone, causing pain and fractures. Bone mineral, called hydroxyapatite, may itself encourage that spread. Flat dish cultures cannot capture a mineral setting. A three-dimensional mineral culture was needed.

Cancer cells grew within the mineralized scaffold in bone-like conditions. The model lets researchers watch tumor-bone interactions directly. Drug tests in realistic settings beat tests on plastic. The system should speed the search for treatments against bone metastasis.
plos-pone-0008949:
Danny Bitton and colleagues built a pipeline to hunt for unknown human proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Protein studies usually match lab readings against lists of already known proteins. Anything not on the list stays invisible, even if the genome truly encodes it. The team instead searched readings against the whole human genome, translated in the computer.

Their pipeline filtered the flood of matches down to credible new coding regions. Several stretches of DNA, not listed as genes, showed real protein evidence. Each find adds a piece to the map of what human DNA actually makes. A fuller protein map sharpens both basic biology and disease gene hunts.
plos-pone-0009049:
Rachel Jenkins and co-authors counted how doctor migration drains psychiatrists from poorer countries, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Health workers have long left poorer countries to work in rich ones. Donor countries lose staff their health systems badly need. Psychiatry, already short-staffed, was the paper's focus.

The team used international data to trace where psychiatrists trained and where they practise. Poor countries train doctors who then serve wealthy health systems. The imbalance leaves mental health care thinnest where burdens are growing. The census gives policymakers numbers for a debate often run on anecdotes.
plos-pone-0009149:
Larissa Estes and co-authors asked women in an HIV programme how a talking computer interview felt, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Audio computer-assisted self-interviewing, or ACASI, asks sensitive questions by recorded voice. Answers given in private come out more honest than face-to-face replies. Few studies had asked the participants about the experience itself.

The women were taking part in an HIV-positive prevention programme. Interviews explored privacy, ease of use, and trust in the machine. Their views can make future surveys both kinder and more accurate. Good data on health and risk behaviour starts with tools people accept.
plos-pone-0009249:
Xu Dong and co-authors published this inflammation modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inflammation is a complex response that shifts over time and defies simple formulas. A single-variable model cannot capture its tangled feedback. The authors turned to agent-based modeling, where many simple actors interact in a simulation.

Their model follows human blood leukocytes exposed to endotoxin, a bacterial trigger of inflammation. Each cell in the simulation follows local rules, and the overall response emerges. Such models can reproduce the nonlinear surges real blood shows. They offer a test bed for ideas about sepsis and other runaway inflammatory states.
plos-pone-0009349:
Otfried Kistner and co-authors published this flu vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A new swine-origin H1N1 flu spread fast and became the century's first influenza pandemic. Vaccines were rushed from labs toward mass campaigns. The team's candidate used whole virus rather than split pieces of it.

In mice, the whole virus vaccine proved highly immunogenic, stirring strong immune responses. It protected animals given the vaccine directly. It also protected through passive transfer, where antibodies from vaccinated animals shielded others. Strong results in both modes supported moving this vaccine design toward people.
plos-pone-0009449:
Rauf Latif, Krzysztof Michalek, and Syed Morshed studied the receptor for thyroid stimulating hormone in PLOS ONE in 2010. That hormone tells the thyroid gland to grow and to release its own hormones. It acts through this receptor on thyroid cells. The receptor is a large protein that can join with copies of itself to form groups.

They found that one building block, a tyrosine, helps keep those groups stable. Small changes there can alter how the receptor is built after it is made. Knowing how the groups form helps explain faults behind thyroid disease. It may also guide drugs that aim at this receptor.
plos-pone-0009549:
Chungen Pan and co-authors read the genome of the 2009 pandemic flu virus in PLOS ONE in 2010. The virus, a swine origin H1N1, caused the first flu pandemic of the century. What let it pass so well from person to person was unclear. The team analyzed the pattern of its genome and how its mutations trended over time.

Certain genomic marks set the pandemic strain apart from seasonal strains. Tracking how those marks change helps trace the virus's adaptation to people. Such clues could flag dangerous strains earlier in future outbreaks. The work turns sequence data into an early warning tool.
plos-pone-0009649:
Rachel Schwartz and Rachel Mueller issued a warning to evolution researchers in PLOS ONE in 2010. Molecular clocks estimate species split times from DNA change rates. Those rates are often said to vary between lineages. The team simulated DNA data that evolved at a perfectly steady rate. They then ran standard tests for rate variation on that clock like data.

The tests wrongly reported variation that was not there. In other words, the method can invent the pattern it seeks. That is a sobering result for a widely used tool. It calls for caution and better tests before claims about uneven clocks are believed.
plos-pone-0009749:
Hector Hernandez-Vargas and co-authors published a cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study maps DNA methylation, a chemical tag on genes, in liver cancer, a fast and late-found disease. The team compared tags in 30 tumors with tags in the tissue around them.

One tag pattern marked liver cancer apart from nearby tissue and from other tumor types, whatever the cause. A second set of tags tracked tumor growth and risk factors such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and alcohol use. A third set was strongly tied to how long patients lived after treatment.
plos-pone-0009849:
Cells must copy their centrioles once, and only once, before dividing. Annekatrin Krause and Ingrid Hoffmann found a trigger for that copying step. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Centrioles are small barrels that help organize cell division.

The trigger runs through polo-like kinase 2, an enzyme that tags other proteins. It phosphorylates NPM, also called B23, on serine 4, adding a phosphate group at one spot. That single tag sets centriole duplication in motion. Precise control keeps cells from copying their division machinery too often. Errors here can leave cells with too many or too few centrioles.
plos-pone-0009949:
Arrow worms are glassy predators that drift in every ocean, yet their species are hard to tell apart. Robert Jennings, Ann Bucklin, and Annelies Pierrot-Bults used DNA barcodes to sort them. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Barcoding reads a short standard gene to identify a species. Samples came from three oceans, giving a wide view of genetic diversity. Arrow worms form the phylum Chaetognatha, an enigmatic group whose evolution is still debated. Genetic data reveal hidden species and redraw the phylum's story. Arrow worms snatch small prey with hooks by the mouth.
plos-pone-0010049:
The authors were Jason Schmidberger, Mark Bate, Cyril Reboul, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper presented software called MrGrid. Solving a protein structure by crystallography can demand heavy computing. Hard cases run faster on high-performance machines, but those machines are not easy for many labs to use.

MrGrid is a portable pipeline for molecular replacement, a common crystallography method. That method uses a known related structure to help solve a new one. A portable, grid-based tool lets more researchers bring big computing power to difficult structures. The authors describe the design for use across different computer systems.
plos-pone-0010149:
The authors were Xiaolin Luo, Qiurong Ding, Min Wang, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study altered a signaling pathway in mouse airways. TGF-beta signaling helps keep airway lining tissue stable. It also plays a role in cancers arising from such lining tissue. Asthma research on it had focused mostly on immune cells.

By disrupting the pathway with a blocker protein called Smad7, the team eased allergic asthma. The same change, though, aggravated lung cancer development in the mice. That trade-off warns that asthma treatments touching this pathway need careful cancer watching.
plos-pone-0010249:
The authors were Christian Willberg, Keith Garrison, R. Brad Jones, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study followed immune responses in early HIV infection. One gene variant, HLA-B35-Px, is tied to rapid HIV progression. A close variant, HLA-B35-Py, lacks that bad record, and the contrast between them has long puzzled HIV researchers.

The team tracked killer T cell responses restricted by these variants over time. Rapidly progressing patients recognized vestigial epitopes, leftover viral targets of little use. That misdirected response may help explain why this variant offers such poor protection.
plos-pone-0010349:
Shubha Gopal, Daniela Berg, Nicole Hagen and others studied how Listeria bacteria eat sugars, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Listeria monocytogenes can cause severe food-borne illness. In soil, water, and the gut, these bacteria meet complex sugars such as maltose and maltodextrin. Using such foods takes special intake machinery. The team set out to find and test that machinery.

They showed the bacteria rely on a switchable transport system to pull these sugars inside. The system belongs to a large family of molecular pumps. It stays off when glucose, a simpler sugar, is present. That order of use is common in bacteria: eat the easy food first. Knowing the intake route may help predict where Listeria thrives.
plos-pone-0010449:
Johan Lundberg, Stefan Jonsson and Staffan Holmin developed a new way to exit blood vessels from inside, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Reaching organs through vessels avoids big surgical cuts. Some organs, though, sit in spots surgery reaches poorly. The team proposed punching out through the vessel wall itself, under control, to reach tissue beyond. They built the tools and tested the method stepwise.

Testing moved from a simulator to rats, then rabbits, with full clinical-style integration. Each stage checked that the exit could be made and sealed safely. A working transvascular route could open treatments for hard-to-reach tumors or organs. It is an engineering-heavy study, unusual among biology papers. The goal is simple: turn blood vessels into doorways, not just roads.
plos-pone-0010549:
Jessica Jordão and colleagues used focused ultrasound to deliver antibodies into mouse brains and shrink Alzheimer's plaques in PLOS ONE in 2010. Antibody treatment for Alzheimer's relies on antibodies that clear toxic amyloid from the brain. Most injected antibody never crosses the blood-brain barrier. Earlier work injected it directly into the brain, which is impractical for patients. Guided ultrasound can open the barrier briefly at chosen spots.

With ultrasound targeting, blood-borne antibodies reached the brain and plaque load fell. The mice carried a strong Alzheimer's model mutation. Non-invasive delivery is the breakthrough this approach promises. Safety of repeated barrier opening remains the key question. Still, the study shows a path around a famous obstacle.
plos-pone-0010649:
Kim Appler and colleagues tracked West Nile virus in mice long after the first illness, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most RNA virus infections clear within weeks. Reports in people hinted that West Nile virus, carried by mosquitoes, might not always leave.

The team searched the brain, spinal cord, and other organs over a long follow-up. Viral material persisted in the central nervous system and in some outside tissues. Lingering virus could help explain lasting symptoms some patients report after recovery. The mouse work gives doctors a model for studying those long tails of infection.
plos-pone-0010749:
Sheila McKenna and Peter Etnoyer surveyed stony corals on Saba Bank, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bank's reefs face damage from shipping, above all from anchors of tankers serving nearby oil terminals. Drawing zones that protect the richest reefs requires a map of what lives where.

The rapid survey recorded coral species and reef condition across the bank. Some areas held far richer and healthier coral growth than others. Those hotspots now stand out on the map. A baseline survey taken before zoning lets officials judge later whether the zones actually protect the corals they were drawn around.
plos-pone-0010849:
Robert Castellino, Benjamin Barwick, Matthew Schniederjan and co-authors published this mouse cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Medulloblastoma is a brain tumor of childhood, and two growth pathways, called PI-3 kinase and sonic hedgehog, are both known to feed it. The team crossed mice prone to these tumors through the hedgehog route with mice lacking one copy of Pten, a gene that normally restrains the other pathway.

Losing even one copy of Pten doubled the share of mice showing tumor symptoms and cut survival. Tumors in these mice showed stronger PI-3 kinase signaling and more blood vessel growth, while hedgehog-linked genes fell quieter. Castellino and colleagues show the two pathways do not simply add up; weakening one brake reshapes the whole tumor. That insight may help doctors match medulloblastoma treatments to a tumor's gene profile.
plos-pone-0010949:
Daniele Dell'Orco, Martin Lundqvist, Cecilia Oslakovic and co-authors published this nanoparticle study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The moment a nanoparticle enters blood, proteins coat it, forming a corona that decides what the body actually sees. That coat is not fixed: proteins arrive and leave until a stable mix settles, and predicting the mix matters for medical uses of nanoparticles.

The authors built a simple dynamic model that forecasts the corona's makeup over time from each protein's binding strength, capacity, and exchange rates. They applied it to human plasma proteins meeting polymer nanoparticles of a defined size, adding new measurements for one blood fat carrier. Dell'Orco and colleagues give designers a way to anticipate a particle's biological identity before animal testing, a step toward safer nanomedicines.
plos-pone-0011049:
Henning Zimmermann, Sebastian Seidler, Jacob Nattermann and co-authors published this liver study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Liver scarring, fibrosis, is driven by macrophages that arrive as blood monocytes after injury. Mouse work blamed the classical monocyte type, but humans also carry a non-classical type marked by CD16, and the authors suspected that overlooked population does the damage in people.

They analyzed blood monocyte subsets from more than two hundred patients with chronic liver disease and nearly as many healthy controls. The non-classical monocytes were elevated in patients and showed inflammatory and scar-promoting behavior relevant to disease progression. Zimmermann and colleagues shift the human story away from the mouse template. If this subset drives human fibrosis, it becomes a measurable marker and a possible drug target.
plos-pone-0011149:
