Nakajima, Nishikawa, Iguchi and colleagues studied a reef coral in PLOS ONE in 2010. This coral releases spawn into the sea, so its young drift on currents. At the northern edge of its range, the team measured how genes flow between groups and how varied those groups are.

Their data map how connected these edge groups are to each other. Connection allows new genes to rescue a fading group, while isolation raises risk. Edge groups may also hold traits suited to cooler water. Protecting their links matters as seas warm and ranges shift, making this a guide for reef conservation.
plos-pone-0011249:
Howard and Merrifield mapped water dependent nature in California for PLOS ONE in 2010. Many wetlands, springs and riverside woods survive on groundwater rather than rain alone. The authors charted where such groundwater dependent ecosystems occur across the state.

Their map links hidden aquifers to visible wildlife habitat. When wells draw aquifers down, those habitats can dry out even far from the pumping site. Water rules that ignore this link can harm nature by accident. The map gives managers a starting point to protect both water supplies and the wild places that share them.
plos-pone-0011349:
Ann-Karin Olsen and colleagues examined in 2010 whether chemicals in the environment can leave marks in sperm that pass to the next generation. Damage to sperm DNA is linked to poor sperm quality and lost pregnancies, and some diseases in children begin as new mutations from the father. Earlier work by the group showed that rodent testis cells repair bulky DNA damage poorly.

The team tracked chemical tags stuck to DNA in mouse sperm and the rise of fresh mutations as sperm were being made. Their results connect exposure of the male germ line to changes that arise during sperm formation itself. That link matters for fathers as well as mothers. Safety testing that only watches the exposed animal may miss harm that surfaces in its offspring, so the paper argues for watching sperm directly.
plos-pone-0011449:
Jiaxing Zhang and co-authors used brain imaging in 2010 to watch how the brain changes as people adjust to high altitude. Moving to thin air starves the brain of oxygen, and newcomers suffer headaches and poor sleep before adapting over weeks. Whether the brain's very structure remodels during that adaptation, beyond short-term chemical shifts, was not well charted.

Scans taken as lowlanders acclimatized showed measurable structural changes in the brain over the adjustment period. The brain thus physically rebuilds part of itself under oxygen stress, not merely coping minute by minute. Documenting that remodeling helps explain altitude sickness and why some people adapt slowly. It also reveals a broader capacity of the adult brain to reshape its structure when the environment demands it, a hopeful sign for rehabilitation science.
plos-pone-0011549:
Kinga Gawlik and co-authors dissected in 2010 which parts of a muscle glue protein can substitute for a missing relative. Laminins glue muscle fibers to their surroundings, and loss of the alpha2 chain causes a severe congenital muscular dystrophy. A related chain, alpha1, can partly rescue the defect in mice, and the team tested which of its globular domains, its bead-like end sections, do the rescuing.

Different domains carried distinct roles in the rescue, with some sections essential and others dispensable. A domain-by-domain map tells protein engineers exactly which pieces a replacement therapy must include. That precision matters for designing shortened substitute proteins small enough to deliver as gene therapy. Children with this dystrophy have few options, so a parts list for a working patch is real progress toward a treatment.
plos-pone-0011649:
Sanne van Kampen and colleagues reported the view from national tuberculosis programmes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. New TB tests are approved at global level faster than countries can put them to work. The Stop TB Partnership needed first-hand information on how far national programmes had got with new diagnostic recommendations.

The authors gathered the programmes' own perspective on adopting new tools. Their account flags practical hurdles, from supply and training to funding, that slow adoption. Closing the gap between a recommended test and a test in routine use is essential if better diagnostics are to save lives.
plos-pone-0011749:
Patric Delhanty and co-authors studied an overlooked form of the hunger hormone ghrelin, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Unacylated ghrelin appears to improve insulin sensitivity and blood sugar control. How it acts is not fully understood, because no receptor for this form has been discovered.

Working in mice lacking the known ghrelin receptor, the team showed the unacylated form rapidly changes gene expression for fat making and insulin signalling in active tissues. Effects without the known receptor imply a second signalling route. Finding it could open new approaches to diabetes and weight control.
plos-pone-0011849:
Munyaradzi Dimairo and colleagues followed patients in Harare, Zimbabwe, for twelve months in a study published in 2010. The patients were suspected of having tuberculosis, but the standard sputum smear test came back negative. Such smear-negative cases have grown common where HIV is widespread, and they are hard for clinics to judge.

The cohort was tracked to measure how many of these suspects were later diagnosed with tuberculosis, and how long that took. Knowing the risk and the timing helps clinics decide how long to keep watching people whose first test misses the disease. In places with limited labs, that timing can decide who gets treatment early and who falls through the cracks.
plos-pone-0011949:
Nathanael McCurley and Ira Mellman compared in 2010 how different human dendritic cells digest what they capture. Dendritic cells present pieces of invaders to the immune system, and careful, limited digestion is their trademark: too much breakdown destroys the evidence. Mouse work had suggested their lysosomes carry unusually few cutting enzymes.

Measuring lysosomal proteolysis across human dendritic cell populations, the team found that cells derived from monocytes digest considerably more than the others. Human populations thus differ from each other, and from the mouse picture. Those differences matter for vaccine design, since the cell type chosen to carry a vaccine shapes how its cargo gets presented.
plos-pone-0012049:
Peter Skorupski and Lars Chittka charted in 2010, with care, the full range of light that the eyes of a bumblebee can catch. The bee kind they used has become a workhorse for tests of how bees see color, and for maze and choice tests that lean on bees telling one hue from the next. Oddly, the base data were not on hand: no one had set down how each of the bee's three eye cell types replies across the whole range of light.

Their tests now give those reply curves in full, from the far red end down into the deep violet rays that we cannot see at all. Choice tests in the lab are only as sound as these curves. With them, a lab can say at last what a bee sees when it picks a bloom, not what a human would guess it sees.
plos-pone-0012149:
Jialei Xie, Igor Vilchez, and Mariana Mateos studied a fruit fly, its tenant bacteria, and a parasitic wasp in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many insects carry bacteria passed down from mother to offspring. Some of these tenants are optional extras, neither clearly helpful nor required, which raises the question of how they persist in wild populations at all.

The fly's Spiroplasma bacteria turned out to protect their host when a parasitic wasp attacked. Wasps lay eggs inside fly larvae, and the bacteria improve the fly's odds of surviving that attack. A defense service like this explains why the bacteria spread: hosts that carry them leave more offspring where wasps hunt.
plos-pone-0012249:
Aniruddha Sengupta, Ulrike Lichti, Bradley Carlson, and co-authors studied selenium-related proteins in skin using mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Selenium in the diet protects skin against sun damage and cancer, and too little of it weakens the skin's antioxidant defenses; people lacking it can show skin and hair problems. The proteins that carry selenium do the actual work, yet their role in skin development was murky.

Removing those proteins in mice disturbed the skin cells' proper function and the skin's development itself. That proves the proteins are not optional extras but core equipment for skin. It also gives a biological basis for the skin troubles seen in selenium deficiency and in some inherited conditions.
plos-pone-0012349:
Ariel Pani, Holly Hobart, Colleen Morris and co-workers scanned the genomes of people with intellectual disability in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Learning disability affects a few in every hundred people, and known syndromes explain only part of the cases. The team focused on patients sent for testing with signs that hinted at Williams syndrome, a known genetic condition.

Using SNP chips that read many genome spots at once, they found rearrangements — missing, extra, or moved chunks of DNA — in several patients. Some changes matched known syndromes, while others were new. Each find gives a family a firmer answer and shows why broad genome scans help when single-gene tests come up empty.
plos-pone-0012449:
Ann Vanreusel, Annelies De Groote, Sabine Gollner and colleagues reviewed tiny worms living at deep-sea chemical sites, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Where methane seeps and hot vents leak chemicals, bacteria feed dense animal communities without sunlight. Free-living nematodes, the most abundant animals there, were the review's focus.

The authors ask whether the same nematode traits and species recur across such sites worldwide and what drives the patterns. Their synthesis shows both shared strategies and strong local differences. As mining companies eye deep-sea minerals, baseline knowledge of these fragile communities is the only way to judge what would be lost.
plos-pone-0012549:
Kelly Andrews, Greg Williams and Phillip Levin tracked sixgill sharks through seasons and life stages, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. How an animal moves decides where it feeds, mates, and meets threats, so movement data underpin conservation. Sixgill sharks are large, deep-living, and poorly known, yet they visit shallow bays where tagging is possible.

The team found movement patterns that shift with the seasons and as the sharks mature. Young and adult sharks use their habitat differently across the year. Such detail lets managers time protections, like seasonal closures, to when and where each life stage is most exposed.
plos-pone-0012649:
Kular, Gogliotti and Opal deleted a gene called Cpd-1 in mice and looked for effects on the brain. The gene's protein belongs to an old family involved in gene control, cell traffic and cell death. It shows up strongly in the developing nervous system, hinting at a brain role.

Their 2010 knockout mice showed only a mild nerve-related pattern, not the severe harm one might expect. A subtle result still teaches a lot, since it suggests backup systems cover for the missing gene. Such studies map which genes the brain truly cannot do without.
plos-pone-0012749:
Piekarski, Place and Zucker tested which hormone forms drive male sexual behaviour in Syrian hamsters. Testosterone runs this behaviour, yet its two main breakdown products each failed to do the job alone, even at high doses. Their 2010 study tried giving dihydrotestosterone and testosterone together.

The pair together restored full behaviour where each part alone fell short. Hormones often work as teams, and this case gives a clean example. The result refines how scientists read hormone replacement studies in other animals, including people.  Hamsters are a long-standing model for hormone and behaviour work.
plos-pone-0012849:
Mulrennan, Tempone, Ling and co-authors tested two standard tools against pneumonia from the 2009 pandemic flu. Early reports showed many pandemic H1N1 patients developed a viral pneumonia directly from the flu. Doctors needed a severity score they could trust and a reliable way to confirm the infection.

Their 2010 study found the CURB-65 severity score unreliable for this pneumonia, and nose-throat sampling likewise unreliable for diagnosis. Naming weak tools in a crisis is as useful as finding strong ones. Their results pushed clinicians toward better tests during that pandemic.
plos-pone-0319549:
Shruthi Venkataraman and colleagues used a national survey of over thirty-seven thousand American medical students. They asked how gender bias during training shapes a young doctor's growth. Students rated how often they were denied chances, insulted, or marked down because of gender. They also rated whether their school had raised them as people and as future doctors.

Women reported far more bias than men. About a third of women faced it, in single events or again and again. For men the share was about a tenth. Students of both sexes who faced repeat bias were much less likely to feel their school had fostered them. The cost showed in both personal and professional growth.
plos-pone-0329049:
Mary Elizabeth Snow and colleagues gathered lived accounts of forced psychiatric care under British Columbias Mental Health Act in Canada. Forced admissions have risen for fifteen years there. Focus groups heard twenty three people who had been held and treated against their will, led by facilitators with the same lived experience. Staff interviews added provider views.

Seven themes emerged. Voluntary options were scarce before crisis hit. Poverty, housing strain, and other social pressures deepened crises. Proof that forced care helps stayed thin in participants eyes, while harms touched patients and staff alike. Peer support stood out as a bright spot. Reform should grow voluntary, community care upstream, the authors argue, so force becomes rarer.
plos-pone-0333649:
Jose Manuel Burgos-Bragado and his team set out a plan for a trial in bowel cancer care. The trial tests work-out help sent by screen, with no live calls. Folk set for bowel surgery oft face a hard road back. Fit work pre and post surgery helps, but trips to a gym can block it. The screen route is meant to clear that block.

Fifty-six folk will be split in two groups by lot. One gets the screen plan: two weeks of work pre surgery, then four weeks post. The rest get the old book of tips. Walk tests lead the checks, with strength, sleep, mood, and life scores in tow. This is a plan, not a set of results.
plos-pone-0336549:
Bahari Yusuf and a team in northern Uganda followed newborns with birth asphyxia in 2026, watching their blood salts. Babies deprived of oxygen around birth often develop off-balance sodium, potassium, or calcium, which can worsen brain injury.

Term babies admitted to Lira hospital had blood tests on arrival and again over two weeks if they stayed. The team recorded mother and birth details, then modelled what predicts imbalance and how babies fared early. Such local figures help small hospitals, where lab tests are scarce, decide which asphyxiated babies need the closest chemical monitoring.
plos-pone-0336749:
Marco Alderighi and co-authors built an artificial intelligence system to predict tourist traffic in Italy's Aosta Valley. Their 2026 paper draws on more than forty-one million vehicle passages recorded at fourteen road sensors, combined with weather data and calendar information. The goal was forecasts that stay accurate when seasons change or sudden events disrupt travel.

The system blends four different prediction methods and constantly reweights them according to recent performance, season, and weather. In tests it beat every single method on its own, cutting average errors by roughly a quarter and holding up well through seasonal swings and extreme weather. Valley managers could use such forecasts to plan staffing, ease congestion, and size tourism facilities.
plos-pone-0339549:
Janet Kobusinge Lubega and colleagues tracked a warning sign in HIV care: virus levels too low to count as failure, yet high enough to hint that treatment may be slipping. Their 2026 PLOS One paper covers Ugandan children and teenagers from 2014 to 2023, using close to a million routine viral load tests.

The share of tests in this low range climbed from about one in ten to about one in six over the decade. The rise appeared in boys and girls alike and was steepest among infants. The authors say watching this signal closely could help clinics act before full treatment failure sets in.
plos-pone-0339949:
Md Khobair Hossain led a team of eight authors on this 2026 interview study inside a clean cookstove trial in Bangladesh. Families in the trial received liquefied gas stoves, and researchers interviewed mothers, husbands, and mothers-in-law about how childcare and housework shifted. The original trial targeted smoke exposure, not family routines.

Gas cooking cut cooking time and workload, freeing mothers to feed, play with, and watch their infants more closely and to juggle tasks with less strain. Hossain calls these spillover gains real but in need of measurement in future quantitative studies.
plos-pone-0340749:
Jonathan Mokhtar and colleagues reviewed nearly six hundred confirmed skin melanoma cases from a specialist lab in the United Arab Emirates from 2017 to 2025. The sunny, multi ethnic Emirates had little published melanoma data. Records covered ancestry, body site, subtype, depth, and invasion signs, with models hunting predictors of thick, dangerous tumours.

People of European ancestry made up nearly three quarters of cases. The spreading surface subtype led, and just under half of tumours were thin. Men grew thicker tumours than women and favoured the trunk, while women favoured legs. A nodular subtype overwhelmingly predicted thick tumours. Sun safety campaigns should target fair skinned residents and men most.
plos-pone-0342949: Chandroth and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on guarding smart home gadgets from hackers. Their system blends a deep neural network with a memory-based model to spot intrusions on consumer device networks. A search method named ACO tunes the system. As homes fill with connected devices, guards that catch attacks early without slowing gadgets down are in demand.
plos-pone-0343349:
Lwanga Nanziri and colleagues examine in 2026 whether phone based money improves life for women and young people in Mozambique. They used a large household survey from a fragile, post conflict country hit by climate shocks. Careful statistical methods tried to separate the effect of the service from who chooses to use it.

Active use, not simply holding an account, drove the gains. Households relied less on growing their own food, smoothed spending, and put more into schooling and health, often through money sent by others. Women gained more say over money. The authors caution that one key assumption behind their method cannot be fully tested.
plos-pone-0344449:
Abdullah Al Rakib and co-authors surveyed people in Bangladesh to ask why antibiotics so often fail against the germs they once killed. Their study links survey answers from more than two hundred and fifty respondents using a statistical model. The model tests how money pressure, weak testing, and mistaken beliefs about medicine connect with overuse of the drugs.

Money incentives, uncertain diagnoses, thin health services, and local beliefs all pushed people toward using antibiotics too freely. The authors argue that fixing the problem takes more than new drugs. They call for better testing tools, rules that curb needless prescribing, and public campaigns that correct common misunderstandings about when antibiotics actually help.
plos-pone-0344649:
Bennett H. Price and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on whether boat noise hushes the spawning choruses of red drum, a prized estuary fish in Saint Andrew Bay, Florida. Male red drum drum together at dusk in spawning season, and those choruses may guide reproduction. Underwater recorders listened across two seasons while the team modeled chorus loudness against vessel noise and weather.

In the first year, louder boat noise went with measurably quieter choruses, and earlier noise predicted reduced calling too, a pattern repeating in year two. At times the chorus dipped below its level just before a boat passed, suggesting fish quieted or left. During peak spawning months, vessel noise appeared in nearly a third of recordings, and on some dates in every single one. Chronic traffic noise, they warn, could be interfering with a behavior these fish need to reproduce.
plos-pone-0345449:
Sujesh Sudarsan, Jonas Van Caeneghem, Ramesh Vinayagam, and Raja Selvaraj turned almond peel waste into a sunlight-powered cleaner for dye-polluted water. Using peel extract as the only helper chemical, they grew flower-shaped zinc oxide particles at low temperature. The 2026 study characterised the material thoroughly, confirming pure crystals built from radiating rods, with a porous texture and a plant-derived coating.

Under natural sunlight the particles destroyed up to about eighty-two percent of a stubborn red dye in four and a half hours, driven mainly by superoxide radicals. After four reuse cycles they kept most of their power. The authors present the route as cheap valorisation of an agricultural residue.
plos-pone-0345549:
Bo Li, Wei Zhou, and Haijun Li built a hybrid AI model for medical scans. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The model outlines organs so doctors can plan treatment. One model family reads fine detail but sees little of the whole scan. Another sees the whole scan but costs heavy computing power.

The new design runs both paths side by side. A fusion step weighs fine detail against broad shape at several scales. On two public scan sets, the model matched expert outlines closely. One set held many organs. The other held the aorta and its branches. Tools like this could cut the long hand-drawing work in hospitals.
plos-pone-0345749:
Aya Atomi and colleagues present a 2026 PLOS ONE study of an exercise program done entirely lying on one's back. The program links steady control of the trunk with smooth, coordinated leg movements. The researchers tested it on healthy young adults because keeping the head, chest, and pelvis lined up is central to standing balance.

In one trial, seventeen men did the program ten minutes a day for two weeks, and a second study followed twenty-two adults with motion tracking during a side-step test. Standing balance, side-step movement, and seated trunk bending improved, while strength and power tests did not change. The authors suggest the safe, low-load routine could aid fall prevention and early rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0346949:
Fengjiao Han, Haiyang Guo, and Yang Zheng study air pollution's effect on people already carrying tangled heart, kidney, and metabolic risk. Their 2026 prospective cohort follows such patients at early disease stages. Five common pollutants were tracked: three sizes of airborne particles, nitrogen dioxide, and ozone. Heart disease outcomes were modelled against exposure, singly and as mixtures. Several statistical engines cross-checked the mixture results.

Single pollutants told a consistent story. Each step up in particle or nitrogen dioxide exposure raised heart disease risk by roughly a third to a half. Ozone alone showed no clear link. Mixture analyses weighed the pollutants together, apportioning blame among them. Lag checks guarded against reverse causation. These patients sit at a dangerous crossroads where hearts, kidneys, and metabolism all strain. Showing that the air they breathe pushes them toward heart disease strengthens the case for protecting this group first when pollution spikes.
plos-pone-0347349:
Frederick Daenen and colleagues interviewed people around Belgium's earliest-stage cancer drug trials: sixteen patients, five family caregivers, and dozens of doctors, nurses, and specialists. Patients in these trials have advanced cancer and slim prospects, yet palliative care, which focuses on comfort and quality of life, is rarely built into the trials. The 2026 study asked why.

Patients mostly prized the trial as a last chance that gave hope and routine. Comfort care, though, arrived late and reactively, if at all. Many confused palliative care with giving up, and trial teams and outside doctors barely communicated. Participants suggested making comfort conversations a normal, flexible part of trial care from the start.
plos-pone-0347549:
Jina Kim and co-workers read the full genome of a newly found freshwater bacterium from Korea and test what it can do. The microbe belongs to a versatile family known for useful chemistry. Their 2026 study assembles its single chromosome completely, proves it is a distinct species, and screens both its genes and its living behavior for valuable traits.

The strain fought other microbes, made compounds that grab iron, and broke down sugars with a wide enzyme kit. It also carried an unusual cluster for using urea and showed early signs tied to anti-obesity and antiviral effects. Lab-grown tests must still confirm much of this promise. Even so, the strain joins the shelf of microbes biotech firms may draw on.
plos-pone-0347649:
Kevin Siebels and his team mapped COVID-19 in the streets of Toronto. They split the spread into three waves, from late 2020 to late 2021. For each wave they asked which traits of a place drove case counts. The traits ran from pay and school years to home size and first tongue. Shots were weighed too.

The drivers changed from wave to wave. Rules on crowds, shop stops, and work from home hit groups in unlike ways. Low pay and low school years kept the worst risk in all waves. The team backs watch systems that track social facts with case counts.
plos-pone-0347749:
Rebecca G Evey and colleagues read the life stories of seven Rice's whales, the rarest baleen whales on Earth, written in their own baleen. Fewer than fifty adults of this Gulf of Mexico species remain. Baleen, the filtering curtain in the mouth, grows steadily and traps hormones as it grows, so drilling along a plate yields a timeline of stress and reproduction hormones spanning years.

Every assay worked on the species for the first time. Two whales thought to have starved showed all four measured hormones surging in their final growth, a pattern seen in other whales after long illness or injury. A female with a known recent pregnancy carried a long stretch of raised pregnancy hormone, proving the method can spot pregnancies. Male yearly cycles, by contrast, left no clear trace.
plos-pone-0347949:
Mariam Komeili, Jessi Robinson, and Hannah Akrigg set out in 2026 a plan for mapping Canadian writing on fair and safe speech language care. Their protocol covers work with Indigenous peoples and with other groups that face unfair treatment. Earlier reviews, they note, often mixed this field with other rehab fields or covered only one age group.

The planned search will cover both journal and grey sources across the whole lifespan. A scale running from basic awareness to full safety will guide how findings are sorted. The aim is a clear map of current practice claims and gaps, to guide teaching and future study.
plos-pone-0348349:
Emrah Altun, Fulya Gezer, and Hana Alqifari extend a classic income distribution model, the generalized gamma. Their version can deliver the standard inequality measures economists rely on: the Gini coefficient and the Theil, Atkinson, and Pietra indexes. Real income data often arrive grouped into brackets, so they estimate the model's parameters with a distance method suited to grouped data and check it in simulations.

They apply the machinery to United States income data from three different years, showing how inequality readings move. To make the method usable, they built a free web tool that computes the measures and draws the graphs for any practitioner. Good inequality numbers underpin tax and welfare debates, so lowering the technical barrier matters.
plos-pone-0348949:
Einat Sandbank and co-workers survey fish and tiny drifting animals across the Polar Front in the Barents Sea, where cold and warmer waters meet. Fronts often gather life, but the Arctic changes fast with the seasons. Their 2026 study pairs continuous sound and water recordings with net samples in spring, summer, and winter.

The front's grip on life proved strongest in spring. Fish and their tiny prey often peaked at opposite ends of the survey lines, and in spring the prey gained a refuge from grazing fish. Melting and forming sea ice also shaped where species gathered. Water temperature was the best single predictor of biomass, so a front famous for richness does not stay rich all year.
plos-pone-0349249:
Sajjan Kumar, Pankaj Kumar, and co-authors tackled a balancing act faced by solar power plants tied to the electricity grid. Plants usually chase maximum power, but the grid also needs spare capacity held back to absorb sudden swings. Their 2026 study proposes a controller that watches both sunlight and grid conditions, then decides how much reserve to keep moment by moment.

The controller blends flexible tracking with maximum-power tracking so the plant can switch smoothly between holding reserve and producing fully. Tests in both simulation and real hardware showed it reacting to live frequency changes while keeping output clean. Electrical distortion fell by more than half against one standard approach. The authors argue such dynamic control helps solar farms support, rather than strain, grid stability.
plos-pone-0349749:
Yuhui Gong and colleagues combined single cell and bulk gene data from glioma, an invasive brain tumour, to build a three gene outlook signature. Survival models with shrinkage selection landed on three genes tied to malignant behaviour. The score was checked in two large patient cohorts from the United States and China and explored for drug response and immune cell links.

The signature sorted patients by outlook in both cohorts. One gene, studied in depth, tracked with more suppressive immune cells and killer T cells alike in tumours, and its partners sit largely on immune and tumour cells. A compact gene score could sharpen prognosis talk and point to new drug targets in a cancer short on both.
plos-pone-0349949:
Annie O’Brien and co-authors re-examined a school social and emotional learning trial in 2026 through a multiverse lens. The question was whether pupils who actually take part benefit, an answer that depends heavily on how taking part is defined.

The original cluster trial covered sixty-two schools and more than two thousand children. The team pre-registered ten plausible model versions, varying five definitions of compliance and two cut-offs. Relational outcomes like bullying and peer support were then read across all versions. Showing every reasonable answer, rather than one chosen analysis, exposes how fragile or firm the intervention's claims really are.
plos-pone-0350049:
HPV testing usually needs a clinic pelvic sample. Many women avoid that exam. Self-sampling could widen screening dramatically. Nigus Telele and colleagues compared two self-collected options. One was a vaginal swab. The other was first-morning urine. Participants were girls and women aged fifteen to twenty-five.

About seven hundred fifty participants joined across three countries. They lived in Bangladesh, Nepal, and Pakistan. Each woman provided both sample types. One laboratory method tested every sample. Shared protocols kept the steps identical. The team measured detection rates and type-by-type agreement. The work feeds a wider project on HPV burden in poorer countries.
plos-pone-0350149:
Maad S Ytemi and A El-Shabasy led a field guide to five plant species in Saudi Arabia. The plants belong to a dry-land group called Commicarpus. They grow mostly in the west and southwest of the country. The species look much alike, so naming them takes care. The team compared stems, leaves, blooms, and fruits. They also sliced plant parts for study under the microscope.

Leaf and stem traits split the species well. The stalk that holds each leaf proved most useful of all. Pollen grains also differed in size, shape, and surface marks. Three species bear very large grains. The team built two keys for naming the plants. One key uses traits seen by eye. The other uses stalk anatomy.
plos-pone-0350549:
Valeria Caragli and co-authors compared doctors with ChatGPT on treatment choices for sudden hearing loss in 2026. The condition, a rapid loss of hearing without clear cause, demands quick decisions, often including steroids, and artificial intelligence advice is untested there.

Records of eighty-six patients were stripped of names and given to the model through staged prompts mimicking team discussion. Its suggestions were then scored against the treating doctors' actual choices. Agreement measures showed where the model matched human judgment and where it strayed. The study treats the tool as a junior colleague to be audited, not an authority.
plos-pone-0350749:
Borbála Német and colleagues validated a Hungarian version of the Skindex-Mini, a three-question tool that gauges how much a skin disease burdens daily life. Dermatologists need fast measures, and this one had only been tested in English and Spanish. Five hundred seventy-eight patients with a range of skin conditions filled it in alongside longer, established questionnaires on life quality, emotion control, and stigma.

The three questions hung together as one scale, sorted patients sharply, and behaved the same across different patient groups. Scores lined up moderately with stigma and distress, and stayed properly separate from general well-being. With reliability and validity in order, Hungarian clinics gain a one-minute screen for skin-related suffering, quick enough for busy visits and useful for flagging who needs a longer conversation about coping.
plos-pone-0351149:
Lu Xing and Xueqi Wu surveyed just under five hundred student preschool teachers in China during internships in spring 2024. Many early childhood graduates hesitate to enter the field, which threatens workforce supply. The survey asked whether feeling matched with a kindergartens values and needs linked with internship satisfaction, and whether confidence and felt skill carried that link.

Fit linked positively with satisfaction, confidence, and felt competence. Confidence and competence each carried part of the fit to satisfaction link, and a chain ran from fit through confidence to competence to satisfaction. Universities and kindergartens should match values early and build skills step by step, the authors argue, to keep interns in the profession.
plos-pone-0351249:
Zilu Shang, Yu Li, Yun Zhang, and Yajuan Gong trace one chain of events behind pain after surgery. Their rat study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Pain following an operation is a very common complaint. The team used a standard model. A small cut is made in a rat's paw. Then they followed an inflammatory signal called TNF-alpha. It travels into the cluster of nerve cells serving the paw.

The signal switches on a controller protein. That protein raises production of a sodium channel. The channel makes pain fibres easier to trigger. Blocking this chain appeals to drug hunters. A medicine could quiet the exact channel surgery leaves overactive. It would not need to dull the whole nervous system.
plos-pone-0351549:
Rating how good a photo looks, without a clean original to compare it with, is the problem Yanru Jia and Longsheng Wei take on in this 2026 PLOS One paper. Phone cameras and sharing apps need such automatic scores, but blur, noise, and compression each damage pictures in different ways.

Their method first trains a vision network that adjusts itself, then arranges sample images in a graph linking damage type, damage level, and picture content. On four public test collections the scores lined up with human judgments better than older hand-built and deep learning methods. Tests removing one part at a time showed each piece added accuracy.
plos-pone-0351649:
Shymaa Damfo and six colleagues combine case records with virus genomics to profile dengue fever in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Dengue has circulated in the country's west since the nineteen nineties, spread by mosquitoes and swollen by pilgrimage traffic, yet its local molecular picture was missing. The team reviewed confirmed cases from the first ten months of 2024 — citizens, residents, and religious visitors alike — and sequenced the genome of the commonest virus type.

Family trees built from the sequence place the Jeddah virus among its regional relatives and catalogue its mutations. Knowing exactly which strain circulates, and how it is changing, is groundwork for any future vaccine or antiviral aimed at this population.
plos-pone-0351749:
Heavy bleeding after childbirth kills mothers worldwide, and quick, skilled action saves lives. María Jose Montiel Bravo and co-authors present a plan, published in PLOS One in 2026, for reviewing whether virtual and augmented reality training helps health workers learn to manage this emergency.

As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet. It sets out which databases will be searched, which study designs count, and how bias will be judged with standard checklists. Two reviewers will screen studies on their own, with a third settling disagreements. The finished review aims to show whether immersive practice truly improves learning.
plos-pone-0351849:
Biao Wang and six colleagues build a prognostic model for glioblastoma around a new chemical tag on proteins. Their 2026 study concerns lactylation, a modification driven by lactate. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive brain tumour, with grim survival. The team merged single-cell and bulk gene data from public cohorts. Nine major cell types appeared in the tumours. One macrophage group scored highest for lactate metabolism genes. Machine learning then distilled the signal into a risk model.

Three key genes anchor the model, including one called CD93. High and low risk groups differed in immune cell infiltration and predicted drug sensitivity. The team validated CD93's behaviour in laboratory cells. Such a model could help doctors sort patients by likely course. It also spotlights lactylation as biology worth drugging. For a cancer where prognosis guides hard choices about aggressive treatment, even modest prediction gains matter to patients and families.
plos-pone-0351949:
Thong Duc Hong and colleagues used engine simulation software to find the best ignition timing for a diesel engine burning diesel-methanol blends. Methanol mixes change how the charge burns, so the spark of combustion must shift with blend, load, and burn speed. Their single-cylinder model, checked against real engine data within a few percent, swept blends up to half methanol across three loads.

For each condition they located the timing that maximized power and the timing that minimized fuel use per unit of work, then fit formulas tying those optima to the inputs. Burn duration ruled the answer, blend came second, and load mattered least, and the relationships were simple straight lines. Engine calibrators get usable equations rather than a lookup table, ready for controllers that must retime an engine as its fuel changes.
plos-pone-0352149:
Rahil Mirabi Moghaddam and four colleagues feed honey bees a special diet. It mixes helpful bacteria with the fibre that feeds them. The question was whether diet can armour bees against heat and cold. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Newly emerged workers ate the supplement for three weeks. Conditions stayed comfortable during that time. Then the bees faced cold, cool, ideal, or hot settings. Survival and antioxidant enzymes were tracked.

Bees on the highest dose survived thermal stress best. They beat lightly dosed and unsupplemented bees clearly. In unsupplemented bees, stress drove antioxidant enzymes sharply up. That is a sign of strain. Supplemented bees stayed calmer, in step with the dose. Their gut microbes were richer too. For beekeepers facing erratic weather, feed may be a cheap defence.
plos-pone-0352249:
Jean-Luc Jung and colleagues carry out in 2026 the first water DNA survey of marine vertebrates in the city waters of Abu Dhabi. The Arabian Gulf is shallow, very hot in summer, and salty, putting sea life near its limits while city activity adds pressure. Water samples from a marina, a new development, a seagrass bed, and a protected mangrove were screened for DNA traces.

More than eighty kinds were detected, mostly bony fish, plus birds, rays or sharks, and one marine mammal. Kind counts were alike across sites, but family tree diversity lagged at the new development and matched richness best at the mangrove. The method supports long term watching.
plos-pone-0352349:
Adrián Díaz-Faes, Pablo D'Este, and Anne Ter Wal study how scientists use their contacts while doing research. Their 2026 paper draws on detailed data from biomedical researchers. Two habits are contrasted. Some scientists hedge, asking several people about the same need. Others compartmentalise, turning to one specialist per need. Networks rich in diversity and gaps were already known to help. This study asks how people actually work those networks.

Hedging paid off. Scientists who consulted multiple contacts for the same resource more often produced high-impact work. The advantage held beyond the benefits of a diverse or sparse network. Under uncertainty, a second opinion is not indecision. It is insurance against one contact's blind spots, delays, or failure. The findings speak to research managers too. Cultures that normalise wide consultation may quietly raise the impact of the science they host.
plos-pone-0352449:
Melina Eitzel and three colleagues use volunteer observations to test whether California's marine parks change human behaviour. Their 2026 study draws on MPA Watch, a programme where trained surveyors record coastal activities. Twelve groups agreed the protocol across the state. From 2012 to 2020, nearly nineteen hundred surveyors logged over thirty-one thousand surveys. They counted more than a million actions at one hundred four sites, inside parks and outside them.

Fishing-type actions told the key story. Consumptive uses ran significantly lower inside the strictest parks than outside. Non-consumptive recreation, like beachgoing and tidepooling, showed no difference. The models corrected for weather, tides, timing, and beach features, and for the biases volunteers bring. Protection, in other words, is not just lines on a map. Ordinary people, watching systematically for eight years, documented that the rules change what visitors actually do.
plos-pone-0352649:
Rodrigues and colleagues showed how an HIV protein weakens the cell's virus alarm system in a 2026 study. The alarm pathway switches on antiviral genes when interferon signals danger. The viral protein, present early in infection and found in patients' blood, was tested in a T-cell line that makes it steadily.

Cells making the viral protein lost a key alarm messenger, which the protein sent for destruction by the cell's recycling machinery. With that messenger gone, interferon could not fully switch on its defenses. The finding helps explain why interferon treatment works poorly against this virus. Blocking the viral protein's trick could restore a natural defense line.
plos-pone-0353349:
Hongliang Sun and three colleagues optimise a factory wireless network. Part of it talks through light. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Ceiling lamps carry the light signals. A radio link backs them up. Several devices share one channel by power layering. Data travel in short packets to keep delay low. The design targets industrial machines. Such machines cannot wait, and cannot fail.

The team derived each user's odds of successful delivery. They defined the service capacity of each channel. Then they built an algorithm. It tunes packet length and power together. The aim is maximum capacity under strict reliability limits. In simulations the hybrid beat light-only schemes. It also beat simpler sharing schemes, especially with short packets.
plos-pone-0353849:
Ravikumar Chinthaginjala and co-authors present in 2026 a layered learning system for predicting how long people live in countries worldwide. Training used tens of thousands of country year records and many health indicators from the World Health Organization. The design stacks several models, adds an explanation method, and adjusts its own error ranges so stated confidence matches real coverage.

On held back test data the system predicted life expectancy within about a year on average, and its confidence bands hit their target closely. Most of the explanatory weight came from population and structural factors rather than single diseases. Planners could use such forecasts to guide health spending with clearer uncertainty.
plos-pone-0353949:
Tamar Zurashvili and five colleagues convene patients and providers in Georgia. Their task was to pick a support tool. It should help people with HIV decide whether to share their status. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Telling family, partners, or employers can bring support. It can also bring stigma. No decision aid existed for the Georgian setting. A structured consensus method worked through nine options. The group met in separate sessions, then a joint one.

Providers favoured digital tools for their reach. Patients favoured face-to-face sessions. They stressed trust and peer involvement. The joint session settled on a blend of both. Local content on law, treatment, and support will be added. Adaptation and pilot testing come next.
plos-pone-0354049:
Qiuyuan Peng, Minglin Wu, and Qiang Feng published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their subject is the sport industry in China between 2018 and 2024. The authors track how work and money shifted toward services inside that industry, and how much value each part of it produced.

Working as a longitudinal accounting analysis, the study follows the same industry accounts across seven years so changes can be compared over time. It looks at where jobs and spending moved as service activities grew, and at how strongly different segments added value. Readers in sport management and economic policy get a year-by-year picture of an industry reorganizing itself around services rather than goods.
plos-pone-0354149:
Yoon and colleagues, in a 2026 study, build a small device that measures radiation dose inside the rectum during prostate cancer treatment. Modern treatment gives radiation in fewer, larger doses, guided by MRI scans, so checking the real dose delivered near the rectum matters for safety. Their device pairs a radiation-sensitive plastic layer with a marker that shows up on MRI, held by an applicator made in five sizes.

One rubber-like material won as the clearest MRI marker. The sensing layer darkens in proportion to dose, its reading settles by two hours after treatment, and its uncertainty was small at clinical doses. In two patients, measured doses ran somewhat higher than the planning computer predicted, by a few percent on average. The authors blame placement wobble in zones where dose changes fast. They present the device as a workable in-body check for MRI-guided treatment.
plos-pone-0354249:
Mohammed Kanani and Ronald Kwon build in 2026 fully automatic tools for measuring body size and shape in adult zebrafish from three dimensional scans. Zebrafish are a major model for bone, muscle, and growth research, but measuring lean volume, body slimness, swim bladder parts, and standard length by hand is slow and varies between observers. Their methods combine built in functions of free image software.

Automatic measures matched hand and partly automatic measures well, while greatly raising speed and removing observer differences. The tools are released as ready macros for a popular image program. Labs can now gather body measures from many fish with far less labour.
plos-pone-0354749:
Kleber Resende Silva and colleagues dissected a small Amazonian plant that lives only on the ironstone outcrops of Carajás, Brazil, to learn how its body survives sun-blasted, drought-prone rock. Their 2026 anatomical study compared wild plants of this threatened species against greenhouse-grown specimens, tracking stems, leaves, and cell structure across wet and dry seasons.

Wild plants were armored: stiff, secondarily thickened stems, thick leaf blades, and mucilage cells riding the veins, none of which the pampered greenhouse plants developed. Dry season leaves lignified their bundles to hold even dying leaves up, and the species barely tolerated cultivation at all. Conservation, the authors conclude, means protecting the outcrops themselves, since the plant's adaptations are inseparable from its harsh home.
plos-pone-0355549:
Hannes Junker and Clara T Schoeder benchmarked the artificial intelligence tools now used to invent new peptide drugs for G protein-coupled receptors, the cell-surface switches targeted by a large share of medicines. Their 2026 two-part study first asked three structure predictors to reproduce ninety-one known receptor and peptide pairings, then asked three generative tools to design fresh peptides from scratch.

The sobering result: predictors often reported high confidence for peptides placed in the wrong position, and some outputs showed signs of memorizing known examples rather than inventing. Generators explored shapes well but wrote weak amino acid sequences, partly fixable with a separate sequence tool. The benchmark gives drug designers a realistic map of where these pipelines can and cannot yet be trusted.
plos-pone-0355649:
Yanjun Liu, Zanfu Ma, and Hao Zhan propose in 2026 a new way to read efficiency scores used to compare units such as cities or firms. Standard scores mix two things: how much a unit makes and how its inputs and outputs are valued by weights the method itself picks. Their work pulls those two strands apart.

Using a peer appraisal table, they build one index for amount related gaps and another for value related gaps. Tests on data from Chinese cities show how changing the assumed technology reshapes both parts. The point is insight into why scores differ, not a fresh ranking method.
plos-pone-0355749:
Yi Yang and colleagues worked alongside caregivers in China who raise autistic children, designing an education programme shaped by the caregivers themselves. Such programmes help families, yet little was known about what Chinese caregivers actually want from them. Their 2026 study ran two focus groups with fourteen caregivers, then showed the group draft videos for comment.

Analysis produced three themes about content and two about delivery. Caregivers asked for practical, everyday guidance and for formats that fit busy family life. The authors' central point is procedural: programme makers should keep asking intended users for input at every stage, not just at the start. The resulting design process itself is offered as a model for community-engaged work.
plos-pone-0355849:
Yang Geng, Jaap van Dieën, and Sjoerd Bruijn compared in 2026 how people keep their balance while standing and while walking. At first glance the two tasks look like versions of one skill, yet their study argues the body stabilizes them through different mechanisms. Standing balance leans on correcting sway in place, while walking balance is woven into the pattern of steps themselves.

Beneath those different tools, the authors find a shared aim at the level of the whole task: keeping the body upright and moving safely. The distinction matters for fall prevention and rehabilitation, since training that improves standing still may not transfer to walking. Their analysis gives therapists a cleaner picture of what to train for each.
plos-pone-0356149:
Hao Dun, Maura Sticco-Ivins, Gianni Bonnici, Hannah Beatty, and Benjamin Kopecky wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It presents a surgical technique for transplanting the aorta in mice. Their method uses a single aortotomy, one opening cut in the aorta, in an end-to-side connection.

Mouse aortic transplants are a standard model for studying vessel disease and rejection, but the surgery is delicate and slow. A simpler technique can make experiments more consistent between surgeons and labs. Cardiovascular researchers who run transplant models in mice are the readers who would adopt or test this shortcut.
plos-pone-0356249:
David J. Varricchio and Heath R. Caldwell published a 2026 paleontology paper in PLOS ONE describing the pelvis and hindlimbs of a troodontid dinosaur from the late Cretaceous Two Medicine Formation of Montana. Troodontids, small feathered relatives of birds, are usually known from scraps, so a growth series from embryo to adult is rare. The Flagg Butte material gives an almost full picture of this stretch of the skeleton for the animal they assign, following recent proposals, to Troodon formosus.

Bone shape stayed remarkably consistent across growth: most adult landmarks appear in the young, the real changes being robustness, fusion, and surface texture at predictable stages. Many foot bones showed pathology, a recurring oddity in troodontid samples the authors document rather than hide. Because growth changes so little anatomy, immature specimens elsewhere can be judged taxonomically with more confidence, strengthening study of large North American troodontids.
plos-pone-0356549:
Sydney F. Hope and coauthors published a 2026 animal cognition study in PLOS ONE testing whether Asian elephants can control an impulse, a basic executive skill. Sixteen elephants at Thailand's National Elephant Institute learned to reach around an opaque box to take food from a side opening. Then came a transparent box with tempting front holes, where success meant ignoring visible food straight ahead and reaching around, as before.

The elephants detoured around the see-through box about as well as the opaque one. That may show strong self-control, or the see-through cues may simply have been too weak to tempt them, and the authors hold both readings open. When the box flipped so the learned direction was wrong, hesitation jumped, proof a real habit had to be overridden, and performance recovered quickly across trials. Elephants now join the comparative map of how inhibition evolves.
plos-pone-0357049:
Mariam Adam Al-Hassan, Jodie Bigalky, and Solina Richter set out a protocol, published in 2026. It will map what helps or hinders pregnant women with dangerous blood pressure disorders. The focus is getting care in poorer countries. These disorders are leading killers of mothers and babies. Delays in seeking help are often the difference between a managed case and an emergency.

The team follows established scoping review methods. It has completed searching and screening the literature. It is now extracting findings on barriers and facilitators. These range from cost and distance to beliefs and clinic failures. No results are reported yet. The finished map is meant to show governments and clinics where the path to care breaks down. Fixes can then target the real obstacles.
plos-pone-0358049:
Yi He published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on spotting deepfakes, manipulated images and videos that fool viewers, without needing labeled fakes for training. Most detectors learn from collections of marked forgeries and still miss subtle edits. He's framework, SDDA, trains itself instead, comparing each image in two domains at once: its ordinary appearance and its frequency pattern, which records fine repeating detail.

Two encoders extract features from both views and an alignment step forces them to agree, while four custom measures flag inconsistencies in the learned features. A contrastive objective sharpens the separation between normal and odd patterns, and the author reports the system stayed robust under compression and lighting changes that often defeat detectors. In the reported experiments it beat leading baselines, especially on manipulation types it had never seen. The design aims at an interpretable detector that does not depend on huge labeled fake collections.
plos-pone-0358349:
Bahetibieke Tuohetaerbaike and colleagues charted in 2026 the course of tuberculosis across China and its Central Asian neighbors, looking back to 1990 and forward to 2050. Tuberculosis remains one of the world's great infectious killers, and this region carries a heavy and uneven share of it. The team analyzed trends in the disease burden across more than three decades of data.

They also weigh the drivers behind the trends and project where the burden is heading by mid century under current patterns. Projections like these let health ministries see whether control programs are on pace and where drug resistant disease threatens progress. The regional view matters because tuberculosis crosses the borders that the region's people cross daily.
plos-pone-0358449:
Monika Talarowska-Dublicka, Aleksandra Gapińska, and Maria Finogenow studied the roots of loneliness in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. They linked primal emotional systems, the deep drives wired into the brain long before language, to the modern sense of loneliness. Between the two sit early maladaptive schemas, lasting patterns formed in childhood.

The team's model traces how deep emotional wiring can harden into adult isolation through those schemas. That chain suggests where therapy might intervene: not only on lonely behavior, but on the schemas carrying the effect. Loneliness is now treated as a health risk in its own right. Work that maps its inner route gives counselors more than sympathy to offer; it gives them points of leverage.
plos-pone-0358549:
Shengxiang Ma and Wei Jiang published a safety study on subway operations in PLOS ONE in 2026. Subway crashes and failures rarely have a single cause; one fault can trigger the next in a chain. The authors set out to find which risk factors sit at the center of those chains.

Ma and Jiang combined real accident data with network analysis, treating each factor as a node linked to others. The factors with the most and strongest links are the ones worth fixing first, since they feed many kinds of failure. For transit operators, that ranking turns a long list of worries into a short list of priorities for training, checks, and design changes.
plos-pone-0358749:
Lin Qin and four colleagues test a waste based recipe for taming swelling soils, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Expansive soils swell and shrink with the weather, cracking roads and foundations, and the standard cements used to stabilize them are costly and dirty. Their binder, called LSP, mixes lime and sodium silicate into phosphogypsum, an industrial byproduct. Lab samples were then punished with repeated drying and wetting cycles to simulate seasons of abuse.

The treated soil packed denser, needed less water, and swelled far less, with the free swelling measure dropping from well over half to under a third. But the weather cycles bit back: strength fell by about a quarter after fifteen rounds, and water passed through more easily as micro cracks spread. Microscopy credited the improvement mainly to phosphogypsum grains physically filling pores. The study maps both the promise and the expiry date of a greener stabilizer.
plos-pone-0358849:
Rajitra Nawawonganun and two colleagues uncover a paradox for clean air campaigners in Thailand, in PLOS ONE in 2026. They surveyed five hundred fifty-seven parents of primary school children in Khon Kaen, a traffic heavy city in the northeast, during the hot, polluted season of 2025. The question was what drives psychological distress about traffic pollution: the exposure itself, or knowing about it.

Distress was widespread, with about sixty-two percent of parents moderately to highly distressed. The strongest single correlate was awareness itself, in a graded pattern. The more parents knew about air pollution, the more distressed they were. The most aware group carried over four times the odds of the least aware. Using an air quality app also tracked with distress. The authors name the dilemma plainly: education campaigns that raise awareness may raise anxiety too, unless paired with ways to act.
plos-pone-0359349:
Talema Moged Reda leads a team of eight in a 2026 PLOS ONE study mapping damaged land in Ethiopia's Southern Main Ethiopian Rift. Erosion and soil decline there threaten farming, water, and local livelihoods, and hot, salty ground adds stress that is poorly documented. The authors set out to chart where the land is most vulnerable so that limited protection efforts can be aimed well.

They combined satellite imagery from Landsat and Sentinel-2 with rainfall records, elevation data, soil information, and field checks, processed through mapping software and machine learning. Separate layers for erosion, land cover, vegetation health, drought, surface heat, and salt were merged into a single vulnerability map. The result gives planners a picture of which parts of the rift need attention first and where the pressures overlap.
plos-pone-0359549: Nguyen and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on why students say they cheat with AI help. The students were undergraduates reporting their own views. The team weighed five drivers: unclear ethics, what the tools make easy, gaps in school rules, study pressure, and comparing oneself with peers. Knowing which drivers matter most can help universities write clearer rules and fairer tasks.
plos-pone-0360249:
Alexa Keeling and Vijay Daniels published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Its subject is the neurological examination, the hands-on set of tests doctors use to check the nervous system. The authors study medical residents, doctors in training, and how confident they feel performing this exam.

Alongside confidence, the study looks at exam avoidance, the habit of skipping parts of the exam or the whole thing. Residents who avoid the neuro exam may miss signs of stroke and other urgent problems. Medical educators can use evidence about confidence and avoidance to fix training where it leaves young doctors unsure.
pmc-10336149:
Zhang, Xiao, Mao, and co-authors review how swelling and immune activity in the brain may help drive diseases that kill nerve cells. Their review covers Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, ALS, and Huntington's disease. Work in these fields once treated brain swelling as a late side effect of damage.

The authors argue the evidence now points the other way as well. Immune activity in the brain can help push the disease forward, not just follow it. That shift matters because it opens new treatment ideas. If swelling helps cause the damage, calming the right immune signals early could slow loss of memory and movement.
pmc-13127249:
Shreya Tiwari leads a 2026 review of molecularly imprinted polymers for targeted cancer therapy. Drug treatment is often limited by poor tumor selectivity, body-wide side effects, and drug resistance. Imprinted polymers are synthetic carriers molded around a target molecule, leaving shaped pockets that recognize it again, like a plastic antibody.

The review covers how imprinting strategy, polymer making, and nanoscale design set binding strength, selectivity, and drug release. Imprinting with small protein pieces, rather than whole proteins, helps target cancer receptors reproducibly. New designs respond to triggers or combine several functions in one carrier. Remaining hurdles include body safety, batch consistency, and meeting manufacturing and regulatory demands.
pmc-13192349:
Christoph Bueschl leads a 2026 software paper presenting AnnoMe, a tool for classifying mass spectrometry spectra in natural product discovery. Finding new compounds of a familiar chemical class requires sorting thousands of spectra into relevant and other, a task usually done by experts or by models trained on huge databases. AnnoMe lets users train their own classifier instead.

Users supply reference spectra labeled relevant or other, and the Python package combines them with structure-informed embeddings, numeric fingerprints of spectra, to train custom models judged by majority vote. A demonstration hunted prenylated flavonoids, plant compounds with an added carbon chain, for follow-up study. Code, documentation, and datasets are freely posted online, the authors note.
pmc-13195049:
Awadh M Ali leads a 2026 analytical chemistry study developing greener quality control tests for avapritinib, a targeted drug for certain stomach and gut tumors. Routine drug checking lacked convenient methods for this medicine. The authors built two high-throughput tests based on charge-transfer complexation, a reaction where the drug pairs with a colored partner compound.

Run in ninety-six well plates with tiny volumes, the colored reactions were measured by light absorption. Both methods proved linear, precise, and accurate across useful ranges, and computer modeling explained why one partner bound the drug more strongly. Ten assessment tools rated the methods highly green and practical, processing about five hundred samples an hour with minimal solvent.
pmc-13197649:
Suttitas Tongkamsai and colleagues tested drug resistance in a poultry gut parasite in Thailand in 2026. Coccidiosis, caused by Eimeria parasites, cuts chicken growth and farm output. Drugs in feed control it, but rotating drug programs have bred resistance, so the team checked three common drugs.

They gathered parasites from Thai broiler farms and infected test chicks under set doses. Four scoring methods rated drug performance, covering lesions, egg output in droppings, and weight gain. Two drugs cut lesions and egg output versus no treatment, but only partly. Results pointed to weakened drug response in the field strains. Knowing which drugs still work can guide farm prevention plans.
pmc-13198049:
Maria Zink and colleagues interviewed nurse leaders in Germany on pandemic workplace changes in 2026. COVID-19 forced fast reorganization in hospitals and long-term care homes. Nurse leaders drove much of that change, so the team asked which changes they judged a success and why.

Fifty-three leaders across management levels in Saxony took part, with added organizational data. Leaders rated thirty-six of fifty-one changes as successful. Wins clustered in infection control, staff scheduling, and teamwork. Good collaboration, leader backing, and staff drive aided success. Barriers included staff shortages, weak infrastructure, and mental strain. Staff acceptance tracked closely with rated success. The lessons may help build tougher care systems.
pmc-13198549:
Fabian Dellefant and colleagues present a 2026 method to read past fire temperatures from charcoal. Charcoal's inner structure changes with the heat that formed it. A laser method called Raman spectroscopy can read that structure, but past work was slow and prone to analyst bias.

Their calibration uses a pine wood reference set and a band ratio to estimate charring temperature. Set rules also flag crystal clustering and weathering by air exposure. A free web tool, CHARM, automates the full pipeline from cleaning to temperature output. Tests on ancient pottery gave sound readings with no sample damage. Volcanic charcoals also yielded readable ranges despite weathering. The tool suits both field areas.
pmc-13202049:
Hearing loss is a leading modifiable risk factor for dementia, and a 2026 study protocol by Lisa M Shulman lays out a three-year comparison of two hearing treatments. The protocol describes the ARCH study, which follows older adults using cochlear implants or hearing aids at an academic medical center.

The study will enroll 210 older adults in six subgroups defined by hearing level, device use, and cognitive status. Its main outcome is change in real-time, patient-reported listening experience gathered through ecological momentary assessment in daily life. Laboratory hearing and thinking tests, plus measures of loneliness, mood, and quality of life, support the comparison through completion in 2029.
pmc-13205649:
Newer tobacco products are popular with teenagers, and a 2026 analysis led by Jinyoung Kim links them to asthma diagnoses in South Korea. Drawing on the national Korea Youth Risk Behavior Survey from 2022 to 2024, the study compares asthma prevalence across patterns of cigarette, e-cigarette, and heated tobacco use.

The dataset held more than one hundred fifty-nine thousand students in grades seven through twelve. Asthma was uncommon overall, yet odds were higher for every user group than for non-users after adjustment in the authors' models. Teenagers using both e-cigarettes and heated products showed the highest odds, and the authors stress the design cannot prove these products cause asthma.
pmc-13206449:
Brain scans must correct for head size, and a 2026 study led by Aliza Brzezinski-Rittner asks which correction method distorts sex differences least. Working with UK Biobank imaging, the authors compare four ways of adjusting for total intracranial volume when estimating how male and female brains differ.

They built a reference standard by matching men and women on age and head size, removing the confound directly. Against that benchmark, simply adding head size as a covariate in the model performed best across brain measures and brain regions. Common smoothing of the imaging data could itself bias the estimates, a caution the authors raise for the field.
pmc-13207849:
An old blue dye might guard aging brains through surgery, and a 2026 review authored by Yu Wu builds the case for methylene blue. The article pulls together early and clinical evidence on perioperative neurocognitive disorders, which strike a large share of elderly patients after surgery and raise later dementia risk.

Proposed mechanisms converge on mitochondria: the dye can shuttle electrons, switch on antioxidant defenses, calm brain-cell inflammation, block tau clumping, and protect the blood-brain barrier. Small randomized trials report that one dose by vein during surgery cut delirium after surgery sharply in older patients having major non-cardiac surgery. The authors call for large trials at many centers to confirm dosing and benefit.
pmc-13207949:
Two decades of pancreatitis research are mapped in a 2026 bibliometric analysis authored by Chenlu Huang. The study retrieves basic research on acute pancreatitis causes and therapies published between 2003 and 2025 from the Web of Science, then visualizes authorship, institutions, journals, and keywords with standard mapping tools.

Six hundred thirty-two publications formed the dataset for the analysis. China produced the most papers while the United States carried the greatest citation impact in the field. Enduring themes included oxidative stress, a master inflammatory switch, and premature enzyme activation, while gut microbes, autophagy, and two forms of cell death emerged as recent hotspots for therapy ideas.
pmc-13244249:
Fatma Elnaggar and colleagues describe a nurse whose eye was infected by a splash of stomach-tube fluid at work. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Infectious Diseases in 2026. The forty-year-old, a contact lens wearer, was caring for a critically ill child when the exposure happened. Cultures from her lens and live microscopy revealed a four-way infection: the amoeba Acanthamoeba plus three bacteria.

Her cornea developed the ring-shaped marks and haze of advanced keratitis, and its inner layer began to fail. Strong anti-amoeba drugs and targeted antibiotics brought the infection under control. The price was heavy scarring, and a partial corneal transplant is now planned to restore her sight. The germs involved normally live in guts and hospitals, not eyes. The authors flag the case as a warning for eye protection and infection control among healthcare staff.
pmc-13244949:
Satoru Munakata and co-authors survey how mice carrying human immune systems have become central tools for studying immune disease. Their review appeared in Inflammation and Regeneration in 2026. Humanized mice are immune-deficient animals engrafted with human immune cells, liver cells, or thymus tissue, building an approximation of human immunity that ordinary lab mice cannot offer. The review traces progress in rebuilding a diverse human immune system inside the mouse.

Recent work layers in patient-specific elements, such as the self-attacking antibodies and T cells behind autoimmune disease, and pairs the animals with single-cell analyses of human tissue. Applications span modeling autoimmune conditions, testing drug candidates, and probing why therapies fail. The authors call these models foundational for both research and drug discovery. Their caveats are practical: reconstitution is still incomplete and variable. The trajectory, though, is toward models that fail less often for mouse-specific reasons.
pmc-13247249:
Bidard, Barrios, and Bianchini interpret a major breast cancer trial in this 2026 letter in NPJ Breast Cancer. The SERENA-6 trial tested switching treatment at the first molecular sign of resistance. When a blood test detected an emerging ESR1 mutation, patients moved early. They left an aromatase inhibitor for camizestrant, an oral drug that degrades the estrogen receptor, before scans showed progression.

The authors defend and explain that design. They argue it is proactive evolutionary oncology: strike a resistant clone while it is still small, rather than waiting for it to dominate. They address doubts about letting circulating tumor DNA guide treatment decisions. They also place the trial among recent setbacks for similar drugs used without targeting. Their reading aims to guide clinicians weighing the switch.
pmc-13248349: Yang and colleagues issued this correction in Cancer Cell International in 2026 for their paper on silencing the uracil-DNA glycosylase gene in colorectal cancer. One citation in the reference list was printed in the wrong form. The notice replaces it with the correct reference, a 2025 article analyzing the 2022 global cancer statistics report and comparing cancer burden in China with the rest of the world. No results or conclusions of the original paper change.
pmc-13249049:
Qi and colleagues followed a treat-and-extend injection plan for wet macular degeneration, in a 2026 Chinese study. Thirty-seven eyes received aflibercept shots, with intervals stretched or shortened by response, over twenty-four months. This approach aims to keep vision gains while cutting clinic visits, and the team also hunted for scan features that forecast success.

Vision improved significantly by three months and held through the study period, while the macula's central thickness fell. Two baseline features, that thickness and fluid under the retina, best predicted who responded well. The authors support using the starting scan to tailor how aggressively each patient is scheduled.
pmc-13249749:
da Silva Martins and colleagues tested semi-wild horses for leptospirosis exposure in Brazil's Roraima state, in a 2026 study. Lavradeiro horses roam Indigenous community lands in the northern Amazon, and leptospirosis, a waterborne bacterial disease, passes between animals and people. Blood from three hundred eighty-seven horses was checked against eighteen bacterial variants with the standard agglutination test.

About sixteen percent of horses carried antibodies, the first documented exposure in this horse population. Adults tested positive more than foals, and horses in flood-prone areas showed the highest rates, near a quarter. Strong reactions clustered in one municipality. The authors urge joint animal and human surveillance and protection of the Lavradeiro as a heritage breed.
pmc-13250549:
Harada and a large team trace how sesame seeds rebuild their protective lignan chemicals as they sprout. Their 2026 Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences paper covers compounds such as sesamin and sesamolin, long studied in seeds. During germination the oily lignans are fully converted into sugar-tagged forms, and the enzymes behind that switch were unknown.

The team found a family of oxygenase enzymes that rework sesamin and sesamolin into new oxidized forms during sprouting. Sugar-adding enzymes then tag those products in a set order, creating the final variety of glycosides. One oxygenase also proved central to making a key sesame lignan during seed formation itself. The work shows how plants reuse and reshuffle their enzyme toolkits as seeds develop and wake.
pmc-13253849:
Annika Schulte and colleagues study how cell junctions are built in a 2026 paper. Tight junctions seal the gaps between surface cells, forming a barrier and passing signals. The team asked how one junction protein, JAM-C, connects to ZO-2, a scaffold protein that links junctions to the cell's inner frame.

Cell tests and lab experiments showed JAM-C binds ZO-2 directly, needing two parts of ZO-2 working as one unit. JAM-C sat only at tight junctions in sorted surface cells. A sister protein, JAM-A, also lowered JAM-C gene activity, a finding the authors link to how junctions sense force.
pmc-13254149:
Trinari and co-authors pool trials of SSRI drugs for children with autism. Their 2026 review searches seven databases for controlled trials against placebo. Parents often face these drugs for anxiety, repeated behavior, or obsessive symptoms, with unclear payoff.

Seven trials with six hundred six children took part. Evidence was too weak to judge effects on repeated behaviors or anxiety, and weak data hinted at little effect on obsessive or disruptive behavior. Overall daily function likely barely changed, while side effects rose slightly. No trial tracked mood outcomes in this group. The authors conclude current evidence shows no benefit and urge case-by-case risk weighing until better trials arrive.
pmc-13254749:
Hannah Biemans, Astrid de Vries, and Reinoud Brouwer study cold therapy after partial knee replacement in a 2026 trial analysis. Patients used a cryo-compression brace, which applies cold and pressure, five times daily for six weeks, or got standard care. Pain, function, life quality, and oxycodone use were tracked.

At six weeks, pain at rest did not differ between groups. The cold group used 46 percent less oxycodone, though the absolute gap was small, at a median of 3.5 five-milligram tablets total. Work and life quality scores improved more with cold therapy but fell short of the meaningful-change threshold.
pmc-13255149:
Jose Alfonso Ontiveros and colleagues report four cases linking a depression drug to new symptoms in a 2026 case series. Bupropion is an antidepressant also used to help people stop smoking. Four patients with mood disorders, none with past obsessive symptoms, developed obsessive-compulsive symptoms after starting the drug.

Symptoms grew in intensity over time on the drug. After bupropion was stopped, symptoms eased notably and fully remitted over time. Standard scales tracked the symptoms and their course. The authors say the brain basis is not yet understood and urge clinicians to watch for this effect when prescribing.
pmc-13255749:
Valfré and colleagues tested how nursery enrichment shapes resilience in more than six hundred piglets on a commercial farm. Litters received a single chain, chains plus a weekly rotated extra object, or several objects at once.
