A subsample later faced an attentional bias test, while the team also scored behavior qualitatively and measured hair cortisol and a brain growth factor in blood.

Attention measures barely separated the groups, but coping behavior did: each treatment showed a distinct pattern of excretion, standing, or escape attempts. Piglets with several objects looked calmer and less tense, while the single-chain group carried higher cortisol and lower growth factor. Enrichment style, the authors argue, tunes stress biology.
pmc-13264549:
Irmand Leblond Mikiela Ndzoumbou and co-authors present a 2026 maths paper on networks of evolution equations, the rules that describe how quantities change over space and time. Older models often assumed every node in a network was the same shape and size. Their framework allows nodes that differ and links at edges as well as inside.

For the single-value case, they prove that flow is conserved and that one positive solution exists. For the multi-value case, they prove like results and show the total mass stays bounded when the system conserves mass. They test the theory on a predator-prey model with two nodes. Computer runs match the theory, and the authors offer the framework for spread and transport problems.
pmc-13264949:
Karoline Louise Imingen Selvik and co-authors wrote a 2026 Norwegian study on family money worries and teen mental distress. They compared what teens feel about family finances with official records of parent income and education. Data came from two waves of the Young-HUNT surveys, in 2006 to 2008 and 2017 to 2019, linked with parent data.

Each wave held more than 8,000 teens aged 13 to 19. Teens who felt their family was worse off than others reported more anxiety and depression symptoms, with the gap a bit larger in girls. Official parent income and education showed little or no link to teen symptoms. Counting parent mental health did not change the pattern, and results were much the same in both waves. The authors say felt financial stress, not recorded wealth, is what tracks teen distress.
pmc-13267549:
Dhathri Priya Bandi and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of gum bacteria in pregnant women with diabetes of pregnancy. Both gestational diabetes and gum disease involve lasting inflammation and may worsen outcomes for mother and baby. The team studied 80 pregnant women, all with gum disease: 40 with diabetes of pregnancy and 40 without.

Samples of plaque from under the gum line were tested for seven known gum pathogens. Women with diabetes carried higher loads of five of them, including Porphyromonas gingivalis. That species tracked closely with deeper gum pockets and loss of gum attachment. Gum measures and blood sugar test results both helped predict pathogen levels. The authors call the link between blood sugar control and gum microbes a two-way street worth clinical attention.
pmc-13267749:
Derrick Bennett and colleagues wrote a 2026 summary of a workshop on statistical reviewing for medical journals. Statistics in medical papers have grown more complex, yet journals struggle to find trained statistical reviewers. A national research group ran an online workshop to close that gap, aimed at people new to the task.

Statistical review checks whether a paper's methods fit its question, were carried out correctly, and are openly reported. The summary shares the workshop's key lessons and practical advice for new reviewers. It covers what to look for, how to write a useful review, and why this work matters for trust in medical research. The authors hope more statisticians and clinicians will take up reviewing.
pmc-13269049:
Natalia Quintero Serrano and Olga Lucía Melo Trujillo published a case report in 2026 about a 76-year-old man with gout. Soon after he gave himself one 75 milligram shot of diclofenac, a pain and swelling drug, he developed a severe skin reaction. The reaction, toxic epidermal necrolysis, makes large areas of skin blister and peel away.

At the hospital, sores covered 40.5 percent of his body surface, with severe mouth and organ damage. His risk score of 5 meant an estimated death rate of about 85 percent. He died soon after arrival despite strong supportive care. A scoring method rated the drug link as only possible, since other drugs were also in his history.
pmc-13269649:
Yair Alvarez-Ricardo and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on three new vanadium compounds built with ring-shaped partner molecules, tested against cancer cells. Their structures were checked with standard lab methods, and one was mapped exactly by X-ray crystallography, a method that reveals atomic layout.

Across six human cancer cell lines, the compounds beat the common drug cisplatin in five, needing lower doses to halve cell growth. One compound was strongest against a lung cancer line, and another against a colon cancer line. Unlike cisplatin, they barely harmed healthy fiber cells. One compound pushed lung cancer cells into late-stage programmed death without tissue-rotting death. Computer studies also showed the compounds stick to DNA.
pmc-13269849:
Luisa Di Paola and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on recovering a pigment protein complex from shellfish waste. Shells of European lobster and Atlantic blue crab hold astaxanthin, a pigment with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. Computer models examined how the complex could carry the pigment for drug and cosmetic use.

Simulations suggested astaxanthin would compete with a cell defender protein at its binding site. Freeing that defender would switch on the cell's own antioxidant machinery. Early lab evidence supported the modeling. The authors propose shell waste as a source of a bioactive agent for diseases tied to cell stress, including cancer. They stress that animal and human studies must first confirm the promise.
pmc-13270249:
Mariana Bastos-Oreiro and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on real-world use of bispecific antibodies in B-cell lymphoma across Spain's GELTAMO network. These drugs grab both a T cell and a cancer B cell to redirect the attack. Thirty-eight centers treated patients whose lymphoma had returned or resisted earlier care.

The study included 168 patients with a median age of 64, split 58 percent large B-cell lymphoma and 42 percent follicular lymphoma. Most, 86 percent, had a planned hospital admission during dose step-up, with a median stay of four days. Unplanned admissions hit 32 percent, led by infections in half of urgent cases. Twenty-nine percent of patients would not have qualified for the pivotal drug trials.
pmc-13270949:
Vincent L. Sorrell wrote a 2026 editorial titled Sound Waves, Rays, and Magnets, on multimodality cardiovascular imaging, the use of several scan types to study the heart. The title names ultrasound, X-ray based computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging, three tools he has worked with for over two decades.

Sorrell tells how mentors trained him first in ultrasound and nuclear heart imaging, and how he was once advised to pick one specialty rather than master both. Instead, he followed the growth of magnetic resonance and computed tomography, trained in London in cardiac magnetic resonance, and later added computed tomography skills for noninvasive imaging of the heart arteries. The piece is a personal career reflection.
pmc-13271149:
Niek Stevenson is lead author of a 2026 journal article presenting an open-source toolbox for joint modelling of brain scans and behaviour. Joint modelling fits behaviour data and MRI data, which track brain activity, together in one model. It accounts for measurement error and for differences between people.

Built into an R software package called EMC2, the toolbox streamlines building behaviour, brain, and joint models. The authors show it on a perceptual decision task done inside a scanner. They explain how to set up design tables, prior guesses, and brain-behaviour links. Joint fitting steadied weak values and cut a known bias that shrinks brain-behaviour links, they report. Code examples are included.
pmc-13271349:
Yi Zhou is lead author of a 2026 review on Fusarium oxysporum forma specialis vasinfectum race 4, shortened to Fov4. That is a highly damaging fungus that causes wilt disease in cotton, especially in the United States. The review gathers what is known from field disease through to the pathogen's genome.

Fov4 genomes are larger and richer in repeated DNA than those of related races, the authors note, though their chromosome layout is still unresolved. Studies have flagged candidate attack factors, including race-specific effector proteins and chemical-making genes. Because the fungus persists in soil and adapts genetically, control relies on mixing resistant cotton varieties, farming practices, and close monitoring, they conclude.
pmc-13272249:
Lena Marie Süß is lead author of a 2026 journal article on blocking P2Y6 receptors to slow kidney fibrosis. Fibrosis is the scarring that drives chronic kidney disease. That disease affects over 850 million people worldwide. Signals from released nucleotides through P2 receptors help activate the fibroblast cells that lay down scar tissue, but their role was poorly understood.

Using precise RNA staining, the team found P2Y1 and P2Y6 receptors in kidney interstitial fibroblasts, with P2Y6 sharply raised in several mouse fibrosis models. Cultured fibroblasts moved more when stimulated by a nucleotide signal. In a mouse kidney disease model, a selective P2Y6 blocker cut expression of a scar-cell marker and of collagen I, a main scar protein. They propose P2Y6 blockade as a new anti-fibrosis strategy.
pmc-13272549:
Ellis Eikenboom, Helena van Doorn, and Anja Wagner wrote a 2026 authors' reply about womb surveillance in Lynch syndrome in the Netherlands. Lynch syndrome raises cancer risk, and their earlier paper questioned whether regular checks of the womb lining help Dutch carriers. The reply answers comments on that paper.

They explain why the subtype of overgrown womb lining did not change their advice, since surgery is advised for any such growth. They note that more growths and cancers were found in the checked group, yet cancers were not less advanced in a way that cut later treatment or improved survival. A much larger study is needed, they argue.
pmc-13272749:
Fang Zhang leads a 2026 study of a protein called SEMA6A in colorectal cancer, cancer of the colon and rectum. The protein was lower in cancer tissue than normal, and low levels linked to more aggressive tumors and a poorer outlook. The team tested what raising SEMA6A does in cells and in animals.

Raising SEMA6A slowed tumors and boosted killing by CD8 T cells, the immune cells that attack cancer. It acted by lowering a protein called ISG15, which otherwise helps stabilize TGF-beta, a signal that shields tumors. Patients with high SEMA6A and low ISG15 responded better to immunotherapy, and raising SEMA6A improved anti-PD-1 treatment in mice.
pmc-13274549:
Xiaocui Ma and colleagues present a 2026 journal article on what shapes bird diversity in a small Chinese nature reserve. Louzishan, in Liaoning Province, offers a test of how plant productivity and habitat variety affect birds across seasons. The team surveyed bird communities in summer breeding season and in winter, scoring greenness from satellites as a stand-in for productivity.

In summer, greener sites held more bird species and more varied bird traits, and species replacement along the greenness gradient drove community differences. Winter flipped the pattern: habitat variety related negatively to species counts, and distance between sites drove differences instead. The authors read this as environment filtering birds in summer but limited movement ruling in winter.
pmc-13274849:
Madisen S Mason and co-authors present a 2026 protocol article for growing a deadly childhood brainstem tumor in mouse embryos. Diffuse midline glioma of the pons is considered universally fatal, and few animal models capture how it starts. The method zaps DNA into the developing mouse pons while the pup is still in the womb, using three electrodes for precise aim.

A single engineered DNA package carries the cancer's signature mutations, including the histone change H3.3K27M, into the progenitor cells lining the fourth ventricle, a fluid space in the brainstem. The embryos then develop large, diffuse brainstem tumors resembling the childhood disease in their molecular makeup. The protocol aims to speed study of the tumor's origins and of candidate treatments.
pmc-13276349:
Yuchen Ping and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on why a prized Chinese medicinal herb tastes of place. Atractylodes macrocephala, one of the famous Zhejiang herbs, varies in potency by region. Traditional thinking credits local soil, but the microbes living around roots may matter more.

The team transplanted herbs across China's four major producing regions. Soil from Pan'an, the classic home region, strongly boosted the active compounds in plants sourced from Bozhou. Gene sequencing of root-zone microbes showed moving reshaped the community and raised its diversity. Eleven bacterial groups stood out as keystone members, rising with the move. Their abundance tracked with root growth and active compound levels. The authors say soil nutrients, microbe-driven carbon and nitrogen cycling, and plant resource shifts together create the herb's regional authenticity.
pmc-13276449:
Dian Kusuma and Hario Megatsari present a 2026 journal article on whether local tobacco laws can cut teen smoking where national action lags. Indonesia has some of the world's highest smoking rates, especially among boys and men. Bogor City tightened its local tobacco rules from 2014 while national enforcement stayed weak.

The team compared Bogor with a synthetic control, a blend of similar districts among nearly five hundred nationwide, over a decade of data. Current smoking among boys fell by about fifteen percentage points versus the control, a cut of over two fifths. Ever smoking dropped by about twelve points. The gaps grew over time, suggesting lasting impact. Adult men showed smaller gains, and their current smoking stayed above the control. The authors back local action plus stronger national measures.
pmc-13277249:
Nevra Koç leads a 2026 study of appetite hormones and body weight in children with inherited metabolic diseases. The diseases covered, including phenylketonuria and maple syrup urine disease, force strict low-protein diets that can blunt appetite. The team compared 43 affected children with 40 healthy children aged one to eighteen.

Two hormones, peptide YY and adiponectin, were higher in the patient group. Other appetite hormones did not differ overall. Yet ghrelin, a hunger hormone, was highest in the thinnest patients. The authors link the shifts to diet, toxic buildup, and organ strain. They urge regular hormone checks and personal diet plans for long-term care of these children.
pmc-13277749:
Seyedeh-Zeynab Hosseinian leads a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of FODMAP foods and indigestion symptoms. FODMAPs are fermentable sugars and related compounds, found in many foods, that gut bacteria break down with gas. The team gathered trials, through October 2025, that compared a low-FODMAP diet with a high-FODMAP diet.

Twelve studies qualified. The low-FODMAP diet eased bloating and early fullness at meals compared with the high-FODMAP diet. Abdominal pain scores, though, ran higher on the low-FODMAP diet in their pooled result. Results varied a great deal between studies, and the authors rate the certainty of evidence as very low. More well-run trials are needed before firm diet advice can rest on this base.
pmc-13278449:
Yannick Elysée Ewane Epée leads a 2026 survey of snail harvesters along Cameroon's Atlantic coast, where giant land snails are a key protein source and income earner. Farming in the region uses more pesticides, raising fears for snail stocks and human health. The team interviewed 211 harvesters across six localities and observed their work.

Fifty-eight percent believed pesticides shrink snail size, while sixty-one percent saw no effect on snail numbers. Collection peaked at night and in October. Statistical links between beliefs and reported harvest amounts were weak, with perceived effect on quantity the only clear predictor. Despite knowing the risks, sixty-three percent had no interest in snail farming, preferring wild harvest.
pmc-13279149:
Sangho Lee and co-authors report a 2026 case, in letter form, of a skin flare tied to a drug for eczema. The drug is dupilumab, and the flare is generalized pustular psoriasis, a rare skin illness with widespread pus filled spots. Their patient was an eighty two year old man with a two year history of eczema.

Two weeks after he started dupilumab, red plaques with pustules spread over his trunk, back, limbs and scalp. Skin biopsy, meaning a small skin sample test, showed changes that fit pustular psoriasis. Swabs found no germ cause, and blood tests were near normal apart from mild shifts. Past reports of this switch are rare, so the case adds a clear warning for skin doctors.
pmc-13279749:
YanLing Yang and colleagues give a 2026 review of safety risks from oral nicotine products. Oral nicotine products, like pouches held in the mouth, form a new tobacco product class. As tobacco rules tighten and health awareness grows, their safety draws more focus. Regulators still lack long term data and full data on additives. The review joins chemical, animal, cell and human group data.

First pages list the main products on sale and their types. Next sections weigh harmful substances found in them and their levels. Health effects on the mouth and on the heart and vessels get systematic checks, with paths of harm traced. Gaps guide future work the authors propose. Clear risk sums can help users weigh use, and help firms and regulators set sound policy to cut health harm.
pmc-13280649:
De Mello and co-authors compare two fat-tailed peptides used in skin care. Their 2026 paper studies C16-KTTKS, sold commercially as Matrixyl, and a variant called C16-RTTRS in which one building block is swapped. Both molecules are reported to boost collagen, the protein that firms skin, but their assembly in water was less clear.

The authors measured how each peptide arranges itself across acidity levels and in two salt forms. The original peptide formed flat nanotapes across most conditions and round micelles only in strong acid, while the variant switched shapes depending on its salt partner. Both peptides were gentle on fibroblast cells at low doses. Each also stimulated collagen production in human skin fibroblasts at very low concentration, with no clear difference between salt forms.
pmc-13281949:
Ju Yeon Kim and colleagues set out a trial plan for herbal care of chronic back pain in a 2026 protocol. Chronic low back pain drags down work and daily life. Standard drugs and hands-on care often give only mild relief. Herbal formulas vary widely in Korean practice. The trial asks whether a flexible herbal strategy is no worse than standard Korean hands-on care. One hundred fifty patients with pain for at least three months will join many centers.

Half get herbal care fitted to each patient for thirty days. Half will get hands-on care twice a week for five weeks, such as needles, cupping, and heat. Raters scoring pain and disability will not know who got what. Scores run to week seven, with cost and harm checks. As a protocol, the paper reports no results. Its value is a fair test design for real-world herbal practice.
pmc-13282049:
Michele Francesco Chiappetta and co-authors tell of a 2026 case of a very rare cancer of the pancreas, the organ behind the stomach that aids digestion. The tumour type carries large, bone-like cells called osteoclast-like giant cells alongside shapeless cancer cells. Scans cannot reliably tell it from other pancreatic masses, so tissue proof is often needed. The patient was a fifty-seven-year-old woman with belly pain and cholestasis, a blockage that slows bile flow.

pmc-13285749:

pmc-13286549:

pmc-13287149:

pmc-13291049:

pmc-13291349:

Million Phiri and co-authors break down in 2026 why modern contraceptive use rose among sexually active women in Lesotho from 2004 to 2023, and how fair that rise was. Four survey rounds gave 22,325 women aged 15 to 49 years, and a split method parted makeup shifts from behaviour shifts.

Use rose from 36.1 percent to 62.7 percent over the span in the survey data for those years. Near nine tenths of the rise came from changed behaviour, not from a changed mix of women in the pool. More women with higher schooling drove the top share of the makeup part. Rich poor gaps shrank and then closed by 2023.
pmc-13308949:
Yuki Makizawa and co-authors report in 2026 two cases of acute aortic tear found during transcatheter valve work, spotted by a throat ultrasound probe while surgery ran. The patients, a woman aged 87 years and a man aged 90 years, each had hard device passage or a valve pop up during the fix.

The probe showed a flap and a false channel in the rising aorta before blood pressure crashed in either case. Both went at once to open surgery for valve and aorta repair, and both left hospital walking with no nerve harm. Hard passage alone should prompt a probe check, since other scans give only snaps in time.
pmc-13309549:
Mahmoud Abdelmagied and co-authors test a heat exchanger with a twisted coil tube in a 2026 lab study. Heat exchangers move heat between fluids, and twisting the inner coil should stir the flow and lift heat transfer. The team compared the twisted design against a smooth-coil version of the same shell layout.

Three twisted coils of differing widths were built and run under opposing flows across a range of flow rates. Heat performance and wasted-energy measures were tracked as coil width and flow speeds changed. Swirl from the twist added flow disturbance beyond the smooth design. The authors report where the twisted layout gains and where it costs, giving engineers data for sizing such units.
pmc-13310649:
Francesco Chierigo and co-authors survey world expert practice on urine leakage during orgasm after prostate removal in a 2026 study. The condition, climacturia, is under-recognized and unevenly checked, even as more men live long after prostate cancer surgery. Its toll on life quality and sexual recovery can outlast other surgical effects.

Experts mapped their checks and treatments across 24 clinical situations, the first such world overview. Care hinged mainly on symptom severity and on whether leakage or erection problems coexisted. Mild cases drew conservative steps, while complex cases drew surgery. Routine screening stayed inconsistent despite wide awareness. The authors propose a starter assessment tool and call for prospective testing of it.
pmc-13310949: A short 2026 correction notice fixes one detail in a trial of online therapy for pelvic pain in endometriosis. Weekly group yoga sessions given by video call were first listed as lasting 120 minutes for 8 weeks in total. The length should read 60 minutes for 8 weeks in total. Authors state the typing error changes no results, conclusions, or other content. The notice itself holds no new data, methods, or findings beyond that single fix.
pmc-13311149:
Márcio Fellipe Menezes Viana writes a 2026 letter on crusted scabies in a healthy baby. A girl aged 3 months came in with a month of itchy rash that spread into whole body redness with thick crusts, mainly on the back and upper arms. Crusted scabies is a heavy mite infestation usually tied to weak immunity, so a healthy infant case is rare.

Blood tests showed high white cells, eosinophils, and swelling markers, with normal immune protein levels and no bacterial infection. Bedside skin scope sped diagnosis and helped control a household outbreak. Early suspicion matters, since heavy mite loads spread fast to contacts.
pmc-13311249:
Abdullah Jajan and Michiel van Nieuwenhoven report a 2026 Swedish cohort study on colonoscopy results inside a fast-track pathway for suspected bowel cancer. They ask how results and referral clues differ by age.

The study covers 3258 patients sent through the pathway from 2016 to 2023 who had a colonoscopy. No cancer was found in patients aged 18 to 40, while the share rose with age to 21.2 percent past age 80 in this cohort. Scan findings, rectal exam findings, anemia, and visible blood each linked to cancer on their own. Stool test results added strong signal where available.
pmc-13311749:
Elizabeth LA Cross and colleagues report a 2026 interview study on the unmet needs in diagnosing cellulitis, a skin infection often confused with other leg problems. Wrong calls lead to wasted antibiotics and missed illness.

Twenty-five British clinicians, from nurses and paramedics to hospital doctors, spoke about hard cases between January and September 2023. Odd or repeat presentations, wounds, darker skin tones, and prior antibiotics made calls harder. Clinicians admitted cellulitis becomes a default label, helped by thin skin training and fear of not treating. They also judged early test ideas and sketched what a good test must do.
pmc-13312249:
Wing Hong Seto and co-authors report, in a 2026 article, the work of the Asia Safe Surgical Implant Consortium to set one standard for how implants are sterilized across the Asia Pacific. A survey of sites in ten countries in the region had found wide gaps between actual practice and world sterilization guidelines, plus uneven infrastructure for infection prevention.

Regional trade groups formed the consortium, which met in Tokyo to build agreed recommendations from expert views and current evidence. The group produced three documents on quality checks in sterilization, standard handling of loaner and implantable devices, and a solid recall policy for sterilization failures. They stress combined physical, chemical, and biological checks, careful records, and fast communication. The authors call for ongoing regional cooperation, investment, and training so sterile supply teams can hold the standard.
pmc-13312349:
Henry Bair writes a 2026 essay on Michel de Montaigne as the first reader of his own body. Montaigne began passing kidney stones in 1578 at age 45, the same affliction that had killed his father. He returned to that inherited pain across his essays, wondering what it means to carry a parent's suffering dormant inside oneself for decades.

Bair contrasts Montaigne's way of attending to his body with clinical attention. Medicine scans for patterns and narrows toward a diagnosis, while Montaigne watched his condition without trying to solve it, aiming to know it rather than classify it. That stance, the essay argues, is close to impossible for trained clinicians, who feel idle without a hypothesis. Bair presents this tolerance for non-diagnostic attention as a discipline modern care has yet to learn.
pmc-13313149:
Ângela Graciela Deliga Schröder and colleagues hunt, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, for gene variants that predispose orthodontic patients to severe root resorption. That is the permanent shortening of tooth roots that braces and jaw surgery can provoke. The complication's uneven toll suggests inherited susceptibility, so the team tested seven variants in four bone-related genes, BMP2, BMP4, RUNX2, and SMAD6.

The study covered 158 patients treated with fixed appliances plus jaw surgery, grading root loss on panoramic X-rays and genotyping cheek-cell DNA. Six of the seven variants showed no link to severe resorption. One stood out: the CC genotype of a SMAD6 variant, rs3934908, appeared significantly more often in patients with severe damage. The authors present the finding as a first susceptibility lead, cautioning that bigger samples and gene-environment work must confirm it before it guides treatment choices.
pmc-13314449:
Anqi Ren and co-workers ask whether the result of a fresh embryo transfer foretells later frozen transfer success, in work published in 2026. The work matters for couples who bank embryos and want a clear sense of their odds on the next try.

The team studied 6491 women who had single blastocyst frozen transfers at a large academic center between January 2016 and June 2024. Women were grouped by their fresh transfer outcome. The groups held 3711 with no pregnancy, 701 with a chemical pregnancy only, 1066 with miscarriage, and 1013 with a live birth, as the counts in the report show. Against the live birth group, the other three groups had lower odds of even a chemical pregnancy next time, with ratios such as 0.58 kept mid-sentence as reported. A good fresh result bodes well for frozen tries.
pmc-13315449:
Artur J Jakimiuk and Marcin Januszewski comment in 2026 on what a landmark Polish trial means for cervical cancer screening. The HIPPO trial was the first large randomized test in Eastern Europe of primary HPV testing against standard cytology inside a national screening program.

HPV testing nearly doubled detection of CIN2 or worse lesions and raised detection of CIN3 or worse as well. That matches wider evidence that DNA testing is more sensitive, at a small cost in specificity. Earlier trials abroad link a strong first-round catch to lower disease in later rounds. The authors weigh whether health systems can handle the follow-on care this shift brings.
pmc-13315649:
Lachlan Coff, Ujala Bashir, and Daniel Bojar review in 2026 how artificial intelligence is changing the study of glycans, the complex sugar chains on proteins and cells. Glycan work has lagged behind gene and protein computing, in part because good training data are scarce and the sugars branch in complex ways.

Deep learning can now read glycan structures from mass spectra. Models fitted to glycomics data can flag likely disease states, and machine learning can forecast how proteins and glycans interact. The review weighs what these tools can do for understanding glycan structure and function, a field long seen as a hard computing problem.
pmc-13315849:
Argyri Chroni and co-authors present a step-by-step protocol in 2026 for pulling out mitochondrial DNA and measuring its overall methylation with liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry. Methylation also acts on the mitochondrial genome, which lacks histones, but studies are often muddied by technical and biological confounders.

The workflow starts with blood and marrow single-cell samples, concentrates mitochondria on a sucrose gradient, then extracts the DNA. Purity checks guard against nuclear DNA contamination before the quantitative methylation read. Clear steps should make results easier to compare across labs studying cancer and cell biology questions.
pmc-13316649:
Michelle Semonella leads a 2026 Italian pilot trial of MobACT, a guided online therapy based on acceptance and commitment methods for adults with chronic pain. Italy had no such online program before, and clinic access to pain psychology stays scarce.

Forty adults were split evenly between the seven-week program and a waiting list. Pain acceptance rose over time in the group as a whole, but the change did not differ between arms during the short pilot window in the reported analysis. The team gathered rich feasibility data: sign-up, staying power, ease of use, satisfaction, and interviews about the experience. Those lessons shape a fuller trial and show how digital care might widen reach.
pmc-13317549:
Fen Zhang and colleagues frame, in a 2026 review, how extracellular vesicles, the tiny parcels cells send each other, could become medicines. Sources range from stem cells and immune cells to plants, milk, and microbes, and each source loads different cargo and behaves differently in the body.

The review weighs delivery routes, from veins to nose, mouth, lungs, and local shots, against diseases in repair, immunity, cancer, brain, and metabolism. Quality rules and world regulations remain patchy, slowing products despite a growing trial pipeline counted to April 2026. Their five-part matching frame links source, route, disease, quality marks, and rules into one planning tool for developers.
pmc-13318249:
Shengyuan Hua and co-authors describe a 2026 genetic study of two Chinese children suspected of having congenital hypotrichosis, a rare inherited condition marked by sparse hair from early childhood. Both children were six years old, and blood samples came from them and from their parents.

Whole-exome sequencing found four different compound heterozygous variants in the LSS gene across the two patients, confirming hypotrichosis simplex 14. Two variants had been reported before, and two were new, widening the known range of changes in that gene. Protein modelling and prediction tools were used to judge the new changes, and poor teeth development in one child may also belong to the condition.
pmc-13318749:
Øyvind Sandbakk and co-authors present a 2026 analysis of sex differences in sprint cross-country skiing. Thirty elite skiers, fifteen women and fifteen men, raced a classical time trial. The qualification run covered 1.3 km on snow. Satellite and motion sensors tracked speed, technique choice, and cycle features.

Men averaged about 14 percent faster than the performance-matched women. The gap was largest uphill, at 19 to 20 percent on those sections. It shrank to 6 to 9 percent downhill in the same race. Men spent more time double poling, about 61 percent against 53 percent for women. Women used diagonal stride more often. Men's cycles ran 9 to 11 percent longer, while rates were similar. The authors say equal distances pose distinct demands by sex.
pmc-13319649:
Gülnihal Eren and co-authors study vitamin D and gum disease in people with well managed type 2 diabetes in a 2026 article. Low vitamin D is common, and gum harm runs high when blood sugar illness and gum illness meet. Whether low blood vitamin D tracks with worse gums, and what gum fluid shows, were the twin questions.

Two groups were compared, 26 people with low vitamin D and 15 with enough, all with gum disease and steady sugar control. The low vitamin D group showed deeper gum harm and more bleeding on checks. Gum fluid levels of vitamin forms and defense bits did not track blood levels, though two fluid measures moved together. Blood shortfall still marked worse gums.
pmc-13320449:
Phaedra Henley and Maria Albin Qambayot wrote a commentary in 2026 on planetary health teaching in Africa and its older sibling framework. Fresh calls urge schools to teach health and planet as one system as climate strain grows. The piece, written in reply to an article by Filho and co-authors, argues that much of that ground was already built across Africa under the One Health banner.

Joint human, animal, and nature health webs, shared rule systems, and cross field courses have run on the continent for years, with Rwanda named as one national case. The two frames share systems thought and cross sector teamwork at their core. New planet health drives should build on those roots and credit African schools as idea leaders, not just test sites.
pmc-13320549:
Di Yuan and Kexin Deng study whether wider digital finance helps the health of older adults in China in a 2026 article. Data came from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, which follows midlife and older people over time. The team used fixed effects models and an instrumental variable check to separate cause from simple links.

Broader digital finance access went with better self-rated health and with less loss of daily function and less depression. Gains seemed to flow through a greater ability and readiness to pay for health care. Benefits were stronger in midwestern areas, among those under 75, with digital access, or living with children. Fair digital skills support is urged so gains are shared.
pmc-13320849:
Clare FitzPatrick and co-authors revisit a worm gene mutation in a 2026 study of the roundworm C. elegans. The gene AGEF-1 helps control membrane traffic inside cells and works with Arf proteins and a clathrin adaptor. A strain carrying the vh4 change was long thought to be a weak loss of function, based on similar looks to gene silencing.

New tests show the vh4 embryos push yolk out of the embryo, an effect reversed by silencing AGEF-1 or its Arf partners but not the adaptor. Structure clues from the yeast version of the protein suggest the change switches AGEF-1 on rather than off. Arf cycling thus seems to split traffic jobs between adaptor and yolk routes.
pmc-13321249:
Kristiana Siste and co-authors run a small randomised trial of brain stimulation plus therapy for gambling disorder in Indonesia in a 2026 study. Online gambling dominates the local problem, and harm can reach partners and family as well. Twenty-seven patients received either real or sham magnetic stimulation over five weeks, alongside standard talking therapy.

The protocol proved safe, with an adverse event rate of 7.2 percent and only mild effects reported in the study. Both groups improved on gambling symptom scores, with no clear gap between real and sham arms. The real stimulation group did cut craving faster and eased gambling beliefs sooner. Larger trials should test dosing and lasting benefit.
pmc-13322849:
Taek Min Nam leads a nationwide Korean cohort study, published in 2026, on metabolic syndrome and malignant brain tumours. The cohort held 3,976,961 adults aged 40 or older who had a health check in 2009, followed from 2010 to 2020 for new brain tumours.

Counts of single syndrome parts, taken one by one, did not link clearly to tumour risk in adjusted models. Grouped by standard cut-offs, people with three or more parts did show a modest higher risk, and risk rose further at five parts. High triglycerides stood out as the strongest single part. The authors suggest lipid checks may help when judging brain tumour risk, alongside wider metabolic care.
pmc-13323249:
Chengjiu Tan and colleagues test what paediatric nurses know about a combined asthma inhaler, in a 2026 survey at tertiary hospitals in Nanning, China. Nurses teach children how to use budesonide-formoterol devices, so gaps in their own knowledge can pass straight to families.

Fifty-seven nurses completed a guideline-based questionnaire, with a mean score near 85 points and most passing the local reference mark of 60 in the results. Nurses on specialist respiratory wards, those seeing more asthma patients and those with more frequent training scored significantly higher. The authors urge targeted training and more clinical exposure, while warning that the small convenience sample limits how far the findings travel.
pmc-13325149:
Huanhuan Wang and co-authors coat drug-carrying vesicles with a chitosan blend to fight skin photoaging in a 2026 study. Sunlight drives oxidative stress that ages skin, and soft vesicles often fall apart before they can deliver their load.

The coating joins caffeic acid to chitosan and wraps transfersomes loaded with oroxylin A, a flavonoid from skullcap root. Coated vesicles resisted fat oxidation and lifted radical scavenging to 89.71 percent on the DPPH test and 72.39 percent on the ABTS test. Skin passage of the drug improved, and ultraviolet-driven cell aging slowed. In mice with light-aged skin, the coated vesicles restored barrier function and eased collagen damage.
pmc-13325349:
Dan Fang and colleagues load the plant compound quercetin into stem cell exosomes to treat liver fibrosis in a 2026 study. Quercetin fights scarring but dissolves poorly, so little of a dose reaches the liver.

Exosomes from human umbilical cord stem cells carried the drug in a mouse model of toxin-driven fibrosis. The loaded vesicles eased scarring more than free quercetin at the same dose, and cell tests showed stronger calming of scar-forming stellate cells. Release lasted up to 48 hours, and the vesicles stayed stable for at least a week. Network analysis and bench checks tied the gain to deeper blocking of the PI3K and Akt pathway.
pmc-13325449:
Qian Xu and co-authors model the shared genetics of 12 cancers in a 2026 study. Many cancers run in the same families, yet the common inherited core behind them was not mapped as one factor.

Genomic structural equation modeling split association data from over 600,000 European-ancestry cases into a shared factor and site-specific parts. The shared factor held 133 separate loci, eight of them new to cancer research. A risk score built from it predicted overall cancer in UK Biobank data and still worked in an East Asian check group. Gene hunting named 132 likely risk genes, and blood protein analysis flagged 23 possible causal proteins, six of them druggable.
pmc-13325849:
Ziyang Wang and colleagues use a recurrent neural network to read material light properties live in a 2026 study. Refractive index shifts under heat, voltage, or strain, but standard fitting is slow and fails on layered stacks.

Their ReflectoRNN framework pulls complex refractive indices straight from reflectance spectra. On generated data it reached a median correlation of 0.998 and a relative accuracy score of 0.968 across test sets. Bench trials on MoS2 and WS2 films over varied bases matched well, and heat-driven exciton shifts followed Bose-Einstein forecasts. The tool could watch materials change during device operation and speed the hunt for new optical materials.
pmc-13327349:
Michael Schotsaert wrote a 2026 first-person account of how vaccine research carried him across borders. He grew up in the Dutch-speaking countryside of Belgium in the 1980s and 1990s, in the same house as his grandfather's medical practice. Early lessons there, from plant care and beehives to a first sheep vaccination, set his direction.

He recalls choosing bio-engineering studies because they joined science with technology and a systems view of how things work. Learning that a killed pathogen, or a piece of one, can train the body to resist later infection anchored his interest. His story shows how childhood curiosity, family example, and engineering training can grow into an international career in vaccine science.
pmc-13327949:
Lujia Tang and fellow editors introduce a research collection on protecting the brain after stroke reopening in a 2026 editorial. Clot removal and dissolving drugs have improved stroke care, yet many patients recover poorly because restored flow itself injures tissue through toxicity, oxidation, barrier leaks, and inflammation. The collection reframes that injury as a treatable continuum.

Contributions span risk sorting, early spotting of harm, and cell-protecting treatments from clinic to lab. Outcomes after successful reopening still vary widely, from a minority harmed in mild stroke to over half in some thrombectomy groups, which argues for personal risk sorting rather than one-size care. Shielding brain cells should stand beside reopening as a core aim, the editors argue.
pmc-13328349:
Ning Li and co-authors test a Tibetan pill in Alzheimer's model mice in a 2026 study. Ershiwuwei Shanhu Pill is used in Tibetan practice for dementia, and the team asked whether it works through gut microbes and blood chemistry. Transgenic mice received 200 mg/kg by mouth daily for two months, eleven per group.

Treated mice performed better in a water maze, carried less amyloid and phosphorylated tau in the brain, and showed calmer brain inflammation. Gut profiling found more Dubosiella and less Bacteroides, while blood metabolites shifted in tryptophan and sugar pathways, including higher fructose 1,6-bisphosphate. A gut-metabolite-brain route may carry the pill's protection, the authors propose.
pmc-13328449:
Pilar Marcos, Arturo Mangas, and Rafael Coveñas introduce a second collection on new glioma therapies in a 2026 editorial. The first volume ranged over molecular targets such as ADORA1 and Fyn, a prognostic RNA study, in-surgery radiation, combined light and field therapies, and the gut's role in brain tumors. This sequel widens the field again.

Contributions run from bench work to patient studies and reviews across many disciplines. The editors highlight three-dimensional tumor spheroids grown by a rotary method, which mimic living tumors better than flat cultures and let a targeted HDAC inhibitor's killing power be read more truly. Together the volumes argue glioma progress will come from many fronts at once.
pmc-13329749:
Antonio M. Amor and colleagues write a 2026 editorial on quality of life for people with neurodevelopmental disorders. Care has shifted from a focus on deficits to a social and ecological view that weighs person and setting together. Quality of life models fit that shift, since they centre what matters to the person across many life domains.

Such models can guide support planning as an input and judge results as an outcome. Some frameworks use signs tied to rights in the United Nations disability convention, linking life quality to true inclusion. The editorial reads the contributions in its Research Topic through that lens. Its aim is to show paths toward inclusion and well-being across the lifespan.
pmc-13330649:
Siqi Guo and colleagues review ginseng flowers as a health food ingredient in a 2026 article. Flowers are a yearly renewable leftover of ginseng farming, long used in East Asian tradition yet little used in industry. The review gathers decades of studies on their chemistry and effects.

Main active parts include ginsenosides of two families, sugar chains, and scent compounds. Reported effects span antioxidant, calming, immune, liver, and heart actions in the summed literature. Trials in drinks and fermented foods show early promise and buyer acceptance. Hurdles include heat damage to key compounds, bitter taste, variable strength by crop, and thin clinical proof. Gentle processing and standards are urged.
pmc-13332949:
William W Wroe and colleagues review the role of excess clotting in delayed brain ischemia after a burst aneurysm, in a 2026 narrative review. The delayed injury strikes roughly 30 percent of survivors days after the bleed and remains a leading cause of disability and death in this group.

Older explanations centered on large artery spasm, but the review gathers clinical and laboratory evidence that aneurysm rupture flips the blood into a hypercoagulable state. Tiny clots in small vessels feed into the delayed damage. So do the sticky DNA webs thrown out by immune cells in a process called NETosis, and clotting byproducts that feed spasm and inflammation. The authors also weigh what growing use of dual antiplatelet and other anticlotting treatment after hemorrhage implies for prevention. They present clotting as a thread tying together most proposed mechanisms of the delayed injury.
pmc-13333349:
Cong-Hui He and co-authors mapped what kinds of fitness services city-dwelling older adults actually want, in a 2026 study using the Kano model of customer needs. Most past work studied what programs supply, not how wants differ among healthy elders, those with chronic disease, and those who depend on care.

Combining expert Delphi rounds, questionnaires, and structured analysis, the team built a demand map for the three groups. Overall demand levels ran low. Healthy older adults mixed must-have basics with features whose quality scaled with satisfaction. Those with chronic disease concentrated on must-have items, and those needing care narrowed further to basic support and care coordination. The authors warn against spreading services evenly or imposing one standard: common foundations should be guaranteed, then each group's sharpest needs handled with targeted extras.
pmc-13333649:
Air pollution during pregnancy and autism in children are the focus of a 2026 population-based case-control study by Mengjie Zhang and co-authors. Fine particulate matter can carry toxic substances deep into the body, and the team asked whether exposure during pregnancy raises risk.

All families were recruited through Xinyang Central Hospital, with details gathered in structured clinical interviews. Exposure estimates for PM2.5 and its parts, including sulfate, nitrate, ammonium, organic matter, and black carbon, came from the Tracking Air Pollution in China dataset. Analysis showed positive links between PM2.5 and autism, with an odds ratio of 5.197 in the main comparison, and monthly estimates pointed to the strongest effects in particular gestational windows. The results argue for protecting pregnant women from polluted air.
pmc-13335649:
Polly Livermore and co-authors tested a conceptual model of illness uncertainty, benefit, and burden in young people with juvenile dermatomyositis in a 2026 UK study. Mental health problems are common in children with chronic conditions, and this rare muscle disease brings its own unpredictability.

Children and young people aged 8 and over were recruited from a UK-wide cohort and biomarker study spanning 15 NHS tertiary pediatric rheumatology services. They completed five validated measures covering quality of life, emotional distress, illness uncertainty, and perceived benefit and burden. The analysis assessed health-related quality of life and tested whether the new model explains depression and anxiety in this group, including which resilience factors protect them. The work aims to show clinicians where support can lift daily life for these families.
pmc-13336549:
Youvalakshmi Saravanan, Vijayasankar Palaniappan, and Kaliaperumal Karthikeyan offer a 2026 review of skin conditions whose names carry the word actinic. The word comes from a Greek term for a ray or beam. In skin care it covers damage from sunlight and from other forms of radiation.

One large section covers actinic keratosis, a rough pre-cancer growth caused by years of ultraviolet light. The authors describe its look on the face, scalp, neck, and hands, plus six forms seen under the microscope. Itching, pain, or bleeding can warn of a shift toward skin cancer. Gathering these conditions in one place helps clinicians name, sort, and treat sun-linked skin damage.
pmc-13336649:
Haipeng Lu leads a 2026 team behind an implantable patch that releases heart drugs on a light-based schedule after a heart attack. Healing after such damage takes long treatment, yet most implants release drugs passively with no way to adjust dosing. Their patch joins a drug-holding gel with a light guide placed under the skin.

A brief flash of light starts a slow, steady release that then continues without more light. Light strength and length act as a code that sets each dose, and the bound drug barely leaks between doses. In rats, three timed doses beat one equal total dose for heart function and calming inflammation. Programmable dosing could better match changing recovery needs.
pmc-13336749:
Lei Cao and colleagues borrow a trick from pancreas inflammation for pancreatic cancer therapy in a 2026 study. In pancreatitis, trypsinogen sparks an aggressive M1-like immune response. The team found trypsinogen can flip tumor-helping macrophages from the calm M2 state to the fighting M1 state through the NF-kappaB pathway.

Their nanoparticles deliver trypsinogen plus JQ1, a drug that blocks the do-not-eat-me signal CD47, straight to those macrophages. In pancreatic cancer models the combo raised cancer-cell eating, reshaped the tumor immune setting, shrank tumors, and extended survival with lasting immune memory. Removing macrophages erased the benefit, proving they carried the effect. A pancreas enzyme thus becomes an immune reprogrammer.
pmc-13336949:
Xiaoyang Lin and colleagues reframe cancer spread along nerves as a team effort in a 2026 review. Perineural invasion, where tumor cells infiltrate nerve sheaths, drives progression and poor outcomes in many cancers. It was once seen as the tumor acting alone. The review treats it instead as a shared ecosystem of tumor, nerve, and surrounding stroma.

Support cells such as cancer-linked fibroblasts and Schwann cells, plus immune cells and matrix, remodel the nerve border and exchange signals that invite invasion. Nerves reorganize and local immunity shifts, building a niche that helps tumors travel neural routes. Breaking this two-way talk could slow spread and improve outcomes.
pmc-13337649:
Kui Yao and Hongling Peng present a 2026 safety analysis of newer ovarian cancer drugs. They drew reports from the United States adverse event system covering mid-2014 to late 2025. The drugs covered include bevacizumab, PARP inhibitors, and immune checkpoint drugs.

More than 200,000 reports covering 33,538 patients entered the analysis, and most involved PARP inhibitors. Signal methods compared how often each harm appeared for each drug. Most events were reported within 30 days of starting treatment. The results map which harms cluster with which drug class, giving clinicians a clearer picture of risks to watch for during ovarian cancer care.
pmc-13339349:
Andrea Soumbasis and co-authors present first registry findings for functional movement disorder in Calgary in a 2026 report. The condition brings uneven, mismatched movements with heavy limits and slow diagnosis. A joint brain and mental health clinic runs the registry.

Seventy-seven patients joined between April 2024 and April 2025 as reported, with 45 women forming 58 percent of the group. Standard records cover movement types, mental health history, care use, and severity scales. Baseline patterns across movement subtypes are compared. The registry aims to replace delayed, split care with proof for treatment plans shaped to each person.
pmc-13339649:
Ismayil M. Garazade, Armando J. L. Pombeiro, and Maxim L. Kuznetsov trace a tin-catalyzed cyanation step by step in a 2026 study. Benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal plus a silicon cyanide source can give a cyano ether or simply hydrolyze to benzaldehyde. Theory and NMR tracked both races.

Cyanation won through silicon transfer, carbon-oxygen break, and ion reunion as modeled. Hydrolysis won when catalyst-bound water donated a proton instead. Tin activated the cyanide partner in one path and made its water strongly acidic in the other, as the authors show. Knowing the branch point helps chemists favor the nitrile product.
pmc-13340149:
Wes Baumgartner heads the author team for a 2026 INHAND reference chapter on fish hormone system lesions, written for toxicology pathologists. Hormone signals in fish closely mirror mammals, yet gland placement and build differ greatly. Spontaneous gland lesions are uncommon in safety studies, with a few exceptions.

Major tissues covered include pituitary, thyroid follicles, pancreas islets, pineal gland, and corpuscles of Stannius. Ultimobranchial gland tumors in zebrafish are noted as a known exception. Standard finding lists and species contrasts help pathologists judge whether a change came from treatment. Shared wording across labs makes safety reading stronger across studies.
pmc-13341649:
Giammarino and colleagues tested in 2026 whether an enzyme-blocking compound called MC1568 can boost the standard antifungal fluconazole against non-albicans Candida yeasts. These species now cause a large share of Candida bloodstream infections and increasingly resist standard drugs. The team compared three approved blockers of histone deacetylases, enzymes that help switch genes, plus the selective compound MC1568, alone and paired with fluconazole.

The MC1568 pairing stood out, working in synergy to cut biofilm growth, the slimy layers yeasts form, and to strengthen killing against three species, including Candida tropicalis. In wax moth larvae, a stand-in host, the pair raised survival in tropicalis infection by about 70 percent over controls. Tests on human retinal cells showed low toxicity for three dose pairings. The authors propose MC1568 as an add-on therapy worth refining for hard-to-treat yeast infections.
pmc-13342049:
Removing a whole lung by robot is reported in the largest single-center series yet, by Ammar Asban and co-investigators in a 2026 study. Their consecutive series covered 21 robotic pneumonectomies performed from January 2019 to December 2024, drawn from a prospective database.

Median age was 70 years; cancer drove 17 cases, and 76% of those patients had prior drug or radiation therapy. Only two cases (9%) converted to open surgery as planned, chest tubes lasted a median of one day, and hospital stay five days. Thirty-day mortality was 0% and 90-day mortality 5%, far below historical figures for minimally invasive attempts at this operation.

pmc-13347349:

pmc-13349849:

pmc-13350449:

pmc-13351849:

pmc-13353149:

pmc-13354949:

pmc-13362749:

The Truce Commission in the land must give first place to a truce for the City of Jerusalem. It must report back on how the call is kept.
un-sc-res-749: Under number 749, the catalog lists a Security Council resolution dated to 1991 in the official UN record. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Nauru, one of the world's smallest countries, is recommended for United Nations membership in Resolution 1249, adopted on 25 June 1999. The Council had examined the Pacific island republic's application, filed as document S/1999/478. Nauru had been independent since 1968 but waited three decades before seeking a UN seat.

The resolution asks the General Assembly to admit Nauru, following the Charter's two-step pattern for new members. When the Assembly acted, Nauru gained a vote equal to that of the largest states, a striking feature of the system. The tiny phosphate island's admission also reflected a late-1990s cluster of Pacific microstates deciding that a UN seat was worth having.

Guides that call this an Ethiopia text have the wrong war. The land at stake is Western Sahara. A UN team, MINURSO, stood ready to run a vote on its fate. That vote had been pledged for a decade. Deep rifts over who could vote blocked it still. Resolution 1349 passed with no dissent on 27 April 2001.

MINURSO won a short stay, to 30 June 2001. The chief's envoy would keep the sides at the table. The hope was plain: crack the old rifts, or find a deal both could take. The chief's report of 24 April had set out the snags. A fresh check on the state of play was due before the term closed. The text backs the 1991 peace plan, but its tone admits the plan was stuck.

Candidates for permanent judge posts at the Rwanda war crimes tribunal are forwarded on 24 December 2002. The tribunal, created in 1994, prosecutes those responsible for the Rwandan genocide and related crimes. Its permanent judges are elected by the General Assembly from a list the Council sends.

The text sends the Assembly the nominations the Secretary-General had received, as the tribunal's Statute requires. The list names 23 candidates from countries in Africa, Europe, Asia, and the Caribbean. The Assembly would elect the judges from among them. Those elected would sit in the tribunal's trial and appeals chambers for the cases still moving through its courts.

Upper Volta, the West African country now known as Burkina Faso, won independence from France in August 1960. Its leaders applied for UN membership at once. Resolution 149 was adopted unanimously on 23 August 1960. The Council considered the bid at its crowded 891st meeting, alongside other African applications that day.

The members recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of Upper Volta. Admission followed that autumn. The country took the name Burkina Faso in 1984. Its UN seat, though, traces back to this text. The resolution belongs to the 1960 wave that transformed the UN. New African votes shifted debates toward ending colonial rule worldwide.

Liberia's Panel of Experts is re-established on 17 June 2004. The panel checks whether sanctions on arms, diamonds, and timber are being obeyed and breached. Liberia's transitional government had appealed for the sanctions to be lifted and asked for an expert visit to judge its performance against the Council's conditions.

The new panel, of up to five experts, would work from 30 June to 21 December 2004. Its tasks include a follow-up visit to Liberia and nearby states to study how the sanctions are being applied and where they are still broken. The Secretary-General is to appoint the experts in consultation with the sanctions committee and arrange the funding for their work.

Congo's armed-group leaders face targeted sanctions in Resolution 1649, adopted on 21 December 2005. Foreign armed groups in the east — the FDLR, the Palipehutu-FNL, the Lord's Resistance Army — had refused to disarm past the 30 September 2005 deadline. The deadline was set by the region's Tripartite Plus Joint Commission. Their attacks threatened civilians and the coming elections. MONUC was acting against them in hazardous conditions.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the travel ban and asset freeze of Resolution 1596 (2005) to political and military leaders of foreign armed groups. It extends them to Congolese militias backed from abroad, above all in Ituri, who block disarmament and demobilization. The measures take effect on 15 January 2006 unless the Secretary-General reports disarmament is being completed, and are reviewed by 31 July 2006. A full strategy for disarming and repatriating foreign combatants is due by 15 March 2006.

The last notification rules on arms transfers to Rwanda's government are ended on 28 March 2007. The measures dated from 1995, passed after the genocide, and required notice of arms supplies to Rwanda. Rwanda's government had asked for them to be terminated, and the sanctions committee had reported on the question.

The measures are terminated with immediate effect. States in the region must still cooperate to prevent arms from reaching illegal armed groups, which the remaining embargoes on such groups address. With this step, the special arms restrictions built around Rwanda in the mid-1990s are fully wound down, twelve years after they began.

The Hague war crimes court needed more judges than its rulebook allowed. Trials from the Balkan wars were still stacked up in 2008. Fourteen stand-in judges were at work. More cases were set to start. Resolution 1849 passed on 12 December 2008. It drew on a plea from the court's president, sent that November.

The Council let the Secretary-General name extra stand-in judges on request. The total could climb to sixteen at a time. The cap in the court's statute was twelve. This break was meant to be brief. By 28 February 2009, the count had to fall back to twelve. The aim was clear: clear the docket and meet the plan to wind the court down by 2010.

Guinea-Bissau, a small country in West Africa, faced fresh instability in late 2010. Soldiers had detained officials on 1 April that year, and some people were still held without due process. Drug trafficking through the country was feeding corruption and organized crime. Resolution 1949, adopted on 23 November 2010, responds to that situation.

The Council extended the United Nations peacebuilding office in Guinea-Bissau, called UNIOGBIS, until 31 December 2011. It urged the armed forces to respect civilian rule. Those detained in April had to be released or given a fair trial. The government was pressed to finish its inquiries into the political killings of 2009. Reform of the security forces and action against the drug trade run through the whole text.

Islamic State terrorism draws a call to arms in Resolution 2249, adopted on 20 November 2015, a week after the Paris attacks. ISIL, also called Da'esh, had struck Sousse, Ankara, a Russian airliner over Sinai, and Beirut in 2015. It held parts of Iraq and Syria, destroyed cultural heritage, and drew foreign fighters from around the world. The Council calls it a global and unprecedented threat.

The Council condemns the attacks in the strongest terms and says those responsible must be held accountable. It calls on member states with the capacity to take all necessary measures, in compliance with international law, on ISIL-held territory in Syria and Iraq. They are to prevent and suppress terrorist acts by ISIL, the Al-Nusrah Front, and other Al-Qaida-linked groups, and to destroy their safe haven. It urges stronger action against foreign fighter flows and terrorist financing, and promises to update the sanctions list.

Resolution 249, adopted unanimously on 18 April 1968, deals with the application of Mauritius, filed as document S/8466. The Indian Ocean island had become independent from Britain the previous month, in March 1968. Its government applied for United Nations membership almost at once.

After examining the application, the Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Mauritius. The sentence is short because admission votes rarely involve debate in the Council itself; agreement is usually reached beforehand. Yet the formality mattered: without this recommendation the Assembly could not act. The resolution records the moment Mauritius, an island east of Madagascar, began its life as a member state of the world organization.

Ten years after it first arrived, the Cyprus peacekeeping force came up for a new term on 29 May 1974. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 22 May, said the force was still needed if peace was to be kept. Cyprus agreed it should stay beyond 15 June. Resolution 349 records the renewal.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. They were also told to speed up their joint efforts toward the Council's goals. The island's calmer climate was to be used well. The force's stay was extended to 15 December 1974. The Council expected that progress toward a final solution might then allow the force to withdraw or be reduced.

The label on this file can mislead. Some notes tie Resolution 449 to the settlement debate. The text itself renews a peacekeeping force. Fourteen members voted yes on 30 May 1979. China took no part. The Secretary-General's report on the force, paper S/13350, sat before the members.

The force was UNDOF, the UN team on the Golan Heights. Its mandate grew by six months, to 30 November 1979. The Council paired the renewal with its stock demand. Israel and Syria had to act on Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. A fresh report was due when the term ended. By 1979, these Golan renewals formed a fixed rhythm of the Council's year.

A week after the State of Israel was proclaimed, war was under way in Palestine. Earlier Council resolutions on Palestine had not been obeyed. Fighting continued on all sides. Resolution 49 was adopted on 22 May 1948.

The Council called on all governments and authorities to stop hostile military action in Palestine. They had to issue cease-fire orders to their forces within thirty-six hours. The order was given without prejudice to any side's rights, claims, or positions. The Truce Commission and all parties were told to give top priority to a truce in Jerusalem. Winning it and keeping it came first. All sides were also told to help the United Nations mediator do his work. He had been appointed only days earlier.

A United Nations force for Croatia, approved in February 1992, received the order to deploy in full that April. The force was called UNPROFOR, the United Nations Protection Force. Its advance teams were already in place. Fighting kept breaking the cease-fire in the areas where the force would be based. Resolution 749 was adopted in April 1992.

The Council approved the Secretary-General's report of 2 April 1992. It decided to authorize the earliest possible full deployment of UNPROFOR. Everyone involved was urged to help cover the force's costs. Its aircraft had to be given complete freedom of movement. All parties were called on to stop the violence. That call applied above all where UNPROFOR would be based. The Council also appealed for cooperation with European efforts toward a cease-fire and a political settlement in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
zoist-vol-07-1849:
The Zoist reaches volume seven with the months from March 1849 to January 1850. Elliotson's journal of cerebral physiology and mesmerism keeps its double brief. Reports of trance surgery now compete with news of chloroform's spread. Mesmerists argue their method is safer and gentler in reply.

Clairvoyant cases, cure narratives, and sharp editorial combat fill the volume. The society of contributors spans Britain's industrial towns and villages. Across thirteen volumes the journal preserves the movement entire. Volume seven shows the cause in its mature, embattled phase. Historians of hypnosis quarry these pages constantly. The voices are those of the practitioners themselves.
